Module 2
Keyboarding Skills and Ergonomics
Module Overview
Strong keyboarding skills are essential for efficient computer use in both personal and
professional environments. In this module, you will build a foundation that will help you type
more quickly, accurately, and comfortably. By focusing on proper technique, posture, and finger
placement, you will not only avoid common physical problems but also increase your typing
speed and accuracy. Whether you are just starting or looking to refine your abilities, mastering
these fundamentals will help you complete computer-based tasks with greater confidence and
ease.
You will learn through a series of interactive labs and activities designed to help you develop
muscle memory and good typing habits. Step-by-step guidance will show you how to use each
finger correctly, practice letters, numbers, and special keys, and apply your skills to real words
and sentences. As you progress, you will have the opportunity to apply your new skills to
classic texts and customized practice, ensuring that your improvement is both measurable and
meaningful.
Module Summary
In this module, you will:
• Use proper keyboarding techniques to improve typing accuracy and speed.
• Apply correct finger placement for all keys, including home row, letters, numbers, and shift
keys.
• Practice typing individual letters, common words, and mixed case using guided exercises.
• Enhance your typing skills by completing word and sentence practice based on classic
literature.
• Incorporate ergonomic strategies to minimize discomfort and prevent repetitive strain
injuries.

Lesson 2A
What is Keyboarding?
Keyboarding is a fundamental skill for using computers in both personal and professional life.
Using proper posture and technique will allow you to not only type more quickly and accurately,
but allow you to work longer without getting sore, and without looking at the keyboard at all.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is proper keyboarding technique to type more accurately?
• What is proper finger placement on the home row?
Why Keyboarding Matters
Keyboarding is the foundation of how we interact with most digital tools in school, work,
and everyday life. When students and professionals can type accurately and quickly, they
spend less mental energy hunting for keys and more on thinking, problem-solving, and clearly
expressing ideas. Strong keyboarding skills make writing essays, reports, emails, and messages
faster and more efficient, which is especially important in timed settings like tests or work
deadlines. It also supports better note-taking, allowing people to capture more information
during lectures, meetings, or training without falling behind.
Beyond speed and productivity, good keyboarding habits help prevent physical strain and
long-term discomfort. Proper posture, hand placement, and rhythm reduce the risk of repetitive
stress injuries, such as wrist and hand pain, that can come from years of poor typing technique.
As more learning, collaboration, and even assessments move online, keyboarding becomes as
essential as reading and basic math. It's not just a "computer skill"—it's a life skill that supports
success across subjects, careers, and daily digital communication.

Lesson 2B
Typing Letters
The letter practice labs are designed to help you learn proper keyboarding techniques and build
muscle memory. Use the highlighted finger to type each letter, and always return to the default

Module 3
Digital Citizenship and Online Reputation
Module Overview
In today's increasingly digital world, your everyday interactions, whether through social media,
messaging apps, or online communities, shape not only your virtual experiences but also your

demands empathy, responsibility, and an understanding of the impact your online actions can

and online safety, you'll gain the tools to create positive digital spaces and protect your
personal information.
Throughout this module, you'll develop the confidence to participate ethically and securely
in a globally connected society. You'll encounter real-world scenarios that challenge you to
make thoughtful decisions, recognize risks, and manage both your emotional and physical
well-being while online. By strengthening these essential skills, you'll become a responsible and
empowered digital citizen, prepared for the challenges and opportunities of the digital age.
Module Summary
In this module, you will:
• Explain what it means to be a digital citizen and why empathy and ethics matter online.
• Describe how everyday posts and interactions contribute to your digital footprint and
personal brand.
• Identify examples of online carelessness and explain their possible long-term
consequences.

Lesson 3A
Being a Digital Citizen
Objectives Covered
6.1 Explain fundamental security concepts and frameworks.
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
Part of digital literacy is digital citizenship, our roles and responsibilities as participating
members of a digital society. Two of the most important aspects of this citizenship are the
responsibility to be empathetic and ethical. How we interact with others online should include a
sense of respect for others and guiding principles that help us determine morally good actions
from poor ones. This sense of respect helps us make and keep the internet a better place for
everyone.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• How do empathy and ehtics apply to digital life?
• What does your digital footprints leave behind?
• Why does what you say and how you communicate matter?
• How can cultural differences affect how people understand what you say?
• How can you know what the right thing to do is in a new situation?
Digital Citizenship
A digital citizen is anyone who connects and participates online. Because the online world
is global and not limited by physical borders, everyone who goes online shares this digital
citizenship.
As a digital citizen, you are expected to:
• Follow the laws and rules that apply to your online activity.
• Use digital tools to empower yourself and others in positive ways.
• Be responsible, respectful, and appropriate in your conduct.
• Show empathy and good ethics in your online interactions.
• Respect other people’s content and follow copyright or usage rules.
• Protect your identity and personal data by learning and using basic security practices.
Online discussions can sometimes get heated. Messages, images, audio, and video can be
distorted or misinterpreted and may lead to bullying, trolling, or gaslighting. As a good digital
citizen, you can:
• Pause or step away before an argument goes too far.

• Report inappropriate, abusive, or threatening behavior on the platform.
• Support others who are being targeted, when it is safe to do so.
As you learn more about digital tools, it becomes your responsibility to recognize common
threats, use technology wisely, and be a positive influence in the global digital community.
Building a Positive Community
Netiquette is a term for online manners and good behavior; it is etiquette for the internet. Good
netiquette helps you build a positive community wherever you interact online.
Community Participation
Online communities depend on the behavior of each member. A helpful way to think about good
netiquette is through three principles that are also used in information security:
• Integrity refers to trust. Share content that is honest and accurate, and do not tamper with or
misrepresent information. In return, you expect others to do the same.
• Availability refers to accessibility. People should be able to access their own content when
they need it. Do not steal, delete, or block other people's data without proper authority.
• Confidentiality refers to privacy. Your content should only be available to the people you
choose to share it with, and you should respect others' choices about who can see their
content.
When creating and posting content, keep these general guidelines in mind:
• Write your own content and avoid plagiarizing or stealing others’ ideas. Take responsibility
for what you post and how it may influence others.
• Review your content before posting. Check text, images, or video for unintended information
or mistakes that may affect your reputation or hurt others.
• Engage with others respectfully. You are never required to respond if you feel uncomfortable
or unsafe.
• Give proper credit when you quote or reuse others’ content. Mention the original creator
and, when possible, link to the source. When in doubt, ask for permission.
• Protect privacy. Share limited personal information about yourself and avoid posting
personal details about others without their consent.
• Be polite and respectful in your language and reactions, even when you disagree.
Platform Etiquette
Different platforms have different purposes and levels of formality. Always remember that online
communication can be misunderstood, so treat every interaction as if it were face-to-face:
be polite, considerate, and attentive. Avoid saying anything online that you would not say to
someone in person.
A general rule for any digital communication is to practice patience. Avoid repeated calls,
multiple messages in a row, or excessive tagging. Send your message once and give others
time to respond, especially for non-urgent topics.
The following table highlights a few common platforms and key etiquette guidelines for each.

Technology and Ethics Facts
Ethics are personal behaviors and principles that build responsibility and trust. Computer ethics
require more than simply avoiding unlawful acts; they guide you to use technology in ways that
respect and protect other people.
Key ethical principles include:
• Confidentiality: Protecting data and information that you are not authorized to share.
• Human Dignity: Respecting the privacy and inherent worth of other people.
• Civility: Following rules of netiquette that promote courtesy and respect in online settings.
• Property Rights: Respecting intellectual property and refusing to copy, steal, or misuse other
people's digital work and credentials.

A code of ethics is a set of rules or standards you adopt to guide your behavior when
using technology. It cannot list actions for every possible situation, but it can identify general
principles of proper behavior that you apply consistently.
Personal Code of Ethics

should focus on honesty, integrity, and respect for others and their
property.
Personal Responsibility Personal responsibility is your commitment to follow your values and

act in difficult or tempting situations.
Legal Compliance Legal compliance means obeying laws and regulations that govern how
computers and data are used. For example, installing key-logger software
on someone else’s computer to capture passwords would be both
unethical and illegal, and may also require you to report such behavior
if you see it.
Professional organizations also publish codes of ethics. For example, the (ISC) 2 organization for
security professionals includes these principles:

• Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
• Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
• Advance and protect the profession.
As you gain more technical skills and access to powerful tools, maintaining a strong personal
code of ethics becomes even more important to keep yourself and others safe.
Show Empathy
Empathy is the ability to imagine and relate to the feelings and experiences of other people.
Being empathetic helps keep relationships healthy, both online and offline.
This topic focuses on practical ways to show empathy online:
• Consider accessibility
• Communicate across cultures
• Respect rules and restrictions
Consider Accessibility
Not everyone has access to the same devices or internet connections you do. Some may only
have a phone, share a single device with their family, or have limited bandwidth. People with
disabilities may also rely on assistive tools to access content.
To show empathy and include others:

• Do not assume everyone will view your content on a specific device or can download large
files.
• Use clear, readable text and simple layouts where possible.
• Add descriptive alt text for images so that people with visual disabilities using screen
readers can understand the content.
Communicating Across Cultures
Cultural differences exist between countries and also within the same neighborhood
or community. Differences in language, age, religion, politics, or priorities can lead to
misunderstandings if you are not careful.
• Keep an open mind and be willing to accept differences.
• Listen closely to what others are saying, practice empathy, and respond respectfully.
• Use your listening and empathy skills to notice differences and look for common ground.

Lesson 3B
Managing Your Digital Footprint
Objectives Covered
1.2 Identify notational systems.
6.1 Explain fundamental security concepts and frameworks.
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
Every time you go online, liking a post, sharing a photo, filling out a form, or commenting on a
video, you leave behind a trail of information. This trail is called your digital footprint. It's made
up of everything that can be connected to you online: what you post, what others post about
you, and even data collected quietly in the background by apps and websites.
Your online actions shape your personal brand and long-term reputation. Small, everyday
choices like a joke, a picture, or a quick reaction post can have consequences years later,
for school, jobs, and relationships. Being intentional about the story you're telling about yourself
online is more important than ever.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is a digital footprint, and how do you create one?
• In what ways do your everyday online actions leave a trace behind?
• Why does it matter that the internet can feel temporary but is often permanent?
• How can careless posts, pictures, or comments affect your future opportunities?
• What choices can you make now to build a positive and intentional online reputation?
Personal Brand
In your everyday life, people form opinions about you based on what you say and do. The same
is true online. Your behavior as a digital citizen helps shape how others see you and the culture
of the online spaces you participate in.
Online Persona and Personal Branding
The version of yourself that exists online is sometimes called your online persona. It is shaped
by what you choose to post and what others post about you. While you cannot control
everything others do, you can be deliberate about how you present yourself.
Personal branding is a term borrowed from marketing and business. It is the process of making
intentional choices about how you present yourself so that your online persona reflects the
image and identity you want to share. Your personal brand is built through messages, images,
shares, likes, and other content you post across different platforms.

Personal branding does not mean being fake or pretending to be perfect. Just like you choose
how to act around others in person, you can choose what you share online so that it matches
your real values and goals.
As a member of the wider internet community, a "netizen", your behavior matters. It shows
others who you are and contributes to the overall tone and culture of your digital spaces.
Lifelong Impacts and Making Responsible Choices
Because the internet is permanent, a poor decision made in a few seconds can damage your
digital footprint and personal brand for years. To protect your personal brand and reputation,
use these simple guidelines when posting information online:
• Show your best self when posting online. Share content that reflects your real strengths,
interests, and values.
• Only post things you are comfortable showing publicly. A useful rule of thumb is to ask,
“Would I be okay showing this to a teacher, parent, or grandparent?”
• Treat others online how you would want to be treated. Avoid joining in on bullying, drama, or
mean jokes.
• Do not post or share content that could be interpreted as violent, hateful, or racist.
• Get permission before posting a picture of someone else or tagging them in a post.
Making thoughtful choices about what you share helps you build a strong, positive personal
brand that can support your future opportunities.
Every Online Action Leaves a Digital Footprint
Everything you do online leaves traces called digital footprints. These traces include the sites
you visit, videos and pictures you post, comments you make, and messages you send. It can
also include activities you might not usually think of as “online,” such as sending text messages
or allowing apps to track your location.
These activities create a trail of data on the internet that can often be linked back to a particular
user or device. Even when you are careful about what you share and with whom, anyone using
internet-connected devices will leave some kind of footprint.
A digital footprint is the collection of data you leave behind when you use digital devices and
online services. It includes:
• What you intentionally share (posts, forms, uploads)
• What is automatically collected about you (logs, tracking data, metadata)
Just as footprints in sand can show where you have been, your digital footprint shows
where you have been in the digital world. It can reveal who you are, what you like, who you
communicate with, and how you behave online.
Your digital footprint is usually divided into two types:
• Active footprint: what you choose to post or share.
• Passive footprint: what is collected about you automatically.
Active Footprint
Your active footprint is everything you intentionally put online, such as:
• Posting pictures or videos on social media
• Commenting on a friend's post or in a Discord server

• Liking a video or photo
• Writing a review of a game or app
• Filling out an online form
• Creating a profile with a bio and profile picture
If you know you are sharing it, it is probably part of your active footprint.
Example: Social Media Post
You post: "Can't wait for our big game at Lincoln High at 7 pm tonight! #GoTigers"
• Active footprint:
• The post itself (text, time, school, event location)
• Why it matters:
• You are sharing where you will be and when.
• A stranger can see your school and possibly your team name.
Manage your active footprint
You cannot erase every trace of what you post, but you can reduce risk and control what
people see:
• Set social media profiles to private when possible, and limit who can see your posts, tags,
and contact information.
• Review old posts and delete or hide anything offensive, mean, embarrassing, or that shares
too much personal information.
• Remember that deleting does not guarantee your content is gone everywhere (screenshots
and backups may still exist), but it can still help protect you going forward.
Passive Footprint
Your passive footprint is data collected about you behind the scenes, even when you do not
type or post anything. Examples include:
• Apps tracking your location in the background
• Websites using cookies and trackers to see what pages you visit
• Your IP address and device information logged when you go online
• "Last seen online" or "active now" status in messaging apps
• Metadata in your photos (time, date, sometimes location)
• Your school or library Wi-Fi logs
If the data is collected automatically, without you posting it on purpose, it is part of your passive
footprint.
Example: Just Browsing
You visit a popular clothing website to look at shoes. You do not make an account and you do
not buy anything.
• Passive footprint:
• Your IP address (which can show an approximate location)
• The shoes you looked at and for how long
• The device and browser you used
• Ads for those shoes may follow you to other sites
You never posted anything, but your visit still added to your passive footprint.

Manage your passive footprint
• Check app permissions and turn off location, microphone, or camera access for apps that
do not truly need it.
• Uninstall apps you no longer use.
• Clear your browsing history, cookies, and site data regularly.
• Be cautious about clicking “Accept all cookies” without understanding what is being tracked.
• On public Wi-Fi, avoid logging in to sensitive accounts (such as banking or important email)
unless you are using a VPN.
The Internet is Permanent
When people say "the internet is permanent", they mean that once something is online, it can
be very hard or even impossible to completely remove it. Even if you delete a post, photo,
or comment, copies might still exist on other people's devices, in backups, or in screenshots.
Websites can be archived, and search engines can save old versions of pages.
In some situations, private conversations such as direct messages or group chats may also
become public. For example, if there is a lawsuit or investigation, digital messages and posts
can be collected as evidence.
To protect your reputation and privacy, treat everything you put online, texts, DMs, stories,
snaps, and comments, as if it could become public and permanent.
Examples of Online Carelessness and Long-term Consequences
Posting a Hurtful Comment
Example:
A student gets angry during an online argument and posts a mean, insulting comment about a
classmate on social media. They call the person names and encourage others to make fun of
them, thinking it is just “venting” and everyone will forget about it soon.
Consequences:
Screenshots of the comment are shown to school staff and the student's parents. The school
may treat it as cyberbullying, which can lead to detentions, suspensions, or removal from clubs
or sports teams. The targeted classmate may never fully trust them again, and the student may
gain a reputation as someone who is cruel or unkind. Those impressions can follow them into
future classes and may even be seen by colleges or employers who look at their online history.
Sharing an Embarrassing Photo of a Friend
Example:
At a sleepover, a student takes an embarrassing photo of a friend making a weird face or
in an awkward situation and posts it online without asking permission. Everyone laughs and
comments on it, and the student thinks it is “no big deal” because they are just joking around.
Consequences:
The friend feels humiliated and may lose trust in the person who posted it. The photo might be
saved or shared by others, and even if it is deleted, it can keep reappearing in group chats or
on social media. This can damage the friendship and make others wonder if they can trust that

student with their own photos. Over time, the student may be seen as someone who does not
respect others’ privacy or feelings.
Posting Party or Rule-Breaking Photos
Example:
A student goes to a party where there is underage drinking or other rule-breaking behavior.
They post pictures and videos on social media showing people holding alcohol, vaping, or doing
dangerous stunts, thinking it makes them look “cool” and that only friends will see it.
Consequences:
Screenshots or reposts can spread beyond their friend group. Coaches, teachers, or school
administrators may see the posts and decide the student has broken school rules or team codes
of conduct. This can lead to suspension from sports, clubs, or leadership roles. Later, colleges
or scholarship committees might see those images and question the student’s judgment and
responsibility, which can affect admissions or awards.
Oversharing Personal Information
Example:
A student freely shares personal details online, such as their full name, school, age, daily
routine, and the places they like to hang out after class. They also post usernames for multiple
platforms and reuse simple passwords, assuming no one will actually use this information
against them.
Consequences:
Over time, this information makes it easier for strangers, scammers, or bullies to target them.
Someone could guess or steal their password and log into their accounts, sending rude
messages or posting inappropriate content under their name. Fixing the damage takes time:
changing passwords, explaining to friends and teachers what happened, and rebuilding trust.
Their online identity may be linked to things they never actually said or did, which can harm
their reputation.
Making “Edgy” or Offensive Jokes
Example:
To get laughs and attention, a student posts “edgy” jokes that include racist, sexist, or
homophobic language, or makes fun of a serious topic like mental health. Friends may react
with laughing emojis, and the student assumes it is just dark humor and that no one will take it
seriously.
Consequences:
Those posts can be found years later by people who do not know the context and may be
deeply offended or hurt by them. Colleges, employers, coaches, or scholarship committees
might see the posts and decide the student is not a good fit for their program or workplace.
Even if the student no longer believes or supports those ideas, the internet does not always
show that they have changed. The old jokes can follow them, harming opportunities and
damaging how others see their character.

Cultivate a Deliberate Personal Reputation
Cultivating a deliberate personal reputation means deciding how you want to be seen by others
and then acting in ways that match that vision. Instead of letting random posts, jokes, or angry
comments define you, you make thoughtful choices about what you share and how you behave,
both online and in person.
Your reputation is built over time from many small actions: what you post on social media, how
you talk in group chats, how you treat people at school, and how you respond when things go
wrong. When you are intentional, you are not leaving your image up to chance.
A deliberate personal reputation does not mean being fake or perfect; it means showing your
real self in a responsible way. You can start by thinking about your strengths, interests, and
values. Do you care about kindness, creativity, hard work, or leadership? Then make sure your
posts and behavior reflect those things. Share projects you are proud of, goals you are working
toward, and activities you enjoy, such as sports, music, art, or volunteering.
You can build and protect your personal reputation by making a few simple habits part of your
routine:
• Before you post, ask yourself, “Would I be okay if a teacher, parent, or future boss saw this?”
If not, do not post it.
• Avoid joining in on bullying, drama, or mean jokes, even if others say it is “just for fun.”
• Support your friends, give credit to others, and apologize when you make mistakes.
• Share content that aligns with your values and the kind of person you want others to see.
Over time, these choices build a strong, deliberate reputation that can open doors for you and
help people see you as the person you truly want to be.

Lesson 3C
Understanding Intellectual Property
Objectives Covered
1.2 Identify notational systems.
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
Every day you use and share creative work, music, videos, memes, photos, school
assignments, apps, and games. All of these are examples of intellectual property (IP)  ideas
and creations that belong to someone. Just because something is easy to copy or download
online does not mean it is free to use however you want.
You will explore what it means to own digital work and why copyrights, licenses, and credits
matter. It's important to learn the difference between being inspired by someone's idea and
stealing their work, and you'll see how plagiarism and piracy can affect creators, students, and
even your own future opportunities.
You'll also practice making smarter choices about what you post, share, and reuse, especially
on social media and in school projects, so that you can participate online in a way that is both
ethical and respectful of others' rights.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is intellectual property, and what kinds of digital work does it include?
• How does copyright protect creators and their work online?
• What is plagiarism, and how is it different from simply being inspired by someone else?
• In what ways can copying or sharing content without permission harm creators and users?
• How can you use, share, or remix other people’s work while still respecting their rights?
Intellectual Property Theft online
Intellectual property theft online is when someone steals or uses another person's creative work
without permission. This includes music, movies, books, artwork, software, designs, and logos.
Just because a file can be copied easily does not mean it is free to use. This kind of theft harms
creators who depend on selling their work to make a living. If people steal their work instead of
paying for it, creators lose money and opportunities, which can discourage them from creating
new content.
There are also legal and personal risks for the person doing the stealing. Intellectual property
theft can lead to serious consequences, such as lawsuits, fines, losing online accounts,
or facing school discipline if it violates school policies. Downloading pirated content from
untrusted websites can also expose your device to malware, viruses, and scams.

To avoid these problems, it is important to respect creators' rights: buy or stream content from
legal sources, use free or open-licensed materials, and always give proper credit when using
someone else's work. Respecting intellectual property online helps protect both creators and
users.
Intellectual Property and Digital Ownership
In the digital world, creators and users both have rights. Digital rights are legal rights for people
to use, access, and create digital information and content. Along with your right to find and
access content, creators have rights that protect their work.
Intellectual property is a term for creations of the mind, such as writing, music, art, inventions,
and brand symbols. There are several ways to protect intellectual property in law.
Digital Rights and Protections
The table below summarizes three common ways intellectual property is protected.
Type Definition
Copyright Protections granted by the federal government to
creators, writers, and inventors. Copyright includes
the rights to reproduce, display, make derivative
works, and distribute the work by sale, rental, or
lending. Copyright is automatically given to creators
of original works; no application is necessary.
Trademark A trademark is a symbol for a company or institution
that is used to identify them. Trademarks include
logos, slogans, names of specific products, or other
iconography tied to the company. A trademark
must be registered and approved and must be able
to uniquely identify the company (not be overly
generic).
Holding a trademark allows a company or brand to
prevent competitors from releasing products with
names or logos that would confuse consumers
into thinking they are purchasing from the original
company.
Patent A patent is a special type of intellectual property
protection for inventions and products. Patents must
be submitted and approved. Having a patent can
be used to prevent others from copying, selling, or
using that particular invention without permission.
Understanding these protections helps you respect others’ creations and better protect your
own creative work online.
Copyright Basics
Copyright and Licensing
A copyright is a legal protection that gives content creators the right to determine how their
creations are used and reproduced. If everything is copyrighted, how can we use things created
by other people? Typically, content is licensed by the copyright holder. A license can be an

informal agreement or a detailed contract. In all cases, the copyright holder can specify terms
of use for their content, granting specific permissions and listing specific conditions for using it.
Copyright and Intellectual Property
Term Description
Intellectual Property Intellectual property refers to works created from the creativity or
intellect of the human mind. They are often protected by copyright.
Common examples include books, paintings, songs, poems, movies, and
inventions.
Piracy Using somebody else's intellectual property without their consent in a
way reserved for the copyright holder, such as downloading a movie
without paying or selling a copy of a CD. Piracy is punishable by fines
and, in serious cases, jail time.
License A contract that specifies who may use specific content, including
information about specific permissions and conditions for using the
media.
Permission A permission in a license refers to ways that licensed content may be
used. For example, a license may grant permission for the content to be
modified or to be used for commercial purposes.
Condition A condition in a license refers to specific things the license holder must
do to use the content. For example, a license may require that the media
be used with attribution to the original creator.
Attribution Giving credit to the copyright holder, often by name. For example:
Photo by: Michael Olsen on unsplash.com

Term Description
Fair Use An exception to copyright law that allows short excerpts of a copyrighted
work to be used for purposes that benefit the public, such as criticism,
teaching, research, and news reporting. Fair use is not a guaranteed right;
it is a legally defensible position.
Public Domain When a copyright expires, the work enters the public domain, meaning
anyone can use it freely. Copyrights usually expire 70 years after the
creator's death, or about 100 years after publication for works by
companies or anonymous creators. Creators can also choose to donate
their content to the public domain.
New creations based on public domain content are not automatically in
the public domain. For example, the original Sherlock Holmes stories are
public domain, but a new Sherlock Holmes movie is not.
Creative Commons Creative Commons is a copyright framework that offers several different
licensing schemes so users can remix, reuse, or share creative works.
Users must give attribution to the owner and follow the terms of the
specific license.
Content published online with a Creative Commons license may allow
reuse for many purposes. A common condition is that the content cannot
be used for commercial purposes, meaning it cannot be used to make
money or sell products and services.
Proprietary Software Proprietary software is any software where the publisher retains
intellectual property rights to the source code. Most software you buy
is proprietary. Generally, the end user has the right to use the software,
but does not have the right to make and distribute unauthorized copies.
Open-Source Software Software where anyone can inspect, enhance, and modify the source
code is considered open source. Open-source software is often free and
can have third-party add-ons to enhance the product. Common examples
are GIMP and the Linux operating system.
Open source is not the same thing as a free license or open
license, which is a license that allows others to reuse another
creator’s work as they wish.
Plagiarism
Plagiarism is when you take someone else's words, ideas, images, or work and present them
as if they were your own. This can happen when you copy and paste from a website into your
assignment, use a friend's essay, or borrow sentences from an article and only change a few
words. It also includes using music, art, or photos you did not create without giving credit.
Any time you use someone else's work without clearly saying where it came from, you are
committing plagiarism.
Plagiarism is considered a serious form of cheating and dishonesty in school and beyond. When
you plagiarize, you are not showing what you actually understand or can do; you are taking
credit for someone else's effort. Schools and colleges expect students to be honest and to
do their own work. That is why they often have strict rules and consequences for plagiarism,
such as getting a zero on the assignment or facing disciplinary action. To avoid plagiarism, you
should always put information into your own words and give proper credit to your sources.
Examples of different types of plagiarism:
• Direct plagiarism: Word-for-word copying of someone else's work without using quotations
or giving credit (attribution).
• Self-plagiarism: Submitting work that includes past work of your own without permission or
acknowledgment.

• Mosaic plagiarism: Borrowing phrases or sentence structures from a source without
quotation marks, even if some words are changed.
• Accidental plagiarism: Forgetting to cite sources, misquoting a source, or unintentionally
paraphrasing too closely. Accidental plagiarism can be just as serious as intentional
plagiarism.
Copyright infringement is related but not the same as plagiarism. Copyright infringement
happens when someone uses another person's protected work, such as music, movies,
books, artwork, photos, or software, without permission or proper rights. Examples include
downloading pirated movies, sharing a paid textbook PDF with friends, posting a full song in
your video without permission, or copying artwork and claiming it as your own. Copyright laws
are meant to protect creators so they can control how their work is used and be credited and
paid fairly. Even if you find something easily online, that does not mean it is free to use in any
way you want.
Some people think they can avoid copyright problems by adding a disclaimer such as “I'm not
the creator of this movie and no copyright infringement is intended” before sharing a Hollywood
movie on YouTube. This does not actually protect you from copyright infringement. It is similar
to walking out of a store with unpaid food while saying, “I'm not the baker of this bread, and
no theft is intended.” Clarifying that you are not the original creator may avoid plagiarism, but
using someone else's media without a license or permission (except in fair use situations) is still
copyright infringement.
Copyright infringement is typically not prosecuted as a criminal offense in the United States
except for large-scale cases. However, copyright holders can sue for damages, and many
individuals and companies are known for aggressively pursuing legal action when their
copyrighted materials are used without a license.
Practical copyright ethics on social media
Practical copyright ethics on social media means thinking about whether you have the right to
post or share something before you hit “upload” or “share.” Just because you find a picture,
song, meme template, or video online does not mean it is free to use however you want. Most
of that content is protected by copyright, which gives the creator control over how it is used.
When you repost someone's art without credit, use a full song in your video without permission,
or upload a movie clip you did not create, you might be breaking copyright rules, even if you are
not making money from it.
One simple way to be more ethical is to always credit the creator when you use their work. If
you share a drawing, photo, or quote someone else made, tag them or mention their name and,
when possible, link back to where you found it. However, giving credit alone does not always
make it legally okay; you still need to make sure the creator allows their work to be reused. You
can look for content labeled with Creative Commons licenses, “royalty-free” music or images,
or use built-in music and sound libraries provided by the social media platform, since those are
usually cleared for use there.
It is also smart to create and share more of your own original content. Take your own photos,
make your own edits, record your own sounds, or design your own graphics instead of copying
others. If you really want to use someone else's work, such as a clip from a show or a piece of
music, use only short portions when it fits fair use (for example, for commentary or criticism),
and still give credit. When in doubt, choose safer options or ask permission directly.
By following these practical habits, you show respect for creators, protect yourself from
account strikes or takedowns, and help make social media a fair and honest place.

Lesson 3D
Building Media Literacy
Objectives Covered
1.2 Identify notational systems.
3.5 Identify common uses of artificial intelligence (AI).
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
You are surrounded by media every day, videos, posts, news stories, memes, ads, and more.
Some of it is helpful and accurate, but some of it is misleading, biased, or created just to get a
reaction. Learning to read media carefully is called media literacy, and it’s an important skill for
making good decisions in your daily life.
You will see how your brain’s common biases can affect what you believe, and how to tell the
difference between facts, opinions, and advertising. It's important to identify who created a
piece of content, what their motives might be, and how techniques like clickbait, ragebait, and
altered or AI-generated media are used to grab your attention.
By practicing media literacy, you can become a more thoughtful and careful consumer of
information. This helps you decide what to trust, what to question, and what to ignore online
and offline.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is media literacy, and why is it important in your daily life?
• How do common human biases influence what you pay attention to and believe?
• How can you tell the difference between facts, opinions, and advertising in the media?
• Why is it important to identify who created a message and what their motives or goals might
be?
• How can you recognize clickbait, ragebait, and altered or generated media so you are not
easily misled?
• What strategies can you use to decide whether a piece of media is trustworthy or should be
questioned?
Common Biases in Human Psychology
Common biases in human psychology are mental shortcuts or habits in the way we think that
can cause us to see information in a distorted way. One important bias is confirmation bias,
which happens when we mostly pay attention to information that agrees with what we already
believe and ignore anything that challenges us. For example, if you think a certain celebrity
is amazing, you might only click on positive articles about them and dismiss any criticism as
"haters." This makes it harder to see the full picture and can trap you in an echo chamber,
especially online.

Another common bias is the bandwagon effect, which is when people start believing or doing
something just because many others are doing it. On social media, this shows up in trends,
viral posts, and "cancel culture." If a post has lots of likes, shares, or comments, you might
assume it's true or worth supporting without really checking the facts. Similarly, halo effect bias
happens when you assume that because someone is good at one thing, like being popular,
attractive, or funny, they must be right or trustworthy about everything else, including serious
topics like politics or health.
In media literacy, recognizing these biases matters because they affect how we interpret what
we see online. Algorithms on apps and websites often feed us more of what we already agree
with or enjoy, which strengthens our confirmation bias. To think more clearly, it helps to slow
down and ask yourself: "Am I liking or sharing this just because it fits what I already think? Am
I believing this because it's popular or because I've actually checked it?" By being aware of
these common human biases, you can make more independent, informed choices about what to
believe, who to trust, and what to share.
Identify Facts, Opinions, and Advertising
Being media literate means knowing how to tell the difference between facts, opinions, and
advertising when you see them in news, social media, videos, and posts. A fact is something
that can be proven true or false, like "The test is on Friday" or "Water freezes at 0°C." An
opinion is what someone thinks or feels, such as "This movie is amazing" or "I hate math."
Advertising is content created mainly to get you to buy something, support something, or
change your behavior, even if it doesn't look like a traditional ad. Recognizing which is which
helps you understand what you're really being told.
Facts are important because they give you solid information about the world. They are based on
evidence, can be checked in reliable sources, and don't change just because someone doesn't
like them. For example, "The school has 800 students" is a fact that can be confirmed by school
records. When you see a statement online, ask yourself: "Can I verify this from a trustworthy
source?" If the answer is yes, it's probably a fact. Being able to spot facts helps you make better
decisions and avoid being misled by rumors or false information.
Opinions, on the other hand, are personal thoughts, feelings, or beliefs. They often use words
like "best," "worst," "should," "love," or "hate." For instance, "The new school lunch is gross" or
"This is the best video game ever" are opinions. They can be based on facts, but they are not
facts themselves because different people can honestly disagree. In the media, opinions appear
in comment sections, reviews, opinion articles, and influencer posts. When you recognize
something as an opinion, you know it reflects how one person or group sees things, not
necessarily how everyone does.
Advertising can be tricky because it doesn't always look like a typical commercial. Sometimes
it's clearly labeled with words like "Ad," "Sponsored," or "Paid promotion," but other times it's
hidden inside a YouTube video, Instagram post, or TikTok. A creator might talk about a product
they were paid to promote or show a brand's logo a lot without saying it's an ad. To spot
advertising, look for content that is strongly pushing you to buy, click, sign up, or "learn more,"
especially if it focuses on benefits and leaves out negatives. Understanding whether you're
seeing facts, opinions, or advertising helps you think more clearly, question what you see, and
become a smarter, more independent viewer.
Identify the Creator and their Motives
When you see any kind of media, a TikTok, YouTube video, news article, meme, or ad, one
of the first questions you should ask is, "Who created this?" The creator could be a single
person, a company, a news organization, a political group, or even a bot. Sometimes the creator
is obvious, like a verified influencer or a well-known brand. Other times, it's hidden behind a

username, a logo, or an anonymous account. Identifying the creator helps you understand how
trustworthy the content might be and what kind of point of view it represents.
Once you have an idea of who made the content, the next question is, "Why did they make
this?" This is about figuring out the creator's motives. Are they trying to inform you, like a news
report explaining a current event? Are they trying to entertain you, like a funny skit or a meme?
Are they trying to persuade you, like a political post asking you to support a certain side? Or are
they trying to sell you something, like an ad for a product or a "sponsored" video? Many pieces
of media mix these motives, for example, a funny video that also promotes a brand.
Knowing the creator's motives helps you spot possible bias. Bias doesn't always mean lying; it
can mean leaving out information, exaggerating certain details, or presenting only one side of
a story. For example, a company's ad for its own product probably won't mention any flaws. A
political group's post might highlight only the facts that support its position. An influencer who
is being paid to promote a product might only talk about the good parts. When you understand
what the creator wants from you, your money, your support, or your attention, you can judge
the message more carefully.
To practice this skill, get in the habit of asking a few quick questions whenever you see media:
Who made this? What do they want me to think, feel, or do? How are they trying to influence
me through emotions, jokes, fear, or excitement? Are there any important viewpoints or facts
that might be missing? By looking beyond the surface and paying attention to the creator and
their motives, you become a more thoughtful, critical viewer. This helps you avoid being easily
tricked or manipulated and makes you more in control of what you choose to believe and share.
Identifying Clickbait and Ragebait
Clickbait and ragebait are types of online content designed to grab your attention and make
you click, often by playing with your emotions instead of giving you solid information. Clickbait
usually uses dramatic headlines like "You Won't Believe What Happened Next!" or "This One
Trick Will Change Your Life!" The goal is to make you so curious that you click, even if
the article or video doesn't really deliver what the title promises. Sometimes, clickbait hides
important details or exaggerates the story to get more views, likes, or ad money.
Ragebait is a more intense form of clickbait that tries to make you angry, shocked, or outraged
so you'll react, comment, and share. Ragebait headlines might insult a group, twist a quote, or
show only the most extreme part of a story: "This Teacher's Rule Will Make You Furious" or
"You Won't Believe What These Teens Did!" The creators know that strong emotions, especially
anger, make people more likely to spread the content without checking if it's fair, accurate, or
missing important context. This can increase drama, arguments, and misinformation online.
To protect yourself from clickbait and ragebait, it helps to slow down and look for warning
signs. Ask yourself: Does this headline sound too extreme or too good (or bad) to be true? Is it
using lots of ALL CAPS, exclamation marks, or emotional words like "shocking," "disgusting," or
"unbelievable"? Before you share, consider reading beyond the headline, checking the source,
and seeing if other reliable outlets are reporting the same story. If a post seems designed only
to make you feel angry or hyped up, be cautious. Recognizing clickbait and ragebait is a key
media literacy skill that helps you stay in control instead of being manipulated by your emotions.
Identify Altered or Generated Media
In today's digital world, it's important to learn how to identify altered or generated media,
images, videos, or audio that have been edited, faked, or created by AI. Altered media includes
things like photos that have been heavily edited with filters, apps that change faces or bodies,
or videos that have clips cut out to change the meaning. Generated media goes a step further
and can include deepfakes (videos where someone's face or voice is replaced with another
person's) or AI-generated images and audio that look and sound real, even though they never

actually happened. These tools can be used for fun, but they can also spread lies, bullying, or
misinformation.
To spot altered or generated media, look closely for clues. In images, check for strange lighting,
blurry edges, weird fingers, mismatched earrings, or backgrounds that don't line up correctly;
these can be signs of heavy editing or AI generation. In videos, watch for unnatural blinking,
odd mouth movements, or audio that seems slightly out of sync with the person's lips. If a
video or image makes a celebrity, teacher, or classmate look like they did something shocking
or totally out of character, be extra careful. Ask yourself: "Where did this come from? Is it from a
trusted source? Are other reliable places reporting the same thing?"
Being media literate means not believing everything at first glance, especially when it comes to
dramatic or emotional content. Before you react, share, or judge someone based on a picture or
video, try to verify it. You can use reverse image search to see where an image first appeared,
check fact-checking websites, or compare the content to coverage from trustworthy news
sources. Remember that altered and generated media can harm reputations, fuel rumors, and
influence opinions. By slowing down, looking for signs of editing, and checking the source, you
protect yourself and others from being fooled or unfairly treated.

Lesson 4A
Understanding the Internet
Objectives Covered
3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.
The internet connects billions of devices and people around the world. Every time you send
a message, watch a video, join an online game, or search for information, you are using this
massive global network. But what is the internet really, and how does it actually work behind the
scenes?
Computer networks link devices together so they can share information. Web pages, websites,
and web servers work together to store and deliver content. IP addresses and URLs act like
digital addresses and directions, helping your device find exactly the right place on the web.
Understanding these basics turns the internet from something that feels like "magic" into a clear
system of devices, connections, and rules that make online communication and information
possible.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is the internet, and how is it different from the World Wide Web?
• How do computer networks and connectivity allow devices to communicate with each
other?
• What are web pages, websites, and web servers, and how do they work together?
• What are IP addresses and URLs, and how do they help your device find information on the
internet?
• In what ways is the internet "everywhere" in your daily life, even when you don't notice it?
What is the Internet?
The Internet is a system of computer networks all over the world talking to each other, without
any one person or group controlling it. Think of the Internet as a large highway that emails,
videos, games, and all kinds of data travel over. Internet technology has made it possible for
people to play games online, send emails, make video calls, chat, share files, and more. It
connects millions of computers, websites, and servers. It's a network of networks.
Some form of Internet technology dates back to the late 1960s, and a United States government
program by the Department of Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. It began as a
way for researchers to share information more easily. Because computers at that time were
large and immobile, taking up whole rooms in some cases, people had to either travel to the

computer's location to see the data on that computer or have magnetic computer tapes sent
through the postal service. This was not very secure or efficient. Over the next decade, more
groups developed other small networks of computers, but each network was isolated from the
others. They did not have a common language or set of protocols.
Protocols
In the early 1980s, the people behind the different networks agreed on one shared language,
one that allowed all the networks to talk to each other and to share information. This shared
language is called the Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (T CP/IP),  and it's still the
way the Internet communicates today.
All the Internet-connected computers follow these rules to maintain quick communication, as
well as the integrity of the data. Data integrity is the idea that data sent over the Internet is
accurate, consistent, complete, and correct when it arrives at its destination. In other words, the
data you receive is the same as the data you asked for. These protocols mean that when you
get data from another computer on the Internet, that data hasn't changed while it traveled to
you.
Internet Architecture
The Internet is a decentralized system, meaning that there isn't one group or person that
holds all the information on the Internet or governs how the Internet runs. Instead, everything
connected to the Internet, from your phone to a university computer, can all do the same things.
Every device can ask for information from others (or act as a client), and every device can
share information with others (or act as a server). This is sometimes referred to as peer-to-peer
architecture. Peer-to-peer architecture allows smaller groups to share information just as easily
as groups with more computing power. Peer-to-peer architecture makes it easier to share files,
stream video, and resist security threats.
Computer Networks and Connectivity
From One Device to a Network
Imagine a single computer sitting in a room with no cables, no Wi-Fi, and no way to connect to
anything else. It can only use the information already stored on it. Now compare that to your
experience today: you can message friends, stream videos, play online games, and look up
information in seconds. The difference is computer networks.
A computer network is a group of devices linked together so they can share information. These
devices can be desktop computers, laptops, tablets, phones, game consoles, smart TVs, and
many others. Even devices like printers, security cameras, or smart thermostats can be part of a
network.
A very small network might exist in a single room or home. Larger networks might connect an
entire school or office building. These different networks can then link together to reach even
more places.
Wired and Wireless Connectivity
For a network to work, devices need some way to send data between them. This is
called connectivity. You can think of connectivity like the paths that connect houses in a
neighborhood:

• Wired connections are like solid roads. Devices use network cables to connect to the
network. These cables carry electrical signals that represent data. Wired connections are
usually very stable and fast, which is why they are common in offices, schools, and data
centers.
• Wireless connections are more like invisible paths through the air. Devices use radio
waves, such as Wi-Fi or cellular signals, to communicate without needing a cable. Wireless
connections make it easy to move around with phones, laptops, and tablets.
On a typical home network, both types of connectivity are often used at the same time. A router
might connect to the internet using a cable from the wall, while phones and laptops connect to
that router over Wi-Fi.
Small Networks, Big Networks
Networks can be built in many different sizes. A small home network might have just a few
devices. A school might have hundreds of computers, printers, and tablets connected. Large
companies and universities might have networks that span multiple buildings or campuses.
Even though the size and complexity can change, the basic idea is the same: connected
devices can share data. A file saved on one computer can be opened on another. A printer
in the hallway can be used by any computer on the network. A game server in one city can send
updates to players in many different places.
When many of these smaller networks are linked together, information can travel a very long
way from one neighborhood or school to the other side of the world.
Public and Private Networks
Not every network is open to everyone. Some networks are meant to be shared with the public,
while others are meant to be kept private.
• A public network is open for general use. The public internet is the largest example. Anyone
with a connection can reach public websites, watch videos, or read online articles.
• A private network belongs to a specific group, such as a company, school, or family. Devices
inside the private network can usually reach the public internet, but outside devices cannot
freely reach into the private network.
A useful analogy is a city with open streets and gated communities. The public roads are like
the public internet; anyone can use them. A gated neighborhood is like a private network; only
people with permission can enter. Devices such as routers and firewalls act like the gates and
guards, controlling who can go in and out.
Some organizations build an intranet, which is like a private “mini-internet” inside the company.
It might use web pages, email, and internal chat tools, but only employees or authorized users
can access it.
Clients, Servers, and Peers
When devices communicate on a network, they often take on different roles depending on what
is happening.
• A client is a device that requests information or services. For example, when you open a
browser and type in the address of a website, your computer or phone is acting as a client.
• A server is a device that responds to those requests and provides information, such as a
website, a file, or a game update.

In many cases, the same device can act as both a client and a server at different times. A
classroom computer might request a web page (client role) and also share a simple file with
another student on the same network (server role).
When devices on a network share directly with each other instead of always going through
a central server, this is often called a peer-to-peer connection. In a peer-to-peer group, each
device, or “peer,” can both send and receive. This model is common in small file-sharing setups
or when friends connect their devices for a shared activity.
Connectivity in Everyday Life
Computer networks and connectivity are part of many everyday activities, even when they are
not obvious. A few examples include:
• Saving a school project to cloud storage and opening it later on a different device
• Joining an online game where players connect from many different locations
• Using a messaging app to chat with family members in another city or country
• Having a smart doorbell send video to your phone over your home network
• Connecting a laptop to a school printer over the school’s internal network
In each case, devices rely on networks to move data from one place to another. Cables,
wireless signals, public and private networks, and different device roles all work together so
that information can travel quickly and reliably, often in just a fraction of a second.
Web Pages and Web Sites
It's pretty common to think that the Internet and the World Wide Web (W W W),  or websites,
are the same, but they're actually different things. The Internet is a huge network of computers
all over the world. The Web, on the other hand, is a collection of interconnected files that use
the Internet to share content such as text, graphics, audio, video, and more. If you imagine
the Internet and the Web as a city, the Internet would be all the roads and highways that
connect different neighborhoods. The Web would be the diners, movie theaters, coffee shops,
and stores along the way.
Web Content
The World Wide Web was created to help organize information. A scientist named Tim Berners-
Lee, who worked in a lab in Switzerland, noticed that big projects were making huge amounts
of data, and that was stored in many different places. Sometimes, scientists even lost data
because they could not find it. He suggested a way to link all the data together like a "web"
using hypertext documents that could be stored on computers called servers. In 1990, he set up
the very first web server and web page. By 1993, websites started to be available for everyone
to use.
You can see the very first website ever created at https://info.cern.ch/
At its simplest, a website is a collection of pages that are all linked together and share
information. Every webpage uses a special kind of code that decides how it looks or appears on
your screen.
This special code is called HyperText Markup Language (HTML) . HTML is what organizes
everything you see on a webpage, such as images, advertisements, and text. It also makes sure
all the parts of the webpage work well together. Thanks to HTML, webpages can look the same
and work properly no matter which browser you use to view them.

HTML is packed with details on all the different parts of a webpage and instructions on how to
display them. It's a key part of making webpages work.
Protocols
HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP)  is the basis of the World Wide Web. This protocol, or set of
rules, allows a web browser to communicate with a web server and request a website, transmit
the website data, and load it on your browser for you to see.
There are many other protocols involved in directing traffic across the web. Some are
concerned with email and other messages, others focus on transferring files, while still more
protocols deal with discovering devices on local networks and improving communication.
Web Architecture
The World Wide Web was originally designed as a decentralized system. This means no single
person, group, or organization owns or controls all the information. However, most Internet
users use only certain social media or messaging applications today. These applications are
owned by large corporations that are centralized and control all the content on their platforms.
This is why many feel the Internet is controlled by a few large companies.
The World Wide Web uses a design called client-server architecture to access and navigate
information. A client, usually a person using a web browser, requests data from a web server.
The server returns the page with the information requested. You can select any links in that
document to request more information from the original web server or possibly create a request
to a different web server. These hyperlinks are the key to the World Wide Web.
The web server is equipped with powerful hardware, specialized software, and is expected to
be running almost constantly. Servers have large amounts of memory, multiple CPUs, and large
storage capacities. In addition to its power, the server will have better quality components than
a traditional desktop, and more of them: servers typically have multiple hard drives and power
supplies. All of these extras allow web servers to fulfill lots of requests in a short amount of
time, and to stay available for nearly its whole lifespan.
IP Addresses and URLs
Finding Things on the Internet
When you want to call a friend, you probably tap their name in your contacts instead of typing
their phone number every time. Your phone quietly looks up the number for you and dials it in
the background. The Internet works in a very similar way.
When you want to visit a website, you type or tap a web address like comptia.com or click a
link. Behind the scenes, your device has to find a specific computer somewhere on the Internet
that can provide that site. To do that, it uses two key pieces:
• IP addresses – the exact “numbers” that identify devices on the Internet.
• URLs – the readable web addresses you use every day.
IP addresses and URLs work together so that you can use simple names, while your device
uses precise numbers to reach the right place.
What Is an IP Address?
An IP address is a unique set of numbers that identifies a device on a network that uses the
Internet Protocol (IP).  You can think of it like a street address for a house. Without an address,

the postal service would not know where to deliver a letter. Without an IP address, the Internet
would not know where to send data.
IP addresses usually look like one of these:
• IPv4 example: 192.168.1.10
• IPv6 example: 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:037 0:7 334
You do not need to memorize these formats, but it helps to recognize that they are numbers,
not words. When your device sends a request across the Internet, it includes both its own IP
address (so the response can find its way back) and the destination IP address (so the data
knows where to go).
What Is a URL?
A Uniform Resource Locator(URL)  is the text address you type into your browser to reach a
page or resource on the Web. It is designed to be easy for people to read and remember, like a
contact name in your phone.
A typical URL such as https://www.example.com/page can be broken into parts:
• Protocol - https:// tells the browser which set of rules to use when requesting the resource.
• Domain name – www.example.com is the main name of the site, made of words and dots
instead of numbers.
• Path – /page points to a specific page or file on that site.
You can think of a URL like a full mailing address written in a friendly format. The domain name
is like the name of the building, and the path is like the room or office number inside that
building.
How URLs and IP Addresses Work Together
Computers and other devices communicate using numbers, but people usually prefer names.
URLs and IP addresses work together to make both sides happy.
When you enter a URL such as comptia.com , your device needs to find the IP address that
matches that name. This process is like asking your phone to “Call Coach” and letting it look up
the correct phone number behind the scenes.
Once the IP address is known, your device uses that number to send and receive data with
the correct web server. You keep working with the simple URL, but the actual communication
happens using the IP address.
The Role of DNS Servers
A Domain Name System server (DNS  server) is a special device that helps translate URLs into IP
addresses, similar to how a contacts app translates names into phone numbers.
The basic idea is:
• You type a URL into your browser, like comptia.com , and press Enter.
• Your device sends a request to a nearby DNS server, asking, “What is the IP address for
comptia.com ?”
• The DNS server looks in its catalog of stored records to find the match.
• If it finds an entry, it sends the IP address back to your device.
After that, your device can contact the correct server directly using the IP address. This all
happens very quickly, usually in a fraction of a second, so you only notice that the website
appears in your browser.

Why IP Addresses and URLs Matter
IP addresses and URLs might seem like background details, but they affect how you use the
Internet every day:
• Ease of use – URLs let you use simple names instead of long strings of numbers.
• Accuracy – IP addresses make sure data goes to and comes from the correct device.
• Speed – DNS servers and stored records help your device find sites quickly.
Understanding the basic relationship between IP addresses, URLs, and DNS helps explain what
is happening when you type a web address and a site appears almost instantly on your screen.
It turns a “mysterious” process into something you can picture and reason about, even as a
first-time learner.

Lesson 4B
Browsing the Web
Objectives Covered
3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.
3.4 Given a scenario, configure and use web browser features.
Using a web browser is one of the main ways to interact with the internet. Any time you search
for information, open a website, stream a video, or log in to an online account, you are using
browser tools and features, even if you don’t think about them. Knowing how browsers work
helps you stay more organized, efficient, and safe online.
Most browsers share common parts, such as the address bar, tabs, and menus. They also
offer options to personalize how pages look, save your favorite sites, and control privacy
and security settings. With a bit of practice, you can adjust a browser to fit your needs and
troubleshoot common problems when something doesn’t work as expected.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is a web browser, and how is it different from other types of software?
• What tools and features do most web browsers share in common?
• How can you navigate websites effectively and find what you need on a page?
• What options are available to personalize or customize how a browser looks and behaves?
• How can add-ons, extensions, and privacy features change the way you browse?
• What browser settings can you use to have the best experiences online and to keep your
private information safe?
• What steps can you take to keep your browser working well and solve basic browsing
problems?
Web Browsers
A web browser is a program or application that allows you to view and use websites. It
works by asking for resources, meaning the contents of a web page or site, from a web
server and displaying them on your computer screen. Web browsers can deliver websites from
local servers (for example, within a school or company's own network), or from anywhere
on the Internet. Tim Berners-Lee is credited with creating the first web browser and the
protocol needed to transfer a webpage from one computer to another. Since their creation,
web browsers have evolved to become one of the most important tools.
There are many different browsers available. At the time of writing, Google's Chrome browser is
the most popular browser worldwide, with Safari, Firefox, Opera, and Microsoft Edge among the
top spots. These well-known products are similar in how quickly they load webpages and how

easy they are to use. Their differences are where they get users' attention. Some have stronger
privacy protections, some use fewer computer resources to run, and others have note-taking
and productivity tools built in to the browser application. Each of these popular browsers has a
large community of users who can answer questions, in addition to the developers who build
and support them.
Type "do a barrel roll" into the Google search box in the middle of the Chrome browser. This is one
of Chrome's many hidden features.
Compatible Browsers
In the past, different web browsers didn't always follow the standards for how websites
should look and work. These rules are made using formats like HyperText Markup Language
(HTML)  and cascading style sheets (CSS) . Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser, once the most
commonly used browser, was famous for not following these rules. A lot of websites and online
tools were made to work just with Internet Explorer, which meant they might not work right on
other browsers.
Today these problems are not very common at all. The popular web browsers follow industry
standards much more closely. There can still be problems with website compatibility, however,
especially on older websites. These websites may have important information, but just aren't
updated very often. If you encounter a compatibility problem, you may need to use an older
browser.
Mobile Browsers
More and more people, no matter how old they are, are using their phones and mobile devices
to go online. It's easier and more comfortable to browse on a phone, and it makes sharing
content on social media much faster. Mobile browsers are designed specifically to work with
smaller touch screens. They have a simpler user interface that's easy to use with just your
fingers. Additionally, websites often load more quickly on mobile browsers, so you don't have to
wait as long.
As mobile browsing has gotten more common, web developers have kept up by making their
sites easier to use. Single-column page layouts make it easier for users to scroll through, and
simplifying the content makes it easier to find important information. Responsive designs adjust
both text and images to fit the screen, because the mobile browser tells the web server to
deliver the mobile-friendly version of the site.
Shared Browser Traits
Modern browsers, both desktop and mobile, share a lot of similar features. One of the most
user-friendly is the ability to search within the address bar at the top of the browser window.
If you type a valid uniform resource locator (URL) , or web address, into the address bar and
press Enter, it takes you to that web page. If you type text that isn't a URL, the browser will
search the web using its default search engine.
Modern web browsers have other similar features, including:
• Navigation buttons: Move backward and forward through webpages you have recently
viewed. If you hold down either button a window of recent history will appear.
• Refresh button: Forces the browser to reload the current website. The F5 key will also do the
same for most browsers.
• Home button: Returns a browser to the default starting webpage.
• Address bar: Displays the name of the website or universal resource locator (URL)  of the
current web page.

• Browser tabs: Allow several websites to be opened in one browser window.
• Bookmarks: Store websites so you can easily visit the same site again later.
Web Browsing Software
Every device with an operating system (OS)  comes bundled, or pre-installed, with a browser
from that OS's parent company. If you have a Windows computer, you'll get Microsoft Edge.
Apple devices like Macs, iPhones, and iPads come with Safari. Linux computers usually come
pre-installed with Mozilla Firefox. But the most popular browser by far is Google Chrome. Only
Android phones and tablets come with Chrome already installed. This is because Google owns
Android. It's interesting that so many people go out of their way to download Chrome on other
devices. It shows just how much people like it, or perhaps how much they've gotten used to
it. You can have several browsers if you want. In fact, it's probably a good idea since some
websites work better on different browsers.
Chrome is the most popular browser, though modern browsers generally have all the same
features. Whatever browser you choose, it's almost certainly going to be the most-used piece
of software on your computer. You can install any browser for free, and it will stay on your
system until you decide to remove it.
Smartphone Browsers
Smartphones come with a browser too, but people don't use them as much as they do on a
computer because many other apps compete for their attention. The major browsers you find
on a PC, like Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, are also available for Android and iOS. Safari is the one
exception, only available on Apple devices. If you sign in to an account linked to a browser, it
will sync your settings and bookmarks. With a smaller screen on mobile devices, you have to
scroll more to see a web page, which can be tiring. Also, the touch interface, which is the main
way to interact, can be less precise, making some webpages harder to navigate.
Website Navigation
There are millions of websites, each with its own design and content. However, there are some
patterns and features that are more common than not. This table will go over some navigation
features on the TestOut website that are similar to many sites you'll see as you use the web.

Personalize the Browser
Internet and website traffic may have started with small groups focused on special interests,
