streams.
You have a choice in which browser you use, and you can choose how to make it work
best for you. Your device operating system will provide a default browser, which means it
will automatically select that browser for you. For example, a Windows computer may come
pre-loaded with Microsoft Edge. An Apple product will default to Safari. If you prefer something
else though, you can download a different browser to your device and set that as your default,
or regular browser. After that, any time you open a website link your device will open it with the
browser you prefer.
Browser Profiles
Browser profiles are one way to personalize this tool. Your browser profile can store a lot
of information about you, including your name, your photo, passwords to different websites,
payment methods such as credit cards, and your address. Storing all these items is optional.
You don't have to save this information in your browser profile. Many people do, however,
because it saves a lot of time when buying something online.
Browser profiles also save you time by keeping your preferences, or settings, the same no
matter which device you use. If you have a saved profile on Firefox, for example, you can
use a different computer but sign in to Firefox's browser and still see your profile information.
When you synchronize, or sync, your account, your browser will collect your browsing history,
preferences, settings, and bookmarks across the many devices that you've used.

Search Engines
Your browser lets you choose a default search engine in its settings. Google is by far the most
commonly used, but there are many others, such as Bing, Yahoo, and DuckDuckGo.
In 2014, Yahoo paid $375 million to Firefox to be the default search engine for the browser. Why
would they spend so much money for this? Because there is a lot of money to be made when
you're one of the most commonly used search engines.
Google was founded by two college students, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, who were studying
computer science. They wanted to make a search engine that was better than the ones
available at the time. There were many search engines already in the market at that time, but
they all had pretty similar functionality. What Sergey and Larry created ended up being much
more effective than the others. The main idea of Google's search method is that if a lot of other
websites link to a website, it means that the website is popular. Being popular means a website
will show up higher in the search results that Google returns when you use it to search.
Customize the Browser Appearance
In a browser, you can change a variety of settings to make it look and feel the way you want.
Most browsers let you pick different colors, patterns, designs, and pictures to make it look the
way you want. Some browsers even let you upload your own pictures to use as a background.
So for example, if you love Star Wars, you can make your browser look like it's part of the Star
Wars universe with backdrops for every new tab you open. Most of these features are free, but
a few might cost a little bit of money.

Accessibility Features
In Chrome, you can choose between light or dark mode. Dark mode can be easier on your
eyes, especially in dim light, while light mode might make things easier to read. If you're using a
laptop outside on a bright day, dark mode with light text can make the screen easier to see.
If you have trouble seeing, browsers can help you out. There's a setting called high contrast
that makes text on web pages easier to see by changing the background colors. High contrast
simplifies the visual elements, such as images, and focuses on text.
You can also zoom in or out on web pages. Each browser and operating system has shortcut
keys available for this. Other browser settings let you change the font style, which can help
some users read the text more easily.
The Chrome browser has a feature that can read web pages out loud to you. You can pick some
text you want to hear or have the whole page read back to you. This is helpful for people who
have a hard time seeing the words on the screen, or if you just want to listen to the information
instead of reading it.
Users with low vision or visual impairments may want to use a different browser entirely. While
screen readers can be helpful, including the Chrome read-aloud feature, most of them will
read every single thing on the screen. A free browser called WebbIE allows low-vision users
to focus on the main content of a webpage, ignoring graphics and links that could cause them
frustration.
Understand Browser Add-ons
You can tailor your browser's functionality by adding extensions or add-ons. Different browsers
may use different names, but the goal is the same: new features for your browser. These are
often developed by third-party companies not associated with the browser.
Each browser has an extension store where you can search for any kind of extension. There are
extensions that tell you the weather, help you write better, and even check prices for things you
want to buy.

Pop-up Blockers
One of the most popular types of extensions is a popup blocker. These help reduce the number
of ads on webpages. They also stop annoying ads and commercials on video sites like YouTube.
There are many popup blockers to choose from, and new ones come out often. Most are quick
and free to download from the online store for each browser.
Extensions and Privacy
Most extensions you can get for free, and the ones that cost money usually don't cost very
much. People who use the extensions can leave ratings, just as they would for other products,
so you can see if the extension is worth your time and effort.
Unfortunately, hackers have found out that extensions can be an easy way to sneak into what
you're doing online. When you have them turned on, or enabled, they might pop up out of
nowhere and try to get you to click on a link. This could take you to a spoofed website, one that
pretends to be something else, to obtain your personal information.
Removing Extensions
Extensions are easy to manage. Inside the extensions window you can enable, disable, or
completely remove an extension. When removing one, you can typically provide feedback to
alert the developers or the browser maker if there's a problem.

Use Browser Privacy Features
The Internet and the Web are public places, for the most part. Anyone can visit, anyone can set
up a shop, and anyone with the right tools can obtain sensitive data. However, there are many
ways to keep yourself safe online. To make sure you're safe while you browse the Internet, you
just need to spend a little time setting up your safety nets.
Autofill
Browsers can remember your usernames, passwords, addresses, phone numbers, and even
credit card details for different websites. Browsers will remember your credit card number and
expiration date, but to reduce the risk of theft, they won't store the 3 or 4-digit security code on
the back of your card.
It's important to understand that keeping your username and password saved is usually fine for
sites like ones with tips for your favorite video games. However, for websites that have your

banking information or other private data, it's better not to let the browser fill in those details
automatically. Depending on what makes you feel safe, you can let the browser remember
your username, but it's a good idea to type in your password yourself each time, or to use a
password manager.
Incognito and Private Mode
If you don't want your browser to track your activity, you can use a special mode. In Chrome,
it's called "Incognito Mode." In Safari, Firefox, and Edge, it's called "Private Mode." You can find
this option in the browser's main menu. While you use it, the browser won't keep track of the
sites you visit or the searches you make.

services advertised herein are not endorsed by any of them.
Another aspect of private browsing is that the browser doesn't store cookies or temporary files.
Cookies are like little notes a website leaves on your computer to remember you by. In private
mode, it only allows cookies that are directly related to the website you're visiting, and it gets
rid of them once you close the page. Most browsers will let you choose to block third-party
cookies, which come from other sites.
Private mode doesn't hide everything. Websites can still see your IP address. For true
anonymity, you need a virtual private network (VPN)  or a proxy. These services route your
traffic through a secure tunnel, hiding your location from the websites you visit.

Maintain the Browser
Keeping your Internet browser running smoothly is important for a fast and safe online
experience. Here are some ways to maintain your browser:
1. Adjust privacy and security settings: Get to know your browser’s privacy and security
settings.
Adjust them to your comfort level to protect your data and browsing habits.
2. Regularly review permissions: Check the permissions you’ve granted to websites (like
location, camera, microphone) and turn off or revoke any that you don't need anymore.
3. Back up your data: Regularly back up your bookmarks and other important data in case you
need to reinstall your browser or switch to a new device.
4. Update regularly: Always keep your browser updated to the latest version.
Updates often include security patches, new features, and performance improvements.
5. Clear browsing data: Periodically clear your browser's cache, cookies, and history.
This can help speed up your browser and protect your privacy.

Browser Cache
Whenever you go to a website, your computer needs to download all the website's assets
(meaning, its text, images, code, and more) from the Internet. If your Internet is slow, this
can take a bit of time. To speed things up, your browser keeps saves some of these assets,
especially images, on your computer's hard drive.
This stored data is called the browser cache. Getting assets from the cache is much faster
than getting them from the Internet over and over. This means websites you've visited before
load more quickly. This practice of caching websites began when the Internet and webpages
were new, and most people only used dial-up services. Internet speeds were much slower. If a
website could be saved to load faster the next time you visit, that's a big plus for the website
owner. It made browsing that particular site a lot easier.
Browser caches are really useful, but every once in a while they can cause problems. If a file
in the cache gets damaged, or corrupted, it can cause some websites or apps to break down.
This happens because your computer keeps using the corrupted file from the cache instead of
getting a new, working one from the Internet. That's why clearing your cache is one of the first
things to do if your browser is behaving strangely.

If you use your browser to keep track of your passwords for your favorite sites, be careful when
you clean out your cache. Most browsers give you the option to keep your saved passwords
safe when you're clearing everything else. After you clear your cache, you might not see a big
change in how fast your browser works. But you will see the most updated version of websites
and some pages might load a bit quicker. Plus, you might fix some problems with websites not
working right. Clearing your cache also makes things more secure, because the cache can hold
onto private and personal information.
Browser Compatibility
Sometimes, websites don't load correctly. You might refresh the page a few times, but it still
doesn't look right. This could be because the browser you're using isn't compatible with the
website. The easiest fix is to try opening the website in a different browser. It's a good idea to
have more than one browser on your computer for this reason. But why does this happen? It's
because some websites were made for older browsers, not the new ones we use today.
When the World Wide Web became mainstream in the 1990s, companies of all sizes hurried to
create website content. Just like today, the people who made those websites designed them
to work best with the most popular browser. For a long time, the most popular browser was
Microsoft's Internet Explorer.
Browsers have changed a lot over the years, and Internet Explorer isn't even supported
anymore. But some companies haven't updated their websites to be compatible with modern
browsers. There are many reasons for this. Maybe the website still works fine, and the company
doesn't want to spend time and money to change it. It could also be that the company doesn't
know how to update it. Another reason might be that very few people use the website, or they
use it so rarely that it doesn't bother anyone.
This compatibility issue is why, in Windows 10, Internet Explorer is still available as an app. In
Windows 11, you can switch the modern browser Edge to "IE mode," where it works like Internet
Explorer used to.

Citations and References
Giving credit to the work and ideas of others is incredibly important, in both formal writing and
informal settings like on social media.
Formal Citations
In formal academic writing, specific citation styles are required. Citations appear both in the
text and in a compiled list known as a bibliography, reference list, or works cited list. Below are
popular citation styles with examples for a book, a scholarly article from an online journal, and a
news article.

Style Description and Examples
APA APA is the most popular and widely used citation
style in the academic world but is not often
used by students before college studies. This is
because APA was developed by the American
Psychological Association as a citation style for
scientific publications and is used in many fields,
especially in the social sciences.
Note that APA citations emphasize the year of
publication in citations and de-emphasize personal
details about the authors, like the first name. This
reflects the need in scientific circles for current
research and a focus on the content and not the
individual researchers.

Style Description and Examples
MLA MLA is the most familiar citation style for teenage
students, as it is used frequently in the humanities
(like English literature) and is taught widely in
American middle schools and high schools.
Note that MLA citations emphasize the author
and de-emphasize the date by not including it in
citations in the text and not including it in the works
cited entry until the very end. This reflects the
importance of the author or artist in creative and
literary works, as well as the timeless nature of art
and literature.

Style Description and Examples
Chicago notes and bibliography The Chicago style has two variants, but only the
notes and bibliography version is discussed here
since the other style is similar to APA.
The Chicago style uses footnote markers in the text
and either a footnote at the bottom of the page or
a bibliography at the end of a chapter or a paper. It
is popular in historical scholarship and a few other
fields. It is not as common as APA or MLA.
Note that Chicago citations are the least intrusive
to the reading experience, without parenthetical
citations at all.
Informal Citations
Even when not writing formal or academic papers, giving credit to original creators is still
important. Never post someone else's work without naming the creator and, where possible,
providing a link to their content directly.

Type Example

Giving someone credit is not the same as obtaining permission to post someone else's work, so
always get permission from the original creator before posting or reusing someone else's work.
Special Considerations for Social Media
Many social media platforms make it easy to give original creators credit. Many platforms allow
users to repost, which is automatically linked back to the original poster. Other platforms have
integrated media tools, whether for music, memes, or more. Music selections will typically play
with the song title and artist automatically embedded, and the app has negotiated permissions
on behalf of its users. Other platforms use complex algorithms to detect music or video from
other posters and send advertising revenue to the original artist automatically. Most memes are
used under the fair use provisions, meaning they often don't require attribution or permission to
use as long as you're not selling them. Regardless of the platform you use, you should always
try to give credit when using ideas, images, music, or art from others. Plagiarism Plagiarism
is the act of using someone else's content and pretending that you are the original creator.
Plagiarism has serious consequences and should always be avoided. Here are examples of
different types of plagiarism:
• Direct plagiarism - Word-for-word copying of someone else's work without using quotations
or giving credit (attribution)
• Self-plagiarism - A person submitting work with past work of their own mixed in
• Mosaic plagiarism - When a person borrows phrases without using quotations

• Accidental plagiarism - When a person forgets to cite sources, misquotes their source,
or unintentionally paraphrases a source. Accidental plagiarism can be just as serious as
intentional plagiarism.

Social Media
Social media platforms can serve different purposes beyond general social interaction. Some

Bluesky allows users to post short messages, videos, and pictures, which can be viewed by

Risks of Social Media
Social media has some obvious benefits in terms of its ability to connect and bring people
together. However, it also comes with some risks. Consider the following precautions:
• The sense of anonymity provided by the internet can lead some people to post obnoxious or
harmful comments that they would never consider making in person. Avoid being a "troll."
• Because extreme and contentious opinions tend to get the most engagement, social media
algorithms will promote them notwithstanding the damage they do to our society.
• Be wary of strangers who might be misrepresenting themselves and their motives for the
purpose of scamming or misleading other people.
• Because it's extremely difficult to erase online information, be careful what you post.
Creating a professional online presence is particularly important when you're interviewing
for a job. Hiring managers will often investigate the postings of prospective employees.
Protect and carefully monitor your digital identity, which includes your patterns of online
interaction and anything you post about yourself on social media.
• If you have children, closely monitor their social media use. Children are often more trusting
of strangers and more likely to share personal information that would make them vulnerable
to predators.

The internet is a free and open environment - anyone can upload articles, images, and videos.

Determining False Reviews
It is possible you will encounter fake and biased reviews when looking at reviews for local
businesses and restaurants. Here are some general tips on how to avoid falling for fake reviews.
• Look at the Dates
• When looking at reviews, be sure to look at the dates of the review. If a product or
business has two or three bad reviews spread across months and suddenly ten good
reviews in the past week, this is a sign of trying to skew the ratings.
• The opposite is true, too. If a series of bad reviews appear in a short amount of time, the
competition may be trying to steal their customers.
• Look at the Details
• If a simple product "changed my life" or a review seems overly detailed about everything
but the product or service, this is a sign of fake reviews.

• Check the Reviewer
• Many sites utilize other logins such as Facebook or Google. Try to verify that the person
writing the review is not a relative of the owner.
• Also check other reviews by the reviewer. If this person has written two hundred reviews
in the last month, they may not be honest. Verify that the reviewer is reviewing products
they have actually used.
• Check if the Reviewer is Verified
• Many websites will label reviewers as "verified purchase" or "check in" for users
reviewing businesses. These reviews have verified users leaving the reviews.

Content Sharing
A large portion of our time is spent on social media. Most of us are consumers, but content
creators work hard to update their content, build audiences, and promote their brand.
Content Ownership
Although you may not think of yourself as a content creator, if you have produced any type of
content online, you are a content creator. A content creator is anyone who has participated in
uploading a post, video, audio, or picture to a social media platform. As a creator, you need to
understand the concept of content ownership.
Content ownership describes who is responsible and accountable for the created content.
Although they create the content that is being distributed, content creators will not always have
full legal rights to their media. Content creators are responsible for the media they upload,
any messages within the uploaded media, and distributing the media. However, when creators
produce content for a company, they typically sign a contract that gives the company full rights
to any media they create.

Content creators need to read and understand the terms of any agreement with employers or
platform providers.
These creators need to read the terms of service when creating accounts on the different social
media platforms. When we create online accounts and get screens for licensing and terms of
service, it is tempting to select next, agree, and check any boxes without reading. As a creator,
this is very important information. The terms of service will explain the social media platform's
role in hosting and displaying your content. Platforms generally hold the right to remove posts,
suspend accounts, and shut down the platform at will. Many reserve the right to use any
content uploaded to their platform in any way the company desires.
The social media platform manages the system that will display your content. It is important
to note that while creators own their content, most platforms hold the right to remove posts,
suspend accounts, and shut down the platform at will. Examples of former platforms that have
shut down their services include Vine and Google+.
Privacy Implications
As a content creator, you will undoubtedly spend large amounts of time online researching,
creating, and editing your content. Those who make a career out of content creation must be
especially careful not to divulge any personal information in their content. There have been
instances where creators have been hacked, physically tracked down and harassed, and forced
to deal with other problems.
Creators should avoid sharing the personal information of others as well. Privacy rights are
highly protected in online environments. Always ask permission before sharing any content
regarding someone else's personal information.
Content Distribution

Lesson 5A
Keeping Your Data Private
Objectives Covered
6.1 Explain fundamental security concepts and frameworks.
There is always a push and pull when it comes to data collection. When you use the Internet,
you do the best you can to keep your information private. Companies also do the best they can
to improve their bottom line. In order to better understand this relationship, you need to know
how data is collected, how it's used and, most importantly, what makes up your data.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What types of personal data do companies collect when you use the internet?
• How is your personal information used by websites and online services?
• What steps can you take to protect your privacy online?
• Why is it important to understand data collection practices?
Personal Data
Technology brings many wonderful tools that enhance our lives. Our ability to store data in the
cloud is one of the many features that make life convenient. Being able to share bits of our
lives, thoughts, feelings, and experiences online with friends and family is another example of
technology making our lives better. However, this can be risky as well. You never know how
others will take what you share, and certain details about you in the wrong hands can backfire
on you. Take a closer look at what matters when it comes to protecting your personal data
online and the digital footprint you leave behind when using the Internet.
Digital Footprint
Everything you do online can be tracked. Even something as simple as browsing a website
or using a search engine is considered data that can be collected and used. Many times, the
information gathered is sold to third parties who use it for analysis, marketing, or both. But it
can also be gathered and used by those with bad intentions toward you. It's always best to be
careful.
For example, cookies are small text files that allow websites to save information about you and
how you're using their platform. They do it so that the next time you visit the same website, it
can automatically show you your preferences or display saved information like your username,
password, or more.

At the same time, the website owners can also access this information about you and use it for
other purposes like analyzing what content you spent the most time on, what new products they
could develop that would interest you based on how you used their services and so on. They
could also use information saved, such as your email address, to send you advertisements. On
the other hand, if a hacker were to discover this kind of information about you, they could use it
in numerous ways to scam you, pretend to be you, sell your information to others, and more.
Being aware of the type of digital footprint you leave behind, such as the types of websites you
visit and the information you provide in what you type, watch, or click on, is important.
The Importance of Your Data
When you go into a store, the workers there don't know a lot about you. They can see your
clothes or if you're with friends and make some guesses, but they can't tell what you might
want to buy. Sometimes, when you're paying, the cashier might ask if you want to join their
discount club. If you say no thanks, that store can't really find out any more about you.
But when you shop online or even just visit a website, you end up sharing a lot more
about yourself. The websites and apps can collect data that tells them where you are, what
other websites you've been to lately, what kinds of things you've bought, and even your
email address. To the people who run these websites and apps, this information is incredibly
important.
Image by mizinra © 123rf.com.
A Data-based Picture of You
Your personal information is special because it's unique to you. Personal information is one way
to describe anything that can show who you are. Social security numbers, insurance numbers,
and passport numbers are some of the most well-known examples of personally identifiable
information (PII) . There's also information that might not seem important by itself, like your first

name, how old you are, and the city you live in. But when you put these pieces together, people
with bad intentions, or threat actors, can figure out who you are.
People have had this kind of information for a long time, even before the Internet was around.
Now, because of Internet connections and the way we use the online world, it's a lot easier for
threat actors to find this information. It’s more important than ever to keep it all safe.
Safely Managing Data
This personal information can be good for businesses that want to know more about their
customers. Companies can use what they learn about you to sell you things you might like.
When you agree to a company's rules (for example, when you sign up for something online), in
a sense you're giving them permission to use your information, or some of your PII. But you also
expect them to keep your data safe and not share it without your consent. Not every company
or organization meets this expectation, unfortunately.
If someone misuses your personal data, it could cause you a lot of trouble. This is called identity
fraud. It's when someone pretends to be you and might try to take your money or mess up your
credit score. Your credit score is important because it helps you get things like home loans or
credit cards. If your credit score goes down because someone did something they shouldn't,
you could have a hard time with your financial future.
Types of Personal Data
Imagine living in a cabin in the woods without Internet. You could still use a computer or tablet,
and you wouldn't have to worry about keeping your personal information safe. But for everyone
else, there are effective ways to keep our private information safe while still staying connected.
The first step in protecting your personal information is to understand exactly what it is.
Direct PII
Personally identifiable information (PII)  includes data that could reveal a person's identity. This
information can be linked directly to you. It's data that you want to protect, because someone
could use it to impersonate you. Some examples of direct PII include:
• Full name (first name, middle name or names, and last name)
• Home address
• Phone number
• Social Security or National Insurance number
• Email address
• Bank account number
• Passport number
• Driver's license number
• Login credentials (a username and password combination)
• Vehicle identification numbers (VINs)
• Browser history
• Social media posts
• IP addresses
A lot of this information is unique to just one person. For example, your passport and driver's
license are issued only to you and no one else. Other pieces of PII might not be specific to just
one person, such as a home address you might share, but it's still private. For safety reasons
you wouldn't want to just give that information out to anyone.

Indirect PII
Some types of personal information are tied to you in less obvious ways, but they're still
important to keep private. These bits of information are more general, or indirect. Each piece
could be true for lots of people, but when you combine them with more specific details, they
can create a complete picture of who you are. That complete picture could lead to identity
fraud. These are a few examples of indirect PII:
• Your postal code or ZIP code
• Gender
• Height, weight, eye color
• Race
• Last name (if it's a common one where you live)
• Job position and employer
It's important to be cautious about sharing too much of your personal information with people
you don't know. This data can lead threat actors directly to you, and cause you a lot of trouble.
Some people might think they don't have much money to steal, or they're not important or
famous, but that doesn't mean they're not targets for identity fraud. Everyone has direct and
indirect data, and PII has become a new type of asset in the digital world.
How Companies Use Your Data
In places where businesses aim to make as much money as possible, they try to sell more
things. In the digital age these companies can gather information about what you like, based
on where you shop and what you buy online. They use this data to show you ads for products
similar to ones you've bought before, or targeted advertising.
Businesses use targeted advertising to make your shopping experience, or even your scrolling
experience all about what you like and need. They can also make their products and services
better with this information. Those same companies can also turn your data into a product and
sell that information to other businesses. Buying and selling data can help companies improve
their bottom line. How it impacts the rest of us is up for debate.
Collecting Data
Think about the things you've bought lately. How did you first learn about them? Maybe a friend
told you, or perhaps you saw an ad while scrolling through social media. The algorithms behind
all the tech used today watch what is looked at online, what you click on, and what you buy.
From this, they figure out what you might like. Then, they show you new things based on that.
This is what makes online marketing so powerful. It's incredibly precise in the products and
content it serves up to you, and all this makes the company more and more money.
Collecting data helps discover new ideas and opportunities never known about before. Think
about music apps. They look at the songs and playlists you like and then suggest new music
you might enjoy. This same idea is used for other things, like different products and services.
Data Analysis
After collecting your data, companies then take a closer look at it. They're looking for a pattern
that you might fit into so they can offer you something you're likely to purchase. If your personal
data, such as your location, age, and interests, line up with what they're selling, then they have
succeeded. This is called data analytics.
Consider someone named Kai as an example. If Kai has been on social media talking about
visiting an animal shelter and has also been shopping for dog toys recently, the company
looking at this data might connect the dots. They could start showing Kai ads for dog beds or

more posts about dogs on social media. If they also know where Kai lives or how old Kai is, they
can get even more specific. Kai might start seeing ads for dog groomers nearby, or events held
at the local dog park.
All of this happens very quickly and at a very large scale with the help of algorithms and
computer processing. Human analysis isn't necessary anymore when tracking huge amounts of
data.
Big Data
Big data is a term that started when computers began collecting huge amounts of data. As the
amount of information kept growing, organizations found ways to analyze it to make decisions
based on insights and trends. They use this information for current and future products,
marketing, and pricing.
Masking Data
Even though there are laws and rules about privacy that offer some protection, not everyone
likes the idea of their personal details or shopping habits being shared everywhere. There are
many independent search engines whose goal is to keep your information private.
DuckDuckGo, BraveSearch, and Swisscows are just a few of these types of search engines.
They offer consumers a browsing experience that's different because it doesn't keep track of
what you search for online. This means your searches stay private. Some of these organizations
allow users to rank results, include child- and family-friendly default settings, and offer stronger
encryption and better levels of privacy. In addition, they're very open and transparent about
how they keep your information safe and make sure you know what's happening with your data.
Monetizing Data
Companies collect a lot of information all the time, and looking closely at this data can help
them make more money. For instance, if you go to your favorite coffee shop every Saturday
at 9:00am,  and lots of other people do something similar, the shop starts to see patterns in
what their customers do. They can use this information to make your shopping experience even
better. One big reason they collect all this data is for targeted marketing or advertising, which
means they show you ads for things they think you'll like.
Data becomes an asset for a company. They can sort through this data to create and make
money from new products or services. Even though you can't touch data, it's incredibly
valuable.
Data Brokers
There are businesses called data brokers whose whole job is to collect, sort, organize, and then
sell a lot of information, all neatly put together for the people who buy it. Your information might
be included in what they sell. When they handle personal data, they are required to follow laws
and regulations about keeping information private.
When companies sell data, they often put together information from people who like similar
things. Going back to Kai and their new dog. If a company knows what Kai has been searching
for online and has Kai's email, they might put Kai's data together with others who like dogs. A
local dog groomer would be happy to pay for this data because it could help them find new
customers. This type of targeted data helps the dog groomer reach out to the right people—
those who live nearby and love dogs. So, if the dog groomer sends ads to these dog lovers,
they're more likely to get more business than if they just put an ad in the newspaper.

You also need to know that this data has to be legally appropriate to use, or licensed. Licensing
is important because ownership, whether that's the individual or the company, depends on
the rules written into a licensing agreement. This means that sometimes companies must get
permission to share or use the data. You can usually find these details in the fine print of a
Terms of Services agreement.
Data as Income
You can actually make money from your own data. A good way to do this is by filling out
surveys, where you share your thoughts and information with companies. When you complete
a lot of surveys, you get points that you can use to purchase products or services. Also,
some mobile apps will give you discounts or prizes if you agree to share your fitness or health
information with them.
Privacy in Social Media
Since it started in the late 1990s, social media has become a big part of everyday life for many
people. Whether they're catching up with family and friends, helping out a cause they believe
in, or growing their business, over 5 billion people around the world (at the time of writing) are
using social media right now. That huge audience generates a huge amount of personal data.
That personal information can be useful for advertisers, who want to sell you things, and for
threat actors who want to take things from you. It's important to know as much as you can
about how to protect your privacy on social media platforms.
Image © 123rf.com.

Who Owns Data on Social Media?
Understanding who owns your data isn't easy. The social media platform you're on decides the
rules for how your personal data can be used. These sites let you control your privacy settings,
like who can see your profile and what you post, who can tag you, and the kinds of ads you
see. But it's important to know that usually, these social media sites own your data. They often
have the permission to use your personal info in ways they want, which might include selling it
to advertisers and other businesses. This permission is part of the agreement you make when
you use their sites.
Think about the pictures, videos, and posts you share with your friends and family. Once you
put them on the platform, the site owns them. By using the site, you're letting the site owners
use your content to show you ads and to track your activity. These sites also keep track of
simple things like where you are, when you log in, and how long you stay on. All this data
belongs to the site owners.
Safely Using Social Media
Keeping your personal information secure is an important part of protecting your personal
safety, professional reputation, and it can help your mental well-being as well. Here are some
ways you can take control of your personal data:
• Adjust privacy settings: Most social media platforms offer customizable privacy settings
that allow you to control who can see your posts, profile information, and photos. Set your
profiles to private, limit posts visibility to friends or followers you trust, and control how
people can search for you.
• Be mindful of what you share: Avoid sharing sensitive personal information such as your
home address, phone number, date of birth, and financial details. Think twice before posting
content that could be used against you or could reveal too much about your personal life.
• Review and clean up your friends list: Regularly review your friends or followers list and
remove people you no longer wish to share your information with. This helps make sure that
only people you trust have access to your posts and personal information.
• Be cautious of quizzes and games: Many social media quizzes and games require access to
your profile information and can collect personal data. Be careful about participating in these
activities, and always check what permissions they are asking for.
• Check and understand the platform's privacy policy: Review the social media platform's
privacy policy to understand how your data is collected, used, and shared. This can help you
make informed decisions about what information to share and how to adjust your privacy
settings.
• Regularly review your activity: Many social media platforms offer tools to review your
activity, such as posts you're tagged in, apps connected to your account, and login history.
Use these tools to monitor and manage your online presence.
By taking these steps, you can improve your privacy on social media and protect yourself from
potential risks.
Privacy in Communications
The ways you communicate and share information, in both personal and business life, have
expanded dramatically. Texting, messaging, emailing, and file sharing are some of the most
common ways, or channels, of transmitting data. It's important to understand the different
privacy expectations for these channels, so you can effectively manage and protect your
personal information.

Texting (SMS)  Safety
The most immediate way to get in touch with someone, aside from a phone call, is to message
them. Texting uses the short message service (SMS)  protocol over a cell phone network, and
doesn't actually use the Internet at all. Texting is incredibly convenient, but it does not have
very good security. The fact that SMS texts are sent in plain text, with no encryption, is just one
reason.
Because SMS texts operate on cellular or phone connections, there is not the same level of
built-in security as there is in Internet communications. Text messages aren't usually a target for
hackers, but they can be viewed and saved by law enforcement. Some carriers store SMS texts
for just a few days, but others store them for much longer. This long-term storage can make
your private information vulnerable to court orders that release your data, or to large-scale
hackers that target the phone company.
Instant Messaging Safety
Instant messaging apps communicate only over the Internet and can be installed on any device
that can connect to a network. Some examples of instant messaging are Facebook Messenger,
WhatsApp, Telegram, and Snapchat.
Instant messaging can be safer than SMS texting in some cases. Apps that provide end-to-end
encryption are the most secure. End-to-end encryption is a method of secure communication
that prevents third parties from reading your data while it's transferred from one system or
device to another. WhatsApp and Signal are two examples of apps that provide this level of data
safety.
Just as with any service, it's important to understand who owns your messages. Facebook and
its parent company Meta have come under fire for the way it has shared or sold its users' plain-
text messages to other companies. Meta has said that this is part of how they do business,
while privacy advocates disagree.
Email Safety
When you send an email using popular services like Gmail or Outlook, they usually don't
encrypt your email. Securing email in this way would be much too expensive for both you and
for the email service. This is because email came about when the Internet was much newer, and
much smaller. It really wasn't designed to be all that private.
On most email services like Gmail and Outlook, you can choose to make your emails secret by
turning on a special setting called encryption. Each service has its own way of doing this, and
usually, you can only do it for one email at a time. But even with this option email still has some
security concerns. Emails are stored in plain text, meaning they're stored in a way that anyone
can read them. This is the case in your inbox and on the email server too. Hackers, authorities,
and the email service itself can read your emails if they work at it hard enough.
File Sharing Safety
A popular way to send files to a website and get files from it is using the File Transfer Protocol
(FTP) . FTP has been used for a really long time, almost as long as people have been sharing
files with each other over the Internet. Back when the Internet was just starting, people weren't
too worried about who might be peeking at what they were sending.
FTP is easy to use, but it sends files and login information (like your username and password)
in plaintext, a way that anyone could read if they tried. This means someone could easily grab
your file while it's being sent. Another issue with FTP is that some networks let people in to their
storage servers anonymously, without knowing who they are. This allows threat actors to read

or download files without anyone knowing. FTP also doesn't automatically encrypt the files for
safety. The standard now is to use secure versions of this protocol.
Safely Using Internet Communications
It's important to be careful and not trust every email you get, especially if it's from someone you
don't know asking for your personal info or telling you to click on a link or download something.
Always look closely at the email address to make sure it's truly from who it says it's from. If
you're not sure, it's a good idea to reach out to the company or person the email claims to be
from, but use their official contact info to do so. You can also use tools that sort your emails and
security programs that can spot and stop these tricky emails, known as phishing attempts, from
getting to you. Protect yourself and avoid these kinds of behaviors:
• Responding to phishing emails: Don't respond to phishing emails that appear to be from real
sources (such as your bank, a government agency, or a familiar service provider) but are
actually attempts by threat actors to steal your personal information. These emails often ask
you to confirm personal details, click on a link, or open an attachment. Some of these emails
pretend that there's some emergency, or that you owe a lot of money. Always double-check.
• Answering unsolicited requests for information: Don't provide sensitive information in
response to unexpected emails or messages that request personal details, account
numbers, passwords, or other PII. Legitimate organizations typically do not ask for sensitive
information via email.
• Not verifying email sender's identity: Always verify the identity of an email sender
before sharing personal or sensitive information. Cybercriminals can spoof, or copy, email
addresses to make them appear as if they are coming from a trusted source.
• Clicking on suspicious links or attachments: Clicking on links or downloading attachments
from unknown or suspicious emails can lead to malware being installed on your device.
This malware can then be used to capture keystrokes, access files, and steal personal
information stored on your device.
Digital Privacy
When the internet is involved, privacy is never a simple issue. The following table summarizes
the privacy you can and can't expect when you use the internet.

controls that let users decide what information is available to which
people. However, any information you share will likely be made available
to third parties, including advertising firms, government institutions, and
others interested in analyzing big data.
Marketing Metadata By agreeing to a company's Terms of Use, you allow them to extract
metadata from your activity. Metadata, or “information about information,”
can include where and when you use the service, what sites you access,

and caution when using company computers for personal use, even when
allowed by the AUP.
Privacy Regulations
Data privacy rules are made to keep people's private information safe, make sure the financial
system is secure, keep the Internet and online businesses reliable, and to protect national
assets from cybercrime. Whether these rules apply to a company depends on what kind of
business it is, what kind of information it deals with, and where it does its business.
There are 194 countries in the world and the degree of privacy laws varies significantly from
one country to another. More than 65% of countries in the world have enacted legislation
to help protect the privacy of their citizens. Of those who do not have laws in place, many
are drafting legislation to keep track of how companies will handle data collected from their
citizens.
Personal Data and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
Privacy, as it relates to your personal information, means that your details should be kept safe
and treated fairly. Fairness and the right to privacy, as the European Union's General Data
Protection Regulation (GDPR)  describes it, means that no one can take or use European Union
residents' personal data without letting the owner know clearly and getting their approval. The
owner would have to give this consent freely, knowing exactly what their information will be
used for, and it should be explained in easy words, not complicated legal talk. The GDPR
also lets the people it governs change their mind anytime, check what personal information
companies have, fix it if it's wrong, or even ask them to delete it. Failure to comply with GDPR
rules can result in incredibly large fines.
Personal Data in the United States
The United States doesn't have as extensive or as strict a set of laws as the European Union
does. Unfortunately, because of the lack of blanket regulations in the United States, companies
in many states can collect and sell personal data as they see fit, without your knowledge.
California has the CCPA (Calif or nia  Consumer Privacy Act), which is designed to provide the
individual with more control and security over personal information. The CCPA is a law that
helps people living in California know what personal information companies collect about them,
why they collect it, and who they share it with. It lets people in California see their personal
information, ask for it to be deleted, or say no to having it sold. This law affects any company,
no matter where it's located, if it sells things or services to people in California, makes
more than $25 million a year, deals with the personal information of 50,000 or more people,
households, or devices, or gets half or more of its money from selling personal information.

The United States also has the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIP A A) . This
law focuses on the health insurance industry and was enacted in 1996, around the time the
Internet was becoming mainstream. HIPAA was designed to make sure that doctors and health
insurance companies keep your medical records safe and private. HIPAA says these groups
must protect your information and can't share it with anyone without your consent.

Lesson 5B
Using Passwords and Encryption Safely
Objectives Covered
6.3 Explain password best practices.
6.4 Identify common use cases for encryption.
Locks protect physical assets like a car or a home. To protect digital assets such as bank
accounts and insurance numbers, you rely on password protection. In this lesson you will
understand the importance of both passwords and encryption. These two concepts work
together to form the foundation of cybersecurity.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What makes a password strong, and why does password length matter?
• What are common password mistakes that put your accounts at risk?
• How do password managers and multifactor authentication improve security?
• What is encryption, and how does it protect your data?
What Needs a Password?
Computers, phones, websites, apps, network devices all have login credentials. These
credentials are a unique combination of a username (or possibly an email address) and a
password.
A good password is one which you’ve made it difficult for hackers to crack. Strong passwords
include all the following elements:
• Uppercase letters, or capital letters.
• Lowercase letters, or small letters.
• Numbers.
• Symbols, such as #@+_$%^ .
• Length.
Changing Passwords
When you first set up some computer equipment, you will typically find a default username
and password already in the system. Routers, modems, IoT devices and more all have default
usernames and passwords. More often than not, the default is "admin" and "password," and
that's the same for every single model of that device. It's good security practice when setting

up the device to change these credentials. If it's the default, anyone can easily discover what
they are with a quick Internet search.
There are a few devices that come out of the box with no password at all. Manufacturers let
the user decide if they think a password is needed. As a general rule, if a device connects to a
network or if it handles sensitive information, you need to turn on the password feature.
Beyond Passwords
Many accounts offer another layer of protection with the addition of two-factor authentication
(2F A) . In addition to the credentials, you will use your smartphone as the second part to the
login process, with either a specific app on the phone or a text message sent to the phone
number on file. The app will ask to confirm that you are logging into a website or account. There
is typically a time limit for you to provide this confirmation, which might mean that you'll have to
make a second or third attempt to confirm your status. These steps make hacking into accounts
significantly more difficult.
Password Best Practices
Industry best practices and guidelines for password security include these things to avoid:
• Avoid sharing passwords: Don't give your password out to anyone for any reason.
• Avoid reusing passwords: If you use the same password in more than one place, such as for
both your bank app and your streaming service account, your password is more vulnerable
to attack.
• Avoid incrementing passwords: This practice uses a base password and adds a number
every time you need to change your password. For example, “password1” followed by
“password2.”
• Avoid using birthdates, pets' names, and other easily guessed details: Especially if you share
this type of information on social media, you should stay away from using it as part of your
password.
• Avoid using only dictionary words: If your password has a regular or common sequence of
only letters, like "balloon" or "marigold" or "photograph" then they are much easier to break.
• Avoid using common patterns and sequences: Don't use repetitive strings, such as “1234” or
“xoxo” or "abc123.”
Ultimately, the best and most secure password is long, uses several types of characters, and
(most importantly!) is one you can memorize.
Password Management
Think of all the websites you visit that require you to create an account with a password to
access them. Now, think of all the apps you use for school, work and daily life. How many of
those also need you to create an account with a username and password? Most people have
dozens, maybe hundreds, of accounts online. If you're following good security practices and
using different credentials for every single one, you will likely need a system to manage all your
passwords.
Some of the most common ways to manage multiple passwords and usernames include:
• Password managers
• Physical documentation
• Digital records

Password Managers
A password manager is a digital organizer for multiple passwords. They can be free, such
as Google Chrome's Password Manager, or they can be paid services such as Keeper and
Dashlane. You can install these organizers as a browser extension or as an app. Every time you
log into one of your accounts the service will record your username and password combination.
The password manager encrypts the password for that site, or generates one that's complex.
These generated passwords might be readable, meaning you can recognize each character, but
they won't be a words or phrases you recognize. This makes it harder to crack. One example is:
X%3a*!4q_e23#Fl4t9
After that you will only need to remember the master password associated with the password
manager service. Also, If you are using a password manager, best practices would be to change
your personal passwords to one randomly generated by the manager, to increase the security
for your accounts.
Screenshot courtesy of CompTIA, Inc., and LastPass US LP.
Password managers can be safer and more secure than trying to keep track of passwords on
your own. For example, most people are in the habit of using the same password for multiple

accounts. If threat actors uncover that password on one website, all the other accounts are at
risk too. By securing all passwords under one password manager you can increase your digital
privacy. Of course, if these password manager services get hacked, your accounts could be
exposed too.
Physical Documentation
Another choice is to write down passwords in a physical notebook and keep them in a safe
place, such as a locked cabinet or a home safe. This extra layer of security can prevent losing
your password collection to a home robbery. Overall, though, this physical type of password
manager can provide peace of mind for those who are not comfortable leaving their passwords
on the Internet.
Digital Records
Keeping track of passwords in a document on your phone or computer is another option. It's
convenient, but not always the most secure. If you do choose this method it's important to take
precautions.
In the movies a hacker might type away at a computer, trying to guess passwords and gain
access to systems and files. In real life, actual hackers write scripts that automate the process.
These scripts look for keywords, including the word ‘password.’ Don't name your file "My
Passwords," and be sure to set some kind of password control settings on the document itself.
Should I Change My Password?
Is it time to change your password? This depends on several factors:
• Is your password very short?
• Does your password include only letters, and doesn't include any numbers or symbols?
• How much of your sensitive information does the website or app have?
• Are you using the same password on more than one site or app?
• Have you heard about any data breaches at the organizations for which you have a
password?
If you've read through this lesson and have a feeling that you might not have the best passwords,
take a few minutes now to change them.
Account Types
Think about what your password is guarding. For example, if your questionable password is
protecting your favorite files on a 3D printing website, you may not need to change your
password. The saved files, while important to you, are not sensitive information. That company
might sell your email address and make money from that, but in this example you have not given
them any financial details. However, if you did use this same questionable password on other
sites, ones where you do share sensitive data, you should update your passwords.
Data Breaches
Did a website where you have an account get hacked? How can you find out if this happened?
You might hear about it on TV or online, or the company itself might tell you. But there are times
when people don't find out until months later. If you hear about a hack it's important to change
your password right away. Also, check if you used the same password on other websites or
apps. Sometimes, a company will make everyone with an account change their password. If you

notice anything suspicious happening with your account, such as messages you didn't send,
that's another sign you should change your password.
It's very common to hear about a large company getting hacked and a lot of private information
getting stolen. One of the first big breaches happened at Target Stores in 2013, when hackers
took over 40 million credit and debit card numbers. Since then, there have been thousands
more data breaches, and it's likely there will be even more in the future.
Will your personal info get stolen? We hope not, but it's hard to say for sure where hackers will
strike next. The best thing you can do is keep an eye on your credit score and stay updated with
the news. Often, if a company's data gets breached, they'll offer a free year of credit monitoring
to help those affected.
Encryption Basics
Encryption transforms clearly understood writing into ciphertext, which is unreadable.
Encryption protects the data and only lets authorized people, people with the key, to read the
message. The key to decoding the material is an encryption algorithm, or the specific steps to
uncover the hidden meaning.
The Caesar cipher is one of the best known early uses of encryption. The Roman emperor
Julius Caesar scrambled written messages to prevent enemies from learning his military plans.
It was a simple system in which letters were transposed to make a message look like nonsense.
Caesar's generals, the people who were intended to get the message, had the key and could
accurately rearrange the letters. If the message was intercepted, though, enemies would not be
able to figure out his plans.
This encryption method works by shifting each letter in the alphabet a certain number of spaces
to the right or left. In the example below, the cipher is shifting to the right by three letters. A
becomes D, B becomes E, C becomes F, and so forth. To decrypt the message, the reader must
know how many spaces to shift the letters.
For example, to encrypt the plaintext word COMPTIA using the Caesar cipher with a shift of 3
letters to the right, COMPTIA would become FRPSWLD.
Try making your own Caesar cipher.

Modern Encryption
Today's encryption is so complex that not even the biggest and fastest supercomputers can
figure them out. Ironically, computers are the ones that make these unbreakable codes. Without
them, it would take people days just to make one secret message.
The modern process of encrypting data involves taking the raw data, in an easily readable
form, and changing it into a form that prevents unauthorized people from reading or using it.
Computers use complex mathematical algorithms to create the encryption keys. Encryption
keys are commonly 128 bits, or characters long. This is another way of saying 128-bit
encryption, the most common type of encryption today. It is 2 to the 128th power, written as
2128. If you were to write out a string of 128 characters, it would look like this:
1100101010011100101001010110010101011001010101100101010110010101011001010110010101
1001
0101011001010101100101010110010101011001010101100101011001010110010101011001010101
1001
How much time do you think it would take to crack encryption this long?
Encrypting Data
Any information could be encrypted, but not all information needs to be encrypted. Government
and industry rules can mean that bank account information is protected, but the business
address is not. Grandma’s secret recipes probably don’t need to be in cipher, but the top secret
recipe for Coca-Cola will be.
Sometimes a group or company will play it safe and encrypt any information that comes to their
computers. Because information can travel quickly from one place in the world to another with
just a few clicks, it is important to keep sensitive data hidden from hackers and other online
attacks. However, the cost of encrypting every single piece of data all the time can be very
high. Knowing when to encrypt information can save a company lots of money.
By understanding what state their data is in, if data is at rest or in transit, organizations can
figure out the best ways to keep it safe. They can decide what kind of protection each type of
data needs, find any weak spots, and decide where to spend money to keep data secure. This
way of looking at data also helps make sure that organizations follow rules and best practices
for keeping data safe.
Encrypting Data at Rest
Data at rest is when data is sitting still, saved somewhere such as on a computer or in the cloud.
In this state, data is held in some form of persistent storage.
Think of it as information that's not going anywhere, like last year's taxes stored in a database,
archived pictures, or committee meeting notes from 5 years ago. When data is just sitting there,
it is possible to encrypt it. You can do this for the whole device, just the databases, or even just
certain files or folders. You can also set up special permissions, such as a list of who's allowed
to look at or change the data. Another method of encrypting data at rest is the lock screen of
your mobile device.
When you encrypt data at rest, you offer another layer of protection beyond the internal
systems in place. However, encrypting data at rest can be more complicated than with data
in transit, because the encryption keys must be kept secure for a longer period of time.
Another part of storing data is keeping encrypted information for only a short time. When you
log into a website, it will keep a session token or session ID. This special code shows who you

are while you're logged in. But when you log out, the token disappears. The next time you visit
the site, a new token is generated and held in this non-persistent storage.
Encrypting Data in Transit
Data in transit, or data in motion, is when data is moving from one place to another over the
Internet or a network. This can happen when you're sending an email, visiting websites, logging
into your computer remotely, or when files are being moved between online storage spaces.
To keep this data safe while it's moving, there are special security protocols that protect that
traveling data.
One type of protocol is the HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) . This is a very
common way to encrypt information transferred over the Internet, from a browser to a website.
Many online shopping sites and mobile apps use HTTPS, making your credit card information
unreadable when you make a purchase.
A virtual private network (VPN)  is another way of encrypting information as it flows from point
to point across networks. Using a VPN prevents threat actors from reading your data. The VPN
protocol creates a safe tunnel, kind of like a secret passage, to keep everything you do online
private. This means that even when your Internet activity goes through equipment belonging to
Internet service providers, nobody can peek at what you're doing.
