Your Adventure with AI Starts Now!
You don't have to be a tech guru to join the AI revolution. Generative AI tools and models are
opening up exciting possibilities, whether you want to be more productive at work, creative at
home, or just entertained by what AI can help you create.
Elements of an Effective Prompt
You've seen how every AI interaction starts with a prompt and how what you include directly
shapes the results you get back. Now it's time to dig deeper into what makes a prompt truly
effective.
There are four key elements that separate a great prompt from a vague one: goals, personas,
context, and constraints. You will explore each one in detail so you can start crafting prompts
that get you exactly what you need.
Start with the Goal: What Do You Want?
Every effective prompt begins with a goal. Goals are simply the desired results or outcomes you
want to see.
If you don't know what you're aiming for, it's hard for anyone, human or AI, to hit the mark!
Ask Yourself:
• What am I hoping to achieve with this prompt?
• What does "success" look like for me?
Examples:
• If you want to get a recipe, your goal might be "quick and healthy dinner ideas."
• If you're brainstorming, maybe your goal is "creative ways to teach math to kids."
Why It Matters: Stating your goal not only clarifies your own thinking but also helps whoever is
responding to you (friend, student, or chatbot) understand how to help you best. A fuzzy goal
gets fuzzy answers; a clear goal gets you exactly what you need.
Tip: Try writing your goal in one sentence before you start crafting your prompt.
Think About Personas: Who Are You and Who Are They?
A persona is a sort of character role in a story. When you set a persona, you're telling the
responder (whether a person or an AI) to take on a specific role or point of view. Think of it like
casting an actor for a part; different personas deliver different performances.
Questions to Consider:
• Who should be answering my prompt? (A  teacher, scientist, comedian, or maybe a helpful
fr iend?)
• Who are you in the scenario? (A  student, a business leader, a curious p ar ent?)
Examples:

• "Explain gravity like I'm 10 years old." (The  responder is now a friendly science teacher, and
you're a child.)
• "Act as if you're a career coach. What advice would you give for switching professions?"
(No w ,  the persona is a knowledgeable coach.)
Why It Matters: Specifying a persona shapes how the response is written, its tone, depth,
language, and focus. Imagine asking a chef versus a nutritionist about food. Each gives helpful
answers, but from different points of view.
Tip: Try including phrases like "as a historian," "like I'm new to this," or "with examples for kids."
Set the Context: What's the Situation?
Context is the "background story." It's the information about your situation that gives meaning
to your request. Good context helps the other person, or AI, give you answers that actually fit
your needs, not just generic advice.
Think About:
• What's already happened?
• Are there any special circumstances to consider?
• What kind of information does the responder need to know?
Examples:
• "I have only 20 minutes to cook, and I'm missing eggs and milk."
• "We're planning a party for 8-year-olds in winter."
Both prompts give important context: time constraints, missing ingredients, type of audience, or
even the season.
Why It Matters: The more relevant background you provide, the more tailored and helpful the
response will be. Without context, you might get suggestions that don't make sense for you, like
a recipe you can't actually make.
Tip: Imagine you're filling in the blanks: 'I need help with ___ because ___.'
Define Constraints: What Are the Boundaries?
Constraints are the limits or rules you'd like followed. Maybe you only want three options, not
ten. Perhaps the answer should be short, friendly, or use no jargon. Constraints help narrow
things down and keep you from getting overwhelmed.
Ask Yourself:
Are there things I want more of? Less of? What should the response avoid or include? How long
or detailed should it be?
Examples:
• "Summarize the following text in one paragraph."
• "List three dessert ideas with under five ingredients."
Why It Matters: Constraints keep things manageable. They prevent "information overload" and
ensure you get answers you can use right away. Plus, they save time for both you and your
responder.
Tip: Use numbers ("Give me 2 examples"), length ("No more than 100 words"), or style hints
("Make it kid-friendly").

Pulling It All Together
Let's see these four elements: goals, personas, context, constraints, in action. Here are two
versions of a prompt.
Weak Prompt: "I need help with a speech." It's vague. Who's speaking? Who's listening? What's
the topic? How long should it be? Endless possibilities!
Strong Prompt: "I'm an 8th-grade student preparing a 3-minute speech about climate change.
As an experienced teacher, could you help me write an introduction that's persuasive and easy
for my classmates to understand?"
Here's why this prompt works:
• Goal: Write an introduction for a speech.
• Persona: The answer is coming from an experienced teacher.
• Context: Speaker is an 8th-grader; audience is classmates; topic is climate change.
• Constraint: Persuasive, easy to understand, fits a 3-minute speech.
The answer to the strong prompt is almost guaranteed to be more relevant, useful, and on point.
Why Effective Prompts Matter
It might sound simple, even obvious. But mastering prompts can save you hours of back-and-
forth and frustration. The more clearly you lay out your needs, the better advice, ideas, or help
you'll get in return, whether from an AI tool, a friend, or a pro.
So next time you're stuck, remember:
• State your goal
• Set the right persona
• Provide enough context
• Add any constraints

Lesson 6B
Improving AI Output with Better Prompts
Objectives Covered
3.5 Identify common uses of artificial intelligence (AI).
Getting a good answer from AI often takes more than a single try. AI tools are powerful, but
the quality of their output depends heavily on how you communicate with them. Just like
a conversation with another person, the clearer and more specific you are, the better the
response you will get back.
In this lesson, you will learn how to spot common errors in AI outputs, such as hallucinations,
bias, and outdated information. You will also explore how to use context files wisely and how to
craft follow-up prompts that refine and improve AI responses over multiple exchanges.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What types of errors can AI produce, and how can you recognize them?
• What are AI hallucinations, and why do they happen?
• How can adding context files improve an AI tool's responses, and what are the limits?
• What should you include in a follow-up prompt to get a better answer from AI?
• How can you use techniques like clarifying questions, added constraints, and self-critique to
guide an AI conversation?
Types of Errors in AI Outputs
Have you ever asked an AI tool a question and gotten a strange or incorrect answer? If
so, you're not alone! As Artificial Intelligence (AI)  becomes an increasingly important part of
our daily lives, from answering your questions online to supporting business decisions at big
companies, it's essential to know about the types of errors AI can make. That way, you'll
be better equipped to spot issues, use AI responsibly, and get the best out of this powerful
technology.
Factual Errors and Hallucinations
What Are They?
Have you ever noticed an AI answering, "Babe Ruth was president in 1923," or "The Eiffel Tower
is located in Australia"? These are factual errors, or in AI-speak, hallucinations. Hallucinations
happen when AI generates information that sounds real but simply isn't true.

Why Do They Occur?
AI language models, like ChatGPT or other AI tools, work by predicting what words probably
come next in a sentence based on patterns in the data they've seen before. They don't "know"
facts; they're just very good at imitating writing styles and using language.
Sometimes, when there's a data gap or ambiguity in your question, the AI "guesses" and ends
up inventing answers that don't reflect reality.
How to Avoid Factual Errors and Hallucinations
• Double-check: Use AI as a starting point, but always fact-check important information using
reliable sources (like official websites or trusted news outlets).
• Ask for sources: Some AI tools can list their sources, always ask for them if you can.
• Show your work: Ask AI tools to explain how they developed the response, or to show their
work.
• Be specific: Vague or open-ended questions increase the risk of hallucination. Try to ask
precise, detailed questions to guide the AI toward accurate answers.
Bias in AI Outputs
What Is It?
Imagine you ask, "What are the best jobs in tech?" and all the AI's examples are about
programmers or managers. That's bias, when an AI's outputs unfairly reflect a specific group,
position, or idea in a response.
Why Does Bias Occur?
The data used to train AI models often comes from the internet or other large datasets.
Unfortunately, this can include all kinds of human biases. If the data is unbalanced or contains
stereotypes, the AI can learn and even amplify those biases.
How to Avoid or Minimize Bias
• Be aware: Recognize that all AI contains some bias, question outputs, especially those about
people or groups.
• Diversify your queries: Rephrase your request to check how answers change.
• Use trusted tools: Some AI tools take extra steps to reduce bias. Use platforms that are
transparent about their approach and information sources, and keep up with the latest
guidelines.
Generic or "Sloppy" Content
What Is It?
If you ask AI for advice on "how to learn a new skill" and receive something like, "Work hard,
practice often, and believe in yourself", that's generic or slop content. It's the kind of vague,
surface-level response anyone could give.
Why Does It Happen?
AI is rewarded for producing "safe" answers that apply to many situations. If your question
is broad, the model may serve up dull or repetitive content because it doesn't want to make
mistakes.

How to Avoid Generic Content
• Be specific: The more detailed your question or prompt, the more specific the answer.
• Follow up: Don't be afraid to ask clarifying or probing questions (e.g., "Can you give me five
creative ways to learn a language at home?").
• Check depth: If the answer seems too shallow, ask for examples, case studies, or
explanations to go deeper.
Outdated Information
What Is It?
AI models are like time capsules; they only know information up until the point they were
trained. If you ask about a recent event like the latest sports scores or recent scientific
discoveries, you might get answers that are old news.
Why Does It Occur?
AI models are trained on data up to a specific cut-off date. Any events or changes occurring
after that time might not be included. The information used for training AI models primarily helps
the system learn how to generate responses, not necessarily to find verified facts.
How to Handle Outdated Information
• Check the date: Before trusting time-sensitive information, verify the AI's data cut-off.
• Use up-to-date sources: If you need recent news or updates, use official websites, news
services, or AI tools with real-time access.
Ethical Risks
What Are They?
Imagine an AI accidentally sharing personal information or copying text from a copyrighted
book. AI can sometimes produce outputs that raise ethical issues.
Why Does It Happen?
Because AI models use vast amounts of internet data, occasionally they can reproduce content
that's private, sensitive, or protected by copyright laws.
How to Avoid Ethical Risks
• Don't expose personal data: Never feed sensitive private information into any public AI tool.
• Check permissions: Before reusing AI-generated text, verify you're not violating copyright.
• Be cautious with confidential content: Always think about privacy when using AI for work or
school.
Misunderstanding Context
What Is It?
Say you ask, "Describe a jaguar?" Do you mean the animal or the car? Sometimes, AI gets the
context wrong and produces off-track content.
Why Does It Happen?

AI can struggle with ambiguous questions or cultural nuance. If your request could mean two or
more things, the model might "pick" one at random, or guess wrong.
How to Avoid Context Errors
• Clarify your meaning: Add context and detail (e.g., "Can you describe a jaguar animal"
instead of just "jaguar.")
• Review and revise: If the AI misinterprets your request, correct it and ask again.
Bringing It All Together
AI is a tool - powerful, helpful, and improving every day. But it still makes mistakes! Here are a
few simple rules to keep in mind:
• Always double-check important facts.
• Be as specific as possible when asking questions.
• Recognize and watch out for bias or stereotypes.
• Ask follow-up questions for depth and clarity.
• Think critically about every answer, especially when the stakes are high.
Nuances of Adding Context Files
Imagine you're assembling a toolkit for a camping trip. You want to be prepared, so you grab a
flashlight, a pocketknife, some matches, and a first-aid kit, and then you start adding more and
more: canned food, a spare tent, four types of sunscreen, ten pairs of socks, and a portable
espresso machine.
Suddenly, your small backpack is bursting at the seams, and you can barely zip it up. Are you
really better prepared, or just overloaded?
Adding context files to a chatbot works much the same way. The instinct is often to give a
chatbot as much information as possible, hoping it'll become more helpful. But, just like your
backpack, there's only so much the chatbot can "carry" in its digital memory. "More" is not
always "better."
Memory Limits: Chatbots Aren't Elephants
While you might wish your AI tool had a razor-sharp memory, in reality it has its limits. Most
AI tools (and even the most advanced AI models) can only hold so much information at a time.
Just like humans, AI tools do not have infinite memories, and the amount they can remember is
described as the "context window." This is the maximum amount of text the bot can process or
"see" at one time.
The good news is that the size of context windows for AI tools is constantly increasing, but it's
still important to think about how to limit the amount of data that you are asking your AI assistant
to consider.
If your context files are too large or too numerous, they'll likely exceed the context window or
just confuse your AI assistant. Some information might get ignored, or the bot may only pick out
bits and pieces. This means the most relevant answer might be left behind, simply because it
lost out in the information pile.

Quality Over Quantity: Be a Thoughtful Curator
Pretend you're making a photo album for a friend's birthday. You wouldn't include every blurry
picture and random snap from the past year. Instead, you'd pick the images that best capture
your friendship, fun memories, big milestones, inside jokes. The same care should go into
selecting context files for your AI tool.
Here's why:
• Relevance rules: Including everything you can think of, just in case, is a tempting trap. If files
aren't directly related to the kinds of questions users will ask, they'll just clutter up the AI's
memory.
• More can cloud clarity: Just as too many toppings can make a pizza messy, too many
context files can actually confuse your bot. It may start mixing up information, taking longer
to respond, or providing wrong answers.
• Efficient bots are better bots: When you provide your AI tool targeted, relevant context files,
it becomes more accurate and helpful. Less searching through useless data means snappier,
clearer responses for your users.
Strategies for Choosing the Right Files
So, how do you pick the best context files and leave the rest behind? Here are some simple
strategies:
Think Like a User: Put yourself in your user's shoes. What questions will they most likely
have? What information do they truly need? Focus your context files on those core topics. For
example, if your audience is mostly beginners, include simple help guides and basic FAQs. Save
the advanced troubleshooting documents for later (or for a different bot).
Edit: Just because you've already written a 50-page training manual doesn't mean your AI
needs all of it. Distill documents to their most useful parts. Cut out repetition, outdated info, and
anything not directly relevant.
Organize for Efficiency: Break up larger documents into smaller, topic-specific files. For
example, instead of one huge FAQ, consider individual files for each major subject area. This
modular approach makes it easier for your chatbot to "grab" the information it actually needs
without wading through unrelated material.
Limitations to Keep in Mind:
Even with careful planning, there are a few realities you can't escape:
• Incomplete digestion: Most AI tools only absorb a summary or "snippet" of each file. Don't
expect them to know every detail.
• Lost in translation: If you try to stuff too much into the context window, the most important
pieces might never get "seen."
Less Really Can Be More
Here's the good news: Smart selection of content nearly always beats quantity of content.
By focusing on key documents, keeping them updated, and making sure they're as clear and
concise as possible, you're creating a "just right" toolkit for your AI tool.
Checklist for Adding Context Files
Here's a quick-start summary for your next chatbot project:
• Prioritize relevance: Only include files that matter for common needs.
• Remove extra: Condense files to essential information, and avoid repeats.

• Stay under memory limits: Remember your bot's "plate" isn't bottomless!
• Break up big files: Make focused, topic-specific documents.
What to Include in Your Second Prompt
When you use AI tools to help you write, brainstorm, or solve problems, the answer you get
back from your very first question is rarely perfect. And that's totally normal!
Think of your first prompt and the AI's initial response as just the start of the conversation. To
really nail down the answer you want, or improve the usefulness and creativity of what you get
back, your second prompt matters even more.
But what should you say in your follow-up? How can you coach the AI so it gives you exactly
what you're looking for?
Ask Clarifying Questions
Before you do anything else, make sure you thoroughly understand the AI's response.
Sometimes the AI may respond using terms that you don't know or explain something in a
way that may confuse you. The great news is that AI will never judge you or get impatient so
never hesitate to ask clarifying questions or ask for a different explanation.
For example, imagine you asked: "What's a good way to measure the success of a new
product." The AI responds with: "There are a number of metrics that are used to measure
product success including NPS, satisfaction rating, and usage data."
If you're unfamiliar with the term "NPS", don't continue with the discussion of the original topic
until you have followed up with: "Can you explain what NPS is?".
Remember, AI isn't a mind reader: it can't tell what you know and don't know. Always review
responses and ask clarifying questions to clear up anything that you don't understand.
Add Elements: Give More Context, Constraints, or Details
To get really refined answers, add extra information in your second prompt. This could be
background context ("It's for a business audience"), constraints ("Needs to be under 300
words"), or other elements the AI wouldn't know unless you tell it.
Ways to Add Elements:
• Add context: "Could you rewrite this for someone who's new to this topic?"
• Add constraints: "Can you shorten the answer to just three sentences?"
• Set a style or format: "Could you make this sound more formal?" or "Can you change this
into a poem?"
Example
You: Write a story about a dog.
AI: Once upon a time, there was a dog named Max. He loved to play fetch...
You: Can you make the story funny, set in New York City, and include a talking squirrel?
AI: Sure! In the hustle and bustle of New York City, Max the dog was no ordinary pet. He and his
best friend, Sammy the talking squirrel, spent their days dodging taxis and hunting for the best
pizza crust scraps...

Adding those specifics gives the AI new "ingredients" to work with, and now you're well on your
way to the exact story you want.
Ask the AI to Critique or Check Its Own Response
Here's a clever trick: you can ask the AI to look at its answer and find ways to improve it, explain
it, or spot mistakes.
Like this:
• "Could you review your answer and make it clearer?"
• "Is there anything missing in your last response?"
• "Tell me if your answer has any weaknesses or could be more accurate."
This not only brings a fresh perspective but can also improve the overall quality or usefulness of
the response.
Example
You: Explain photosynthesis in simple terms.
AI:  Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make food from sunlight, water, and
carbon dioxide.
You: Read your answer and see if you can make it even simpler and more suitable for a 6-year-
old.
AI:  Sure! Plants make their own food using sunlight. It's like they eat sunlight and water, and turn
it into food to help them grow.
You've just made sure the answer matches your audience, and it's written for a young child to
understand.
Tips for Crafting Great Follow-Up Prompts
• Be specific: The more details you provide, the better the answer.
• Don't be afraid to ask again: If you're not happy yet, tweak your follow-up or give more
context.
• Try combinations: Mix clarifying questions with new constraints ("Can you explain this again,
but use more examples and keep it under 100 words?")
• Invite improvement: Ask the AI to double-check itself or make revisions for clarity, style, or
depth.
In Summary
The magic of using AI isn't just in your first question, it's in what you do next.
Your second prompt is your chance to clarify, add details, and collaborate with the AI to create
something uniquely helpful.
Treat your interaction like a conversation, and don't hesitate to guide, correct, or challenge the
AI to get what you really want.

Using AI Responsibly

AI tools are incredibly useful, but they come with real risks that you need to understand.
Every time you interact with an AI chatbot or assistant, you are sharing data, and the output
you receive may contain bias, copyright issues, or inaccurate information. Knowing how to
recognize these risks is just as important as knowing how to use the tools themselves.
In this lesson, you will explore the rules and risks that come with AI usage, including data
privacy, copyright considerations, and company usage policies. You will also examine how bias
enters AI outputs and learn practical strategies for using AI safely and responsibly in school, at
work, and in your personal life.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What are the main risks of using AI, including data privacy, copyright, and bias?
• How can sharing personal information with AI tools put your privacy at risk?
• What is bias in AI, and where does it come from?

Risks and Rules for AI Usage
AI can be incredibly helpful, but like all technology, it comes with a set of rules and risks you
need to be aware of. Whether you're using AI for work, school, or fun, knowing these risks will
help you use AI wisely and safely.
Break down the most important risks you might face, and what "rules of the road" to follow to
stay out of trouble.
Data Privacy: Protecting Your Personal Information
AI learns from data and sometimes, that data is your information: what you type in prompts and
even your voice or photos that are included in prompts.
Data privacy means keeping that information safe, both for yourself and others.

What's the risk?
• Accidentally sharing sensitive info: You might enter your address, phone number, or
passwords into an AI tool without thinking about where that information goes, and who might
see or use it later.
• Data leaks: Not all AI systems have strong security. If a system gets hacked, the information
you provided could end up in the wrong hands.
• Tracking and profiling: Some AIs use your data to create a profile about you, your
preferences, habits, even your weaknesses, for marketing or other purposes.
Best Practices
• Be cautious about the details you share with AI tools. Don't give away sensitive information
such as passwords, financial information, or confidential work details.
• Check the privacy policy before you use a new AI service. Find out how it collects and uses
your data.
• If you're using AI at work, make sure the tool has been approved and meets company
security standards.
Copyright and Legal Issues: Using Content the Right Way
AI tools can generate text, images, music, and even video. It's amazing, but it's also a
legal minefield. Much of what AIs produce is based on material they've learned from books,
websites, art, and more. Some of this material may be protected by copyright.
What's the risk?
• Using unlicensed material: If you use an AI tool to generate an image or text, and then use
that output for your business, in a presentation, or online, you might be breaching copyright
laws if the content closely imitates someone else's protected work.
• Attribution issues: Sometimes, it's not clear who "owns" work created by AI. If you publish
AI-generated work, you might need to credit both yourself and the tool, depending on usage
policies.
Best Practices
• Always check the terms of use. Some AI tools prohibit commercial use or require you to
credit the tool when using its output.
• If you're generating images or content for business, look for AI tools that guarantee the
content is safe for reuse.
• When in doubt, create your own original content or get proper licenses for source material.
Company Usage Policies: Follow the Rules at Work
Most workplaces now use some form of AI, whether it's a chatbot for customer support, an
analytics tool, or a writing assistant. But not all AI tools are approved for use, and some could
expose your organization to risk.
What's the risk?
• Leaking confidential information: Entering company secrets or private documents into a
third-party AI can compromise security.
• Breaking company rules (even by accident): Your company might have specific policies
about what data you can use in external systems, and violating them can lead to serious
consequences.

• Compliance and audits: Some organizations need to follow laws like HIPAA (in healthcare) or
GDPR (in Europe) about how data is stored and used.
Best Practices
• Always check with your manager or IT department before using a new AI tool at work.
• Use only company-approved tools for handling work data.
• Take security and privacy training seriously, and ask questions if you're not sure.
Biased or Incorrect Information: Don't Believe Everything You See
AI is powerful, but it's not perfect. It learns patterns from the information it's trained on, which
means it sometimes picks up mistakes, stereotypes, or outdated ideas. Even more, AI tools can
make "educated guesses" that sound convincing, but are actually wrong.
What's the risk?
• Spreading misinformation: A chatbot that gives you a wrong answer without you realizing it
isn't accurate.
• Biases in results: If the training data reflects biases, the AI's responses might reflect those
biases too.
• Poor decision-making: Relying too much on AI recommendations for hiring, lending, or
diagnosis, can lead to unfair or even harmful outcomes.
Best Practices
• Always double-check information from an AI, especially for important decisions.
• Use AI as a helpful assistant, not as the final authority.
• If you see something biased or questionable, report it to the service provider or your
company.
Staying Smart with AI
AI is a tool, and like any tool, it works best when you use it thoughtfully. Here are a few simple
rules to follow:
• Be curious, but cautious. Explore what AI can do, but don't overshare or trust it blindly.
• Keep learning. AI is changing fast. Keep up with new rules, tools, and guidance from experts.
• Respect the rules. Whether at work or at home, stick to approved uses and always check the
fine print.
• Speak up. If you see a risk, mistake, or ethical concern, don't be afraid to raise it.
Privacy in Artificial Intelligence (AI)
What is artificial intelligence (AI) ? Think of AI as a machine that can figure out how to solve
problems and create new content mostly on its own. But, to start, people need to give it some
help. For example, technicians might give the machine lots of text so it can learn how words
and sentences work together. This is called machine learning (ML) . The machine reads through
large sets of data, learns the patterns and structures that make up those sets of data, and can
generate new content.
Privacy, Surveillance, and Consent
Previously, you focused on privacy as "don't paste sensitive data into AI." Here, you'll view
privacy and data use as a question of consent and power. AI tools often collect, store, and

analyze prompts, uploads, and interactions. That data can reveal a lot about people, even if they
didn't fully understand or agree to how it would be used.
• On an individual level, someone's story, mental health details, or confidential work could be
fed into an AI tool without their permission. Over time, their data might be used to profile
their habits, preferences, or vulnerabilities.
• At the community level, certain groups may be monitored or profiled more heavily if AI-
powered systems are used for tracking or prediction. Constant data collection can make
people feel watched, changing how they behave or speak.
• At the broader world level, when AI tools normalize extensive tracking and profiling, it
becomes easier to justify more surveillance in everyday life. Legal protections often lag
behind technology, so rights and expectations of privacy can erode before clear rules exist.
Key questions to ask yourself: Did everyone whose data is involved have a real choice about it
being used this way? Am I treating other people's information with the same respect I'd want for
my own information?
Safely Using Artificial Intelligence
You can help keep your personal information and work safer from AI models, and preserve your
privacy. It's important to avoid the following:
• Using AI-powered health apps: People might use health apps that use AI to watch over their
health or figure out if they're sick. They put in private health details without checking to see
if the app keeps their information secure. If the app doesn't protect their data well or shares
information with other companies, their private health details could be shared with others or
used in ways they don't want.
• Participating in online AI experiments: Joining online AI tests or studies that ask for your
personal information without really looking into how your data will be used, kept, or shared
is not ideal. Some AI experiments might use your information to make their systems smarter
without clearly asking for your consent to use your data in every possible way. This could
lead to your private information being shared when you didn't want it to be, and cause
privacy breaches.
• Uploading photos to AI facial recognition services: Putting your own pictures on websites
or apps that use AI to recognize faces, without thinking about how these pictures might
be kept, used, or who might see them, can be risky. These pictures could be used to train
generative AI models without your consent. This could lead to unauthorized surveillance or
identification.
• Interacting with chatbots and virtual assistants: It's not a good idea to share personal details,
business information, or sensitive data when you use AI-powered chatbots and virtual
assistants. At the very least, you should understand how those companies store, process, or
share your information with third parties. If they share your information widely, this can lead
to privacy violations, targeted advertising, or scams.
To avoid these problems, it's important to review and understand the privacy rules of AI
services before you share your personal information. Look for services that keep your data
safe, have clear rules on how they use your data, and let you control who they share your data
with and how you can delete it. Be careful about how much personal information you give out,
even to AI apps that seem harmless, and think about what it means for the future if you add your
private data to AI collections.

Biases in AI
You probably have a favorite song or a favorite snack. That's normal; we all have preferences
and patterns our brains fall into. In many ways, artificial intelligence (AI)  learns from patterns
too. But sometimes, just like us, AI can fall into so-called "biases."
What Is Bias in AI?
Bias in AI happens when a computer program, especially one that uses learning and data to
make decisions, starts to favor certain things over others unfairly. You might think of AI as
neutral or "just numbers." But the truth is, the way AI thinks and learns depends a lot on us, how
we build it, what data we give it, and the choices we make along the way.
The Data It Learns From
At the heart of most AI is a huge treasure chest of data, pictures, words, numbers, and records.
If this data reflects bias in the real world, the AI will learn it, too. For example:
• Historical Bias: If your data comes from a time or place where people were treated unfairly,
the AI may learn those same unfair decisions.
• Selection Bias: If some groups are underrepresented in the data, the AI may perform worse
for those groups.
• Measurement Bias: If some things are measured or labeled in skewed ways, for example,
using test scores as the only measure of "good students", the AI will carry that into its
predictions.
Everyday Example: Think about building a recipe app, but almost all your recipes are from one
type of cuisine. The app's "best recipes" will be biased toward that style, even if there are
delicious options from around the world.
Blind Spots and Missing Information
AI can only learn from what it's given. If some experiences, backgrounds, or situations aren't
included, AI won't learn to recognize them.
Everyday Example: Imagine a voice assistant that doesn't recognize certain accents because
it's never been trained on them. People with those accents will have a harder time using the
technology.
Who Builds the AI
People bring their own viewpoints, experiences, and assumptions into the design. A team that's
diverse is more likely to notice blind spots or ask questions like, "Does this work for everyone?"
If everyone on the team thinks alike or shares the same background, it's easier to miss hidden
biases.
Why Bias in AI Matters
You might wonder, "Is this just a technical problem, or does it really matter?" The answer is, yes,
AI bias can have big effects on real people. Here are a few ways:
• Unfair Decisions: If you're using AI assistants to help you make important decisions, biased
recommendations from AI can lead you to make poor decisions.
• Reinforcing Stereotypes: If AI keeps serving up the same old stories, images, or
recommendations, it can trap people in stereotypes.
AI is being used in more places, such as schools, hospitals, banks, and police departments. If
left unchecked, AI bias can make inequalities worse, not better.

Copyright Considerations
Intellectual Property, Creative Work, and Labor
Copyright and IP aren't only legal topics. There are also ethical questions about respect for
people's time, creativity, and effort. AI systems are trained on huge collections of text, images,
code, and other content, which is often created by humans who weren't individually asked or
credited. When AI-generated content is treated as if it came from nowhere, it can erase the
people whose work helped make it possible.
• On an individual level, artists, writers, musicians, developers, and other creators may see
their style or work imitated without recognition or compensation. People may also be
tempted to present AI-generated work as entirely their own, which raises questions about
honesty and ownership.
• At the community level, creative communities, especially those already underpaid or
marginalized, may feel exploited if their work is used by tools that don't credit them. Open-
source and sharing communities can be strained if contributions are scraped and reused in
ways contributors didn't intend.
• At the broader world level, cheap, AI-generated content can devalue some types of creative
and knowledge work. Tension grows between rapid innovation and fair compensation for the
people whose work helped make AI powerful.
Key question to ask yourself: Am I using AI in a way that respects the people and communities
whose work and ideas made this output possible?
AI is a Great Teacher
Have you ever wished for a teacher who always has the answers, never gets tired of your
questions, and explains things in a way that makes sense just for you? That's what it's like to
use an AI chatbot to learn something new. With just a few clicks, you have access to a world of
knowledge right at your fingertips.
Flexibility
One of the best things about using an AI chatbot as a teacher is how flexible it can be. You can
ask about almost anything, from how photosynthesis works, to how to write a formal email. The
AI listens to your questions and customizes its answers every time. If you don't understand an
explanation or need a different example, just ask! AI can instantly rephrase ideas, give you more
details, or simplify things depending on what you need.
Patience
Another great advantage is that an AI chatbot never gets frustrated or impatient—no question is
too simple or "dumb." Unlike being in a classroom, you never have to feel embarrassed asking
basic questions or admitting you don't understand. The AI is there to help, not to judge. You're
free to move at your own pace, take your time, and dig as deep as you want into any subject.
And if something is still unclear? Go ahead and ask again. Ask for more details, a different
example, or a step-by-step explanation. The AI is infinitely patient and never runs out of energy.
It's like having a teacher who's available anytime you need them—ready to guide you, explain
things as many times as you want, and help you build real understanding on your terms.
So, next time you're curious about something or need a little extra help, don't hesitate to use AI
as your personal teacher.

Understanding Operating Systems

Once all of the computer hardware is connected and turned on, it needs something that
interprets all of the electronic signals into something we can use. An operating system is the
program that communicates between the hardware and other software, and it's what lets us use
computers every day.
In this lesson, you will explore what an operating system does, how it manages hardware
and software, and the different types of operating systems available. You will also learn
about system software such as device drivers, utility software, and firmware, and see how
an operating system starts up through the boot process.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What does an operating system do?
• How does an operating system interact with hardware and applications?
• What are the differences between device drivers, utility software, and firmware?
• What are the main types of operating systems, and how do they differ?
• How does the boot process work when a computer starts up?
• What tools does an operating system provide for managing tasks, applications, and
services?
System Software
Unlike application software, which is designed for the end user, system software controls
computer hardware and coordinates the interaction between hardware and application
software. An operating system is the most common example of system software. Three other
types are utility software, device drivers, and firmware. The table below takes a short look at
each one.

Table 14:  System Software
Term Description
Utility Software Utility software analyzes, configures, and optimizes the computer. Unlike
application software, which benefits the end user directly, utility software
is used to support and maintain the computer system itself. Common
examples include backup software, compression software, disk cleaners,
and antivirus software.
Device Drivers A device driver is software that helps an operating system communicate
with hardware devices, such as printers, video cards, scanners, and
cameras. Users install the driver for their specific device, which translates
signals from the operating system into instructions the hardware can
understand.
Firmware Firmware is preinstalled, read-only software on a device that tells it
how to work. In many ways, it's like a low-level operating system.
Firmware can be found in televisions, remote controls, game consoles,
printers, cameras, music players, and even automobiles. Sometimes,
manufacturers release firmware updates that fix bugs and add new
features.
Operating System Basics
An operating system (OS)  manages computer hardware and software resources, and provides
common services for computer programs. One of its main jobs is to allow the user to interact
with the computer. Learning about operating systems will help you expand your understanding
of technology.
A computer needs both hardware and software to be usable. Without hardware, you can't type,
see the screen, or interact with the computer at all. Without software, the hardware is just a
bunch of metal, plastic, and silicon.
Interfaces
Operating systems provide an interface, or point where a human and a computer interact. You
interact with an OS through either a command line interface (CLI)  or a graphical user interface
(GUI) .
The strengths of a CLI are better control over programs and the whole system, quick navigation,
and using scripts for faster results. A CLI also uses fewer system resources, which is great for
older computers. However, there are challenges too. It's easy to mistype characters, which can
cause mistakes, and you get little feedback as you type. CLIs are harder to learn than GUIs
because you have to remember many commands.
Ease of Use
An operating system creates an environment where different software applications can run. The
application software is the program or group of programs that lets you accomplish different
tasks, like browsing the web, sending emails, or designing graphics. Thanks to the OS, software
developers don't need to worry about writing code to access the hard disk or to send a graphic
to a printer; they can rely on the OS to do these things for them. The OS acts as a go-between
for the hardware and applications, letting developers focus more on improving programs or
building better pieces of hardware.
Because of this convenience, there are only a few operating systems available today, owing to
the fact that it's difficult to make software that works across many different platforms. And over

time, an operating system might change so much that old software doesn't work anymore. For
this reason, changes to an OS have to be done very carefully.
Processing Instructions
One fundamental difference between operating systems is the number of instructions that the
central processing unit (CPU)  can handle. This difference applies to the OS, too.
Computer hardware and software are designed to operate with either 32 bits or 64 bits of
instructions at one time (and that "one time" is as short as one billionth of a second). Operating
systems work similarly, able to manage 32-bit or 64-bit at one time. As systems have advanced,
64-bit has become the standard size for today's CPUs and OSs. One significant benefit of
64-bit systems is the ability to address more memory, where 32-bit systems were limited to
4GB of memory, 64-bit systems jump to 16 exabytes, which is equal to one billion gigabytes
(GB).  This is enough memory for systems in the foreseeable future.
One way to look at the difference is through an analogy. Imagine trucks going down a highway
carrying goods across the country. If there were 32 lanes on this highway and 32 trucks moving
in tandem, each going 65 miles per hour (mph), when they reach their destination, they would
have moved 32 loads. Now imagine the same highway, except this one has 64 lanes and 64
trucks, also going 65 mph. When they reach the same destination, they would have moved
twice as much cargo.
This is how CPUs and operating systems compute, but with 32 or 64 bits of data at one time.
This is why a 64-bit processor at 3GHz is going to be faster than a 32-bit processor also with
3GHz speed.
Types of Operating Systems
Operating systems (OSs)  serve many different functions. Just like software programs that
specialize in certain types of work, operating systems can be customized to specific tasks.
Some OSs are designed to support different hardware types, like mobile devices or servers.
Others target different types of users, matching the resources and expertise available in an
organization. There are too many Operating Systems for this course to describe them all in
detail, but here are some of the overall types of operating systems.
Embedded Operating Systems
An embedded operating system is a low-cost operating system that uses few system resources
and is made for a single purpose. These special computers and their OS are often optimized
for real-time processing. Examples include those used in cars and medical devices. Many
consumer electronics, like video game consoles, also have an embedded OS.
Open-Source Operating Systems
Open-source applies to applications, software programs, and operating systems as well. Open
source means that the code used to create a piece of software is available for anyone to look
at and use. It doesn't always mean that the software is free (though many are), but it does
mean that developers can change how the software works, as long as they make the changes
available to everyone else in turn. The open-source model makes software creation faster and
better managed, considering how many hands a program might pass through. When it comes to
operating systems, Linux and Android are two of the most well-known examples.
Linux is an open-source OS created by Linus Torvalds in the early 1990s. The name "Linux"
comes from combining his name, Linus, with "UNIX," which is the system he was building upon.
Linux followed the same design structure: a multi-user and multitasking environment.

Commercial Operating Systems
A commercial OS is an operating system for which you have to buy a license to install and
use, generally on only one device. Commercial OS code is also kept secret by the developing
company, rather than shared out like open source code. Some products are more flexible than
others about the "one license, one device" rule, but Windows (by far the most popular desktop
operating system in the world) is very specific. You must have purchased a license to install and
use Windows on your machine, and it cannot be shared.
When it comes to personal computers, there are four popular operating systems: Microsoft
Windows, Apple macOS, Linux, and ChromeOS. For smartphones, there are two most common
operating systems: Android and iOS. Apple has also created a special type of iOS for iPads
called iPadOS.
All of these operating systems have different versions or numbers. The different versions have
upgraded features, or different functionality, or allow the system to work better with newer
technology. This is important to understand, because some newer OS versions need more
resources than older computer hardware can provide.

Screenshot courtesy of Microsoft.
Windows
Microsoft does not release major updates to its Windows operating system regularly. For
example, there were almost six years between Windows XP and Windows Vista, but only two
years between Vista and Windows 7. The main reason for the quicker update was that many
people didn't like Vista. After Windows 7, Microsoft released Windows 8, then Windows 10, and
now Windows 11. Each new version of Windows comes with new features and better security.
Many of the behind-the-scenes tools in Windows look and work the same, while the main
desktop always gets a new look with the new version.
Windows may look different from other operating systems, with a unique interface, but they all
function very similarly. Almost any adjustment or tweak you can make in Windows can also be
done on a Mac. For example, if you want to set your favorite photo as the wallpaper, it's easy to
do on both systems. In Windows, you just right-click on the picture and select "Set as desktop
background." If you want to make your mouse pointer bigger or your icons smaller, you can do
that with just a few steps on both systems.
Apple macOS
In comparison to Microsoft, Apple is very consistent with its macOS updates; you can expect
a new version every autumn. For many years, they named their OS versions after big cats,
like Cheetah, Mountain Lion, and Snow Leopard. When they ran out of cat names, they started
naming them after famous places in the western United States, like Sonoma, Ventura, and
Catalina.
One important thing to know is that macOS only works on Apple computers. The other three
operating systems (Windo ws,  Linux, and ChromeOS) can run on many different brands of PCs.
macOS is built on the same general design as UNIX, a mainframe operating system created in
the 1960s. Because Apple designs both the hardware and the software, it can make macOS
very secure and very stable. It's much less likely that you would get a virus on a Mac, though
not impossible.
macOS has always had a dock at the bottom of the screen, with icons for common functions
and your favorite programs. You can easily add or remove items from the dock based on what
you use. The dock can also be moved to the left or right side of the screen, but not to the
top because the macOS menu bar is there. The small Apple logo in the upper left corner is the
closest thing to the Start menu in Windows. In addition to the menu, there are system settings
and icons for running programs in the upper-right corner.

Application Management
Desktop applications are programs designed to help you do specific tasks on a computer,
like browsing the Internet, making a presentation, or doing calculations. Your operating system
plays a role in getting these programs to work properly.
Installing Applications
When you install a program, your OS adds it to a list of all the software on your computer.
In Windows, you can find this list in Settings under "Apps," where you can modify, repair, or
uninstall applications.
Windows also lets you restrict app installations to the Microsoft Store only. This provides extra
security because Microsoft checks and verifies all software on the Store.
Using Applications
Programs are designed to work with certain types of files. For example, photo software
opens .jpg files while Microsoft Word opens .doc file types. But more often than not, more than
one program can open the same type of file.
To use the .jpg file example, you can choose which program you want to use for viewing and
editing your .jpg files in the "Default apps" section under "Apps." Apps are listed alphabetically,
and each one shows the file types it can open. You decide which program you want to use for
each file type.
At the bottom of the list of programs, there's another option called "Choose defaults by file
type." This lets you select the default program to open a specific file extension. It's similar to
choosing by the list of apps but approaches it from the file type side.
Startup Applications
Many programs you install are designed to start automatically when your computer turns on.
If you want to control which apps start automatically, you can use Task Manager. To do this,
right-click on the taskbar and select "Task Manager." Then, go to the "Startup" tab. Here, you
can select all the apps you don't want to start automatically and click "Disable" to confirm.
When you're done, close Task Manager.

As your computer gets older, more apps will add themselves to the startup list, which can cause
your computer to boot up slower and use more resources in the background. It's a good idea
to regularly check which software starts up with your computer and disable any apps you don't
use often. This is like doing spring cleaning for your computer, keeping it running smoothly.

Lesson 7D
Managing Files and Folders
Objectives Covered
3.1 Identify components of an OS.
3.2 Explain the purpose of operating systems.
Almost everything you do on a computer involves files, from the documents you create to
the applications you run. Understanding how files are organized, stored, and managed is
essential for working efficiently with any operating system. Whether you are saving a document,
downloading a photo, or finding a file you worked on last week, you need to know how your
computer keeps track of everything.
In this lesson, you will learn how operating systems use file systems to manage storage, explore
how files are organized into folders and directories, and discover the role of file attributes such
as permissions, encryption, and compression. You will also examine different file types and
extensions, learn to organize, copy, move, and delete files using File Explorer, and understand
how file compression reduces storage and transfer sizes.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• How does an operating system use a file system to organize and manage data on a storage
drive?
• What is the purpose of file and folder attributes such as permissions, encryption, and hidden
status?
• How do file extensions determine which application opens a file, and how can you change
the default?
• How do you organize, copy, move, rename, and delete files using a graphical file manager?
• What is the difference between lossy and lossless compression, and when is each type
used?
Disk Management and Files
The operating system (OS)  takes care of all the background tasks when you work with files,
including sorting files into pre-determined locations. When you download a program, Windows
by default will drop it into the Downloads folder. When you save a picture, Windows will store
it in your Pictures folder. The OS handles everything necessary for this to happen, quickly
and efficiently. Every time you or the computer needs to access a disk or open a file, the File
Explorer utility jumps into action.
File Explorer is the file management interface for Microsoft Windows. Within this interface, you
can create, delete, open, or rename files and folders. The files can be stored on a local disk
(meaning, a storage disk within your computer), a connected drive such as an external hard

drive or flash drive, or on other devices connected through a network server. With Windows,
the traditional location for files on the primary drive is referred to as the C:  Drive.
Screenshot courtesy of Microsoft.
When you select “This PC” within File Explorer you have access to files and folders stored
both locally and externally. This includes any removable devices, such as a flash drive, and any
connected network drives, like a shared server. The New Technology File System (NTFS)  is
Microsoft's utility to organize the files and folders on any storage media.
NTFS abilities go beyond file organization. It can also divide or partition storage drives, giving
you more than a C: drive. Dividing up a storage drive allows you to organize your files to your
liking. For example, you may want to keep your tax documents separate from your project files,
so much so that you put them on separate drives. The NTFS utility can make this happen. After
dividing, the resulting drive letters will follow the alphabetical sequence, from C: to D: to E: and
so on in sequence, as long as no other devices are using one of those letters.
The reason Windows' primary drive defaults to the third letter in the English language, C, is
because A:  & B: were used, in the early days of computers, to designate floppy disk drives.
Apple's macOS and Linux also have disk management utilities for handling files. With Apple,
the user sees the “Finder” application, which works very similar to File Explorer, with one key
difference. The Finder is also one of the primary locations for launching applications. In Linux
systems there are many different utilities to manage files and folders. It is beyond the scope of
this course to name them all.
Maintaining Hard Disk Drives
Mechanical hard disk drives (HDDs)  are, at the time of writing, a very common and
comparatively inexpensive form of storage. Users save files and delete files from their HDD

every day as a normal part of daily operations. When you delete a file, that removal creates a
gap of free space in the drive.
When you save a file, the file management system fills in any available gap with the new file.
However, new files are very rarely ever the same size as the gap. This size imbalance means
that the file management system divides your new file into parts to fit the different gaps. The
system will put one part of the new file into one gap on the drive, and a second part of your file
into a different gap of free space.

As this process takes place over time, files can become fragmented. Newer files may be divided
across many different parts of the disk.

This can really slow down your computer's performance, because those files take much longer
to load than usual. It's not surprising, considering the OS has to find all the file pieces and put
them back together!
To combat this situation, Windows uses the Defragment and Optimize Drives utility to scan
every file on the drive and consolidate them, a process also called defragmentation, or defrag
for short. This moves all the parts of the file together and improves performance.
Working with Files
A drive is used to store files. Folders help organize these files on each drive, making them
easier to find. You can also put folders inside other folders for better organization. You can also
set permissions and control who can access them. This allows you to limit who can see or use
the files inside. Operating system (OS)  files can be kept separate from user files, and regular
users can be prevented from changing them. Each user can have their own storage space that
other users can't access unless the folder is shared.
An operating system organizes storage using a hierarchical file system. The top level is the root
folder, which in Windows is labeled C:\ . Subfolders branch out from the root, and their locations
are described using paths separated by backslashes, such as C:\ Windo ws \Syst em32\ .
Directories are very well-suited to organizing data on different levels of hierarchies, as well as
managing complex metadata. Metadata are the characteristics and properties of files stored on
a computer. Think of a file like a package that has been shipped to you. When it arrives, that
package has a lot of information on it. The name and address of the person who sent it to you,
your name and address, some barcode labels, and perhaps a sticker saying "Fragile" are all on
the outside of the package. These labels tell us important information about the package and its
contents. This is what metadata does for a file.

The file system supports a variety of attributes and metadata, including the following
characteristics.
Compression
The file system can reduce the amount of disk space that files take up. To do this, the file
system can apply an algorithm, or a set of instructions, to the file to efficiently store the data
without losing any information. It's important to note that compression can only apply to files
that are not already compressed. You can't just keep making files smaller and smaller over
and over. For example, a file type such as JPEG is already quite compressed. Applying the
compression algorithm won't actually change that file at all.
Many, many versions ago, the Microsoft operating system added file compression that could be
applied to an entire hard drive. This was added as a feature because at the time, storage was
expensive and it didn’t take a lot of programs and data to fill up a drive. As storage capacity
began to outstrip the average user's needs, this compression became unnecessary. However,
take a look at Windows root C: drive properties and you will see there is still a box which can be
checked for the legacy purposes: “compress this drive to save disk space”.
Encryption
The file system can automatically encrypt data in a file when you save it. This means the file
can only be opened if you have the encryption key. This keeps the data safe even if the disk is
stolen and put into another computer.
Permissions
The file system keeps an Access Control List (A CL)  for each file or folder. The ACL records
which user accounts are allowed to read, write, or control an object. Some of the permissions
include:

• Full Control: Users can do anything with the files, like read, write, change, or delete files and
folders.
• Modify: Users can read and write files and delete folders.
• Read and Execute: Users can view files and run programs.
• List File Contents: Users can see what files are in folders.
• Read Only: Users can only view the files and folders.
• Write: Users can add files or subfolders.
There are also advanced options and special permissions. An IT department will set
permissions at the folder level, and all files in the folder will inherit the same permissions.
Journaling
The file system tracks changes or intended changes in a log. If there's a sudden power loss and
a write operation is interrupted, the journal can be used to recover the data or at least restore
the file system to a good working state.
Limitations
File systems can have limits on their maximum capacity and the size of individual files. This is
useful if you want to allocate a certain amount of storage to employees so they don’t store all
their personal videos on the company server.
Hidden Files
Files and folders with this attribute do not appear in directory listings unless the option to view
hidden files and folders is enabled.
Naming Rules
Very old file systems limited file names to eight characters plus a three-character extension.
Modern file systems support longer file names (usually up to 255 characters) and complete
directory paths. They also allow the use of Unicode (a text character standard for computers) in
the name and can distinguish between uppercase and lowercase letters. File systems also have
reserved characters that cannot be used in a file name. These include: ? * / \ < > : “ and|
Types of Files
Files are containers for the data that's used and modified by the operating system and
applications. A file can be part of the operating system itself, an outside piece of software,
or a specific file you have on your device, like a picture. Common types of files include:
• Multimedia files: These include pictures, videos, and audio files.
• Document or text files: These range from plain text documents to Adobe PDFs to Google
Docs, which can be saved online or locally.
• Data files: These include spreadsheets and databases.
• Executable files: These are software programs that run on your computer, like a browser or
your favorite game.
• Archived files: macOS uses Disk Image (.dmg) files to distribute software, but for archiving
purposes, it commonly uses standard formats like .zip. Like Linux, macOS can also use
archive formats such as .tar.gz.
• Internet files: These include web pages in .html format, as well as cache and cookies.

You can use a period as part of the main portion of the filename, too. It's the last period that
delimits the file extension.
Many file types work across Windows, Apple, and Linux platforms. However, some are specific
to each operating system and are handled differently. Executable files are the best examples:
• Microsoft Windows uses .exe files (executables).
• Apple macOS uses .app files (applications).
• Linux uses .elf files, which stand for Executable and Linkable Format.
Files follow a similar naming pattern to folders, but the last part of a filename represents the
extension. On Windows, every file will have an extension that determines the default application
it will be opened with. Essentially, the extension describes what type of file it is and how the
operating system should use it, in other words, which application to associate it with. Operating
systems do not add extensions to folder names.
You'll be able to tell what the extension is easily because it's separated from the rest of the
filename with a period. Traditionally, extensions were three characters long, but today they can
be longer, like four or five characters. For example, MyDocument.docx has a four-character
extension. Most extensions use letters, but some have numbers, like .mp3 for music. By default,
extensions aren't visible to the user, but this can be changed in the file menu by choosing to
show hidden items.
File extensions can change without warning. Sometimes an update changes the extension, and
sometimes a program takes over an extension that didn't belong to it before. When you click
on a file, and it doesn’t open with the right program or doesn’t open at all, Windows will try to
help by saying, “Look for an app in the Microsoft Store.” Sometimes this fixes the problem, but
usually, you will need to go into Apps from Settings and set the default program back to what
works best.
Managing Files
Files store information, and they need to be labeled so the system knows what is being stored
where. For example, if you make a presentation with a few slides and try to save it, you'll be
asked to give it a name first before you can proceed. Once it's named and saved, it's there
permanently on the computer for you to access. If you were to close the presentation program
and then double-click on that file, your computer would know to open the program and the file
together.
Every file on your system has two things that make it unique: its filename and its path. The
filename is just the name you choose to give the file. The path shows all the folders that the
file is contained in, starting from the main drive down to the current folder. For example, a file
named "Project paper" might have the path: "C:\ Users \ User1\Document s \Pr oject  paper.docx."
You can have two files with the same name, but they can't be in the same folder.
Organizing Files
To keep data organized, files can be sorted into different folders. A Windows system comes
with several default folders already created, such as Windows (for OS files), Program Files
(for installed applications), and Users (for your personal documents, pictures, and more). You'll
spend most of your time working in the Users folder and its subfolders.
When you work on a computer for the first time, you log in with your credentials (your username
and password), and you have an environment set up just for you. This is called the user's
profile. Inside the user's profile are several folders to help organize information. You can easily
start to create new folders by right-clicking inside the folder where you want the new one to
be. Then you'd select "New" > "Folder". You can also click the "New Folder" button on the

top ribbon bar. After that, Windows lets you give the folder a name. To keep things even more
organized, you can create folders inside other folders. For example, "Documents" is meant to
hold your documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and more. You could make a new folder
called "Spreadsheets" inside of "Documents" and put all your spreadsheets in there, making it
easy to find your work.
Copy and Move Files
You can and should organize your files and folders in the way that works best for you. Using the
Home tab in the File Explorer ribbon bar, you can copy, paste, rename, move/cut, and do many
other things with your files and folders. When you move or cut a file or folder, it will be copied
to the new location, and the original will be deleted. On macOS, there's no 'Cut' command.
Instead, files are copied to the new location, and you have to go back and delete the original file
if you want to move it over completely.
There is a setting in Windows to change the "double-click" to launch a file or program to a single
click. When set in File Explorer Options, hovering over an item with the mouse acts as the selection,
and the single click opens the item. This is a handy way to save mouse clicks in day-to-day
computing.
Renaming Files
If you need to, you can rename files and folders. Besides using the ribbon bar in Windows,
you can also right-click on the file or folder and choose "Rename" from the pop-up menu that
appears. Another way is to press "F2" on your keyboard. With all of these options, the file or
folder name will be highlighted, and you can type in the new name that you want it to be called.
Deleting Files
There may be times when you'll need to remove a file or folder from your computer. When you
delete something in Windows, it's not immediately gone. Instead, it goes to the Recycle Bin in
case you want to get it back. On macOS, deleted files go to the "Trash," which works like the
Windows Recycle Bin. While the name "Recycle Bin" sounds better for the environment, it's the
same thing: it's the final holding spot for files and folders before you decide to permanently
delete them.
In the Recycle Bin, you have two options: to restore something, click on it, and select "Restore
the selected items." To permanently delete everything, click "Empty Recycle Bin." On macOS,
you can delete apps as well, which go to the Trash. Remember, even though deleted files are
out of your everyday view, they still take up space on your computer until you permanently
remove them from the system.
Windows File Management Facts
A file's extension determines which application will be used by default to open it. Some
examples include the following:
• .txt - a text file, which opens with Notepad by default
• .pdf - an Adobe Acrobat Reader file
• .jpg, .bmp, or .png - an image file, which opens with the Photos app by default
• .zip - a compressed file that contains other files, which opens with File Explorer by default
• .wav, .mp3, .wma, or .m4a - an audio file, which opens with Microsoft's Groove Music app
by default in Windows 10 and Media Player in Windows 11
• .doc or .docx - a Microsoft Word document
• .xls or .xlsx - a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet file
• .ppt or .pptx - a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation file

• .accdb - a Microsoft Access database file
In Windows, file extensions are hidden by default. If you access a file's properties, you can
view its extension as well as customize which application that particular file type opens with by
default. To do this, complete the following steps:
1. Access the file's properties.
2. To the right of Opens with, select Change .
3. Choose the desired default application and then select OK > OK .
File Compression Facts
Compression reduces the size of files, making them easier to store and faster to transfer over
a network. There are different types of compression, each with trade-offs between file size and
data quality.
Lossless Compression
A compression algorithm that doesn't affect the original data. In other words, the uncompressed
file will be exactly the same as the file before compression, bit for bit. Common lossless file
types include:
• GIF
• PNG
• PDF
• ZIP
Lossy Compression
A compression algorithm that slightly alters the data to make it easier to store. Lossy
compression takes advantage of the limitations of human sight and hearing, and is usually used
for images, videos, and audio files. Common lossy file types include:
• JPG
• MP3
• MP4
Run-Length Encoding
A common lossless compression algorithm. Instead of storing each bit of a file, it stores how
many of each bit appear in a sequence. For example, instead of storing thirty zeros in a row,
it would just store the number thirty, followed by a zero. It can also store repeated patterns in
data, such as identical pixels in an image.
Compression Artifact
Sometimes, when a video is compressed to a very small size using lossy compression, patches
of pixels appear that have less visible detail than the rest of the image. These are called
compression artifacts. They often appear in educational videos (such as the ones in this course)
because file size is prioritized over video sharpness, which allows the videos to stream well on
suboptimal hardware.

Lesson 7E
Configuring Windows Settings and Accounts
Objectives Covered
3.1 Identify components of an OS.
3.2 Explain the purpose of operating systems.
6.1 Explain fundamental security concepts and frameworks.
6.3 Explain password best practices.
The Settings App is where you configure nearly every aspect of Windows. From adjusting
display resolution and scaling to personalizing the desktop background, lock screen, and
taskbar, the Settings App gives you centralized control over how your computer looks
and performs. It also includes options for managing devices, apps, power consumption,
accessibility, and privacy.
Windows also uses user accounts to control who can access the system and what they are
allowed to do. Understanding the difference between standard and administrator accounts,
how to create and manage accounts, and how to set strong passwords are essential skills for
keeping a system secure.

As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:

• How do display settings like resolution, scale, and orientation affect usability?
• What is the difference between a standard user account and an administrator account?
• What are the characteristics of a strong password?
• How do you personalize the desktop background, lock screen, and taskbar?
Windows Settings
The Settings App is the central place in Windows to customize how the computer looks and
functions. Within the Settings App are several options you can use to configure the system.

Windows User Account
