Lesson 7F
Maintaining Windows
Objectives Covered
2.4 Given a scenario, install and configure common peripheral devices.
3.1 Identify components of an OS.
3.2 Explain the purpose of operating systems.
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
Once you are comfortable navigating Windows and managing files, it is time to learn how to
keep the system running smoothly. Windows relies on background services and processes to
function properly, and tools like Task Manager and Task Scheduler give you visibility and control
over what is happening behind the scenes.
This lesson also covers device drivers and system updates. Device drivers are the software
that allows your operating system to communicate with hardware like printers, keyboards, and
video cards. Windows Update automatically downloads security patches and bug fixes, but
understanding how to manage updates and install drivers yourself is essential for maintaining a
reliable system.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• How can you use Task Manager to monitor performance and manage running processes?
• What are system services and how can Task Scheduler automate tasks?
• What is Plug-and-Play and how does it help when connecting new devices?
• When would you need to manually install a device driver, and where can you find one?
• How do you use Device Manager to check on or update device drivers?
• What options does Windows Update provide for managing and pausing updates?
• Why is patch management important, and what is a zero-day attack?
Task Management
All Microsoft Windows systems include a Task Manager, which is a program that allows you to
monitor how your computer is performing at any given moment. It displays information about
the software, processes, and services running on your computer. With Task Manager, you can
find out things like how much computing power each task is using or which users are logged
onto the computer.
Using Task Manager
You won't find Task Manager listed in the Start menu, but there are several ways to access it.
You can press Control + Alt + Delete at the same time and choose Task Manager from the

menu that appears. You can also type task manager in the Windows search bar, or right-click
any empty area of the taskbar and select "Task Manager" from the pop-up menu.
Task Manager is especially useful for handling programs that aren't responding. You can quickly
end programs or processes to stop them from running.
Each process uses its own memory and system resources. Sometimes a program freezes or too
many programs are running, which can slow down your computer. By closing certain programs
in Task Manager, you can free up memory so other programs and the operating system run
better.
Screenshot courtesy of Microsoft.
Task Manager shows important details like which programs are using the most central
processing unit (CPU) , memory, disk, and network resources. High resource usage from any
single program can slow down your computer.
The "Processes" tab lists all running programs and background tasks. You can highlight a
program and click "End Task" to stop it immediately. By sorting by memory or CPU usage, you
can quickly identify which programs are consuming the most resources and end them to free up
performance.
Network Performance
The "Performance" tab shows real-time graphs and statistics for CPU, memory, disk, network,
and GPU usage. This is useful for diagnosing slowdowns and identifying hardware bottlenecks.
System Services
A service is a program on Windows that runs in the background without you needing to interact
with it at all. These services help with different tasks on your computer, like signing in, browsing
the Internet, or searching for files. Both Windows and other programs, like antivirus or backup
software, can install services. Programs like Adobe Acrobat take advantage of services to
optimize performance.

If you want to see which services are running, type "services" in the Windows start menu. From
the Windows tool that pops up, you start or stop services and change their settings, like forcing
them to start automatically when you turn on your computer.
Screenshot courtesy of Microsoft.
Knowing which services are running at any given time is important because they support
important functions like printing, Windows updates, and Bluetooth, among others. When your
computer boots up, many of these start automatically without your direction. But you have
ultimate control over what they do on Windows, and you can pause, resume, or restart them
when you want.
Task Scheduler
As you're working with services and tasks, you might need to set up when certain ones should
run. Task Scheduler is a Windows tool that automatically starts an application or runs a script
based on events.
Task Scheduler sets tasks to run at specific times. A task can be a simple application or a
batch file (a file with commands). They can be set to run once at a future date or on a regular
basis, maybe daily or weekly. You can access Task Scheduler through its own console or in the
Computer Management console. The Computer Management Console is a tool that helps you
manage various parts of Windows in one place.

Screenshot courtesy of Microsoft.
Tasks that are often scheduled to run regularly include backups, malware scans, and system
updates. Triggers are the conditions that start these tasks, like a specific day, time, login, or
other system events. You can set up Task Scheduler to run a program, send an email, or show a
message when the trigger occurs. It's a powerful tool that's often underutilized.
If you have the free version of an anti-spyware or anti-malware program, one of the limits is not
being able to schedule scans. You can set up Task Scheduler to run a weekly scan on the program.
Now you've got the free version and a perk of the paid version!
Plug-and-Play Installation
When you connect a device to a Windows PC, it often uses Microsoft's Plug-and-Play (PnP)
technology. This means Windows detects the new device and tries to install a driver for it. The
system checks the hardware ID and searches its database of drivers to find the right one. The
goal is to make it easy for users, especially those who may not have much technical knowledge,
to set up the hardware right away without any problems. The driver helps the device work
smoothly.
To check the status of your devices, open the Windows Device Manager. The alphabetical list
will show you which devices didn't install with Plug-and-Play and need attention.
Devices connected via USB are hot-swappable, meaning you can add or remove them while the
system is running. If a device isn't hot-swappable, you need to restart the system when adding
it or shut it down before removing it. Another benefit of Plug-and-Play is that Windows manages
resources like Input/Output addresses, interrupt request numbers, and memory access to help
prevent conflicts.

Driver Installation
Windows includes an inventory of generic drivers that will sometimes provide full functionality
for a piece of hardware, and other times will provide only basic functionality for devices. For
example, with a standard keyboard or mouse, the basic functionality is normally all that is
needed. However, your unique situation may require full functionality, either because of a work
or school policy, or because you want to optimize a piece of equipment like a gaming mouse.
In addition to the repository of default drivers, Windows will also try to locate a driver through
Windows Update. If no driver is available for the hardware, you will need to obtain one from the
device manufacturer.
It's important to know the exact make and model of the hardware, and the correct version
of Windows. For example, Windows 10 and Windows 11 have different drivers. Also, before
Windows 11, older versions of Windows came in 32-bit and 64-bit versions. It's important to
install a driver that matches your computer's 32-bit or 64-bit version, or it won't work.
In addition to the manufacturer's website, there are many other websites that offer free driver
downloads. Be careful with these sites because some might include corrupt software or
malware with their download. To help avoid problems from bad drivers, Microsoft has a rule that
all drivers must be digitally signed to prove they are safe. This process goes through Microsoft
Windows, and once the driver is checked and verified, it can be installed on your computer.
Drivers and Devices
For hardware to work properly, it needs software called a driver that tells the operating system
how to use it. On Windows, if the exact right driver isn't installed, the hardware isn't going to
work. Over the years, Windows has gotten better at finding the right drivers for the installed

hardware on its own. But there may still be times that you'll need to find the correct driver and
install it manually yourself.
To view device drivers, open Device Manager in Windows. From there, you will see an
alphabetical list of every piece of hardware connected to the computer. If there is a problem
with any of the drivers, Windows will let you know with a symbol to the left of the device name.
There are a few symbols: a yellow exclamation point, a red cross or blue question mark, or a
black downward arrow.
Screenshot courtesy of Microsoft.

Each icon is a variant on the idea that the driver may be missing or corrupt. You can update,
disable, uninstall, or check for hardware updates to these drivers. You will need to use these
options when a device is acting up or not acting correctly.
Windows usually downloads and installs the latest drivers for your device through Windows
Update. But some devices don't update automatically. In those cases, you might need to update
the driver yourself. When you choose to update the driver, a new window will pop up with two
choices: "Search automatically for drivers" or "Browse my computer for drivers."
The automatic search is useful when drivers can be downloaded through Windows Update.
Companies that make hardware like video cards, sound cards, and Bluetooth devices offer
driver packages on their websites for users to download and install. Updating drivers can fix
problems with a device and sometimes make it work better.
Updating device drivers is often listed as a way to fix problems with hardware. However, the
success rate of these tweaks is not as high as it would appear. It doesn't hurt to see if an update
will fix a problem, but don't get your hopes up.
Windows Update
Windows includes a feature called Windows Update to keep your operating system up to date.
The default setting for Windows Update is to automatically identify, download, and install
operating system updates for you. It is possible to manually force Windows to check for
updates by selecting the Check for updates button. These updates can occur in two different
methods:
• Some updates will be installed in the background while the system is running.
• Other updates require the system to be shut down and restarted for them to be applied. By
default, updates will be automatically installed during a restart when you are not using the
system. Windows will display a prompt and allow you to reschedule the restart.

Image 1:  Configuring Windows Update in the Settings App
To access Windows Update select the Windows Start icon and then Settings. From the Settings
App, select Windows Update.
Pause updates
While it is not recommended to turn off updates, there are times when you need, or want,
to prevent updates. The Pause updates option allows you to stop updates for one to three
weeks. However, there is a maximum of 35 days. Once the time expires or you select to resume
updates, Windows will download and install the latest required updates. Pause will often be
disabled until the updates are installed.
A few examples of when you would pause updates include:
• It is common for professionals who are traveling on business, giving presentations, and
using limited network connections to disable updates.
• If there is an error that occurs during an update, you may need to pause updates to continue
working until the issue can be resolved.
• When using slow or secure network connections, allowing Windows to constantly check for
and download updates can affect performance and could be restricted.

Update history
Reviewing a list of installed updates can help you identify whether you are protected by critical
security updates. Selecting Update history will list of all installed updates.
Advanced options
Advanced options allow you to take control of when the updates are downloaded and installed
instead of relying on the default settings. Some key settings are:
• Recieve update for other Microsoft products: enable this function to have updates for
Microsoft Office or other Microsoft applications included in the list of available patches.
• Get me up to date: this option instructs Windows to restart, even if it is during regular hours,
if an update requires it.
• Download updates over metered connections: enabling this option will instruct Windows to
check and install updates on metered connections. This could cost you more depending on
the connection plan.
• Notify me when a restart is required to finish updating: determines if you receive a
notification when the system needs to restart due to an update.
• Active hours: by default, Windows will not restart during the hours of 8:00  AM to 5:00  PM.
Select this option if you need to adjust the time range.
• Optional updates: enable this option to include notifications of updated drivers or features.
Windows Update does not provide maintenance for non-Microsoft applications installed on the
system. To update these applications, you must go the vendor's website and manually check for
updates, or refer to the documentation to enable automatic updates.
Software Patching and Updates
Software is always changing, and operating systems (OS)  are constantly being improved and
expanded. Productivity software gets both minor and major updates in the background. Many of
these updates are meant to make programs work better and to improve security, and are usually
free of charge. They can also add new features and make the software work better with new
hardware. As IT professionals, it's important to always keep operating systems and software up
to date with software patches.
Patch Management
Patch management is an important maintenance task to make sure computers run reliably and
securely. It involves several steps, like checking for software updates and testing them before
deploying them to all the company's computers. IT professionals test the patches to make sure
the update doesn't cause problems with the existing system. If it works well, the update is then
put on all computers on the network and checked again. Finally, the IT team documents or
writes down the changes they made.

Screenshot courtesy of Amazon.
Microsoft Patches
Microsoft products follow a support lifecycle policy. Windows versions get about 10 years of
mainstream support. During this time, they receive all kinds of updates, including new features,
security fixes, and bug fixes. After this period, the OS enters the extended support phase,
where Microsoft still provides free security updates to keep systems safe, but any non-security
updates are not available without an additional paid support agreement. Once an OS reaches
the end of its life, Microsoft will no longer support it at all. The OS will still work, but Microsoft
won't fix bugs or provide patches for security issues.
In 2003, Microsoft established a regular cadence of updates on the second Tuesday of the
month. While there were updates at other times, the second Tuesday of every month was
known as "patch Tuesday" to allow administrators a dedicated day to push out updates to their
systems. In 2015, they stopped this practice to help reduce the chances of cyber attacks. One
common attack is a zero-day attack. This type of attack takes advantage of a vulnerability, in
either software or hardware, that the vendor didn't know about before. They are called zero-day
because the exposed system has been known for zero days by the vendor. This means that the
vendor hasn’t had the opportunity to provide a patch to fix the problem.
Updating Non-Microsoft Software
Software from companies other than Microsoft also gets updated from time to time, but not as
often. When these updates are available, you might see a prompt asking if you want to update

when you open the software. Technicians can also manually check the publishers' websites for
any new versions of the software.

Lesson 7H
Backing Up Files and Storage
Objectives Covered
2.3 Compare and contrast storage types.
5.1 Explain the value of data and information.
5.4 Explain basic data backup concepts.
Nearly everyone who has worked with a computer has a story about losing their data, usually
at the worst possible time. Hardware failures, software problems, cyber attacks, and accidental
deletions can all cause data loss. To avoid costly and uncertain recovery efforts, it's important
to understand both how data is stored and how to protect it through backups.
In this lesson, you will explore the different types of local and network storage, learn which data
to prioritize when creating backups, compare system and cloud backup strategies, and discover
how to restore deleted files and test your backups.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What types of local storage do computers use, and how do SSDs, HDDs, optical drives, and
flash drives compare?
• What are Storage Area Networks (SANs),  Network Attached Storage (NAS),  and file servers,
and how do organizations use them?
• What data should you prioritize when creating backups, and why are personal files the most
important?
• What is a system backup, and how do incremental backups help keep a system recoverable?
• How does cloud storage provide backup solutions, and what are its limitations?
• How can you restore deleted files, and why is it important to regularly test your backups?
Computer Storage
Computers need long-term storage to keep information when they are turned off (called
persistent storage). Without it, they would lose data every time they shut down. The most
common types of computer storage are also called local storage.
Connections and Transfers
Before we talk about different types of storage drives, we need to describe how data moves
between the central processing unit (CPU)  and memory.
Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (SA T A)  is the interface and communications standard
for transferring data from the motherboard to a storage drive and back again. The drive could
be a mechanical hard drive, a 2.5-inch SSD, or an optical drive. The SATA standard includes

a specific connection type, along with a cable and identical connectors on a motherboard and
drive.
SATA is the connector used in servers, desktops, and laptop computers. SATA supports disk
hot-swapping, which means you can change the drive while the computer is powered on.
This feature is often used in servers, which can't afford downtime. Motherboards usually have
multiple SATA ports, letting you connect a variety of SATA-based devices.
Solid State Drives (SSD)
Desktops and laptops use a special type of flash storage called solid state drives (SSD) . SSDs
are much faster and last longer than hard drives, but they are more expensive per unit of
storage. Many people don’t need a lot of storage and often use cloud storage, or renting space
on someone else's computer, to add more storage capacity.
SSDs connect to the motherboard using either an M.2 or SATA interface. M.2 is the hardware
specification, or size and shape, of the SSD. Most people prefer M.2 because it provides a
faster connection than SATA.
Image ©123rf.com.
The motherboard and the SSD use both a connector, either M.2 or SATA, and a protocol or set
of rules to transfer data. That protocol is called non-volatile memory express (NVMe) , created
specifically for transferring data to and from SSDs. When you combine an M.2 connection with
NVMe, you get incredibly fast data transfers.
If you add more SSDs to your computer, you can take advantage of the PCIe expansion slots
and their interface. The PCIe interface is better and faster than the older SATA interface, which
was mainly used for traditional hard drives or optical drives. PCIe is a computer interface used
to connect high-speed parts, like video cards and other expansion cards, to the motherboard. It
makes data transfer speeds to the motherboard much faster. PCIe is most commonly used with
M.2 SSDs.

Hard Disk Drives (HDD)
For decades, people used hard disk drives (HDD)  as the most common type of long-term
storage. Hard disks store data on magnetic disks inside a protective case. Because technicians
usually install hard disk drives inside computers, moving them between systems is difficult. If
you need a portable hard drive, you can use an external drive that connects to the computer
with a USB cable.
Hard disks can store large amounts of data, but their moving parts can fail over time or if they
get shaken too much. Hard disks are relatively cheap and can hold a lot of information.
Hard disks come in two sizes: 3.5 inches and 2.5 inches. The 3.5-inch size is common in
desktops, and the 2.5-inch size is common in laptops. This measurement represents the
approximate diameter of the disk inside the drive. The drives spin at a set speed, with 3.5-inch
HDDs spinning at 7200 revolutions per minute (RPM)  and 2.5-inch HDDs spinning at 5400 RPM.
The capacity of an HDD keeps increasing, with some of the biggest drives holding over 20TB.
To give you an idea of how much that is, songs in MP3 format are about 1 MB per minute. With
20TB, you could hold 5,000,000 songs! As technology improves, these numbers will likely get
even bigger.
Optical Drives
Desktop computers and some laptops used to include an optical drive. Optical drives store
information using light instead of magnetism. They read microscopic light and dark spots on
the bottom surface of disks to represent binary 1s and 0s. You can install three types of optical
drives in a computer or connect them externally using a USB connection. Those three types of
optical drives are CD-ROM,  DVD, and Blu-ray.
Optical drives are backwards-compatible with older optical disks. This means that newer
technologies can read older types of storage. For example, a DVD drive can also read CD-ROM
disks. Similarly, a Blu-ray drive can read both DVD and CD-ROM  disks. However, an optical
drive specifically designed for CD-ROMs  will not be able to read the newer Blu-ray disks.
Optical disks can store a lot of data. Blu-rays can hold 25GB, DVDs can hold 4.7GB (some can
double this capacity), and CDs can hold 700MB. The downside of optical media is that they
are slow to read and write. Optical discs are also susceptible to physical damage; if the bottom
of a disc gets scratched, the computer may not be able to read it. Optical discs come in both
read-only and read-write formats. Writing information to a read-write disc (called burning) can
be slow.
Flash Drives
Flash storage uses special non-volatile memory chips to store data. This means you can remove
power from a flash storage device and its contents will stay intact. The most common flash
drives connect to a computer via USB ports, either USB Type A or USB Type C.
Once you connect a flash storage device and the operating system recognizes it, you can store
data on it and read data from it, just like with an internal drive. Flash memory devices have the
following advantages:
• Portability: You can easily move a flash storage device from one system to another. (In
Windows, make sure to eject the device before unplugging it from the USB port or card
reader.)
• Capacity: They provide a lot of storage capacity in a small physical package.
• Flexibility: Flash storage works well in many devices, including digital cameras,
smartphones, digital camcorders, and tablets.

External Hard Drives
You can connect external hard drives to computers to add more storage space. For desktops
and laptops, you usually use a USB Type A or USB Type C connector.
External drives come with a case that protects the drive and provides access to the connection
ports. The capacity of an external drive can range from 500 GB to over 10 TB.
Network and Shared Storage
Organizations generate and collect large amounts of data that must be stored, managed, and
backed up. Depending on their needs and regulatory requirements, some organizations must
retain data for extended periods. Several network-based storage solutions help businesses
manage this data efficiently.
Storage Area Networks (SAN)
Typically, businesses and organizations keep the servers and network equipment in the same
office as the employees. But if they have a lot of data, or multiple business locations, they may
need many servers. To make things easier, they could set up one centralized location away
from the office to manage and back up all this information.
The IT department can set up Storage Area Networks (SAN)  so everyone who needs the data
can access it quickly through high-speed Internet connections. In these cases, users won't
even know the data is stored somewhere else.
SANs are fast-moving networks that let server computers share large amounts of data with
each other. They also have special equipment so people can tap into their apps and programs.
SANs are great for putting all the storage from different computers into one place. It's common
for them to connect in with fiber cables so that the data inside will travel extremely fast. SANs
communicate on a block level, which is a more direct and speedy way, breaking up data into
chunks so it can be found quickly.

Images © 123rf.com.
Network Attached Storage (NAS)
A network attached storage (NAS)  is a smaller scale version of a SAN. These boxes connect to
a local area network (LAN)  using a wired Ethernet connection. Once connected, users on the
same network can see and access shared files and folders. A NAS usually has multiple hard
drives set up in a configuration called a redundant array of independent disks (RAID) . This setup
helps prevent data loss if one of the drives fails. For extra protection, a backup solution stores
the same data somewhere else, preferably off-site.

Images © 123rf.com.
File Servers
Powerful computers or servers were first used as file servers, putting all necessary information
in one place. Once set up, IT decides who gets access to what data. File sharing was a powerful
feature even before the rise of the Internet. The data could also be easily backed up. Imagine
backing up a single computer; it's not too hard. But backing up each individual workstation
would be much more difficult. A server is a powerful computer expected to be up, or working,
almost all the time, often referred to as 24/7 or 99.9% of the time. This feature is essential for
keeping workers productive.
What Data Should I Back Up?
Most people understand the importance of saving copies of their data files somewhere in case
of an emergency. This is called "backing them up." To do this, you make a copy and put it
in a different location. If there is a major event, such as a cyber attack or a hard disk failure,
you have a way to get all your valuable information back, or at least a good portion of it. The
problem is that making duplicate copies can take a lot of time and effort, so many people don't
do it regularly. That's unfortunate because it's much easier to save electronic data than paper
files.
File Backups
Users can often confuse backing up a file with having a copy of the file. They might move,
but not copy important files to an external USB flash drive, often because they don't fully
understand the importance of backups. Simply moving the file would delete the file from their
computer and move it to the USB drive. Later, when the external USB drive fails, the user loses
the data completely because it was saved only on the USB drive. The second location could
easily have been the original computer where the data was created.
Backing up files is all about saving what users create. These are the most important parts
of computer backups. For example, an employee might spend hours working on a report or
creating an animation; these are the things you want to back up. The rest of the computer (like
its operating system and apps) can be reinstalled, but once files are lost, they are gone for
good.

Backup the Essentials
The good thing is that you don't need to back up operating system files one by one because
they aren't critical. If the OS crashes, reinstalling it is relatively simple. The same goes for
programs; reinstalling them is usually easy, too. This is even more true now that software is
available online instead of on physical media like DVDs. You can usually log in to your online
account and download the program again.
However, you may want to keep the customizations you made to a certain program. It is smart
to back these up separately if possible. Then you can merge the changes with the replaced
program after you restore it.
Think about how important your personal files are. What would happen if you lost one? How
would you get it back? Your personal data files are difficult or even impossible to recreate.
Losing a school project would be frustrating because you'd have to type it all over again. Even
worse would be losing family vacation photos from years ago; you can't go back and take those
pictures again.
System Backups
In addition to backing up your data files, it's also important to back up your whole computer
system. Setting up a computer takes time. You need to install the operating system, all the
updates, the hardware drivers, the necessary programs, and any settings to make the system
run well. Because this takes so much effort, saving everything with a system backup makes it
much easier to recover your computer if something goes wrong.
Regularly backing up your entire computer is more complicated than just copying some folders
or files to an external hard drive. System backups usually involve creating a fully bootable disk
image. This means taking a full snapshot of your system at a given time. If you manage to
do that successfully, you'd follow up with incremental backups. Most of the operating system,
applications, and other files don't change much on a day-to-day basis. Incremental backups
only save the files that have been added or changed since the last backup occurred. If your
system crashes because of a failed hard drive or virus, you can restore it by using the last full
backup and then all the incremental backups made since then.
Another benefit to making a full system backup is that it preserves all your important data and
application settings. If you back up all the key data folders, such as Documents, Pictures,
Desktop, and other user folders, your system will likely be fine. However, occasionally a
user saves their personal data in a less common location. Employees at companies with IT
departments need to take care not to save their important data in a less common location,
such as creating a folder called "My Stuff" on the root C: drive without the technician knowing.
Otherwise, the data might not get backed up.
Something to think about as a technician is how much time a fix will take and, just as importantly,
how much of your personal time will it take? If a system recovery is an hour, but you only need to
spend five minutes to get it started and then can let it complete on its own, that free time can be
spent on other tasks.
Cloud Backups
The rise of cloud storage, or using space on another computer through the Internet, has
changed the way many businesses back up their data. In some cases, cloud storage can fill
the need for a company to have an offsite backup location. It offers a convenient, flexible, and
scalable option compared to traditional backup methods. However, one downside is that cloud
backups need a lot of network bandwidth and a reliable Internet connection. This means that
backing up and restoring data from the cloud can take much longer than using local storage
devices.

Cloud storage solutions are increasingly common for both homes and businesses alike.
Companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft give users some free cloud storage space when
they use their products. There are also business-oriented options like Dropbox and Amazon.
You can use these services with a web browser or an app on your smartphone or tablet. On
Windows 10, there's a built-in cloud storage service called OneDrive, which you can access
through File Explorer.
Backup Services in Business
Backup services like Carbonite are very popular, especially for businesses where data
continuity is crucial for daily operations. Carbonite installs a program on the user's computer
and automatically backs up any files or folders it's told to. Businesses see investing in cloud
storage as similar to buying insurance; they want to prevent anything that could halt their
operations and cost them money. The storage cost is usually considered part of their other
business expenses. Storing the data off-site is the most beneficial aspect of this investment. If
something is lost or deleted at the main location, there's now a way to get it back.
Very large businesses don't always make a full copy of an individual user's computer. Instead,
all users' data is stored in the cloud. If a laptop is then lost or stolen, for example, the owner
can get a new one with the company's basic setup. With Microsoft System Center Configuration
Manager, setting up a new laptop or desktop is incredibly fast, taking about 30 minutes from
start to finish. A user just signs in to the new computer, logs in to OneDrive, and their files are
restored.
Microsoft also saves all user settings, such as browser bookmarks, email signatures, and
desktop backgrounds, in the cloud so the user can easily move from one computer to another.
Users can be living far away, get a new laptop shipped to them, and then just sign in to set
everything up with a fresh install of Windows. This makes things easy for the IT staff, the
executives, and the employees.
Restoring Data
Operating systems give you a second chance with deleted files by adding an extra step before
they're completely removed. In Windows, the Recycle Bin, and in macOS, the Trash, move files
out of your main folders but keep them just in case you want them back.
There is a key difference between Microsoft and Apple when it comes to deleting applications,
however. On Apple computers, you can drag unwanted applications to the Trash, and you can
still get them back if you change your mind. On Windows, when you delete an application from
within Settings, it's gone for good and doesn't go to the Recycle Bin.
You can also skip the Recycle Bin/Trash and permanently delete files and folders by holding
down certain keys. On Windows, press Shift + Delete. On macOS, press Option +
Command keys (next to the spacebar) while hitting delete. You can also drag the item to the
Trash in the lower right corner of the screen. Both operating systems have different icons to
show a full bin with at least one item inside, and they change to an empty bin when there's
nothing in there.
Backup Testing
You'll want to test your backups from time to time to make sure they're working properly.
Imagine thinking that you'd been backing up all your files for months, only to find out that a
really important personal file was never saved! Here are some things to look at when testing
your backups:

• Error Detection: Problems with the backup media (the physical parts of the backup device)
or with their configurations can cause backup failures. Depending on the error, the whole
backup might be canceled, or some data might not go through. Backup software usually
has ways to check if the backup worked and will report errors in a log file. This makes the
backup process take longer, but generally that time doesn't interfere with work because
most backups are done during off-hours, like in the middle of the night. In the end, it's well
worth the trouble.
• Configuration: When you create a new backup job (and periodically after that), it's a good
idea to make sure that all the data is there as planned and being backed up as expected.
• Test Restore: It's also a good idea to test if you can successfully restore your backups. Do
this in all cases. When you get new backup software, when you test old backup media, when
you check a new backup job, or if you just do random spot checks to save time. When you
do a test restore, you should save the data to a different folder so you don't accidentally
overwrite what's already there.

Lesson 8A
Exploring Common Applications
Objectives Covered
3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.
Software is what makes computers, phones, and other devices useful. From writing a document
to streaming a movie, every task you perform on a device relies on some type of application.
Understanding the different categories of software and what they are designed to do is an
important part of being comfortable with technology.
In this lesson, you will explore the major types of software people use every day,
including productivity suites, communication and collaboration tools, diagramming and graphics
applications, entertainment and gaming software, and educational platforms. You will also learn
how cloud-based software works, why learning one program helps you pick up others, and how
remote assistance tools allow technicians to support users from anywhere.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is the difference between commercial and free productivity software, and what are
some examples of each?
• How does SaaS differ from traditional installed software, and what are its benefits and
drawbacks?
• What types of software are used for communication and collaboration in the workplace?
• What are some common uses of diagramming, imaging, and video editing software?
• How can learning one software program help you use other programs more effectively?
What is Software?
Software is a set of instructions that tells a computer what to do. The computer's operating
system (OS)  reads and follows these instructions. It's important to know that application
software is made for a specific operating system. Most of the time, it's made for Microsoft
Windows, because that's the most popular OS in the world. If a software developer wants to
make a lot of money, then Windows is the safest bet, because over 1 billion devices are using it!
But there's also a lot of software made for Apple's macOS and Linux systems, too.
Smartphone Applications
Smartphone applications, or apps, started coming out in the 2000s and have become a $200
billion business. Just like software for computers, mobile apps include productivity tools, social

media, and games. But they're designed to work better on mobile devices, which have smaller
touchscreens.
Some things are suited perfectly for mobile phones, like instant messaging apps. Before
everyone had phones in their pockets, something similar existed for computers, but it was a
little bit more clunky. If you got a new message, you couldn't just pull your phone out and
respond; you had to go to your desktop computer to use the app.

The same is true of entertainment. Streaming video and audio from our phones lets you watch
movies and TV shows, or listen to our favorite songs, wherever you are. Social media apps are
also very popular on mobile devices. You can share stories and pictures with your friends and
family, or comment on a classmate's status. Mobile games are fun, simple ways to pass the
time, and navigation apps help us to not get lost.
Additionally, you don't even have to go into the bank to know how much you have in your
account or to pay your bills. It's all available on your bank's finance app. Many large companies
will have their own apps as well, making it easier for customers to use their services.

What is Productivity Software?
Productivity software helps people create documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and more.
These tools save time by replacing manual processes with digital workflows.
Commercial Software
Microsoft Office is a widely used productivity suite that includes Word for documents, Excel
for spreadsheets, PowerPoint for presentations, and Outlook for email. Microsoft also offers
online versions of these tools. Apple provides its own free suite for Mac users, including Pages,
Numbers, and Keynote.
Free Software
Google offers a free suite with word processing and spreadsheet tools that support real-time
collaboration on shared documents. Open-source alternatives like OpenOffice and LibreOffice
provide similar functionality to Microsoft Office and run on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
SaaS and Web-Based Software
Many of the productivity tools discussed earlier are available as both installed software and
web-based applications. Instead of installing a program on your hard drive, you can access it
through a web browser. This model is called Software as a Service, or SaaS.
How SaaS Works
With SaaS, the application runs on a cloud server rather than on your local device. You access
it through a browser like Chrome, Edge, or Firefox. Because the processing happens in the
cloud, SaaS apps can run on almost any device with an internet connection, regardless of its
operating system. This makes it easy to switch between a desktop computer, a laptop, and a
phone without losing your work.
Benefits and Drawbacks
SaaS applications are convenient because they do not take up storage space on your device
and are always kept up to date by the provider. They also make it easy to collaborate with
others in real time. However, they require an internet connection to work, and many charge a
monthly or yearly subscription fee. If you stop paying, you may lose access to the software and
the files stored within it.
Common Examples
Google Workspace (including Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides) and Microsoft 365 (online
versions of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint) are two of the most widely used SaaS platforms.
Other examples include project management tools, email services, and even design
applications. As internet speeds continue to improve, more software is moving to the web-
based model.
Software for Every Job
You may have noticed a theme. Different types of work need different software. Even with these
differences there is a lot of common ground across software types.
For example, many types of employees need Internet access to do their jobs. Email is a given
because it's an easy way to share ideas and objectives with others in the company. Online

collaboration has become a normal part of a job, and is, or will become, common across
industries.
Hospitals have special software for medical staff. This software is crucial because it stores
patient records. Auto mechanics use software to keep track of repairs and expenses. They also
look up diagrams for replacing parts on different cars. The banking industry has specialized
software to help calculate current interest rates. Event planners have their own types of
applications. There is literally software available for every type of job.
But remember, if it all seems daunting to learn about so many different programs, learning one
is like learning many. You'll almost certainly be able to transfer your knowledge to another
program or another industry. No time is wasted; what's important is to get started and to try to
have fun while doing it.
As a technician, you'll use your knowledge to help a company with its software needs. In large
companies, different departments might use programs that other departments don't. Having
a basic grasp of the software that exists will help you keep the office running smoothly for
management and allow you to excel at your job much faster.
Diagramming and Graphics Software
Diagramming software is made for a specific purpose, so you may not encounter it as often.
It's used to make visual representations of projects, in other words, diagrams. For example,
flowcharts can illustrate a project's steps so a team can understand the process better. Some
of this software is used in IT departments to create network diagrams for large networking
projects. Diagrams are great for helping everyone understand the structure of a project or task
and stay on the same page.
Digital Whiteboards
Online whiteboards are perfect for brainstorming together as a team. Miro is an example of an
online workspace where everyone can add to team whiteboards. It doesn't have to be just text;
it can be pictures, videos, and links to other websites. Miro's goal is to make remote work as
productive and collaborative as face-to-face work. It also works great during times of remote
learning in schools because teachers and students can work on the whiteboards as if they were
in the classroom.
Lucidchart is a popular web-based app that makes it easy to create charts, whether they are
simple or complex. Since everyone can see the charts, it's easier to get a better idea of the
scope of the project. Both Miro and Lucidchart have mobile apps for Android and iOS devices.
While it's nice to be able to view charts on your phone, the small screens can make it hard to
see complex diagrams clearly.
Digital Imaging Software
Imaging software helps you capture, edit, and process digital pictures. Common tasks include
cropping, resizing, rotating, adjusting brightness and contrast, and adding text or design
elements. You can preview changes and compare the original with the edited version before
saving.
Video Software
Digital video editing software ranges from professional tools like Adobe Premiere and Final Cut
Pro to free options like iMovie and Microsoft Clipchamp. Most computers come bundled with
basic video editing software that can handle common home projects. Smartphone apps and
built-in social media editors also provide quick mobile editing options.

Digital Image Facts
One of the most amazing developments in computer technology is the ability to create and
display high-quality images. Before computers, photographers shot pictures onto film, which
had to be developed in a laboratory before the pictures could be printed on paper. Now, anyone
with a smartphone can take a photograph and instantly share it with someone on the other side
of the planet.
Image 1:  RGB Colors
RGB Display
Computer monitors are made up of tiny red, green, and blue lights called an RGB display.
Each set of three lights is called a pixel. By combining these primary colors of light at varying
brightness levels, each pixel can display any color on the visible spectrum. Combining two
colors produces the secondary colors: red and green make yellow, red and blue make magenta,
and green and blue make cyan.
Raster vs. Vector Images
There are two main types of digital images. Raster (or bitmap) images store the color of each
individual pixel, making them ideal for detailed photographs. However, raster files use a lot of
storage space and become pixelated when scaled up. Vector graphics store points and curves
instead of individual pixels, making them scalable without losing quality. Vectors are commonly
used for logos and fonts, but they require specialized software to create and usually lack the
fine detail of raster images.

Digital Sound & Video
In the early days of recording, sound and video had to be recorded and stored using analog
methods, which means they had to physically represent the images and sound waves they
wanted to record. If you’ve ever seen a movie played from a film reel or listened to a vinyl
record, you’ve experienced analog recording. Today, however, most sound and video are
recorded digitally, which means they are encoded as ones and zeros.
Digital Sound
Sound is caused by vibrating objects that create pressure waves in the air. Digital recordings
capture this continuous wave by dividing it into discrete segments, each assigned a value called
a sample height. Bit depth determines how much memory stores each sample (e.g., 8-bit vs.
16-bit), while sampling rate measures how many samples are taken per second. Most modern
recordings use 44.1 kHz and 16-bit depth for high-quality audio.
Digital Video
Videos consist of a sequence of still images (frames) shown in rapid succession. Frame rate
measures how many frames are displayed per second, with most digital video running at about
30 fps. Resolution measures the pixel dimensions of each frame; higher resolution means a
clearer image. Color depth determines how many colors each pixel can display. Eight-bit color
supports 256 colors per pixel, while 24-bit color supports millions.
Communication Software
Beyond productivity and creative tools, some of the most commonly used software is designed
for communication. Whether you are sending a quick message to a friend or coordinating a
project with coworkers, communication software keeps people connected.
Email
Email remains one of the most widely used forms of digital communication. Providers
like Microsoft Outlook, Google Gmail, Apple iCloud, and Yahoo Mail let users send and
receive messages, attach files, and integrate with calendar applications. Email is essential
in both personal and professional settings for sharing information and keeping records of
conversations.
Messaging Applications
Instant messaging apps allow users to send quick text-based messages from a phone or
computer. Common examples include SMS text messaging, Apple iMessage, WhatsApp, and
Slack. These tools support both one-on-one and group conversations, making them a fast
alternative to email for everyday communication.
Video Conferencing
Video conferencing tools like Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet allow people to hold
face-to-face meetings over the internet. These tools are especially important for remote
workers and students who need to participate in meetings or classes from different locations.
Most video conferencing apps also support screen sharing, chat, and recording.

Collaboration Software
Collaboration just means to work together. Collaboration software is software that helps
everyone work together effectively when it comes to technology. The goal is to make it easy for
groups of people to focus on a common goal or task. This is especially important today, when
it's more common that coworkers or classmates aren't in the same location.
Communication Apps
There are many software tools available for improving teamwork, such as Slack, Microsoft
Teams, Google Workspace, and more. The essential features of these apps are the Instant
Messaging and video conferencing, which makes working remotely much easier.
These apps are crucial for filling in that face-to-face communication gap. A Zoom call can take
the place of a meeting in the conference room, and a team Slack channel can substitute for the
water cooler talk that lets coworkers get to know each other. Remote work saves companies
money by reducing the need for office space and personnel, so even though it's a little more
complicated, it's in their interest to find ways to replace the interpersonal communication that
used to happen at the office and keep everyone feeling involved.
"To Zoom" has become a verb in its own right, meaning to have a video conference call. The
biggest problem with a Zoom call is dealing with the different time zones of people working in
different parts of the United States or the world. For example, if some people are on the East
Coast and others are on the West Coast, there's a three-hour time difference between them.
When the East Coasters are leaving for lunch, the West Coasters are just starting their day. It
gets even harder when some people are in North America, and others are in Europe, Asia, or
Africa. Think of the 12- to 14-hour time difference between the United States and China. It could
be noon in one place and midnight in the other. But then again, you can work in your pajamas no
matter what time of day it is!
File Sharing
An early part of working together online was file sharing. You could upload a file to a cloud
storage service, and then email a link to someone so they could access it. Services like
Dropbox, OneDrive (which used to be called SkyDrive), and iCloud have been offering this for
over a decade. They let you store a limited amount of files for free, but if you need more space,
you can pay a small monthly fee.
The benefit to this is that it's so easy to share large files this way. Email services usually limit
attachments to about 25 MB. Also, sharing files in the cloud is better than emailing them back
and forth. You can work on a file while automatically saving it to the cloud. And the person you
shared it with can make changes without waiting for you to send it back. This way, you know
that you're always working on the most up-to-date version, which isn't always the case with
email.
Cloud service providers also keep older versions of files in storage, so you can go back to an
earlier version if you need to. For example, you mess something up enough that it's better to
just start over from an earlier point. Since there are backups, you don't have to worry about
losing something forever. There's probably going to be some version of a file that you can
retrieve if something happens to your local computer, like an accidental deletion, ransomware,
or a system crash.

Gaming and Media Software
Software is not only used for work and communication. Entertainment software is a major
category of applications that people use every day for streaming media, sharing content, and

Video and Audio Streaming
Video streaming services let users watch movies, television shows, and user-created content
on demand. Audio streaming services provide access to music, podcasts, and audiobooks. The
content available varies by platform, and most services offer both free and paid subscription
options. Because streaming delivers media over the internet, it does not require downloading
large files to your device.
Gaming Software
Gaming is one of the largest segments of the software industry. Games are available on
computers, smartphones, tablets, and dedicated gaming consoles. Online gaming services

Social media platforms allow users to share photos, videos, and updates with friends, family,

Educational Software
In addition to entertainment, software plays a major role in education. From online courses to
interactive study tools, educational software helps people learn new skills at their own pace and

Learning Management Systems
A learning management system (LMS)  is a platform that delivers and tracks educational content.

Online Learning Platforms
Online learning platforms offer courses on a wide range of subjects, from programming and
graphic design to business and science. Many platforms provide video lessons, quizzes, and
hands-on labs that let learners practice what they have studied. Some courses are free, while
others charge a fee or offer certificates upon completion.
Study and Reference Tools
There are also many apps designed to help with studying and research. Flashcard apps,
note-taking tools, and citation managers help students organize information and prepare for

make the most of study time.

Lesson 8B
Managing Software Safely
Objectives Covered
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
Whether you are managing a personal device or working in IT, knowing how to find, install,
and remove software safely is essential. Software is available from many sources, including app
stores, publisher websites, and third-party download sites, but not all of them are trustworthy.
Downloading from the wrong place can expose your system to viruses, malware, and other
security threats.
In this lesson, you will learn how to identify safe sources for software, understand how app
stores review and distribute apps, and explore different types of software licensing. You will
also walk through the steps for installing software on both Apple and Windows systems, and
learn when and how to remove software you no longer need.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What are the risks of downloading software from untrusted sources?
• How do app stores help ensure that software is safe to install?
• What is the difference between open-source and proprietary software?
• What are the common types of software licenses, and why do they matter?
• How do you install and remove software on Apple and Windows devices?
• Why is it important to remove unused software from your system?
Where Do We Find Software?
For the first few decades that personal computers were available, software was sold only at
physical shops. Retail stores had a few programs on floppy or compact disc (CDs)  you could
buy, while stores that specialized in computers and tech had a bigger selection. As the Internet
became more popular, people began to download their favorite programs more often than they
bought packaged software. Software companies actually liked this change because it saved
them money. They didn't have to manufacture CDs, put them in fancy boxes, and ship them out
to stores anymore.
Know Your Sources
Walking into stores and going through shelves full of software back in those days could be fun.
You never knew what you were going to find. Shopping online for software now can be fun, too.
However, when you work in IT or manage your own system, it's important to make sure that

the software you download is coming from a trustworthy source. The last thing you want is to
be the one who accidentally brought a virus onto the company network, or who let the home
network get hacked.
When shopping online, you can be sure your software is safe and malware-free by getting that
software directly from the source. Make sure you're on the software producer's website, and
you know your purchase will be safe. Sometimes, threat actors create fake websites that look
similar to the real ones, often by using a misspelled version of the correct site's name. Luckily,
these fake sites usually don't copy the real site's content. Instead, they use other tricks to make
money off of you, such as getting you to download harmful programs onto your computer.
There are so many programs available for download these days that it can get overwhelming.
Like most people, you'll probably search the web for answers. This is another place where
problems can arise, so make sure to go over a website carefully before proceeding with
its suggestions. Just visiting a website won't harm your computer, but clicking on a pop-up
window or downloading a file can. Trust your instincts and just exit the site if something feels
off. If you're unsure, pop open a new tab in your browser and look for reviews about the
site or product. If the top results show a lot of issues or complaints, look for something else.
Remember, there are so many companies competing to make the best software out there that
there will almost always be another option.
Trusted Sources for Software
Programs on tablets and phones are called apps. You might have some that came pre-installed,
and you might have downloaded others from the mobile app store. These online stores offer all
kinds of content, like games, productivity tools, photo-editing software, and more. The apps will
be organized in categories, with each one having its own icon, like a book cover. You can also
read reviews about them from other customers in the app store or by searching online.
What Is an App Store?
An app store is a platform where users can search for and download a variety of apps for
different devices. In most app stores, the majority of apps are free, but there are some that
you have to purchase. One exciting thing about these stores is that they're constantly being
updated with new content to explore. When you open an app store, you'll see a home page with
suggestions, new releases, and popular downloads.
Major companies like Apple and Google have their own app stores for their smartphones and
tablets. The apps available in these stores are chosen by the company that runs the store.
This means that before an app is released, it goes through a review process to make sure it
works well with the company's devices, is of good quality, and doesn't have any harmful or
inappropriate content.
Because of this review process, app stores are one of the safest ways to install software.
The Microsoft Store, Google Play Store, and Apple App Store all work to ensure that only
trusted apps are available for download or purchase, reducing the risk of accidentally installing
malicious software.
App Distribution
Downloading an app is easy. First, you need to create an account that links your device to the
specific app store. Once you find the app you want, you'll be able to click a 'Get' button or
something similar. Then the app will be installed on the device. Usually, if you've purchased an
app, it's yours to keep. This means that you can delete it from your device and re-download it
later without paying again. This is nice for when you get a new phone because you can log back
into your account, and your apps will automatically download to the new one.

Another feature of app stores is that they provide updates when developers release them.
These updates are meant to fix bugs or address complaints users have made. Sometimes,
developers also add new content and features to keep people interested in their product.
Updating is done through the app store, which usually has a section for this purpose. These
updates are almost always included in the original purchase price.
Common App Stores
Apple's App Store is the main place to get content for products like the iPad, iPhone, and Mac
computers. It connects with a user's Apple ID to share content across all their Apple devices.
There are actually two app stores in the Apple world: one for mobile devices running iOS and
one for computers running macOS. These stores also offer digital media like music, videos,
eBooks, and podcasts.
Amazon not only sells physical products but also offers a variety of apps for its own devices
and tablets. These include the Kindle line of products and smart devices like Alexa smart
speakers. Some Amazon apps can be used on different platforms, including the Kindle Reader.
Google Play is the main place to get content for Android and Google devices. In 2012, it
combined several separate digital stores, including Books, Games, Movies & TV, and Music,
into one big store that offered all these apps together. It comes pre-installed on Android phones
and tablets and has a huge selection of programs that are easy to find and add.
The Microsoft Store (formerly called the Windows Store) offers apps for computers and devices
running Windows or using Microsoft technology. This includes Windows tablets and all versions
of Microsoft's gaming platform, Xbox. When Windows 10 came out, Microsoft combined several
different digital stores into one. This new store includes the Windows Marketplace, Windows
Phone Store, Xbox Music, Xbox Video, and Xbox Store. You can download media directly onto
an Xbox system just like you can with other Microsoft products.
Software Licensing
You might not think too much about whether the software you install on your computer or
phone is properly licensed. As an individual, you may feel like a small fish in a big ocean of
consumers. But when you work in an IT department with hundreds of computers, following
software licensing rules is an important business concern. Software publishers don’t appreciate,
and can prosecute, people who use their products without paying for them. A license is a type
of receipt that permits you to run the product you paid for. Installing unlicensed software breaks
copyright laws. You can be fined for this behavior. Beyond that, it's simply wrong.
When you first install a software program, you have to read and agree to the rules for using
it, which is called the End User License Agreement (EULA) . These rules can be different
for different programs, but usually, they say that you can only install that particular software
program on one machine. That's why you need to be extra careful if you're in charge of an
office environment where all the machines need to have the same piece of software installed.
The good news is that software makers don't expect large companies to buy individual copies
for each person. Instead, they offer companies a blanket or site license, which lets them install
the software on as many computers as they need for one price. This makes things easier for the
IT department because they don't have to keep track of licenses for every single computer.
Subscription Model
A big change in software ownership over the years has been the shift to monthly subscription
plans. Developers came to realize that they could end up making more money this way. Before
this model became popular, many consumers would buy the software and not upgrade to a new
version (and pay for that new version) for a long time. With a subscription plan, you pay every

month and always get the latest version and updates. You can also expect better security and
performance, and direct access to the software's tech support team.
Product Keys and Serial Numbers
A common way to link purchased software to its owner is by using a key or serial number
specific to that product or license. These keys or numbers are long strings of unique letters and
numbers given out after purchase to prove ownership. Usually, you must enter this key or serial
number when you install the software, which also registers it with the developer. In the past, you
would find these keys somewhere in the box or on the label of the CD case. Nowadays, most
licenses are emailed out. The main purpose of these keys is to help prevent piracy.
Open Source vs. Proprietary
Since the early days of computers, there's been a small industry of independent programmers
creating free-to-use software programs. This is known as freeware or open-source software.
Open source means that the code used can be viewed and even modified by anyone. So if
you know how to program, you can change the source code to make the software look or
work differently. You can even add on your own features. In addition to that, if you change
something, you can redistribute your modified version to others. There are some open-source
licensing rules you'd need to follow, but they're much less restrictive than rules created by big
companies.
In fact, open-source software is usually a collaborative effort. Programmers from around the
world all add their own touches to the code until there's a final product. One of the most
common examples of open-source software is the Linux operating system.
On the other hand, there is proprietary software, which is made by companies that sell it
for profit. Some of the well-known companies that make proprietary computer and gaming
software are Microsoft, Adobe, Sony, and Oracle. To use their products, you need to buy a
license and agree to their terms and conditions.
Piracy
Software piracy occurs when someone makes or shares copies of a software program without
permission. It is illegal to use these unauthorized copies, known as pirated copies. Pirated
software is dangerous because it can have viruses hidden inside, or the program might have
been changed in ways that make it less stable and more likely to crash. This creates a big
security risk and is a major concern for IT departments. If you use pirated software, you will
not get security updates or support for the product. There are also serious legal risks, like the
possibility of lawsuits and significant financial penalties.
Installing Software
Most software installs in the same basic way. Not every app will have all these same steps, but
this is the most common method.
1. First, you'll open the program and agree to the license agreement.
2. Next, you're asked where on the system you want it installed.
3. Then, you click to start the installation.
4. Finally, the software installs in a few seconds.
Sometimes you may need to restart your computer to finalize it. After the software is
installed, there are often settings you can change. It's a good idea to adjust these early
on to get the best use out of the application.

While these steps give you the general outline, there are some differences between the major
manufacturers.
Apple Software
Apple computers have three common ways to install software.
• The App Store: The App Store is Apple's official place for iOS and macOS apps, where you
can browse through millions of choices. The nice thing is that Apple checks these apps for
security and compatibility.
• Installation packages: A lot of Apple software for macOS comes as installation packages
with a .pkg file extension. You can download these packages from the developer's website
or from websites that aggregate or collect software.
• Disk image files: Software might be distributed as a disk image file (.dmg). You can
download these files from the developer's website as well. When you open a .dmg file, it
mounts a disk image onto your computer. You can then drag and drop the software into your
Applications folder to install it.
Windows Software
There's a wider variety of websites that offer software for Microsoft Windows, compared to
what's available for Apple. It's common practice to visit a publisher's site to get software. Some
websites collect all kinds of software in one place. Be sure to review these websites to ensure
they are reputable.
Installing software on Windows has been pretty much the same process for a while now. Most
files come as an .exe, which is an executable file. After you download it, you double-click on the
file to start the installation. On Windows 11, the software is usually saved in one of two folders:
Program Files or Program Files (x86). You'll see a series of prompts, like the license terms and
choosing the installation location. Sometimes, you might need to restart your computer after the
installation is done.
You can also install apps directly from the Microsoft Store, which comes preinstalled with
Windows. The Microsoft Store verifies apps for security and compatibility, making it one of the
safest ways to add software to your system.
The x86 in program files is in reference to 32-bit software, which goes back to the x86 architecture
on Intel processors from decades ago.
Downloading Software Safely
Before installing an app downloaded from the internet, make sure the website or publisher
is a trusted source. Download the installation file and scan it for viruses and other malware
before running it. Most anti-malware programs, like Windows Defender, will scan downloaded
files automatically. When you're confident the file is safe, run it and follow the on-screen
instructions.
In some cases, you may still encounter software distributed on a CD or DVD. To install from a
disc, insert it into the drive and follow the on-screen prompts. If the installation doesn't begin
automatically, you may need to adjust your computer's AutoPlay settings. After a disc-based
installation, check the vendor's website for any available updates.
Removing Software
Sometimes you install software on your device, and for whatever reason, it just sits there
unused and forgotten. In IT, it's a good practice to remove any unused software. This can help

you avoid potential threats that could end up harming your network. Old programs can be a
security risk because they might no longer receive updates. Also, keeping unused software can
cause issues with license compliance, so in most cases it's better to just remove it.
Another reason to remove unused software is to free up storage space on your hard drive.
Getting rid of these programs can improve your system's performance. Many programs run in
the background and use up resources, which can slow your computer down.
Different manufacturers have their own ways of removing unwanted software.
• Apple: On Apple's macOS, you just drag and drop. Find the app you don't need anymore
in your Applications folder, click and grab the icon, and then drag it to the trash can in the
bottom right of your screen. If you change your mind and haven't emptied the trash yet, you
can go back into the trash can and then drag it back to your Applications folder. It will work
just like before.
• Windows: With Windows, removing an app requires a few more steps. First, open Settings
and go to Apps. Find the app you want to remove and click the three dots on the right. Then
choose the option to Uninstall. (Cer t ain  programs can't be uninstalled; they only have the
option to "Modify").
If an app is being stubborn and won't uninstall the normal way, which does happen
occasionally, you can use special software to help. One of the best tools for this is Revo
Uninstaller.
Some computers come out of the box with extra software and trial versions (unkindly referred to
as "bloatware"). Once you know you don't need these programs, you should remove them, too.
If a software program stops working, the best solution is often to uninstall it and then reinstall it.
Some programs have a "Repair" option, which can be faster and preserve your custom settings.
You might also see a "Change" option, which lets you add or remove parts of the program to
your liking.

Everyday Uses for Word Processors
Word processors are not just for writing essays. Here are some ways you might use one in

Common Word Processing File Formats
Word processing files come in different formats depending on the software that created them.
Knowing the common formats helps you open, share, and convert files between programs.
• .docx — The default format for Microsoft Word. Supports rich formatting, images, tables,
and tracked changes.
• .odt — The open-source format used by LibreOffice Writer. Most word processors can open
it.
• .pages — Apple Pages' format. Other programs may not open it directly, so you may need to
export to .docx or PDF before sharing.
• .pdf — A read-only format that preserves the exact look of your document. Useful for
sharing a finished file when the reader does not need to edit it.

• .txt — A plain-text format with no formatting at all. Useful when you only need the words and
nothing else.
Word Processors vs. Other Tools
A word processor is not always the right tool. Understanding how it compares to other options
helps you choose the best one for the task.
• Word processor vs. spreadsheet — A spreadsheet is designed for numerical data, formulas,
and calculations. Use a word processor when your document is mostly text with some tables
or images.
• Word processor vs. presentation software — Presentation software creates visual slides for
speaking to a group. Use a word processor when the reader will consume the content on
their own and needs full paragraphs of detail.
• Word processor vs. text editor — A plain text editor like Notepad saves only raw text with
no formatting. Use a word processor when you need fonts, colors, images, headers, or page
layout.
Mobile Word Processing Software
Mobile devices also have options for word processing, including all the ones we've discussed
and others made just for smartphones. These can be really handy for quick document creation
and editing, especially if time is of the essence and you're not at a computer. Like Google Docs,
mobile options rely on online storage, but they also let you access your documents offline.
Some of these mobile apps are free, while others might have a one-time cost or a monthly

Everyday Uses for Spreadsheets

Common Spreadsheet File Formats
Spreadsheet files come in different formats depending on the software that created them.
Knowing the common formats helps you open, share, and convert files between programs.

multiple worksheets.

need to export to .xlsx or .csv before sharing.
Spreadsheets vs. Other Tools

helps you choose the best one for the task.

tables in a document. Use a spreadsheet when you need to calculate values, sort data, or
work with more than a handful of rows.
• Spreadsheet vs. database — Databases are designed for very large data sets and for
connecting related tables together. A spreadsheet works well for smaller data sets that one
person or a small team manages.
Mobile Spreadsheet Software

downloadable spreadsheet apps, but they're not as commonly used because the screens are
so small and you have to try to work with the touchpad. But, at the end of the day, these apps
