Text and Phone Apps
Your smartphone comes with built-in apps for making phone calls and sending text messages.
These are the most basic communication tools on any mobile device, and understanding how
they work will help you stay connected in both personal and professional settings.
Phone Apps
Every smartphone includes a phone app that handles voice calls over a cellular network. When
you make a call, your voice is converted into a signal and transmitted through your carrier's
network to the person you are calling. Most phone apps also include features like a contacts list,
call history, voicemail, and the ability to set up conference calls with multiple people.
In addition to traditional cellular calls, many smartphones support Voice over Internet Protocol
(V oIP)  calling. VoIP apps like Google Voice, Skype, and WhatsApp use your internet connection
instead of a cellular signal to place calls. This can be especially useful when you are connected
to Wi-Fi but have weak cell reception, or when you need to make international calls without high
carrier fees.
Text Messaging Apps
Text messaging, or Short Message Service (SMS)  allows you to send short written messages
through your phone carrier's network. You can also send photos, videos, and audio clips
using Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS).  These services are tied to your phone number,
so anyone with a cell phone can receive your messages regardless of the device or operating
system they use.
Many smartphones now also support Rich Communication Services (RCS),  which is an updated
standard that adds features similar to internet-based messaging apps. With RCS, you can
see typing indicators, read receipts, and send higher-quality images, all through your phone's
default messaging app.

Choosing Between Phone and Text
Phone calls and text messages each have strengths depending on the situation. A phone call
is better when you need to discuss something quickly or when the tone of your voice matters.
Text messaging works well for short updates, sharing links or images, or when the other person
may not be available to talk right away. In a work environment, understanding when to call
versus when to text is an important part of professional communication.
Messaging Apps
Messaging apps go beyond traditional texting by using your internet connection to send
messages, images, videos, and files. These apps have become some of the most widely used
communication tools in the world, both for personal conversations and workplace collaboration.
Personal Messaging Apps
Apps like WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, iMessage, and Telegram allow you to send
messages to individuals or groups over the internet. Unlike SMS, these apps typically require
both you and the recipient to have the same app installed. In return, you get features that
standard texting does not offer, such as read receipts, typing indicators, voice messages, video
clips, and end-to-end encryption for privacy.
Many personal messaging apps also support group chats, where multiple people can participate
in a single conversation. Group chats are useful for coordinating plans, sharing updates with
family members, or staying in touch with a circle of friends.
Business and Collaboration Messaging
In the workplace, messaging has moved beyond simple chat. Collaboration platforms like
Microsoft Teams, Slack, and Google Chat organize conversations into channels or groups based
on projects, departments, or topics. This structure helps teams stay organized and find relevant
discussions without scrolling through unrelated messages.
These platforms also integrate with other productivity tools. For example, you can share files,
start video calls, assign tasks, and connect third-party apps directly within the messaging
interface. This makes them a central hub for day-to-day work communication, reducing the
need to switch between multiple applications.
Messaging Etiquette
Because messaging feels casual, it can be easy to forget that your messages leave a record.
In a professional setting, you should keep your messages clear and respectful. Avoid sending
too many short, fragmented messages in a row, as this can be distracting to the recipient. If a
conversation becomes complex or requires detailed discussion, it may be better to switch to a
phone call, video call, or email.
Email
Email is one of the oldest and most reliable forms of digital communication. Whether you are
sending a quick note to a friend or submitting a formal report at work, email gives you a way to
deliver written messages, attach files, and keep a record of your conversations.
How Email Works
When you send an email, your message travels from your email provider's server to the
recipient's email server using standard internet protocols. The recipient can then read your

message whenever they check their inbox. This makes email an asynchronous form of
communication, meaning both people do not need to be online at the same time.
Every email address follows the same format: a username, the @ symbol, and a domain name.
For example, in the address jsmith@example.com, "jsmith" is the username and "example.com"
is the domain where the mailbox is hosted.
Webmail vs. Desktop Email Clients
There are two main ways to access your email. Webmail services like Gmail, Outlook.com, and
Yahoo Mail run entirely in your web browser. You do not need to install anything, and you can
check your email from any device with an internet connection. Webmail is a popular choice for
personal use because it is free and easy to set up.
Desktop email clients like Microsoft Outlook, Mozilla Thunderbird, and Apple Mail are
applications installed on your computer. These programs download your messages and store
them locally, which means you can read and organize emails even when you are offline.
Desktop clients are commonly used in business environments because they offer advanced
features such as calendar integration, contact management, and support for multiple email
accounts in one place.
Key Email Features
Most email services share a common set of features that help you manage your
communications:
• Attachments: You can send files such as documents, images, and spreadsheets along with
your message.
• CC and BCC:  Carbon copy (CC)  sends a copy of the email to additional recipients. Blind
carbon copy (BCC)  does the same but hides those recipients from other people in the
message.
• Folders and labels: You can organize messages into folders or apply labels to keep your
inbox manageable.
• Search: Built-in search tools help you find specific messages by keyword, sender, date, or
attachment type.
• Spam filtering: Email providers automatically detect and separate unwanted or suspicious
messages from your inbox.
Calendaring
A digital calendar is more than just a place to mark dates. Calendaring software helps you
schedule events, set reminders, coordinate with other people, and manage your time across
personal and professional commitments. Most digital calendars sync across your devices, so
your schedule is always available whether you are at your desk or on your phone.
Common Calendaring Tools
Several calendaring applications are widely used today. Google Calendar is a free, web-based
tool that integrates tightly with Gmail and other Google services. Microsoft Outlook includes a
full calendar alongside its email and contacts features, making it a popular choice in business
environments. Apple Calendar comes built into macOS and iOS devices and syncs through
iCloud. Each of these tools offers similar core features, so the best choice often depends on
which ecosystem of apps and services you already use.

Key Calendaring Features
Digital calendars include features that make scheduling easier and more reliable:
• Events and appointments: You can create entries with a title, date, time, location, and
description. Some calendars let you add video call links directly to the event.
• Reminders and notifications: You can set alerts to notify you before an event starts, helping
you stay on track throughout the day.
• Recurring events: If you have a meeting or task that repeats on a regular schedule, you can
set it to recur daily, weekly, monthly, or at a custom interval.
• Shared calendars: You can share your calendar with coworkers, family members, or
classmates so everyone can see each other's availability and avoid scheduling conflicts.
• Invitations: When you schedule a meeting, you can send invitations to other people. They
can accept, decline, or suggest a different time, all from within their own calendar app.
Calendars in the Workplace
In a professional setting, calendaring software plays a central role in coordination. Teams use
shared calendars to schedule meetings, track deadlines, and reserve conference rooms. Many
organizations rely on calendar integration with email and messaging platforms, so meeting
invitations and updates flow automatically between tools. Developing good calendaring habits,
such as keeping your availability up to date and responding promptly to meeting invitations,
helps your team work together more efficiently.
Videoconferencing Apps
Videoconferencing apps allow you to have face-to-face conversations with other people over
the internet. Whether you are attending a remote class, joining a work meeting, or catching up
with family in another city, these tools bring the experience of an in-person conversation to your
screen.
How Videoconferencing Works
Videoconferencing uses your device's camera, microphone, and internet connection to transmit
live audio and video to other participants. Most apps use Voice over Internet Protocol (V oIP)  to
handle the audio portion of the call, which means the sound travels over the internet rather than
through a traditional phone line. As long as you have a stable internet connection, you can join a
video call from a computer, tablet, or smartphone.
Popular Videoconferencing Apps
Several videoconferencing platforms are widely used today:
• Zoom: Known for its ease of use and reliability, Zoom is popular for business meetings,
online classes, and personal calls. It supports features like breakout rooms, screen sharing,
and virtual backgrounds.
• Microsoft Teams: Integrated with Microsoft 365, Teams combines video calls with
messaging, file sharing, and collaboration tools. It is widely used in corporate and
educational environments.
• Google Meet: A browser-based option that works with Google Workspace. It requires no
software installation and is accessible to anyone with a Google account.
• FaceTime: Built into Apple devices, FaceTime offers a simple way to make video calls
between iPhones, iPads, and Macs.
• Skype: One of the earliest video calling apps, Skype supports video calls, voice calls, and
messaging across multiple platforms.

Common Videoconferencing Features
Most videoconferencing apps share a set of core features that improve the meeting experience:
• Screen sharing: You can share your screen so other participants can see a document,
presentation, or application you are working with.
• Chat: A text chat panel runs alongside the video call, allowing you to share links, ask
questions, or comment without interrupting the speaker.
• Recording: Many apps let the host record the meeting so people who missed it can watch
later.
• Mute and camera controls: You can turn your microphone or camera on and off during a
call, which is useful for reducing background noise or maintaining privacy when you are not
speaking.
Tips for a Good Video Call
To get the most out of a video call, make sure you have a reliable internet connection and
a quiet environment. Position your camera at eye level so you appear natural on screen.
Use headphones or earbuds to reduce echo and background noise. If you are joining a
professional meeting, mute your microphone when you are not speaking and be mindful of
your surroundings, since other participants can see what is behind you.

Rules of Netiquette
Netiquette refers to the rules of etiquette that should be observed while using computer
networks, such as the internet. Using a computer to interact with other users tends to impart a
sense of anonymity, which can cause you to behave in ways that are impolite or even offensive.
To keep this from happening, all network users should adhere to a set of guidelines called
netiquette. The overarching rule of netiquette is this: Don't do or say anything to another person
online that you would not do or say if you were looking at them face to face.
Several more specific guidelines will help you achieve this goal.
Table 26:  Guidelines of Netiquette
Guideline Description
Show Consideration for Other
Users' Time
Before making an online post or sending an email, make sure it is worth
the time of those who will read it. A common violation of this rule occurs
when someone forwards a mass email message of questionable origin to
everyone in their address book. Before doing this, consider the following:
• Verify the authenticity of the information you're sending.
• Ask yourself whether the recipients actually need (or even want) to
read it.
Use Appropriate Spelling and
Grammar
The anonymity of the internet frequently makes users careless about
following spelling and grammar rules. This can make a message difficult
to read and can even make it impossible to decipher.
Avoid using all capital letters. On the internet, this is considered shouting.
Write Clearly and Concisely A lot of internet users are careless about how they communicate ideas
in messages and posts. To respect other users' time and to make sure
your ideas are communicated correctly, be sure your posts and email
messages are:
• Clear. Read through your message and make sure your point is clearly
stated. Remember, the reader may not have the same background
that you have. Will they understand what you are trying to say?
• Concise. Be brief and to the point. Nobody likes to wade through a
ten-page email or post trying to find important information.
• Readable. Use understandable terms when you write. Many internet
users prefer to use shorthand terms in their posts and messages,
such as u r ("you are") and idk ("I don't know"). While using
shorthand can reduce the amount of time needed to compose
a message, it makes it much more difficult to read. It can also
obscure the meaning and intent of your message, resulting in
misunderstandings.

Guideline Description
Avoid Being a Troll A troll is someone who deliberately tries to create conflict among users.
Expressing your opinion is encouraged on the internet; however, trolls
are not usually interested in engaging in a healthy dialogue. Instead, they
seek to cause contention and disrupt the conversation. Trolling tactics
that are commonly used include:
• Posting provocative, offensive, and even hateful messages to incite a
response from other users.
• Posting off-topic messages in an attempt to start an argument.
• Posting obscene or menacing messages to harass another user.
If you encounter a troll, the best response is to just ignore them.
Obey the Law Be familiar with the laws in your jurisdiction surrounding computer use
and cybersecurity, and abide by them. For example, all fifty states in the
United States have laws to stop cyberbullying. In the United Kingdom,

Hertz, Bytes, and Metric Prefixes
How fast is your internet connection? What size hard drive do you need? How much memory
does your computer currently have? How much cloud storage do you need? These are common
questions when working with computers and networks. The answers will include terms that you
need to be familiar with.
Hertz
Hertz is a measurement of how many times a repeating process happens per second. If you
clap your hands one time a second, you are clapping at 1 Hertz. If you clap your hands 10 times
every second, you are clapping at 10 Hertz.
The term Hertz is used to describe the speed at which a device runs. The internal parts of a
computer, laptop, tablet, or phone need to work together to process and move data. To do this,
all devices use a master clock to keep devices synchronized.
The signal the master clock produces is called a square wave. A square wave has sharp edges.
It rises, then moves to the right, then drops and moves to the right. The amount of time it moves
to the right is the same after a rise or a fall. When the square wave rises is the start. After the
fall, the wave moves to the right, which is the end of the wave.
The process of moving up and over, then down and over, is called a single cycle. Here is an
example of multiple cycles together. If all four cycles happen in one second, then this clock
signal would be running at 4 Hertz (4Hz).

Metric Prefixes
Most modern computers run at extremely high clock speeds, some in the Gigahertz (GHz).
The most recognized device that uses Hertz in its specifications is a computer's Central
Processing Unit (CPU).  If your computer has a 3.4 GHz processor, it is capable of processing
3,400,000,000 operations per second.
Metric Prefixes Modern computers and networks process data at super high speeds, and
modern storage devices are able to store extremely large amounts of data. Because the
numbers being used are so large, we use metric prefixes to help us.
For example, a computer has a hard drive capable of holding 500 billion bytes of data. You
would have to label it as a 500,000,000,000-byte hard drive. It's much easier to express it with
a metric prefix. Using a metric prefix, we could rewrite the size as a 500-gigabyte hard drive.

Storage Units
Most people don't think much about what's stored on their devices when they're not in use, but
all our devices need to have storage capacity to work properly. Storage in a computer is called
"persistent" because it holds data even when the power is turned off. This data can include

the operating system like Windows or iOS, as well as all the apps and user files added to the
system.
Each piece of data has a file size, which is the number of bytes it takes up. Computer storage
for files has grown to be measured in gigabytes (GB)  or terabytes (TB).  These units can also be
used for memory and storage drives. A gigabyte (GB)  is about one billion bytes. A terabyte (TB)
is one thousand times bigger than a gigabyte!
How and for how long data is stored differs between memory and storage drives. Memory is
"non-persistent" or "volatile" storage, which means it only holds data while the computer is
powered on. A solid-state drive (SSD),  on the other hand, keeps the data permanently.
The smallest addressable unit in memory is a byte. Once you gather 1024 bytes, it is called
a kilobyte (KB).  This number isn't the usual 1000 you're used to, because computers count in
binary, not decimal. For example, two to the 8th power is 256, and two to the 10th power is
1024. These are common numbers in computing because they are "round" in binary.
As you keep multiplying up to 1024 kilobytes, you get to the next storage unit: megabytes
(MB).  After megabytes come gigabytes (GB),  then terabytes (TB),  followed by petabytes (PB),
exabytes (EB),  zettabytes (ZB),  and yottabytes (YB).
Most files today are measured in megabytes (MB).  Music and photos are good examples. Larger
files, such as videos, are usually measured in gigabytes (GB).  Only small text files are measured
in kilobytes (KB)  these days.
Adding commas to numbers greater than 999 is not common in IT communications. This is because
different regions separate the thousands digit in different ways. For example, European standards
use the period to separate thousands and a comma for decimal points, while in North America this
is reversed. Additionally, the comma in programming is used to separate items when coding. To
avoid confusion around the world, it was simply decided to leave off any punctuation.
Throughput Units
Throughput measures how much of something passes through something else in a certain
amount of time. The term isn't limited to just computing. It can also mean things like the number
of pages you can read per hour, the number of patients a doctor sees in a day, or the number
of customers visiting a store in a week. All these examples are different ways of describing
throughput. It measures how fast things move or get done.
With computers, this means how much data moves through the system in one second. With
networking, it's similar but slightly different; it’s about how much data moves from one place
to another in one second. You can also think of it as the amount of data passing through the
network at any given moment.
It's important to know that throughput is not the highest or lowest amount. Throughput is the
total amount over a certain block of time. Think of it like a bus: if the network were a bus,
throughput would be like counting all the passengers the bus carried in one day.
In fact, one of the main jobs when managing a network is to monitor throughput so you can
make changes if necessary. A slow network can make everyone unhappy and less productive.
Moving Bits
When you talk about how much a storage drive or memory can hold, you use bytes to measure
that capacity. But when you talk about how fast data moves, you use bits, which are much
smaller than bytes. In fact, one byte is equal to eight bits. Network transfers break it down to the
smallest units possible, bits per second. But when you check your Internet speed, the results
are shown as Mbps, which means megabits per second. If you want to send a video to a friend
over the Internet, the speed is measured in megabits (Mb)  or gigabits (Gb)  per second.

Bandwidth
When talking about sending data over the Internet, the term bandwidth is used. Bandwidth is
the highest amount of data that a network can handle at once. For example, if a network has a
bandwidth of 50 megabits per second (Mbps),  it can't send data faster than that number.
Going back to the bus analogy, think of it like this: bandwidth is the maximum number of
passengers the bus can carry at one time. Bandwidth describes the bus's seating capacity, and
throughput describes how many people the bus actually transports in a certain amount of time,
carrying passengers over many trips throughout the day.
Throughput Units
To restate the throughput measurements, when data is moved between parts within a computer
or between different computers on a network, this is measured in bits per second (bps). Just
like with storage, using bits per second can make for very long numbers, so larger units are
used to make it easier to understand. Here are some of those units:
• Kilobits per second (Kbps):  One thousand (1, 000)  bits per second. Slow network links are
measured in Kbps.
• Megabits per second (Mbps):  One million (1, 000 , 000)  bits per second. Wireless networks
and residential Internet links typically have this rate of throughput.
• Gigabits per second (Gbps):  One billion (1, 000 , 000 , 000)  bits per second. The latest PC bus
standards and networks can support this higher level of throughput.
• Terabits per second (Tbps):  One trillion (1, 000 , 000 , 000 , 000)  bits per second. This sort
of capacity is found in major telecommunications links between data centers, cities, and
countries.
Throughput Obstacles
Multiple factors can affect a network's throughput. Some things that can slow it down are
latency, errors that cause data to be sent again (retransmissions), and the communication rules
(protocols). Some protocols have built-in features like congestion avoidance and flow control,
which can impact throughput. If a data packet gets lost, it might need to be resent. If this
happens a lot, it can cause more congestion and slow down the network.
Your Internet Service Provider (ISP)  gives you a certain amount of bandwidth. You might have
a plan for 50 Mbps or 100 Mbps, which means that those are your expected download speeds.
However, the actual speeds you get might be different from what is advertised. Inside your
home network, speeds between devices can be faster because they don't depend on the
Internet bandwidth.
It's common for ISPs to underpromise and overdeliver. You may be paying for a 100 Mbps package,
but doing a speed test will probably yield slightly faster speeds. This is an easy way for ISPs to
make customers feel good by giving them a little something extra, at no cost to the ISP.
Another obstacle can be the amount of traffic passing through the network. If there's a lot of
traffic on the network at once, congestion occurs, making everything slower. The more traffic
there is, the harder it is for data to move quickly, just like cars on the freeway.
The cables you use also affect your network speed. The network can only be as fast as its
slowest part. For example, if you have fast cables and network cards but a slow network switch,
the switch is going to slow everything down. This is called the weak link.
"I worked with a client whose network was inexplicably slow. We could not figure out
what the problem was. The ISP was functioning just fine, the routers and switches
were new and double-checked, older laptops were replaced. Finally, we looked at
the network cable inside the building. Whoever built the building decided to save
money by installing CAT 3 cable, when the standard was at least CAT 5e at the time.

A smaller CAT number means less capacity, so business at that client was incredibly
slow."
-- R. Turner, network administrator
Processing Speed
Processing speed describes how fast the computer itself works during a given operation or
task. A computer's speed is measured by its internal clock and its processors, also known as
the central processing unit (CPU).  This speed is measured in Hertz (Hz) , where 1 Hz means one
cycle per second. A cycle would just be how many times a process reoccurs.
For example, if you clap your hands once every second, you're clapping at 1 Hertz. If you clap
10 times every second, you're clapping at 10 Hertz. Hertz (Hz)  are used to describe how fast a
device runs.
Clock Speed
On a computer, laptop, tablet, or phone, the internal parts move data around using a
synchronized clock. All these devices use a master clock to stay synchronized, or to stay
working together smoothly.
The signal from the master clock is called a square wave. These square waves work for
computers because they represent binary digits: the 1s and 0s. The wave goes up and over,
then down and over in one cycle. If you see four cycles happening in one second, the clock
signal is running at 4 Hertz (4  Hz).
Over the years, processors, just like other major computer parts, have gotten better. At first,
processors were measured in Megahertz (MHz),  which means 1 million cycles per second. This
speed was common for the first 20 years of personal computers. But as technology improved
and we got to over 1000 MHz, we started measuring them in Gigahertz (GHz),  which means 1
billion cycles per second.
Today's processors usually run at between 2 and 4 GHz. The largest producers of Windows-
based CPUs, AMD and Intel, have processors that tend to run within this range. And the fastest
CPUs can reach up to 6 GHz. If your computer has a 3.4 GHz processor, it can handle 3.4
billion operations per second. Think about that for a moment: over 3 billion operations in just
one second! Can you think of any other machine that works that fast?
It's hard to get CPU speeds faster than they are now, as this amount of activity creates a lot of heat.
Heat is an enemy of computers, especially laptops.
Even though servers are powerful types of computers, they don't have specialized processors.
Servers use the same kind of processors as the ones in your home computer. They actually get
their enhanced performance from having multiple CPUs work together.

Lesson 13B
Connecting External Devices
Objectives Covered
2.4 Given a scenario, install and configure common peripheral devices.
2.5 Compare and contrast common types of input/output device interfaces.
While the internal components are what make a computer work, it is the external devices, also
called peripherals, that you see and interact with every day. Peripherals include keyboards,
mice, monitors, webcams, speakers, and other input/output devices. Understanding how to
connect, configure, and troubleshoot these devices is essential for anyone who works with
computers.
In this lesson, you will explore the different types of peripheral devices and how they connect
to a computer. You will learn about input devices like keyboards and mice, output devices like
monitors and projectors, and how to identify common ports and connectors including USB,
HDMI, DisplayPort, and audio jacks.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What are peripheral devices, and how are they classified as input or output?
• What types of connections do keyboards and mice use, and what are the advantages of
wired versus wireless?
• What ports and connectors are commonly used to attach peripherals, and how do USB,
HDMI, DisplayPort, and Thunderbolt differ?
• How do webcams, microphones, projectors, and speakers connect to a computer, and what
is casting?
• What is Plug-and-Play, and what does it mean for a device to be hot-swappable?
• How do monitors and touchscreens differ from other output devices?
Keyboard and Mouse
The majority of users interact with computers using a keyboard and mouse. Sometimes, you
may also use a touchscreen along with these devices. If your computer has a touchscreen,
you can simply touch the screen just like you would click the mouse. Additionally, in Windows,
you can bring up an onscreen keyboard, which serves as a handy alternative to the physical
keyboard.
Using the Keyboard and Mouse
A touchpad sits below the keyboard on every laptop, and you use it to move the pointer.
However, many people find the touchpad uncomfortable and prefer using an external wireless

mouse. Lenovo first made laptops with a small mouse in the middle of the keyboard, called
a trackpoint. Other laptop makers followed with similar setups, often in their business-class
systems. With some practice and finger movements, you can make the mouse pointer move
quickly around the screen.
Some keyboards have returned to an old technology that was almost abandoned because of
cost. These keyboards use mechanical switches for each key. When you press them, they make
a distinctive sound and provide tactile feedback. They are popular with programmers, gamers,
and tech enthusiasts.
Designers have created keyboards and mice to be more comfortable to use. Spending many
hours in front of a computer can cause injuries to your hands, arms, and shoulders from
repetitive movements. Ergonomic designs position the keyboard in a way that is easier on your
upper body.
Some keyboards include a built-in mouse, usually on the right side of the keys. These work
great for multimedia setups in a family room, especially when using the television.
Surprisingly, modern US and US-Int er national  keyboards have the same layout for letters and
numbers that typewriters have used since 1874. This layout is known as the QWERTY design,
named after the first six letters on the top left of the keyboard, next to the tab key. This layout
has become widely known, but it is not the only keyboard layout available. For example, French
language speakers can use a layout called AZERTY, which positions the letters for faster typing
in French.
Inventors August and William Dvorak created another layout called the Dvorak layout. This
layout aims to let you type faster and be more ergonomic. Both Microsoft and Apple allow you to
switch your keyboard to the Dvorak layout, but unless you physically move your key caps, you
will have to memorize the letter positions.
Connection Types
Wireless technology helps get rid of many cords around our computers. You can connect a
keyboard, a mouse, or both wirelessly using the same USB adapter. The input devices send
a radio frequency (RF)  signal to the adapter plugged into the computer. Bluetooth mice and
keyboards also work with laptops and sometimes desktops, just like their RF counterparts. The
operating system usually loads the drivers needed for full functionality without any issues.
However, a programmable keyboard might need a special driver to be fully operational.
While wireless connections help keep things neat, wired connections are still very popular.
Wired connections give power to the device, so you don't need to charge it separately. For
example, you don't need batteries for a wired mouse like you do for a wireless one. USB
connections are the most common type of wired connectors. Today, most new and high-quality
devices use USB Type C connectors. Even though USB Type A is older, it's still a very common
connector for input devices, and in the electrical infrastructure throughout the world. Many
homes, airports, hotels, and other public places have USB Type A ports in their electrical outlets
for charging.

Video and Audio Devices
Beyond monitors, there are many other audio and video peripherals worth understanding.
Cameras and Microphones
Laptops have had built-in webcams since the early 2000s, but they really became part of daily
use in 2020, when Zoom calls became as common as brushing your teeth. Webcams not only
let people see each other, but also usually have a microphone, making them a great substitute
for what comes standard on a laptop. They can be used for video calls, and major operating
systems have speech recognition software that uses the microphone. This software is very
good at listening to your voice and typing the words into the computer.
Tablets and smartphones also have cameras and microphones. Early phones had to have a
microphone to receive voice input, and cameras were added soon after. Camera quality kept
improving, and another camera was added to the front of tablets and phones. Taking selfies
would be very hard without the front camera on your phone. FaceTime and Google Meet let
you make video calls with friends, family, and co-workers. These features work because of the
cameras built into every mobile device.
Microphone quality can vary a lot. Some microphones sound tinny and hollow, while others
give rich, full audio close to a professional recording studio. All-in-one computers have built-in
webcams, and some headphones also include a microphone, so you can hear and talk at the
same time. People often use these headphones for online multiplayer gaming or when they want
to keep the sound from bothering others.
Network Connectivity
A smart TV adds the ability to connect to the Internet, giving users a portal to streaming
content. With this access, they can watch TV with free and paid services, listen to music, and
browse the Internet (even if browsing with your remote control is a bit cumbersome). Many
smart TVs can be joined with smart speakers, making it easy to jump into a user's favorite
shows. There are many creative uses for smart televisions. One example of this is a fitness
class that can be streamed right to the TV, bringing the gym to the family room.
One of the conveniences of a smartphone, tablet, or laptop is the ability to wirelessly connect
to a larger display. Once connected, the device can transmit audio and video. "Casting>" is a
popular way to do this. It lets your mobile device send a signal to a projector or TV. The most
popular casting options are Google Cast (used with devices like Chromecast), Apple AirPlay and
Miracast.

Projectors
Projectors work with computers to pass along what’s being displayed on the computer screen.
Most often, they will be paired with a laptop, allowing the presenter to show the small screen
to more people on the projector. The presenter can also choose to mirror the displays of the
screens, showing the same content on both, or span them in a way which allows one view
on the projector and a different display on the laptop. This can be useful for a presenter, for
example, if they are showing slides. This gives them the ability to look ahead at the next slide in
their presentation while showing the current slide to the audience.
Speakers and Headphones
Speakers and headphones let you hear sound from things like online TV, movies, live events, or
music. The operating system (OS)  on your computer also has sounds to make your experience
better and to give alerts. For example, when you start your PC, it plays a startup sound. When
you plug in a USB flash drive, Windows makes a sound to let you know it recognized the device.
Early computers had a basic internal speaker that made simple beeps to let you know if you
clicked wrong or if a program was working. Now, both speakers and headphones have gotten
much better at providing great sound. Speakers can now offer options like 5.1 surround sound
and stereo output with rich bass and treble.
High-end audio uses a format called Sony/Philips Digital Interface Format (SPDIF).  Many high-
end motherboards have this digital audio interface built into the back. To use it, you also need
speakers designed for SPDIF. This setup can provide excellent sound quality.
Connecting Audio and Video Peripherals
The 3.5mm audio jacks on the back of computers are color-coded to indicate whether they are
for input or output. There is a pink jack designated as the standard for input. This is the place
to plug in a microphone. If you are using a set of speakers or headphones, they would plug into
the green jack, which is for output. There may be additional 3.5mm ports, but these two are the
most common. Some speakers will also add another 3.5mm jack on one of the speakers to plug
in headphones.

Images © 123rf.com.
To support their mobile devices, Apple made the Lightning plug and socket, a proprietary or
special set of connectors. This plug charges the battery, moves data, and sends audio signals
to headphones and speakers. In 2021, the European Union decided that all makers of small
electronics, like smartphones, must use the USB-C  connector. Because of this, the Lightning
connector is now being switched to USB-C.
Apple also created the Thunderbolt connector, a high-speed data transfer cable and connector.
Thunderbolt connectors use the USB-C  standard, with high data transfer speeds, the ability to
charge laptops, and connect multiple monitors.
Some speakers connect through the 3.5mm audio port and add a USB Type-A connection to
boost the audio power. This works because USB provides a little bit of power. It's a handy way
to make your speakers louder without needing another power plug.

Windows Printing Facts
The following provides step-by-step details for each of these tasks, as well as how to manage

In order for your computer to send documents to a printer, several components are required.

Component Description
1. Computer The computer that will assist with routing print jobs to the printer.
2. Application The application creates print jobs and sends them to the printer.
3. Printer Driver The printer driver is software running on the system that contains

4. Connecting Medium The printer can be connected to the computer in a number of ways,

When you print a document, the following process occurs:
1. The application you are using sends the print job to the printer.

3. The printer driver will reformat the print job so the printer can understand and process it.
4. Windows waits for the printer to become available.
The printer must be:
• Turned on.
• Not jammed.
• Finished printing all other print jobs.
5. Windows moves the print job from the print queue to the printer.
6. The printer prints the document.

Printers and Scanners
Even though many organizations use digital storage, paper is still important. Printers are a key
part of today's technology and are used in many different areas. Public services, healthcare,
and schools still use printed forms and records. Businesses also need to print things like
receipts, price tags, menus, and flyers, even if they use a lot of digital systems.

Printer Basics
There are two main types of printers: laser and inkjet. Businesses, government offices, and
schools usually use laser printers, while individual consumers more commonly use inkjet
printers for convenience and cost savings. Laser printers can be combined with copiers in a
larger-scale build, ideal for many institutions, though many models can fit on a desktop. Inkjet
printers are more commonly found in the desktop size.
The laser printer uses toner cartridges filled with toner, a powder-based print medium. They
are called laser printers because they have a laser inside them, which develops the image onto
a drum, and as the drum spins, it attracts the toner, which transfers and then fuses it to the
paper. Inkjet printers use cartridges filled with ink, which are ejected onto the paper in very
small droplets.
You will find laser printers in black and white and color varieties, while inkjet printers always
print in color. Both types of printers use the same three colors: yellow, magenta, and cyan
(blue). The printer can blend these three colors to create any color of the rainbow.
You can set up a printer to work best for you. To save paper, you can print on both sides if your
printer has that feature, and you can set this option as the default in the operating system. To
save color ink or toner, you can print everything in black and white, and temporarily change the
setting to color for specific print jobs.
A fun addition to the printer family is 3D printers. They create objects in three dimensions using
resin, a liquid that hardens into solid shapes, or filament, a type of plastic string that melts and
forms layers. However, the size of their build area limits them. In consumer-level 3D printers,
this area is a square or rectangle with dimensions of around 8 inches by 7 inches by 7 inches.

Image © 123rf.com.
Scanning Technology
Some printers include software that can scan an image and "read" the characters, turning them
into a document that you can edit, search, and save like a regular document. This software
is called Optical Character Recognition (OCR).  More powerful all-in-one printers have a useful
feature called an Automatic Document Feeder (ADF),  which allows you to place a stack of
documents in the top feeder and have them scanned or copied automatically.
When it became popular to connect scanners to computers, manufacturers quickly combined
them with printers to create all-in-one devices that can print, scan, and copy. Even today, some
of these printers can also send faxes. While you might think of scanners as part of all-in-one
printers, some companies make dedicated scanners that can quickly scan documents. These
dedicated scanners are common in offices with lots of paper because they make it easy to turn
paper documents into electronic files.

Connecting Printers and Scanners
Printers connect to a computer or network using either USB, an Ethernet cable, or a wireless
connection. Almost all modern printers have USB and wireless (also called Wi-Fi) connections,
and most also have an Ethernet port. You can use USB and one of the network options at the
same time.
However, a printer can't use both wired and wireless connections at the same time because it
needs an IP address to be part of a local area network (LAN).  Most printers can only have one
IP address, so when one network connection is used, the other is turned off.
Image courtesy of CompTIA.
Uninterruptible Power Supplies
Businesses and organizations do a lot to protect their data and equipment, like creating off-site
storage and buying strong security systems. These steps are usually too expensive for most
people. So, how can the average person protect their data? One good option is to use a battery
backup system.
A battery backup stores energy to use if the main power in a building or home goes out. This
battery backup is called an uninterruptible power supply (UPS).  You place it between the wall
outlet and the devices that need emergency power. In addition to keeping power on during a
blackout, the UPS has filters that stop damage to sensitive electronics from electrical spikes and
surges. It also has multiple outlets, so you can plug in several things at once, like a computer,
monitor, network equipment, and other accessories.
All network and server setups are expected to have a battery backup. You can measure a
battery backup's capabilities in two ways: VA and run time. VA, which stands for volt-amperes,
indicates the maximum electrical load the UPS can handle. Run time tells you how many minutes
the UPS can supply power before it runs out.

Image by magraphics© 123rf.com.
Using the UPS
Unplugging a computer to turn it off isn't a good idea. It's better to use the operating system
to shut it down. Battery backups often come with software and a USB connection that monitors
the power. If there’s a power outage, the battery backup will tell the computer to shut down
properly. This stops sudden shutdowns that can harm the operating system. When the OS is
damaged, the computer might act strangely or not start up correctly.
When the UPS notices that power isn't coming in, it beeps at regular intervals. This alerts
people nearby about the power problem. You can replace the internal batteries in a UPS, so you
don't have to buy a whole new unit. This saves money and helps the environment.

Lesson 13D
Installing a Motherboard
Objectives Covered
2.2 Explain the purpose of common internal computing components.
2.3 Compare and contrast storage types.
The motherboard is the central circuit board that connects and powers all the components
of a computer. In this lesson, you will explore the different types of motherboards, their
specifications, and the role they play in both desktop and mobile devices. You will also learn
about the various buses, expansion slots, and proprietary designs found in laptops, tablets, and
smartphones.
Additionally, this lesson covers the essential firmware that controls the motherboard, including
BIOS and UEFI. You will discover how firmware starts the computer, manages hardware checks,
and how modern UEFI provides advanced features and security. By the end of this lesson, you
will understand the key steps and considerations for installing and configuring a motherboard in
a variety of devices.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is the function of a motherboard in a computer system?
• How do motherboard specifications affect compatibility with CPUs, memory, and expansion
cards?
• What are the differences between desktop and mobile (laptop, tablet, smartphone)
motherboards?
• What is the role of firmware (BIOS/UEFI)  during the boot process?
• How do you identify and install the correct motherboard for a given device?
The Motherboard
The motherboard is a large circuit board that acts like the computer's spine. It links all the parts
together and sends electrical signals between them.
As you saw in the video, motherboards come in different sizes and form factors, including
standardized designs like ATX and micro-ATX, as well as proprietary designs made for specific
systems. This topic takes a closer look at the specifications, buses, and expansion slots found
on desktop motherboards, as well as the proprietary motherboards used in laptops, tablets, and
smartphones.

Motherboard Specs
A motherboard is made to work with specific types of central processing unit (CPU)  and
memory, and will have sockets designed to hold those specific types of components. The most
widely used brands of CPU are Advanced Micro Devices (AMD)  and Intel.
AMD CPUs and Intel CPUs are very different and can't be swapped with each other. Each type
of motherboard will have sockets for certain AMD or Intel CPUs. The socket that holds the CPU
uses a zero insertion force (ZIF)  mechanism to push the processor into the motherboard and
keep it in place securely. This helps prevent the motherboard from bending, which could cause
permanent damage.
There are fewer options when it comes to memory and how it works on motherboards. Memory
types have been pretty standard over the years, with the Double Data Rate (DDR)  family
being the most common in recent decades. DDR memory changes every 4–6  years, and each
generation has different slot connectors. The latest one is DDR5. The most important thing
to remember is that as long as you match up the parts that are designed to work together
correctly, your computer will run well.
Computer Buses and Expansion Slots
The motherboard is what connects peripheral devices, such as they keyboard, mouse, printer,
and speakers, to the computer's CPU. The motherboard has all the connectors and circuits
needed for these devices to link up with the CPU. If you look closely at a motherboard, you'll
see the many connectors and ports where different computer parts can be attached. If you look
even closer, you'll notice small groups of parallel wires on the surface. These wires form buses,
which are groups of wires that connect different devices together.
A bus is a communication system that lets data move between different parts internally. The
word "bus" comes from the Latin word "omnibus," which means "for all." If you take a close look
at a motherboard, you'll notice that it has many small wires running across it. These tiny wires,
or circuits, make up the bus, which is printed on the circuit board (PCB).  The computer bus is
responsible for transferring power, data, and clock timing.
One of the great things about a motherboard is its expansion slots, which let you add more
features to your computer. Over the years, the design of these expansion buses has changed.
Because the bus design depends on the motherboard and CPU, it's good to know the types
of bus systems that have been used and are still in use. Older systems had a peripheral
component interconnect (PCI)  bus. But today's systems have what are called PCI express
(PCIe)  slots.
The PCIe slots on the Motherboard come in different sizes, x1, x2, x4, x8, and x16, with x1 and
x16 being the most common. The speed of PCIe slots has also increased over time, from 1.0 to
5.0, with each new version being twice as fast as the one before. But to take advantage of a
slot's speed, a motherboard will need to support it.

Image © 123rf.com.
When you're looking to buy a motherboard, try to get one with four memory slots. This way,
adding more memory later won't be as expensive. For example, your new computer might come
with 2 sticks of 8GB memory, for a total of 16GB. There's a chance you'll want more memory in
a couple of years. If the system you buy has four memory slots, you'll have two empty slots to
add more memory to. But if you only have two slots, you'll have to remove the old memory to
add more, which can be costly.
Laptop, Tablet, and Smartphone Motherboards
Not all motherboards follow the ATX standard. Laptops, tablets, and smartphones use
proprietary motherboard designs that are unique to each model.

Type Description
Laptop Motherboards
Laptop motherboards fall into the proprietary form
factor type.
• The motherboard and the case are designed
specifically for each model.
• If the motherboard needs to be replaced it must
be replaced with a specific model.
• Laptop motherboards are not designed to be
modular. The CPU and other components are
soldered onto the motherboard and cannot be
easily replaced.
Tablet Motherboards Like laptop motherboards, tablet motherboards are
a proprietary form factor.
• All parts, including CPU, memory, and storage,
are soldered onto the motherboard and can be
difficult to replace.
• Normally, if a tablet malfunctions the entire
device is disposed of and replaced.
Smartphone Motherboards
Like tablet motherboards, smartphone
motherboards are a proprietary form factor.
• All parts are soldered onto the motherboard and
can be difficult to be replaced.
• Normally, like a tablet, if a smartphone
malfunctions the entire device is disposed of
and replaced.
The Firmware and BIOS
When a computer is powered on, the basic input/output system (BIOS)  or Unified Extensible
Firmware Interface (UEFI)  is what starts up and checks the hardware components on the
motherboard. This is the beginning of the boot process. It happens before the operating system
loads and is made possible by a low-level set of instructions called firmware—that's what the
BIOS and UEFI both are. The UEFI is responsible for the power-on self-test (POS T)  and is the
first software to run when a computing device starts up.

The term BIOS has been used for so long (many decades, in fact) that it's hard for techs to switch
and call it UEFI. If you hear someone mention a motherboard's BIOS, they probably mean UEFI,
unless it's a very old system.
The BIOS provides industry-standard code that starts up the essential parts of the computer by
performing checks on critical hardware components such as RAM, CPU, and peripherals. You
won't see this very often, though. Most motherboards nowadays use the newer UEFI firmware.
UEFI has a modern look, supports bigger storage drives, lets you use a mouse, and has better
security when booting. And computers with UEFI can start up in the old BIOS mode if needed.
You can upgrade the UEFI by "flashing" the code on its read-only memory (ROM)  chip. This
is best done from time to time to help the motherboard work better. You can download the
new firmware from the PC manufacturer, such as HP or Lenovo. Or if you have a custom-built
system, you can get the firmware from the motherboard manufacturer instead—ASUSTeK and
GIGABYTE are popular ones. The UEFI is non-volatile, which means it keeps its settings even
when the computer is turned off.
The term "flashing" dates back to early BIOS chips, which were literally flashed to update the
coding. This was done with a beam of light that erased the chip and allowed it to be reprogrammed.

Lesson 13E
Connecting Internal Components
Objectives Covered
2.2 Explain the purpose of common internal computing components.
2.3 Compare and contrast storage types.
1.4 Explain the troubleshooting methodology.
A computer is made up of many internal components that work together to process information,
store data, and display output. Understanding what these parts do, how they connect, and how
to troubleshoot them will help you make informed decisions when upgrading, purchasing, or
repairing a computer.
In this lesson, you will explore the central processing unit (CPU)  and how it connects to the
motherboard, how memory (RAM)  temporarily stores data for fast access, and how storage
drives keep your files safe when the power is off. You will also learn about graphics processing
units (GPUs),  sound cards, and power supplies, and discover basic troubleshooting steps for
diagnosing common hardware problems.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What does a CPU do, and how do Intel and AMD processors connect to the motherboard
differently?
• What is the difference between volatile memory (RAM)  and non-volatile storage (HDD ,  SSD)?
• How do DDR generations improve memory performance, and what is a DIMM?
• When would you need a dedicated GPU instead of integrated graphics?
• What does a power supply do, and how do you determine the right wattage for a system?
• What are the first steps you should take when troubleshooting a hardware problem like no
power or no display?
The Central Processing Unit (CPU)
As you learned in the video, the central processing unit (CPU)  is the computer's brain,
processing billions of instructions per second at speeds measured in GHz. This topic takes
a closer look at the different CPU manufacturers and connection types, optimization features
like multi-core processing and cache memory, and the cooling systems that keep CPUs running
safely.
CPUs are also categorized by the number of bits they can process at one time. Modern CPUs
process 64 bits, while older ones processed 32 bits. A 64-bit CPU handles 64 bits of data at
once, making it faster than a 32-bit CPU.

CPU Manufacturers
Intel and AMD are the main companies that make processors for consumers and servers, and
they've led the market since the late 1970s.
Different CPUs connect to the motherboard in different ways. All Intel CPUs use a land grid
array (L G A)  design, which means they have hundreds of little pads on the underside. Most
AMD CPUs use a pin grid array (PG A)  design, which means they have hundreds (sometimes
thousands) of pins.
These pins or pads fit into the motherboard socket, which has the same layout. So, if an AMD
CPU has pins, the motherboard will have an equal number of matching pads.
Image ©123rf.com.
In the last decade, at time of writing, Apple started making its own CPUs for its systems. Apple
doesn't call them just CPUs because its chips have the memory built in. This includes not
just the cache memory but also the main memory, which Apple calls unified memory, used by
the computer. With the memory and CPU 'under the same umbrella,' computing time is faster.
Another improvement in Apple silicon is its efficient processing, which doesn't use a lot of
power, leading to longer battery life on its laptops.
Another important type of processor is the ARM processor. These processors use a simpler set
of instructions for computing and are very common in smartphones and other mobile devices.

Optimizing CPUs
As computers got faster, manufacturers wanted to make CPUs even quicker. They did this by
adding more "brains" or cores onto a single chip. Today, CPUs have multiple cores to boost
computing power. CPUs can have 4, 8, 16, or even more cores.
CPUs can also almost double their computing power without adding another core. Intel calls this
hyperthreading, and AMD calls it simultaneous multi-threading.
CPUs have a small amount of cache memory. Cache is a special type of memory that stores
data the CPU uses frequently, making it faster for the CPU to access this data. Adding cache
memory helps the CPU work even faster.
Even though CPUs don't have moving parts, they get very hot. This is because they process
billions of instructions every second. To keep them cool, they are built with both active and
passive cooling. Manufacturers will use a heatsink, thermal paste, and a fan to remove the hot
air, depending on the size of the computing device.
Images ©123rf.com.
The Memory
As you saw in the video, random-access memory (RAM)  is the computer's short-term memory.
It temporarily stores the programs and data the CPU is actively using. RAM is volatile, meaning
everything in it is lost when the computer is turned off. This topic explores the differences
between volatile and non-volatile memory, memory features like DDR generations and dual-
channel architecture, and how to determine the right amount of memory for your needs.
You might wonder, why not use the storage drive that already holds everything? The problem is
that storage drives, like mechanical drives and solid-state drives, are too slow to keep up with
a CPU. If storage replaced memory and interacted with the CPU instead, the computer would
move very slowly.

Volatile vs Non-Volatile Memory
Random access memory (RAM)  and read-only memory (ROM),  used in the firmware and BIOS
system, might look similar at first glance. Despite both being pieces of memory, they do serve
different purposes.
Random access memory (RAM)  has these features:
• Volatile: Stores data temporarily, while the computer is powered on, and does not save data
while the computer is turned off.
• Fast: Data can move in and out of RAM very quickly, making it easy for the computer to
process many instructions at once.
• Removable: Memory modules or sticks clip into slots on the motherboard, and can be
replaced as needed.
Read-only memory (ROM)  has these features:
• Non-volatile: Stores data permanently, even without power.
• Slow: Data retrieval from ROM is a comparatively lengthy process, and ROM does not
contribute to processing speed.
• Permanent: Manufacturers permanently attach ROM chips to boards within devices.
• Programmable: Some types of ROM have code or instructions that can be rewritten when
needed, such as when firmware updates are released.
Memory Features
Many of today's desktops, laptops, and smartphones have between 6GB and 16GB of memory.
If you want a more powerful system, you can add more RAM, maybe 32GB or more, and servers
can have even more memory. These aren't strict rules, though. Servers might have more or less
RAM, and you can add as much memory as your motherboard can handle.
When you look at a memory stick, you'll see gold contacts on both sides. This is called a dual
inline memory module (DIMM).  DIMMs were introduced in the 1990s and are still the standard
format for memory today.

Image © 123rf.com.
Memory has other characteristics in addition to its capacity. Memory speed doubled around
2000, or the turn of the 21st Century. This faster speed was termed Double Data Rate (DDR)
and speed jumped up to 200 MHz (megahertz, or one million hertz), twice as fast as previous
memory rates. As the industry continued to improve, memory moved on to DDR2 a few years
later, doubling in speed again. Every following generation of DDR has doubled the speed of the
previous generation and has followed the basic naming structure. From DDR3 to DDR4 to DDR5
in today's computers, at the time of writing.
Another characteristic of memory is that it’s interchangeable across different brands and
models of computers. For example, if you have a new HP computer and want to put some
of that memory into a new Dell, you can easily do that. This works because both use DDR5
memory, so it will work in either system. However, one tech company doesn’t always follow
the same rules: Apple. Unfortunately, on their laptops and all-in-one systems, they solder the
memory onto the motherboard, making it impossible to change.

Image © 123rf.com.
When a computer crashes a lot, a bad memory stick could be the reason. Windows includes a
built-in tool to test the memory. You can find it by typing ‘Windows Memory Diagnostic’ in the
Start search box. This program takes some time to run, depending on how much memory your
computer has. To check all the memory, the tool reboots your computer and starts checking the
RAM before loading Windows again.
How Much Memory?
One of the most important things to understand about computers is that memory handles what
is actively loaded when your computer is turned on. People often ask, "How much memory
should I have?" The answer depends on how many programs you run and how many tabs you
have open during a computing session.
For example, if you only work with one program at a time and close it before opening another,
you don’t need a lot of memory; 8GB would be fine. However, if you multitask with multiple
programs and lots of tabs in your browser, you’ll want more memory. Consider getting 16GB to
help your system run smoothly while you switch between websites and programs.
The future of memory technology looks bright. Manufacturers keep increasing memory
capacity, and this trend will likely continue. The growth in memory capacity has been amazing,
with computers now having over 50 times the storage they did just 25 years ago.
Manufacturers also focus on using less power, especially for laptops, to extend battery life.
Additionally, memory speeds are getting faster, which helps make computers run more quickly
overall.

The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)
As you learned in the video, a graphics processing unit (GPU)  handles all of a computer's visual
output. Most Intel CPUs include integrated graphics that share system RAM with the CPU, which
is enough for basic tasks. Most AMD CPUs need a separate graphics card. This topic covers
dedicated graphics cards for high-performance needs, as well as resolution, frame rates, and
the specialized memory that makes modern GPUs so powerful.
Enhanced Graphics
Computers that are used for gaming, video editing, and 3D modeling and animation need a
dedicated GPU for more powerful graphics processing. In order to provide this additional power,
you can install a dedicated graphics card. The best dedicated graphics cards, also called video
cards, are expensive because they include the graphics chip, along with their own specialized
RAM and cooling.
Video cards offer multiple outputs, like HDMI and display ports, so you can connect more than
one monitor. Also, remember that graphics cards use a PCIe x16 interface to install into the
motherboard of a desktop computer.
There is a graphics card for every budget. Integrated graphics are the cheapest, while high-end
graphics cards can cost a lot of money, sometimes over $1,000. Many companies make video
cards and GPUs, but Nvidia is the biggest and most popular one in the market.
Image by nikkytok © 123rf.com.

Resolution and Frame Rate
A video card makes incredibly realistic images by using higher resolution, faster frame rates,
and special video memory.
Video resolution is represented by two numbers. These numbers tell you how many pixels make
up the image, both across (horizontally) and up and down (vertically) on a screen. For example,
a common resolution is 1920 x 1080, also called 1080p. Higher resolution means more pixels,
which gives you more realistic images with better details. Moving up to 4K displays means a
resolution of 3840 x 2160, which is twice as good as 1080p.
Frame rates are measured in Hertz (Hz),  which describes how often a display updates. A higher
frame rate makes graphics and animations look smoother, especially when the action gets
faster. Frame rates range from 30–60  frames per second (fps) and can go up to 120 fps on
some high-end graphics cards. Also, ray tracing is a technique that makes the lighting in a
scene look real by accurately showing reflections and shadows, just like in real life.
Video cards and their GPUs have their own processing and memory systems. This is similar to,
but slightly different from, the CPU's processing capabilities. The GPU has cores, or individual
processors, that are designed to speed up graphics processing. These cores work together to
handle multiple tasks at the same time. Because they compute at a very high rate, they also
have fans to keep the unit cool.
The video card also has memory that is different from traditional memory. The GPU video
memory is specialized for fast rendering, made to meet the specific needs of a GPU. A modern
video card might have 16GB of Graphics Double Data Rate (GDDR6)  memory. The ability to
handle a lot of smaller tasks very quickly is one of the strengths of a GPU that makes it ideal for
artificial intelligence (AI),  as well as video and graphics development.
