Lesson 14A
Understanding Networks
Objectives Covered
2.2 Explain the purpose of common internal computing components.
2.5 Compare and contrast common types of input/output device interfaces.
2.8 Identify basic networking concepts.
Networks are everywhere. Every time you check your email, stream a video, pay with a credit
card, or connect your phone to a Bluetooth speaker, you are relying on a network to move
information between devices. Understanding how networks work is essential for anyone who
uses modern technology, whether at home, at school, or in the workplace.
In this lesson, you will explore what a network is, how computers communicate using the client/
server model and protocols, and the key components needed for a network connection. You
will compare wired and wireless connections, learn how Ethernet cables are built and tested,
and discover the protocols that make web browsing, email, file transfer, and troubleshooting
possible.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What are the three components every computer needs to participate in a network?
• How do a client and a server establish a connection using the three-way handshake?
• What are the main differences between wired and wireless network connections?
• How is an Ethernet cable constructed, and what tools are used to make one?
• What do protocols like TCP, UDP, HTTP, and DNS do, and how do they work together?
• What utilities can you use to troubleshoot network connectivity problems?
What is a Network to Me?
Whether you realize it or not, you are always surrounded by networks that constantly share
information. The ideas about time and place are changing. The world feels like a global village
where distance doesn't stop you from connecting for business, school, or social reasons. If you
live in an area with a strong digital infrastructure, it's hard to imagine life without all the network
systems that are so important to your daily life.
You might think of things like secure browsing and email as obvious examples of networking,
but there are other ways networks impact the way you live.
Networks in Daily Life
Every time you use a debit or credit card, the store's register is connected to other computers
through a network. Your card details are automatically sent to your bank or credit card company

to check and update your balance. This also happens when you shop online, such as when you
purchase a movie ticket or order food through a delivery app.
The world of entertainment is also more and more dependent on networks. When you connect
your mobile device to your Bluetooth earbuds, a wireless speaker, or connect to your car, you
have a direct connection from one device to another. A short-range connection like this is also
known as a personal area network (P AN).  Streaming services have changed how we watch
television, movies, and more. Digital cameras can connect directly to local networks, making it
easier for more people to create and share content.
In addition to their impact on leisure time, networks bring safety into people’s lives. Networked
communication systems are important for controlling transportation. They help manage things
like traffic lights, pedestrian crossings, air traffic control, and train signals.
Networks are a bigger part of your life than you might have thought. They are involved in almost
every part of modern life. When you understand them better, you can make your personal
devices work better for you. If you really like learning about how networks work, there are many
job opportunities in many different fields that focus specifically on network operations.
What Does a Network Do?
A network is a group of computer systems connected together so they can share information.
The Internet is the largest possible example of this. In a network, all the computers can ask for
and send information, but usually most computers ask for information, and only a few send it
out.
Think of a computer network like a school. Most of the computers on a typical network are like
students who take instructions and receive information. A few computers are like teachers who
give out the information. It's most likely that you're using one of the many devices that receive
information, such as when you click on the next page in this course, or when you check your
email. The computers that give you this data are part of a smaller group that shares out data
with you and with people all over the world.
For computers to share information over a network, several key components must be in place.
Each computer must have network media, a network interface, and network protocols.
• Network media: The pathways that connect computers together. Media, when we're talking
about networking, describes the different ways we store or transfer information. Computers
move information across wired connections using coaxial cables, Ethernet cables, or fiber
optic wire. Information can also move wirelessly, through radio signals in Wi-Fi. Computers
must have either a wired or a wireless connection to be part of a network.
• Network interface: An interface is the point at which two different systems interact with
each other. A network interface is where your computer makes a connection to the bigger
network. Each computer needs to have a network interface, which is a special spot for it
to plug into the network (with cables) or to connect wirelessly. This is typically done using
a piece of hardware called a network interface card (NIC).  NICs are often included in the
original computer build, but can be added later if your computer doesn't come with one. If
you upgrade your system with a NIC after you buy it, this is called an expansion card, and
it's easily installed on your computer's motherboard.
• Network protocols: A shared set of protocols, or rules, serves as a common language among
computers. These rules are set up at the operating system (OS)  level. All the computers on
the network must use the same protocols so that they can understand each other as they
share data back and forth.

Using Networking Components
A wired system, one that uses cables to connect to the network, will most often use Ethernet
cabling as its network media. Those cables use specialized sockets and plugs to make this
connection. The IT industry calls these RJ-45  or registered jack type 45. The RJ-45  standard
makes it easy for industry professionals and for computer manufacturers to create network
connections. The RJ-45  plug or clip attaches to the ends of the cable. One end plugs into your
computer, and the other end plugs into the socket on the wall plate. On the other side of the wall
plate is another network cable. If you're at home, this belongs to the internet service provider
(ISP).  If you're at work or at school, this network cable belongs to the organization, and it runs
to other networking devices before connecting to the Internet.
Images © 123rf.com.
Wireless networks use radio signals instead of cables to communicate. Connecting to a Wi-
Fi network is a bit more complex. A computer needs a wireless network interface. Different
computers have different ways of connecting to Wi-Fi. Many desktop computers already have
Wi-Fi built in, but others need something called a wireless network adapter. The easiest way to
add Wi-Fi to these computers is by plugging a small device called a USB wireless adapter into a
USB slot. Laptops usually have Wi-Fi built in, so you don't have to add anything. But you might
have to turn the Wi-Fi on.
Once you have a wireless network adapter set up, or you have your laptop's Wi-Fi turned on,
you can then connect to a Wi-Fi network. On a Windows computer, click on the Network icon
that's usually at the bottom-right of your screen. A menu will pop up showing all the Wi-Fi
networks it can find nearby. Pick the one you want to join and click "Connect." Then, if it asks
for it, type in the Wi-Fi password and click "Next." Some public Wi-Fi networks in places like
cafés or libraries won't need a password.
Connecting to a Network
For computers that use Windows, Microsoft has set up a few ways to check if your computer
is hooked up to a network or the Internet. One way is by looking at a special icon that appears

in the bottom-right corner of the screen, in the area called the system tray. If your computer is
connected with a cable, you'll see an icon that looks like a computer. If you're using Wi-Fi, you'll
see an icon with curved lines that look like waves. The number of waves shows how strong your
signal is. If you can't connect to the internet, the icon changes to a picture of a globe with a
"no" symbol over it.
Used with permission from Microsoft.
Going further into Windows Settings gives you more details about your computer's connections.
The network settings tell you if you're connected with a cable or wirelessly, and they also show
you other options you have, like to use VPNs, share your internet with other devices as a mobile
hotspot, or use proxies.

Used with permission from Microsoft.
Wired Network Connectors
This topic looks more closely at the twisted pair copper cables used inside homes and offices,
specifically how Ethernet cables are built, and you can make your own.
Image by Thuansak Srilao © 123rf.com.

Inside an Ethernet cable, there are eight wires grouped into four twisted pairs. Each pair is
assigned a color: orange, green, blue, or brown. One wire's insulator (the plastic covering) is
mostly white, striped with the color, and the second wire has an insulator with a solid color.
When you're ready to connect the wires, you need to untwist them and line them up in a certain
order in the connectors. This order can follow either the T568A or the T568B standard.
The order of the colors is important because devices can't communicate properly without the
correct alignment.
Images © 123rf.com.
In T568A, the green pairs are wired to pins 1 and 2, and the orange pairs are wired to pins 3 and
6. In T568B, these pairs swap places, so orange is terminated to pins 1 and 2 and green to 3
and 6. It's important to avoid using a mixture of the two standards. T568B is probably the more
widely deployed of the two.
Making Cables
You can make Ethernet cables yourself with some tools and a little bit of know-how. Raw cables
are sold in large hardware and home improvement stores, as well as online, in lengths of 100 to
1,000 feet. You can then cut these lengths to the exact size you need. After cutting, you'd either
attach RJ-45  clips to the ends or connect the cable to a wall jack.
Learning to make cables yourself is useful if you want to get a job in IT eventually. Sometimes,
you'll need a cable with a specific length, but you won't have one that's the right size. Also,
when you need to run cables to devices, especially through ceilings and walls, it's easier to
move them around without the RJ-45  clips getting in the way.
Here are some of the basic tools needed to make your own Ethernet cables:
• Crimper: A crimper is a tool that helps connect an RJ-45  cable to its clip. To do this, you
first make sure that the eight wires inside the cable are in the right order according to the
T568 standard you're using. Then, you put them into the clip, and next, into the crimper. You
squeeze the crimper to secure everything together. After you've done this on both ends of
the cable, you should use a cable tester to check if all the wires are set up correctly.
• Punch Down: A punch-down tool is used to push each of the eight wires into a patch
panel or a wall jack. When you press the cable into the right spot with this tool, it makes a
satisfying click sound. Before you start punching, it's very important to check that the tool is
facing the right way so everything is done correctly.
• Cable Tester: A cable tester checks if a new cable, or one already connected to a patch
panel or wall jack, is working. It quickly tells you the status of each of the 8 wires. The tester

uses lights or an LED screen to show you the statuses so that you know if the cable was
made in the right way. More complex testers can even tell you how long a cable is.
• Toner Probe: A toner probe is a useful tool for figuring out where a network cable starts or
ends. It comes in two pieces. One piece plugs into the network, usually at a wall socket, and
emits a sound or a tone (that's why it's called a toner). The other piece is the probe, which
you move over the various network cables to listen for that sound. This helps you determine
which cable goes with which port. It's a big time-saver, especially when the network cables
aren't clearly marked.
Wireless Network Connectors
An access point (AP)  allows wireless or mobile devices to connect to the network. The AP
can connect to the network using a cabled connection, and can provide wireless connections
to other devices such as smartphones, tablets, and laptops. At first, only large companies
and government organizations had APs, but now anyone can have them at home, with new
improvements in technology. When you have several APs working together, it's called a mesh
network, which works great for covering large areas with Wi-Fi.
Images © 123rf.com.
Most of the time, enterprise APs are connected to the main network with an Ethernet cable.
But the ones you might have at home usually just pass the Wi-Fi signal from one AP to another
without cables. You could buy packages of two, three, or more APs to put around your house if
you wanted. Then all your devices would have a stronger Wi-Fi connection. The more coverage
you need, the more APs you could add.
Common Networking Protocols
Beyond those core protocols, there are additional protocols and tools worth understanding for
email, file transfer, network management, and troubleshooting.

Email Protocols
You just pressed send on an email message. How will it get to the recipient? What protocols are
used to send and receive email? Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)  is the protocol used to
send messages from one person to another. There are two common protocols you should know
about for retrieving messages:
• Post Office Protocol (POP)  version 3:  POP3 is an older protocol that is being replaced by
IMAP. It allows for email messages to be retrieved on a single computer. It is important to
know that POP3 removes the message from the email server and stores it on the device
used to access email. These messages will not be accessible by other computers.
• Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)  4 : This protocol is preferred to get your email
messages. It keeps the message on the server but allows you to modify it as if it were stored
locally. As a result, multiple devices (computer, phone, etc.) can be used to access the email
messages.
File Transfer Protocols
File transfer protocols provide the ability to send and receive files over the internet.
• File Transfer Protocol (FTP):  This is the standard protocol used to transfer files between a
client and a server.
• SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP):  This is the secure version of FTP that uses another
protocol called SSH or Secure Shell Protocol to protect the information being transferred.
Network Services
There are many protocols in this category but we selected one common protocol that you
should know about.
• Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP):  DHCP helps network administrators assign IP
addresses to the devices on their networks. Instead of going to each device and manually
configuring the IP address, DHCP will assign an address when the device connects to the
network.
Common Troubleshooting Utilities
Utilities are small programs that are built into the operating system. There are two commonly
used methods to solve network problems.
• The ping utility sends a message from one computer to a target computer over a network
and then listens for a response. This utility allows you to perform a quick test to determine if
there is connectivity between the computers. If it doesn’t get a response, there’s something
wrong with the connection. If it does, then you know there is a physical connection and the
IP address configuration is correct, and you need to look somewhere else.
• The tracert utility follows the path of a packet of information across the network to its
destination. It displays each router, called a hop, through which the information passes on
its way. It usually lists the hop number, the time it took, and the IP address and name if
available. It is used to see if one of the links takes a long time, indicating a problem. If it
stops and displays timeout messages, then you know something is blocking that path. That
is where you need to start looking.

Lesson 14B
Using Network Types
Objectives Covered

2.5 Compare and contrast common types of input/output device interfaces.
Networks come in many shapes and sizes, from a small home setup connecting a few devices
to a massive corporate system spanning entire countries. Understanding the different types of
networks and how they are organized helps you make better decisions about how to connect,
share resources, and stay productive.
In this lesson, you will explore the different types and sizes of networks, including PANs, LANs,
and WANs. You will learn how network topologies describe the physical and logical layout
of connected devices, compare the client-server and peer-to-peer networking models, and
discover how wireless technologies like Bluetooth and mobile hotspots let you connect on the
go.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What are the different types of networks based on size, and how do PANs, LANs, and WANs
differ?
• What are common network topologies, and how do they affect performance and reliability?
• How do the client-server and peer-to-peer networking models differ?
• What are the key features and advantages of a local area network?
• How do wide area networks connect distant locations, and what role do VPNs play?
• How do Bluetooth and mobile hotspots provide wireless connectivity between devices?
Network Server
In the client-server model, servers are dedicated computers that provide services to all the
clients on the network. Examples of network services include email, file sharing, online gaming,
voice over IP, and printing. By consolidating all network services to a server, clients can all
have equal, unrestricted access to the services. The table below describes a few basic kinds
of servers. Keep in mind that each of these services can be consolidated on the same physical
hardware.

Table 30:  Server Types
Term Description
Mail Server Mail servers provide email service to a network. In many ways, they're
like virtual post offices. They store incoming mail and send outgoing
messages, either to users on the same network or on other networks
around the world.
Web Server Every site you've visited on the World Wide Web, including this one, has
been hosted on a web server. Web servers store web pages as hypertext
documents. Whenever they get a request for one of their pages, they
transmit the appropriate file to the requester using HTTP.
Database Server Database servers store databases, which are huge repositories of
organized data. Clients on the network can send queries to the database
server, which returns specific information about the data. Clients can also
use queries to add, remove, or change data as appropriate.
Gaming Server Gaming servers keep track of events in multiplayer video games. Most
online games have players simultaneously sending inputs via their mouse
and keyboard (or controller). The game server receives all these inputs
and re-transmits them to the other players, making the game play out in
real time for everyone involved.
Networking Models
There are two important models that describe how computers interact on a network: client-
server and peer-to-peer.
The client-server relationship is a basic concept in networking. It's one way of looking at how
one computer (a server) and another computer (the client) on the same network talk. The client
requests information and resources, and the server fulfills those client requests. The servers
are powerful, dependable computers that are expected to be available all the time, every day,
without taking a break.
In addition to the client-server model, where one computer requests and others respond,
computers can have a peer-to-peer relationship model. It's a meeting of two equals. Both
computers can request resources, and both can provide resources to fulfil those requests.
Peer-to-peer architecture allows smaller groups to share information just as easily as groups
with more computing power. Peer-to-peer architecture makes it easier to share files, stream
video, and resist security threats.
Local Network Types
A local area network (LAN)  is a group of connected computers that are physically close, usually
in the same building. These computers are linked up using a centralized device called a switch.
Think about a school's computer lab, where all the computers are connected. Everyone could
save their work on the same computer, or to the same server, or print out documents on the
same printer. Everyone uses the same Wi-Fi from the same router to get to the internet. Your
home probably has a LAN, too, with your family's phones, tablets, and computers sharing the
internet through a router.

Images © 123rf.com.
LANs can be small, like the Wi-Fi network at your house, or they can be much bigger, like in
a large company. That's called an enterprise network. Setting up a LAN has lots of benefits.
For example, every computer or device on this type of network can share resources with each
other. The most important thing they can share is an Internet connection. They can also share
files, printers, and anything else on the network itself.
Local Area Network Examples
An intranet is a private LAN, a bit like a miniature Internet that's just for people in the same
company or organization. It works a lot like the Internet, but it's not part of the global Internet
that everyone in the world uses. Only people who with permission can get access. Intranets are

great for sharing files and collaborating together at work. You can share all sorts of things like
documents, spreadsheets, or slideshows. And these files are stored safely, can be backed up,
and can be shared over and over again without the worry of being stolen by someone from the
outside.
You might hear the term small office, home office (SOHO).  This is a network made for a small
business that you can set up in any office space or at home. The most important part of this
setup is the router. A SOHO router can do more than the regular routers people have at home.
Thanks to technology getting better over the last few years, working from home has become a
lot easier and more common. A SOHO is a great option for this scenario.
Key Features of Local Area Networks
There are some primary elements that make up a LAN. First, there are one or more people
called network administrators who oversee the LAN. These admins try to make sure that
everything on the LAN is safe, and they decide who can use what. If you were an admin,
you could control other computers on the network right from your own computer! This remote
access can help save a lot of time, especially when there may be hundreds of computers
connected to the network.
A LAN network is typically very fast, because all the devices are close to each other. It
uses network devices called switches and routers to connect all these close-together pieces.
Switches help move data around, and the router manages the connection to the wider internet.
To keep everything secure, a LAN will also have firewall put in place. These might be built in
to the router or be a separate device that stops hackers from getting in. Security is important
because a LAN also connects to the Internet.
One of the best things about a LAN is that everyone can share one internet connection, which
means you only have to pay for one internet service provider (ISP).  And things like printers can
be shared, so you don't need as many extra devices cluttering up space. The sharing resources
part is a huge benefit of learning how to set up a LAN.
Wide Area Network Types
Large organizations link many local area network (LANs)  together to make a wide area network
(W AN)  that can cover huge areas, like whole countries or even the whole world. For example,
if you have an enterprise that has a headquarters and branch offices spread across different
cities, each branch will have its own LAN, and all these company LANs will be connected into
the larger WAN. A router is usually used to make the connection between a LAN and a WAN, but
sometimes dedicated telecommunication lines are used as well.
A private network is how businesses keep their data safe from the outside Internet. Only
computers authorized by the company can use their network. This is essential for those
companies that want to keep their internal information secret.
WANs are managed from one central location so that the IT team can look after the whole
network from one place. This is possible because the same rules apply everywhere, no matter
the location. This makes the job a lot easier.
WANs provide many advantages, such as allowing all users in a company to use the same
applications, firewall, and resources. This is beneficial because otherwise each device would
have to be installed on individual machines, costing more time and money. The biggest
advantage of the WAN is seamless communication and sharing of information across the
organization.
Many WANs are used with a virtual private network (VPN).  A VPN allows users in remote
locations to use the Internet to connect to a WAN and access all the network resources as

though they were in their company's main office. The VPN keeps the network private through
data encryption.
Wide Area Network Examples
A metropolitan area network (MAN)  links smaller LANs into one larger, centralized network.
Think of it like this: if each LAN is a small neighborhood, then a MAN is a big city that connects
all those neighborhoods together. A MAN is bigger than a neighborhood but not as huge as a
whole country (that's what a WAN is like). You'll probably find MANs used mostly by colleges,
big cities, or even by towns that are close to each other.
There are also wide area networks based in the cloud. One example would be Amazon Web
Services (A WS).  It uses the power of cloud networks to stay turned on almost all the time and
has the flexibility to shrink or grow depending on what a specific company needs.
The Internet is really just a giant WAN that connects lots of smaller networks from all around the
world. The difference is that where many WANs are privately owned, the Internet is for everyone.

Every time you browse the web, stream a video, or send an email, your data passes through a
series of networking devices that guide it to the right destination. Understanding what these
devices do and how they work together is essential for anyone who uses or manages a
network, whether at home or in a business environment.
In this lesson, you will explore the roles of modems, router, switches, and firewalls, and learn
how network interface card connect your devices to the network. You will also examine network
addresses, ports, and protocols, and compare the different types of Internet connections
available today, including cable, DSL, fiber, cellular, satellite, and fixed wireless.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What do modems, routers, switches, and firewalls do, and how do they work together in a
network?
• What is a network interface card (NIC),  and how does it connect a device to a network?
• What is the difference between a physical (MA C)  address and a logical (IP)  address?
• What are network ports, and how do they help direct traffic to the correct service?
• How do cable, DSL, fiber, and cellular Internet connections differ in speed, equipment, and
availability?
• When might satellite or fixed wireless Internet be the best option, and what are their
limitations?
Networking Devices
This topic covers additional details about modems, router types and configuration, switch
features like PoE and VLANs, and how firewalls protect your network.
Modem
A modem is a device that takes the signals from your internet service provider (ISP)  and
translates them into a form your devices can understand. It "modulates" and "demodulates" the
signals, which is how it got its name.

A modem maintains your connection to the ISP. It sits between two networks, your own home
local area network (LAN)  and your ISP's network, and allows data to move between the two.
Usually, your ISP will provide the modem for you, though you can purchase and use your own.
On the consumer side (that's your side), the plugs are made to be universal, so just about any
device with a network connection can join up. In most cases, the modem will probably come
with a router as well, which lets you connect your devices either with cables or wirelessly.
Router
A router moves data between networks using IP addresses. Inside most home routers, there is
also a built-in switch that handles local traffic. Routers have Ethernet ports on the back where
you can plug in devices such as your desktop computer. They also send out Wi-Fi signals so
that your phones, tablets, laptops, and smart home devices, the ones on the Internet of Things
(Io T),  can connect to the internet wirelessly.
Image © 123rf.com.
Routers are available in two different types:
• Consumer routers: These are ideal for small offices or homes, because their signal strength
is not very strong, and is best suited to smaller areas. Consumer routers offer both wired and
wireless connection options.
• Commercial routers: This type of router has both a stronger signal and higher capacity,
making it perfect for large companies that rely on constant traffic management. Commercial
routers offer only wired connections.
Routers have an area called the interface that you can access either on a web browser or with
a command line interface (CLI).  On the interface, you can set things up the way you want, such
as giving your Wi-Fi network a name or setting a password. Maintain your router by updating its
firmware whenever a new version becomes available.

Switch
Switches can be small, with just 4 connection ports, or very large, with up to 96. Each port has
an RJ-45  connection for your Ethernet cable.
Some switches can send electricity through the cables along with the data. This is called Power
over Ethernet (P oE).  It's handy for devices like Wi-Fi routers, security cameras, and office
phones that require power to work. Some switches also have ports for fiber cables, which let
data travel over longer distances.
There are two types of switches:
• Unmanaged switches: This type of switch allows you to simply plug in an Ethernet cable,
and it will work. An unmanaged switch does not allow for any type of configuration or
changes to its performance.
• Managed switches: This type of switch lets the user control how it operates or configure
its settings. One example of this feature is the ability to set up a Virtual LAN (VLAN)  on a
managed switch. This allows you to make a small, separate network within a larger one. It's
like having a private room in a big house, where only certain devices are allowed in.
Firewall
In practice, every network that connects to the Internet needs a firewall. Your home router has
one built in, and businesses use dedicated firewall appliances with more advanced features.
Firewalls are like filters. They let good data in and keep bad data out. How can data be bad?
One example of bad data is when someone might try to send packets of data programmed to
steal your personal information or a company's top-secret files.
Firewalls can help by splitting the network into separate areas that keep critical systems sealed
off from the internet. Additionally, they can manage virtual private networks (VPNs),  which let
data tunnel safely through the internet, encrypted.
Network Ports
When your computer is part of a network, it's moving a lot of information very quickly. The
network needs to have rules, or protocols, to help guide the traffic so it gets to the right place.
Just like the post office accurately delivers your mail by reading your street address and postal
code on the envelope, network traffic is easier to manage with network identifiers such as IP
addresses and ports.
Network ports are unique numbers that the operating system assigns to different types of
network traffic. They work like parts of a mailing address, sending deliveries to specific
places. Port numbers help to direct the information on a network, depending on what kind
of information it is. For example, when you send an email to your co-worker, the bundle of data
includes the port number 587. It's like a special ticket that sends the data to a corresponding
port on your co-worker's computer.
Some port numbers are reserved for the most common services, like email or for transferring
files. Other services get a port number only when they're in use. Once that service is done
using the port, the number goes back to being unassigned. Some types of ports are turned off.
Just as warehouse doors can be opened or shut, closed ports mean you cannot enter.
Port Forwarding
Port forwarding is like telling a letter carrier to send your mail to a new address if you're not at
home. You would still want to receive your information, even if you were at a different location.

That's essentially what you're telling the router or firewall it has to do with the packets of
information when you use port forwarding.
A common port for this is port 3389, used for the remote desktop protocol (RDP)  on a graphical
user interface (GUI).  This basically lets you connect to any other Windows computer anywhere
in the world!
To make this happen, you have to set things up correctly on both computers and the internet
router, which is a bit like making sure both doors are unlocked and open so you can walk
through.

Port Scanning
Network administrators use port scanning tools to check which ports are open on a computer
or server. A port scan sends requests to a range of port numbers and reports back which ones
responded. This helps administrators understand what services are running on a device and
identify potential security risks.
An open port means a service is actively listening for connections on that port number. For
example, if a port scan shows that ports 80 (HTTP)  and 443 (HTTPS)  are open, you know
the device is running a web server. If unexpected ports are open, it could indicate a security
vulnerability that needs to be addressed.
Port scans typically report ports in one of three states:
• Open: A service is actively listening and accepting connections on this port.
• Closed: The port is accessible but no service is listening on it.

• Filtered: A firewall or other security device is blocking access to the port, so its status
cannot be determined.
Port scanning is an important part of network security. By regularly scanning the devices
on a network, administrators can find and close unnecessary open ports before an attacker
exploits them. Common port scanning tools include Zenmap, which provides a visual interface
for scanning a target IP address and displaying the results in an easy-to-read format.
Network Addresses
Think of a small network, like one in a small office. It's small enough to have only a couple
of desktop computers, a printer, and a server. Each one of these devices has its own set of
addresses which allow it to communicate with all the others.
Network addresses are essential components in computer networking, enabling devices to
communicate with each other. There are two primary types of network addresses: physical
addresses and logical addresses. Understanding these differences is crucial for network
design, troubleshooting, and ensuring efficient communication within and between networks.
Physical Addresses
Every device, whether it's a computer, a Wi-Fi adapter, or something else, comes with a special
code called a media access control (MA C)  address, also called a physical address. This code is
unique to each device, hardcoded into the device's network interface card (NIC),  and it cannot
be changed. Here's an example of a MAC address:
70-D9-5B-36-C2-EE
You can see there are six parts, each with two numbers or letters. These two characters are
hexadecimal numbers, separated by dashes ( - ) or colons ( : ). The hexadecimal numbers
represent a 48-bit binary number. This number is used by switches in a local area network
(LAN)  to direct packets of data to their proper destination. Each MAC address is unique to each
device, hardcoded into the device's NIC, and it cannot be changed.
Physical addresses have these characteristics:
• Duration: Physical addresses are permanent and hardcoded into the NIC.
• Use case: Physical addresses are used for local network communication.
• Notation: Physical addresses are represented in hexadecimal format.
• Assignment: Physical addresses are assigned by the NIC manufacturer.
Logical Addresses
To make sure that every device on a network can be found, each needs its own unique Internet
Protocol address (IP  address). Logical addresses are like special codes that software gives out,
but these codes can be changed, either by a network administrator or by an automated system
called the dynamic host configuration protocol (DHCP).
One of the most common forms of logical addressing is the IPv4 addresses. Think of it like a
phone number, but for computers and other devices. Just like you write your phone number in
a specific way (first the country code or area code, then exchange prefix, and so on), the IP
address has a special pattern too. It looks like four sets of numbers written with dots in between
them, for example:
192.168.1.1
This way of writing is called dotted decimal notation. Each part of the address is known as an
octet, or group of 8 bits.

In IP addressing, we call a group of 8 bits an "octet," but not a byte. Why is that? It's because the
word "byte" is so closely related to the concept of storage. Using "octet" is a way to be clearer
when talking about IP addresses.
The IT community will express, or write, an IPv4 address in only one of two ways. We can write
it in dotted decimal notation, where each octet is a number between 0 and 255:
131.107.2.200
We can also express an IPv4 address in binary. In this case, each octet is an 8-digit binary
number, as in this example:
10000011.01101011.00000010.11001000
For the majority of people, the dotted decimal notation is easiest to read. This is by far the most
common way to write IPv4 network addresses.
Here are some key things to remember about IPv4 addresses:
• They are made of 32 bits.
• The address is split into four octets (which means four groups of 8 bits).
• Each octet is separated by a period, or dot.
IPv6 Addresses
The IPv4 system had been working fine until recently. The problem is that as more devices
(such as phones, tablets, and computers) connect to the internet, we're starting to run out of
IPv4 addresses! Servers, routers, and other Internet-connected devices are moving away from
IPv4 addresses to IPv6, because it offers more combinations of unique numbers.
These are a bit different. They're made up of eight sets of four hexadecimal numbers. And
that small detail makes a huge difference. While IPv4 could give us over 4 billion different
addresses, using IPv6 can give us a huge number of them. Imagine a 1 with 36 zeros after
it—340 undecillion addresses, that's how many!
Here's an example of what an IPv6 address looks like:
59C2:339A:0000:4BE5:C12D:6842:1F3E:09E2
It's a pretty long number, 128 bits long, to be exact. This means that by using IPv6 addresses,
the global community won't run out of internet addresses anytime soon.
Logical addresses have these characteristics:
• Duration: Logical addresses can be either static or dynamic, and can change over time.
• Use case: Logical addresses are used for communication across different networks.
• Notation: Logical addresses are represented in either decimal (IPv4)  or hexadecimal (IPv6)
format.
• Assignment: Logical addresses are assigned by network administrators or dynamically by
DHCP servers.
The Network Interface Card (NIC)
Most motherboards today include a built-in NIC, while some high-end motherboards and server
boards feature two or more network ports. NICs come in wired (RJ-45 ) and wireless varieties.
The topic cover NIC speeds, form factors, and driver considerations in more detail.

Image © 123RF.com.
NIC Characteristics
The most important feature of a NIC, whether wired or wireless, is its speed. Early wired NICs
ran at 10 Mbps. Nowadays, 10 Gbps is becoming common for local area networks (LANs).
Most offices today use 1 Gbps speed, providing fast connections to servers and the Internet.
Remember, these speeds are only as fast as the slowest part of the network.
A network interface card that connects to a motherboard slot is called a PCIe x1 card. If it's a
wireless card, it will have antennas sticking out the back to make the signal stronger. It's more
common to use USB Wi-Fi or wired adapters instead.
With a USB adapter, you can easily plug it into a desktop or laptop. It might seem strange to use
a Wi-Fi adapter on a laptop, since laptops already have built-in Wi-Fi. However, if the built-in
Wi-Fi stops working, you can quickly fix it by plugging in a USB adapter. These adapters come
with either a USB type A or USB type C connector.

A NIC also has something called a MAC address. This is a unique code made up of six pairs of
hexadecimal numbers, unique to every device, that allows the device to connect to a network.
Windows usually does a good job of automatically loading drivers for most wired NICs, so they
work right away. However, wireless adapters can be a bit trickier and often need a driver to
work correctly.
You might wonder, "How can I download a driver from a website if I don't have Internet
access?" This is when having access to a second computer is helpful. You can use the second
computer to download the driver to a flash drive, and then use the flash drive to move it to the
computer with the waiting NIC.
Cable Internet
Coaxial cable is a copper-based cable run from an internet service provider (ISP)  into a
neighborhood, then to a home or business. This is called cable Internet.
This list summarizes the basic elements of cable Internet:
• Equipment required: Coaxial cable, modem, router
• Speed: 10 Mbps up to 2 Gbps, depending on location
• Latency: 10 ms up to 50 ms
Cable TV started a long time ago, even before the Internet was around. At first, it was for people
living in rural areas who couldn't get TV signals because they were too far from big cities and
TV stations. Cable TV offered more channels than the regular TV you could get through an
antenna, and people really liked it. So, the cable companies thought it would be a good idea to
also bring cable to people living in big cities and the suburbs. They didn't know back then that
the cables they were putting down could one day be used for the Internet.
The physical coaxial cables are made up of four different components. At the center is the inner
conductor, typically made of a solid wire coated in copper or silver. Transmissions on a network
travel along this inner wire in the form of electrical signals. To protect the transmissions, the
wire is surrounded by an insulator, and around the insulator is a metallic shield. To complete the
cable, the entire assembly is coated with a plastic jacket. The most common coaxial connector
is the F-type connector, which has a swiveling head that screws onto its port.
Image by destinacigdem © 123rf.com.

Image created by Colin and reproduced under the Creative Commons Attribution ShareAlike 3.0 license.
Today, cable is the most popular way to connect to the Internet. Cable is fast, doesn't have
much delay, is usually on without interruptions, and is reasonably priced. In some places, cable
Internet can go as fast as 2 Gbps, which is more than what most homes or small businesses
need. But for those who want super-fast Internet, it's a great choice. The latency, or how long it
takes for data to go back and forth, is usually between 10 ms and 50 ms. This is good enough
for browsing the Internet and for people who like to play online games.
Cable Internet is different from other Internet services because the connection to a house or
business is shared with other people nearby. That shared connection was noticeable in some
areas years ago, when everyone in the neighborhood got on the Internet at the same time. But
now, cable Internet has gotten a lot better at sending a lot of data through the cables, so even if
everyone is online at the same time, most people won't see their Internet slow down much at all.
Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)  Internet
Digital Subscriber Line (DSL),  one of the original broadband offerings, is a common way for
small offices or homes to get Internet service. Just like cable Internet, DSL uses infrastructure
that was put in place before the Internet became common. Telephone lines can carry Internet
signals the same way they carry your voice, as long as the telephone wire is of good quality.
The Internet data travels over the telephone line using high frequencies, which are outside the
range that voice calls use.
This list summarizes the basic elements of DSL Internet:
• Equipment required: Telephone line, modem, router
• Speed: 5 Mbps up to 30 Mbps (rarely up to 100 Mbps), depending on location and wire
quality
• Latency: 20 ms up to 50 ms

Most telephone wires are made of copper, which is a highly conductive metal that is very
efficient at carrying electrical signals. Copper is not only good at conducting electricity, but it's
also flexible and strong, making it perfect for phone wires.
Telephone or DSL wires are usually set up in a twisted pair cable. This means that the copper
wires are twisted around each other in pairs. The reason they're twisted is to keep away
unwanted signals from outside and to stop the wires from interfering with each other's signals.
Each copper wire is covered with an insulating plastic material to keep it from touching other
wires and to protect it from environmental damage like water and rust. There's also an outer
layer, or jacket, made of plastic materials that wraps around the coated wires. This jacket
helps protect the wires from getting damaged by things like sunlight, water, and changes in
temperature. This makes sure the phone wires work well, no matter the weather.
Image © 123rf.com.
Most residential DSL services are asymmetric (ADSL),  meaning that downloading is faster than
uploading. Businesses and freelance professionals who work with videos and sound prefer
to use a different kind of DSL, called symmetric (SDSL)  connections. This is because both
downloading and uploading speeds are the same in SDSL, which is great for sending and
receiving large files. Usually, DSL Internet can go as fast as 30 Mbps, but there are some that
can reach up to 100 Mbps.
DSL's ping or latency times are similar to other ISP options, with average rates between 20 ms
and 50 ms.
Your DSL Internet speed depends a lot on the quality of the telephone wiring and how far
you are from the local phone company's exchange or hub. The farther away you are, the
weaker the Internet signal gets. When the signal gets weaker, the Internet slows down. This is

called attenuation, and it's one of DSL's main drawbacks. The maximum range of DSL wiring is
typically about 3 miles (5  km). In addition, the DSL or telephone wires in some areas may also
be of relatively poor quality and be more likely to experience signal interference. To help solve
this problem, some telephone ports are fitted with a microfilter to prevent the data signals from
interfering with other traffic on the same line.
Fiber Internet
Some of the larger digital subscriber line (DSL)  companies realized many years ago the limited
Internet capability of copper wires, and found a solution in fiber Internet.
This list summarizes the basic elements of Fiber Internet:
• Equipment required: Fiber optic cable, router
• Speed: 100 Mbps up to 25 Gbps
• Latency: 10 ms to 25 ms
Fiber optic cables work by using light to carry information, sometimes as fast as 70% of the
speed of light. They have a central core made of clear plastic or glass that the light travels
through. Around this core there is a special layer of reflective cladding that acts like a mirror.
When some of the light strays out of the core, this mirror-like layer bounces it back into the
middle so it keeps going along the cable. Then, there are one or two layers that wrap around
this cladding to keep the central core safe from getting broken or damaged. Finally, all of this is
covered with a plastic outer layer.
Image © 123rf.com.
Fiber cables terminate, or end, in a few different types of connectors. The subscriber connector
(SC)  and the local connector (L C)  are the most common. The SC is a push/pull design, allowing
for simple insertion and removal. The LC is a small-form-factor connector with a tabbed push/
pull design. LC is similar to SC, but the smaller size allows more cables to be attached in a
smaller space. LC is a widely adopted form factor for higher Internet speeds.
Image by YANAWUT SUNTORNKIJ © 123rf.com.
Small form-factor pluggable (SFP)  transceivers are important in many networks based on fiber
optic cable. They help switches and other key parts of the network talk to each other. SFPs
are popular because they are small, can connect in different ways (using copper or fiber optic
cables), and can be hot-swapped, or changed out without turning off the system.

While it is more expensive, the SFP is less likely to experience electromagnetic interference and
can save on power costs. This type of port is best suited to large-scale deployments, such as
businesses with large networks.
Image by Zdenek Maly © 123rf.com.
Infrastructure
Fiber Internet is different because it doesn't need a modem. Instead, it uses something called
a fiber-optic network terminal. This changes the Internet signal into a form that your devices,
like phones and computers, can understand. Unfortunately, fiber was not built out along with
the other technologies, cable and DSL, decades ago. And therefore, fiber is still not widely
available.
Fiber Internet is a newer way to get Internet to homes and was not set up a long time ago,
like cable and DSL Internet. To get fiber Internet directly into homes and businesses, Internet
service providers (ISPs)  have to spend a lot of money, so it's not available everywhere. A
common solution that's used in cities and some rural areas is called Fiber to the Curb (FTT C).
This means the ISP puts in a fiber network that ends at a big box or cabinet on a street close by.
Then, the last step from the cabinet to each house uses ordinary telephone wires with a special
kind of DSL called Very High Bit Rate DSL (VDSL)  to make the connection.
Speed
Fiber optic cable is a connection type that allows for very high-speed symmetric connections.
This means that if you have 500 Mbps download speed, you will have the same 500 Mbps
upload speed. Fiber has been able to hit speeds of 25 Gbps. It is the fastest of all connection
types we discuss in this course.
Latency is also very low with fiber, normally coming in at a rate that works well for surfing and
gaming. An average ping rate may be from 10 ms to 25 ms.
Fiber Internet is also very reliable, with uptime or availability as good or better than any other
service. Another advantage of fiber is its ability to travel over a great distance. All of this leads
to faster load times and higher quality streams.

Wireless Internet
The newest player in broadband service is wireless Internet, offered by cell phone companies.
Using the same cell coverage that works with your phones, cellular carriers are beginning to
offer the option of home or small business Internet.
This list summarizes the basic elements of wireless Internet:
• Equipment required: Modem, router
• Speed: 40 Mbps up to 300 Mbps
• Latency: 1 ms up to 30 ms
Cellular technology delivers an Internet signal to your home without cables. Your Internet
service provider (ISP)  sends digital information using cellular radio waves, which travel from
one cell tower to another. Devices that use this kind of Internet, like your phone or modem,
receive these radio waves to connect to both the Internet and the telephone network.
One good thing about wireless Internet is that you can put your modem anywhere in your
house. With other types of Internet, you have to connect it to the wall plate where your cable
comes into your building. But with a wireless modem, you just need to plug it into an electric
socket. Just remember, if the signal isn't strong, you might have to move the modem closer to a
window.
Images © 123rf.com.
The 6th generation of wireless Internet, called 6G and 6E, is the newest kind of network
technology. It's much faster and more responsive than the older versions. With 5G, you can
download things at speeds between 40 to 300 Mbps and upload between 10 to 50 Mbps. This
speed is good enough for most things you do online. The latency, or ping rate, is also pretty
quick, usually around 30 milliseconds. 6G and 6E are even faster, though they're not yet (at the
time of writing) as widespread as earlier generations like 5G. More and more places are getting
6G, so its coverage is growing.
Another advantage of wireless is that it gives people more options to choose from when
they're deciding on Internet service providers (ISPs).  For a long time before 4G, 5G, and 6G/6E
wireless Internet became popular, not much had changed with ISP choices. Because there are

so many companies offering 5G and 6G/6E Internet coverage, and because their cell coverage
is expanding, consumers have more options than ever when choosing an ISP.
Other Wireless Connections
Unlike cable Internet, mobile or cellular Internet, and fiber, the Internet types covered here are
less well known. These methods of connecting to the Internet can be useful in certain situations
where traditional Internet doesn't work well, or isn't available.
Satellite Internet
Satellite Internet is often the only option in rural areas where other types of Internet can't reach.
Usually, satellite Internet is not as fast as other types of connections, but people are willing
to accept these drawbacks because it's the only choice they have. Internet service providers
(ISPs)  don't want to lay cables for hundreds of miles to reach far-off places.
Satellite Internet is not available only to remote locations! If you're almost anywhere in the world,
you may still have the option to get to the Internet through a satellite.
Three companies offer satellite Internet: HughesNet, Viasat, and Starlink. HughesNet and Viasat
have been around for a long time, giving people satellite Internet for many years. Starlink is
newer and started offering satellite Internet in 2020. All of these companies use satellites that
orbit the Earth. They make sure there's always at least one satellite close enough to the antenna
you set up at your place, so you can get the Internet signal.
Just like with other kinds of Internet, you'll need a modem and a router to connect your devices.
While a satellite doesn't rely on cables or other physical connections, you will need to have a
satellite dish to receive the data. Most people attach the dish either to the roof or to the side of
their building. The satellite company can help with positioning the dish in the right direction to
get the best possible signal.
The speed of satellite Internet is on the low side of average. The download speed can be
anywhere from 12 Mbps to 250 Mbps, and upload speeds are almost always 3 Mbps. The
latency, or ping rate, is a bit of an issue because it's usually over 100 ms. This happens because
the Internet signal has to travel a long way: from your dish to a satellite in space, then back
down to Earth to connect to the Internet server, then back to the satellite, and finally back down
to Earth again to reach your dish. This means things like online gaming are not likely to work
well on satellite Internet because of the slow response times.
Two final drawbacks to satellite are data caps and weather. Data caps mean that there might
be limits on how much data you can use, depending on your plan. If you go over this limit, your
Internet could slow down quite a lot. Bad weather can also impact your Internet signal. Heavy
thunderstorms, snow, and dust storms can interrupt your satellite service.
This list summarizes the basic elements of satellite Internet:
• Equipment required: Satellite dish, modem, router
• Speed: 3 Mbps up to 250 Mbps
• Latency: 100 ms and over
Fixed Wireless Internet
In places where it's hard to get fast Internet, like fiber or cable, there's another way to connect
using an antenna. This method is called fixed wireless. It uses a special outdoor antenna that
can handle all kinds of weather, from big storms to heavy snow. It's not as common as other
Internet types, but it's a good choice for people who don't have many options. The Internet

signal is sent from towers using radio frequency waves through the air straight to where you live
or work.
For fixed wireless to work correctly, the place where you're setting up the antenna needs to be
within 10 miles of the tower. Also, there can't be anything blocking the line of sight between
the tower and the antenna, like buildings or trees. The signal can come from towers on top of
buildings or even water towers. You would install the antenna on the outside of a building, and
then a cable runs from the antenna to a modem inside your home to a router.
Speeds of fixed wireless can vary, but are generally 15 to 30 Mbps for download speeds.
However, in the right environment, speeds can be as fast as 100 Mbps. Upload speeds will
be much slower, as low as 1 Mbps or less. Latency or ping rate is within the range of other
services, on average, from 20 to 60 ms. The cost for fixed wireless tends to be higher than
other forms of broadband.
This list summarizes the basic elements of fixed wireless Internet:
• Equipment required: Antenna, modem, router
• Speed: 1 Mbps up to 30 Mbps
• Latency: 20 ms up to 60 ms
Wireless Antenna Types
The type of antenna used in a wireless connection determines how far and in what direction the
signal travels. Choosing the right antenna is important for getting the best performance out of a
wireless network. There are two main categories of wireless antennas:
• Omnidirectional antennas send and receive signals in all directions equally, creating a 360-
degree coverage pattern. These are ideal for general-purpose wireless access points where
devices may connect from any direction, such as in a home or office. The trade-off is that
the signal is spread out, so it doesn't travel as far in any single direction.
• Directional antennas focus the signal in one specific direction, creating a narrow beam
that travels much farther than an omnidirectional signal. These are also called high-gain
antennas because they concentrate the signal strength into a focused path. Directional
antennas are the best choice when you need to create a point-to-point wireless link between
two specific locations, such as connecting two buildings across a parking lot or campus.
Because the signal is focused, it also avoids broadcasting to areas where coverage isn't
needed, which improves both performance and security.
When deciding which antenna to use, consider what the wireless connection needs to
accomplish. If devices will connect from many locations around the antenna, choose
omnidirectional. If the goal is to connect two fixed points over a longer distance, choose
directional.

Lesson 14D
Working with an ISP
Objectives Covered
1.3 Compare and contrast common units of measure.
2.7 Compare and contrast common internet service types.
2.8 Identify basic networking concepts.
To connect to the Internet, you need an Internet Service Provider (ISP).  ISPs are the companies
that maintain the infrastructure, from cables and satellites to cell towers, that deliver Internet
access to homes and businesses. With so many providers and plan options available,
understanding how ISPs work helps you choose the right service for your needs and budget.
In this lesson, you will explore what ISPs offer, how tiered service plans work, and the
equipment your ISP provides to get you online. You will also learn how to measure Internet
performance using bandwidth, latency, and throughput, and understand what those numbers
mean for your everyday experience.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is an ISP, and what services do ISPs typically provide?
• How do tiered service plans work, and what factors affect which plan you need?
• What equipment does an ISP provide, and what does a modem do?
• What is the difference between bandwidth and throughput?
• How are Internet speeds measured, and what do upload and download speeds mean?
• What is latency, and how does it affect your Internet experience?
What is an Internet Service Provider (ISP)?
To get on the Internet, you need to subscribe to an Internet Service Provider (ISP).  Even though
all ISPs provide you with access to the Internet, there are different ways they can make this
happen. They might be the company that gives you cable TV, your phone company, or your cell
phone service. Some companies only give you Internet, while others might offer Internet along
with cable TV or cell phone service. All of these companies maintain their own infrastructure,
meaning the Internet delivery equipment, and offer technical support to their subscribers.
Many ISPs will also offer email addresses and website hosting. Email addresses,
typically offered free of charge, will use the ISP's domain name. For example,
"YourName@ProviderName.com." Keep in mind that when you leave the ISP, you might not
be able to keep this address. Some providers will host a website and register a domain name for
you. This service is typically available for an additional fee.

The majority of providers offer tiered service plans. This means that they have 2 or more
different Internet speeds available, with different price points for each level. For example, a
basic service may give you an average speed and cost $50 per month, while the next tier up
offers a speed that is three times faster and costs $100 per month. The needs of your home or
business depend on the number of devices you have that need to connect to the Internet, and
how much bandwidth the devices will be using.
Each ISP has limitations based on its infrastructure and your location. Every ISP in your area will
have its good points and drawbacks. It's important to know what makes them different so you
can choose the best one for what you need.
Understand ISP Equipment and Performance
When you're selecting an Internet Service Provider (ISP),  you need to think about a few
important things. Consider how much it costs, what other customers say about it, and look
at independent performance reports that show how well it works. Depending on where you live,
you might have many ISPs to choose from, or you might be more limited. It's also key to know
what kind of equipment you need and how fast you want your Internet to be.
It is also worth noting that any data you transfer over an Internet connection is processed by, and
may be stored on, the ISP's computers. When you use an ISP, you are trusting them not to snoop
on your unencrypted Internet traffic.
Equipment
Your Internet service provider uses their infrastructure to transmit the Internet signal to your
home or organization. This means that each ISP deploys its own cable, establishes its own
satellites, or sets up its own cell towers. For example, in older neighborhoods where houses and
roads were built before everyone started using the Internet, an ISP might have to dig up the
ground to put in cables. In places where people are building businesses and homes for the first
time, ISPs usually install their cables when the other basic services like water and electricity
are being set up. This infrastructure brings the Internet up to the building. After that, different
equipment takes over inside the building to make sure you can connect to the Internet.
Most companies use a modem, a device that modulates and demodulates, or changes, the
Internet data. It changes the Internet signal into a form that your devices, like phones and
computers, can use. After the modem changes the signal, it sends the signal to your router, a
device that has ports for wired connections and also sends out a wireless signal. The router
then forwards the signal information to your devices. This way, all your devices, from computers
to tablets, can use the Internet.
Speed
The most common way to compare Internet service providers is to look at how fast they are.
ISPs measure their performance in upload and download speed, or bandwidth, and in latency.
Latency, also known as ping rate, is how long it takes for a signal to get from your computer to
the Internet server. This time is measured in milliseconds, which are thousandths of a second
(one millisecond is just 0.001 of a second). Most people who use the Internet are comfortable
if the time is 50 milliseconds or shorter. If the time is between 10 and 20 milliseconds, that's
considered very good. If you like gaming online, you probably pay a lot of attention to how fast
your Internet service provider's (ISP)  latency speeds are. If these speeds start to get too slow,
your game doesn't react as quickly as it should, which can make it tough to do well.
When you see an Internet plan, it usually shows two bandwidth numbers: one for download
speed and one for upload speed. Both speeds are measured in millions of bits per second
(Megabit s  per second, or Mbps) or in billions of bits per second (Gigabit s  per second, or Gbps).

Most of the time, your ISP gives you a lot more speed for downloading, something like 80%
to 90% of your total Internet speed. This means only 10% to 20% is left for uploading data
to the Internet. This kind of connection is called an asymmetric connection because the
download speed is much faster than the upload speed. As Internet speeds get even faster,
this difference gets bigger, sometimes going up to 95% of the total for downloading and
only 5% for uploading. ISPs do this on purpose because most people use the Internet more
for downloading, like watching videos or browsing websites, than they do for uploading. One
example of someone who does need more upload speed might be a YouTube creator, who
would be uploading large files of content on a regular basis.
The speeds of Internet service discussed here range from as slow as 10 Mbps to as fast as 1
Gbps, or 1 billion bits transferred every second. Some Internet service speeds are even higher
with multi-Gigabit speeds offered in some areas. Another term you will hear to describe Internet
connections is broadband, which means a high speed connection that's always available. The
term "high speed" can be a little bit vague, so in the United States the Federal Communications
Commission (FCC)  has defined it as at least 100 Mbps of download capacity, and 20 Mbps of
upload capacity.
If you're curious to check your Internet performance, go to www.fast.com to see your speed.

Lesson 14E
Creating a Home Network
Objectives Covered
2.5 Compare and contrast common types of input/output device interfaces.
2.8 Identify basic networking concepts.
2.9 Explain the basic capabilities of a small wireless network.
A wireless local area network (WLAN)  lets you share an Internet connection with every device
in your home or small office without running cables through walls and ceilings. Once a router
is set up, phones, tablets, laptops, and printers can all connect and share files, print jobs, and
Internet access. Understanding how wireless networks work, what equipment you need, and
how to connect your devices will help you build a reliable home network.
In this lesson, you will explore how small wireless networks operate, compare Wi-Fi standards
and frequency bands such as 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz, and learn the steps for connecting
a device to a Wi-Fi network. You will also examine how newer standards like Wi-Fi 6E improve
speed and reduce interference.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is a WLAN, and what can devices on a small wireless network share?
• How do signal strength and router placement affect wireless connectivity?
• What are the key differences between the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz frequency bands?
• How have Wi-Fi standards evolved from 802.11b through Wi-Fi 6E?
• What steps do you follow to connect a mobile device to a Wi-Fi network?
• Why should you disable the auto-join hotspot setting on your device?
Understanding Small Wireless Networks
A small wireless local area network (WLAN)  is a good way to spread an internet connection
around. Think of the Wi-Fi router as the center of a circle, emitting Wi-Fi waves in every
direction. Anything like your phone or computer inside of that circle can pick up those waves
and connect to the Internet.
The best part of small wireless networks is how simple it is to share an Internet connection.
Once you link your computers, tablets, or printers to the network, they can start sharing files
and print jobs immediately. Plus, if you're not at home or you're away from the office, you can
still utilize your network from just about anywhere with remote access.
Learning the requirements of a Wi-Fi network can help you set up the best one for your needs.
If everyone using your network wants different things, from super-fast Internet to document

sharing, you will need to set up a network that allows all these things to happen. Selecting the
right equipment means everyone can get what they need.
"One of my small office clients called me out to figure out why one of their printers
was unreliable. They had checked all the mechanical stuff (there was ink in it, there
was paper, there were no paper jams), so I was there to check on the networking
side. Sometimes the printer worked, sometimes it didn't, and there was no pattern or
reason to it. By looking at the whole network I found the solution. The wireless signal
strength at the printer's location was very weak. It was too far away from the router,
and the printer was just barely getting a connection. Sometimes the connection
would just drop off altogether. I recommended that the client either connect the
printer to the router by using a cable, or add a wireless access point between the
router and the printer."
-- Rob P., network technician
Securing Your Wireless Network
When you set up a wireless network, one of the most important steps is making sure it's secure.
Without security, anyone nearby could connect to your network and use your Internet, or worse,
access your personal files. That's why every home router lets you set a password and choose a
security mode.
The security mode tells the router how to protect the data traveling through your network. Think
of it like choosing the type of lock for your front door. Here are the main options you'll see:
• WP A2-PSK  (Wi-Fi  Protected Access 2 - Pre-Shared Key): This is the most common security
mode for home and small office networks. It requires every device to enter the same
password (the pre-shared key) to join the network. WPA2 is considered secure for everyday
use and is supported by nearly all modern devices.
• WP A3:  This is the newest security standard. It provides stronger protection than WPA2, but
not all devices support it yet. If your router and all your devices support WPA3, it's the best
choice.
Along with the security mode, the router uses an encryption algorithm to scramble the data
so that outsiders can't read it. The most common algorithm is AES (Adv anced  Encryption
Standard). AES is fast and very secure. When setting up your router, you should always make
sure it's using AES encryption. Older options like TKIP are slower and less secure, so avoid
them if possible.
To secure a wireless network, you'll typically log into your router's settings through a web
browser, navigate to the wireless security page, select WP A2-PSK  as the security mode,
confirm that AES is the encryption algorithm, and then set a strong password. A strong
password is long, includes a mix of letters, numbers, and special characters, and is hard for
others to guess.
Testing Network Connectivity with Ping
Once your network is set up and devices are connected, how do you know everything is
actually working? One of the simplest ways to test if two devices can communicate is by using a
command called ping.
Ping is a small program built into every computer. It sends a quick message to another device
on the network and waits for a reply. If the other device responds, you know the connection
between them is working. If it doesn't respond, something might be wrong, like the device is
turned off, disconnected from the network, or there's a problem with the cables or Wi-Fi.
To use ping on a Windows computer:

1. Right-click the desktop and select Open in Terminal (or search for PowerShell in the Start
menu).
2. Type ping followed by a space and the name or IP address of the device you want to test.
For example: ping Home-PC2
3. Press Enter.
The results will show one of two outcomes:
• Reply from [address]: This means the other device received your message and responded.
The connection is working.
• Request timed out or Destination host unreachable: This means the other device didn't
respond. It could be powered off, not connected to the network, or there may be a problem
along the way.
Ping is a quick and easy way to check whether your network is healthy. If a device isn't
responding, you can start troubleshooting by checking if it's powered on, connected to Wi-Fi, or
plugged into the network with a cable.
Wireless Band Options
The 802.11n Wi-Fi standard (also called 4G Wi-Fi) was the first to use two wireless frequency
bands for improved data rates. Those were the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequency bands.
Then came the 802.11ac (5G  Wi-Fi) standard, which was even faster, reaching speeds of up to
1.3 Gigabits per second (Gbps).  However, it only worked on the 5 GHz band. The older 2.4 GHz
band is still in use on older (also called legacy) wireless standards like 802.11b/g/n. Today we
have 802.11ax (6G  and 6E),  which is widely supported by modern devices.

Bands and Wireless Function
The 2.4 GHz frequency band is like a busy street that other devices such as cordless phones,
microwaves, and Bluetooth also use. This can cause traffic jams, making things not work as
smoothly. That's why 5 GHz is a better choice. Think of 5 GHz as a less crowded street with
more lanes (or channels) so that everyone can get where they need to go without bumping into
each other. In other words, there is less interference. Your router keeps things running smoothly
on this frequency band.
But there is a catch: when it comes to how far the signal can go, 2.4 GHz can travel longer
distances than 5 GHz. Again, 5 GHz offers a faster connection. So if you want speed and don't
mind being a bit closer to your router, 5 GHz is the way to go.

Troubleshooting Connectivity
Objectives Covered
1.4 Explain the troubleshooting methodology.
2.9 Explain the basic capabilities of a small wireless network.
Network connectivity issues are some of the most common problems you will face when
working with technology. Whether it is a weak wireless signal, a disconnected cable, or a
misconfigured device, knowing how to identify and resolve these issues is an essential skill.
Understanding wireless network standards, speed factors like latency and attenuation, and the
OSI model gives you the foundation to pinpoint where problems occur.
In this lesson, you will learn about wireless network standards and the factors that affect
network speed. You will also explore the OSI model and its role in troubleshooting, then
walk through the CompTIA Troubleshooting Methodology, a structured six-step process for
identifying, resolving, and documenting network problems.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What are the key differences between older and newer Wi-Fi standards, and how do they
affect network performance?
• How do latency, attenuation, and interference impact wireless network speed?
• What are the seven layers of the OSI model, and how can they help you troubleshoot
network problems?
• What are the six steps of the CompTIA Troubleshooting Methodology?
• Why is it important to identify the problem and establish a theory before attempting a fix?
• How should you document your findings after resolving a network issue?
Wireless Network Standards
The properties of radio waves are the same as other waves you might know about, such
as ocean waves. These properties include amplitude (the height of peaks and the depth of
troughs), frequency (the number of peaks per unit of time), and phase (the angle of a wave at
a point in time). Modulation, which is what a modem does to the Internet signal, changes one or
more of those properties to encode data into a signal.
There are many different types of communication that use radio waves. Broadcast television,
AM and FM radio, military communications, garage door openers, satellites, Near Field
Communication (NFC),  and mobile phones all use radio waves to transmit information.
Near Field Communication (NFC)  is a type of wireless technology that works over short
distances. You can use it with smartphones and smartwatches to talk to or share files, or even

pay for things, with other nearby devices. It only works when the devices are very close, less
than 2 inches apart.
Wi-Fi standards use modulation to keep other radio waves and electronic signals from
interfering with Wi-Fi signals.
Standardizing Wireless Communications
The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)  established technical standards for
wireless communications and has been revising them as technology improves. These 802.11
standards, better known as Wi-Fi, define specific ways that a modem encodes data into a radio
signal.
The numbers "802.11" are part of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
index, and aren't related to wireless performance.
