For someone working on wireless networks, it's important to know the variations in types
of Wi-Fi. These differences between generations affect network performance, what features
the network can support, and what devices are compatible with the wireless signal. When a
professional sets up Wi-Fi to cover an entire office, they have to think about how strong the
signal is and whether it will work in different office locations.
Wireless Network Speed
How fast does a website load on your computer? In most cases, you expect websites to load
pretty much instantly, almost as soon as you click or tap. When you measure how fast a website
loads, it's like calculating how fast a car is going on the road. Just like a car has a speedometer

that displays its speed, the internet speed tells you how much data is being pushed from one
place to another, usually starting from the point of the central server.
Latency
When you click on a link or type in a website address, you usually have to wait a bit for the
website to show up in your browser, right? That waiting time is called latency or lag. This is the
delay that occurs during the sequence of steps when packets of data travel over the Internet.
The shorter the wait, the better your internet connection is (at least, as it relates to latency). We
measure how long the wait is in milliseconds (ms), or one-thousandth of a second.
The IT industry measures latency by running a test called ping, named after the command that
starts it off. You may hear the term "ping rate" to describe latency.
Excellent latency times are short, in single digits, and good ones are under 50 ms. With rates
over 150 ms, you'll start to notice delays. Even if your internet is fast at downloading, you might
still have a slow ping rate, which can make things feel sluggish.
Gaming is the area most concerned with low latency. With online games, small delays can really
affect your performance and cause you to fall behind your opponents (and probably annoy your
teammates, too). It's definitely not good if there's a lag between you pressing a button and
when that action actually occurs in the game, if for nothing else than the fact that you won't get
to respond quickly to whatever happens next. So, getting your ping rate or latency lower can
really make your online gaming experience better, if that's something you're into.
But know that there's not always something you can do. Latency can get worse if the network is
juggling a lot of data, or if there are lots of people using the internet at the same time.
Attenuation and Interference
As you move away from a wireless router, the signal strength of your device diminishes, and
your internet connection slows down. This is attenuation, or the loss of signal strength. You can
see the number of bars of signal strength drop as you move farther from the source of your
signal. You might also see a compromised signal if you are behind or beneath certain types of

walls or ceilings, depending on the type of building material. Even trees and other vegetation
can block or reduce the power of your Wi-Fi signal.
Interference is unwanted signals or noise that collide with and degrade the Wi-Fi signal. These
signals or external sources can clash with the intended transmission, causing your wireless
data to become distorted and hard for your device to decode. Other types of radio wave
transmissions typically don't interfere with Wi-Fi, because different signals are designed to
operate in different bands. However, microwaves, baby monitors, and your neighbor's wireless
network can disrupt your wireless signal. The effects are the same as you would experience
with attenuation: a decrease in the Wi-Fi signal strength and network speed.
Standardize the Troubleshooting Process
Problems in your computer system can happen for many reasons that you can't control, and
some that don't seem very clear. Devices might stop working, old cable connectors can come
loose, and software may get corrupted. Whether you're working on your own computer or
a network, you will make everyone on the network happy by fixing problems and keeping
systems working smoothly. To do this well, you need to know the basic tools and steps for
troubleshooting a network. Fixing problems is an important part of tech knowledge and abilities.
Some problems can be very complex, and therefore it's important to follow the steps outlined.
The first step is to use a troubleshooting process that gives you a clear and complete set of
steps, called a standard operating procedure (SOP),  to fix IT problems. This procedure includes
finding out what the problem is, thinking of a possible solution, trying out the solution, and
making sure the problem is fixed. The CompTIA Troubleshooting Methodology is one example.

Identify the Problem
The first step in fixing a problem is to figure out what the problem is, and how widespread it is.
To identify the problem, you should talk to the user, watch the problem happen, understand the
symptoms, and check if anything has changed in the system recently. This step is crucial as it
sets the foundation for diagnosing and resolving the issue effectively.
If one user can't print, but their back-up printer down the hall is working, that doesn't have the
same urgency as a user who can't get on the Internet. Staying productive is an important part of
overall tech goals.
Interview Users
Ask users what they were doing when the problem started and if they noticed anything strange
before it happened. For example, they might tell you that before they left the office yesterday,
they tried to shut down their computer, but Windows said it was going to install a feature
update. This big update might have affected a program, and now it won't load correctly. Try to
get as much information as you can. Putting in some detective work can really help here.
Duplicate the Problem
If you can, it's best to see the problem yourself to get more accurate information. Try to repeat
what the user did to see if you get the same result. Seeing exactly what the user experienced
helps you understand the problem better, especially if the user doesn't fully understand the
process or does things differently. If you can replicate the problem, then you can move on to
figuring out how to fix it.
Identify Symptoms One at a Time
After you replicate the problem and confirm that it's still there, you need to write down all the
important symptoms and error messages. Symptoms could be things like a program not loading
or a common action not working. Error messages, which often show up in pop-up windows, are
meant to help fix the problem. The average user might not understand these messages, and you
might not either at first, but writing down what you see will help you find the solution.
You figure out a problem in your system by looking at the symptoms. By knowing what
usually causes these symptoms, you can test each possible cause until you find the right one.
Sometimes, symptoms come from more than one cause. This kind of problem is less common
but much harder to solve.
Understand Recent Changes and Review Documentation
Many help desks have a knowledge base, which is a place where they keep information
about common problems or issues specific to their environment. These knowledge bases are
collections of what support technicians have learned over time. You can search them by issue,
symptom, or error message. Troubleshooters usually check the knowledge base early in the
process so they don't waste time trying to solve problems that are already known.
It's also important to know what has happened recently to the system you're working on.
The knowledge base might be the best place to check if anything has changed recently, like
new software versions, different settings, or recent updates to the operating system. On the
individual computer, you can check the history of Windows updates in the Settings app under
"Update History." You can also look for recently-installed apps on the computer, which might be
causing the problem.

Establish a Theory of Probable Cause
If you get clear and accurate answers to your questions in the first step, you'll know how
serious the problem is. You'll find out how many users or systems are affected and where to
start looking for the problem. By figuring out where the problem started, you'll have a good
starting point. Check previous help tickets, especially if they are for the same computer, server,
or part of the network.
Question the Obvious
Don't ignore an easy solution to a problem. What seems like common sense to you as a tech
might not be obvious to someone else. For example, if a desktop computer isn't on the Internet
and the Windows symbol at the bottom of the screen shows a globe with a tiny X, it means the
network connection is broken. You know that the night before, your coworkers moved to new
cubicles and took their computers with them. Don't be afraid to check behind their system to
make sure an Ethernet cable is plugged in.
There's a funny but sometimes true saying about fixing system problems: "Have you tried rebooting
the system?" Even though it sounds simple, restarting the system can sometimes fix problems and
is easy to do with little downside.
Consider Multiple Approaches
Don't just focus on one way to fix a problem. Internet issues can be caused by problems in the
operating system (OS),  or by a physical problem with one of the network components, or by a
problem with your Internet Service Provider (ISP).  For example, a good way to check Internet
issues is to try a different operating system. This can help you see if the problem is with the
installed OS. With a bootable Linux flash drive, you can plug it in, turn on the computer, boot
from the flash drive, and have a fully functional operating system for testing. Once the OS is
loaded, test the Internet. If it works, then the problem is with the OS. If it doesn't, the problem is
somewhere else, and you can move on to the next option.
Start At One End of the System
Work step by step, either forwards or backwards, from one point to the next. If a system doesn't
have Internet, start by testing the RJ-45  port on the back of the computer. Then check the
Ethernet cable, then the cable's connection to the wall jack, and finally the port on the switch at
the other end of the cable.
Test the Theory
By questioning the obvious and using a step-by-step approach, you should gather enough
information to come up with an initial idea or theory about what might be causing the problem.
Remember, you might be wrong. Without jumping to conclusions, use your troubleshooting skills
and tools to test your idea. This idea will be the basis for your testing and confirmation in the
next step.
Theory Confirmed
If your idea is confirmed, figure out the next steps to fix the problem. This means making a plan
of action. Some fixes will be simple, while others might be more complicated. For example, if
Windows keeps crashing and you find out it's because of a failing hard drive, the obvious step
is to replace the drive. After replacing the drive, load the operating system and test the system
again to make sure it boots to the desktop without any issues.

Theory Not Confirmed
If your theory is not confirmed, come up with a new idea or ask for more help. Take a breath
and step back to look at the situation again. You might need to gather more information. Did you
miss something when you were trying to identify the problem?
It's important to remember that asking for help is a key part of troubleshooting. If you can't
find a solution or figure out what's causing the problem, you need to ask for help. This help
can come from checking the documentation again, looking it up on the Internet, or asking your
coworkers or manager. You should try to solve the problem on your own first, but if you can't,
it's important to get more help so you don't get stuck.
Solving a problem often means breaking it down into smaller parts. For example, if you can't
connect to a network, figure out if the problem is with the hardware or the software. This helps you
get on the right track and not waste time going in the wrong direction.
Establish a Plan and Implement the Fix
The fourth step in the troubleshooting process is to make a plan to fix the problem and then
put it into action. This means creating a detailed plan based on what you found out about the
problem. The plan should list the steps needed to fix the issue, whether it's an easy fix or a
more complicated one. Once you have the plan, you will follow it to fix the problem and then test
to make sure the issue is solved.
Make Sure You Understand the Process
Think through the process in your head or write it down. Make sure you have the tools and
equipment you need, and the proper administrative rights to make any changes. Also, think
about whether the fix will cause a lot of downtime for the organization. You might need a quick
temporary fix that you can do right away, and then do the permanent fix later when it won't
bother as many people, such as after hours or on the weekend.
Make sure to get any needed approval or components for your plan. Some plans are simple, like
replacing a network cable, and don't need approval from a higher-up. Others are more complex,
like shutting down a server to install new memory. This type of step will need approval. Some
hardware or software issues need resources that your department already has. Other times, you
might not have what you need, and you'll have to order it. There might also be times when the
software needs to be installed on the company server, and only the server admin can do that.
Identify Potential Effects
Think about what might happen when you fix the problem. For example, if you replace a
network cable, make sure it's the same speed or faster than the original one, or the user might
complain about a slow connection. This is easy to mess up because network cables have small
print showing their speed, which can be hard to see. Another example is if you have to reinstall
the operating system because it's corrupt, make sure to back up the user's data first to avoid
making them upset.
Backup Important Data
This is one of the most important parts of tech work. If you drop a laptop and break the screen,
it's disappointing, but the screen can be replaced. If you short out a system and need to replace
the motherboard, it's another setback. While these are frustrating, they don't compare to the
huge impact of losing data. If a user says their information is backed up, ask them to explain
how and where it's backed up. Be very careful and back up the data if you have any doubt.

Implement the Solution
You followed all the steps and procedures; now it's time to fix the problem. It's important to
solve a problem by making only one change at a time and seeing what happens. It can be
tempting to try a lot of solutions at once, reboot the computer or network device, and hope
everything is fixed. While this might work, the problem with this approach is that you won't
know which action actually fixed the issue. By making one change at a time, you'll know what
worked, which will help you and your team the next time a similar problem comes up.
Or Escalate the Issue
You probably won't be able to fix every problem. A junior tech, someone just starting in their
career, might not have full access to some of the most critical systems. In these cases, you
may need to ask a more experienced technician to help. Problems can range from software
to operating systems to network hardware, creating a wide variety of issues and solutions.
In larger companies with bigger IT departments, some staff members have specialized roles,
focusing on things like networks, voice over Internet protocol services (V oIP),  or servers. You
might look at an issue and realize it needs the expertise of someone in one of those roles.
Don't be ashamed if you can't solve the issue; the vastness of IT makes it nearly impossible for
anyone to be an expert in all areas.
Confirm the Solution Works
Next, you need to test the results of your fix. This means making sure everything is working
properly, both from your perspective and from the user's point of view. If the problem might
happen again, you can take some extra steps to prevent it from coming back.
Confirm Functionality
You've fixed the problem and checked that everything is working as expected. Now, you should
have the user work with the system to make sure the issue is fully resolved. Sometimes, users
do things in unusual ways, which can make them think there's still a problem when it's really
just a matter of training them on the right way to do things.
Have the user go through all their typical tasks, like printing, sending and receiving emails,
and logging into the websites they use most often. Make sure they see that their system is no
longer having issues. You should also watch for any new problems that might have come up
because of the fix. Sometimes, fixing one problem can cause another. For example, you might
fix a security problem, but in doing so, some users might no longer be able to access resources
they used to.
Put in Preventative Measures if Needed
In addition, if any other steps can be taken to prevent the original problem from recurring, look
to implement them as well. If, for example, a problem was an Ethernet cable that keeps falling
out of the back of a printer, causing it to go offline. While it was easy to put back in place, why
does it regularly come loose? On closer inspection, you see the clip on top of the RJ-45  cable
end, which snaps into the port, is broken. Replacing the entire cable now will reduce the chance
that the problem could happen again.
Document Your Findings
Finally, the issue is resolved! Before you finish up, you need to write down what happened.
Documenting your findings helps you remember what you did to fix the problem, making it
easier to solve similar issues in the future. It also lets others see the steps you took and the

solutions you found, which can be helpful for teamwork and training. Plus, good documentation
can prevent repeated mistakes and save time by providing a reference for fixing recurring
problems.
Add to the Knowledge Base
Effective documentation makes it easier for other technicians to troubleshoot similar problems
in the future. While you work through a problem and solution, write down your actions step
by step. Remember to include what you did and what happened, even if things didn't go as
expected. This helps clearly show the steps you took. Also, if a fix is delayed because you need
to order parts, make sure to document up to that point. Don't wait until the job is completely
done, because you might forget some details.
Another reason to keep good documentation as you go through the process is to let others
know what you have tried so far. This documentation is also helpful if your changes cause
new problems. With good records of what you did, it's easier to undo your changes or adjust
settings.
Explain in Detail
Provide as much detail as possible, especially about what it took to fix the problem. You might
have tried several solutions before finding the right one. Mention the methods that didn't work
and give the most detail about the fix that did. This documentation can be very helpful if the
problem comes back months later. You'll be glad you wrote everything down, and it will feel
good to have solved the problem.

Module Overview
Cloud computing and virtualization power many of the services and tools you use every day,
from online storage and collaboration apps to virtual machines running behind the scenes.
In this module, you will explore what “the cloud” really means, how cloud platforms deliver
resources over the internet, and how virtualization makes it possible to run multiple operating
systems and environments on the same physical hardware. Whether you are backing up files,
sharing documents, or connecting to remote desktops, understanding these concepts will help
you use modern technology more effectively.
Throughout the module, you will learn how different types of cloud services work, compare
local and cloud storage options, and practice using shared storage to collaborate with others.
You will also examine the basics of virtualization, including virtual machines, hypervisors, guest
operating systems, containers, and remote access tools, and see how they are used in both
home and business environments. Guided activities will give you practical experience working
with cloud storage and virtualized environments, so you can recognize when and how to use
these technologies to support your work, learning, and everyday tasks.
Module Summary
In this module, you will:
• Explain what cloud computing is and describe common cloud services and platforms used
for storage and applications.
• Compare local and cloud storage options, including the benefits, tradeoffs, and typical use
cases for each.

environment.

remote desktop access.

Lesson 15A
Understanding the Cloud
Objectives Covered
2.3 Compare and contrast storage types.
2.6 Compare and contrast virtualization and cloud technologies.
5.4 Explain basic data backup concepts.
Cloud computing has changed how people and businesses use technology. Instead of relying
entirely on local hardware, cloud services let you store files, run applications, and access
computing resources over the internet. Understanding cloud technology is essential because
nearly every modern device and service depends on it in some way.
In this lesson, you will learn what cloud computing is and how it compares to on-premises
solutions, explore the three main cloud service types (SaaS,  PaaS, and IaaS),  examine public,
private, and hybrid deployment models, and compare popular cloud platforms like Google
Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Amazon Web Services.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is cloud computing, and how does it differ from on-premises solutions?
• What are the differences between SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS?
• What are the benefits and drawbacks of using cloud services?
• How do public, private, and hybrid cloud deployments differ?
• What do major cloud platforms like Google, Microsoft, and Amazon offer?
What is the Cloud?
One of the easiest ways to explain cloud services is by thinking about sharing the workload. In a
regular client-server setup, companies handle their own servers, storage, and networking. They
buy costly and complicated hardware, hire experts to manage it, and can't easily adjust as their
business grows or changes. This is called on-premises management, and it's the traditional way
of setting up and running systems and software. The equipment is kept in the same place as
the business. Before cloud services, this was the only choice. Benefits to on-premises systems
include lower long-term costs and complete control over the IT setup.
With cloud services, companies can let a cloud provider take care of some or all of these tasks.
Cloud Service Types
Cloud services can be defined by what they offer you. The simplest service is called Software
as a Service (SaaS).  This lets you use a program through your web browser over the Internet. A

popular example is Gmail, which is part of Google Workspace. With Gmail, you can access your
email and other tools that are stored on Google's servers. The cloud service provider (Google,
in this case) takes care of the hardware, the operating system, and the software updates.
There are also bigger on-demand services, like Platform as a Service (PaaS).  With PaaS, you
get more advanced IT tools, including operating systems. PaaS is usually for developers and
database administrators. They use the platform to create applications or database services
needed by the company without having to build the platforms themselves. For example, a
database administrator no longer has to request a server, install an operating system, and
then install a database platform such as Microsoft SQL Server. Those tasks have all been
offloaded to the cloud service provider. PaaS can also grow and change quickly, giving a stable
development platform as needs change.
Another type of cloud service is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).  IaaS gives you physical
equipment such as servers, routers, and storage. Big businesses often use IaaS because it can
be cheaper than buying the equipment themselves. Having servers on-site requires a lot of
support. Servers take up a lot of space, need reliable power, constant cooling, and physical
security. All these needs mean high costs for businesses. By letting a cloud service provider
handle these costs, businesses can save a lot of money and time. Popular IaaS providers are
Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.

Cloud Storage
"The cloud" is an increasingly common way to talk about resources on the Internet. The idea
of cloud storage is similar to the idea of renting a storage unit when you have more things than
your house can hold. Cloud storage is renting space on another company's computer. Because
high-speed Internet access has become so common in many places, the cloud has become a
very popular storage option for both individuals and businesses.

Cloud Storage Benefits
Cloud storage offers several compelling benefits. One is elasticity, which means the storage
resources can expand or contract based on your workload and business needs. If you find that
you need to add storage, that is an easy shift. If you need less storage, you can make that
change too, though you should check your contract for the agreed-upon details.
Another benefit is that if you need more space, the cloud provider can give it to you right
away. This is called scalability. Cloud resources, including storage, can scale up easily and
accommodate a business or organization's growth.
Beyond automatically saving your files, cloud storage keeps different versions of them, so you
can go back to an earlier version if you change your mind about edits. For individual consumers,
cloud storage costs are typically low, usually just a few dollars per month for tens of gigabytes
of data.
Cloud storage also makes collaboration easy. You can easily share a file with someone else. You
can choose different ways to share, from letting the person only view the file to giving them full
editing rights.
Cloud Storage Providers
Many companies offer cloud services through their own and other companies', data centers. A
data center is a dedicated location that holds thousands of servers. All the big tech companies
have their own online storage. Apple provides iCloud, Google offers Drive, and Microsoft
delivers OneDrive. Other companies like Dropbox and Box also compete in this space. The
well-known providers focus on security, using encryption and advanced virus protection to
keep threat actors away.

Screenshot reprinted with permission from Apple Inc.
Ransomware attacks can lock up files on your local computer, but strong firewalls protect files
stored in the cloud from these threats. Cloud storage works closely with your operating system,
so you can access your files just like they were in File Explorer or Finder. It appears as just
another folder, but it includes automatic backups and access to your files from any computer
with an Internet connection. Simply open a browser and log in to your cloud storage. Remote
access and redundancy make it easy to keep your important files safe and secure.
Microsoft joined the cloud storage game later than others and needed to get people's attention. To
do this, they first offered 25GB of free storage to their users. This service is now called OneDrive.
Cloud Storage Drawbacks
People don't often talk about how much it costs to use the cloud. It's great to have all the
remote features and so much storage space, but cloud service providers charge a lot for
this convenience. Some IT departments with limited budgets need to decide which files or
resources should be in the cloud and which should stay on their own computers (often called
"in-house"). The benefit of keeping things in-house is that it saves money.

Cloud computing has some environmental downsides. Data centers, which are the main part of
cloud computing, use a lot of electricity to run servers and other equipment. This high energy
use can lead to more carbon emissions, especially if the electricity comes from non-renewable
sources. Data centers also need a lot of water to stay cool, which can be a problem in places
where water is scarce or during droughts. Additionally, big data centers take up a lot of space,
which can change how the land is used and disrupt local habitats. Building and running these
centers can affect local ecosystems and wildlife.
To reduce these environmental problems, many cloud service providers are using renewable
energy sources, making their data centers more energy-efficient, and adopting eco-friendly
practices. However, the overall impact of cloud computing on the environment is still a big
concern.
Shared Storage
On a home computer system, data is usually saved on a local storage device such as the
system hard disk drive. But computers used in a business environment will likely use shared
storage to make information more manageable.
To do this, the network administrator creates a shared folder on a server within the network.
Employees are then required to save all of their work-related files in the shared folder instead of
on their computer's local hard disk. This makes it much easier for the administrator to manage,
back up, and control access to the organization's data. Because the folder is shared, you can
access it from your computer and save information to it just as if it were on a local storage
device.
In order to access a shared folder, your user account must be granted access to it. Depending on
how your workstation and server are configured, you may be required to provide a username and
password to access the shared folder.

Lesson 15C
Using Virtualization
Objectives Covered
2.6 Compare and contrast virtualization and cloud technologies.
3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.
Virtualization lets a single physical computer run multiple operating systems at the same
time, each in its own isolated virtual machine. This technology powers everything from server
consolidation in data centers to safe testing environments on a desktop. Special software called
a hypervisor manages how the computer's processor, memory, and storage are shared among
these virtual machines.
In this lesson, you will learn what virtualization is and how it is used, explore the differences
between Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors, understand how guest operating systems work inside
virtual machines, and discover how remote desktop tools let you access and control computers
from anywhere. You will also see how containers and virtual servers make IT infrastructure
more efficient and secure.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is virtualization, and what are common uses for virtual machines on desktops and
servers?
• What is the difference between a Type 1 and a Type 2 hypervisor?
• What is a guest operating system, and how does it run inside a virtual machine?
• How does a hypervisor manage CPU, memory, and storage for virtual machines?
• What is remote desktop, and what tools are commonly used for remote access and support?
• What is container virtualization, and how does it differ from traditional virtual machines?
What is Virtualization?
Virtualization technology has been available for decades. Early computers were very expensive,
with personal computer prices ranging from $440 to $9,875 (in US dollars) in the 1970s. With
virtualization, users could make their computers act like they had another, separate system
running on it at the same time. So instead of buying a new, separate computer for $1,500, you
could spend $300 on components to get a second operating system running on the computer
you already have!
At the time of writing, inflation and rising costs mean that the personal computer price range of
$440 to $9,875 in the 1970s is equal to a price range of $3,100 up to $47,500 today.

When you use virtualization, you partition off a safe and separate space on your computer for
the virtual machines (VMs).  Virtual machines are sometimes called guests, and they are the
computer systems that run commands, open programs, and save files. In other words, they do
all the things a typical computer does. VMs do this within your original physical computer, often
called a host.
Imagine your computer is a large apartment building. Different families (operating systems, in
this analogy) live in their own apartments (virtual machines) within the larger structure. Walls
are separating the apartments from each other, and every family has their own home with
everything they need. Things like a kitchen (CPU),  a living room (memory), storage space (hard
disk), and a door to the outside world (network link) are all available to each family.
Just like families within an apartment building can borrow a cup of sugar or chat in the
hallways, virtual machines can communicate between themselves if they are connected through
a network. In most situations, VMs are organized so that they don't share information directly
with the host computer, as this type of connection can be a security risk.
Virtualization Uses
Virtualization is especially useful for servers. Servers are powerful computers that can manage
a huge number of tasks at once. They can easily run more than one operating system without
any loss of performance. They have so much capacity that they can divide up the memory and
storage space so each operating system has its own little section to work in. This is one of the
biggest advantages of virtualization: resources get used very efficiently. All that capacity on
servers doesn't go to waste.
Virtualization software can also be used on desktop computers for various purposes. Some
typical uses of desktop virtualization are:
• Virtual labs: Used to create a research lab to analyze viruses. As the malware is contained
within the guest OS, it cannot infect the researcher's computer or network.
• Support legacy software applications: If the host computers have been upgraded, software
may not work well with the new operating system. For example, Windows 7 could be
installed, which can natively run older programs.
• Development environment: Test software applications under different operating systems and
resource constraints. This is a quick and easy way to run through new software to see if
there are any issues.
• Training: Lab environments can be set up so that students can practice using a live
operating system and software without impacting the production environment. At the end
of the lab, changes to the VM can be discarded, and the original environment is available
again for the next student to use.
The presence of other guest operating systems can be completely transparent to any single OS.
Each OS "thinks" it’s working with its own CPU, memory, hard disk, and network link. However,
the guest operating systems can be networked together, or they may be able to share data
directly through the hypervisor (though this is not commonly done for security reasons).
Remote Desktop
A remote desktop connection lets you control a computer from a different location as if you
were sitting in front of it. You see the remote computer's screen on your device, and your
keyboard and mouse inputs are sent to the remote machine. This technology is widely used for
IT support, working from home, and accessing virtual desktops hosted in data centers.

How Remote Desktop Works
Remote desktop uses a client-server model. The computer you want to control runs a remote
desktop server (or host) service. You connect to it using a remote desktop client application
on your local device. All communication between the two happens over a network connection,
typically encrypted to keep your session secure.
When connected, the remote computer sends screen images to your device and receives your
keyboard and mouse inputs in return. Files on the remote machine stay on the remote machine
unless you specifically transfer them. This makes remote desktop useful for situations where
sensitive data should not leave a secure network.
Common Remote Desktop Tools
Several remote desktop and remote support tools are available:
• Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP):  Built into Windows Professional and Enterprise editions.
Lets you connect to another Windows computer over the network. The remote machine must
have Remote Desktop enabled.
• TeamViewer: A cross-platform tool that allows remote access and remote support without
complex network configuration. The remote user installs TeamViewer and shares a session
ID and password.
• Quick Assist (Windo ws):  A built-in Windows tool for remote support. A helper generates
a security code and shares it with the person who needs help, then connects to view or
control their screen.
• Chrome Remote Desktop: A free, browser-based option from Google that works across
Windows, macOS, Linux, and Chrome OS.
• Virtual Network Computing (VNC):  An open-source protocol that works across different
operating systems. Popular implementations include RealVNC and TightVNC.
Remote Desktop Use Cases
Remote desktop technology serves several important purposes:
• IT support: Technicians can troubleshoot and fix problems on a user's computer without
being in the same room or even the same building. This is especially valuable for help desk
teams supporting remote workers.
• Working remotely: Employees can connect to their office workstation from home and access
all their files, applications, and network resources as if they were on-site.
• Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI):  Organizations can host virtual desktops on centralized
servers using hypervisors. Users connect to their virtual desktop remotely using a thin client
or any device with a remote desktop client. This simplifies management because IT only
needs to maintain the server-side virtual machines.
• Server administration: System administrators manage servers that may be located in data
centers far away. Remote desktop or SSH (Secur e  Shell) connections let them configure,
update, and monitor servers without physical access.
Security Considerations
Because remote desktop gives full control over a machine, securing the connection is critical:
• Strong passwords: Remote access accounts should use complex passwords to prevent
unauthorized access.
• Multi-factor authentication (MF A):  Adding a second verification step (like a phone code)
makes it much harder for attackers to break in.
• Encryption: Most remote desktop tools encrypt the connection so that screen data and
keystrokes cannot be intercepted.

• Firewall rules: Only allow remote desktop connections from trusted networks or through a
Virtual Private Network (VPN).
• Disable when not needed: If you don't use remote desktop, turn it off. An open remote
desktop port is a common target for attackers.
Hypervisors and Guest Operating Systems
Type 1 Hypervisors
A bare-metal hypervisor, also called a Type 1 hypervisor, is special software that works directly
on a computer without needing Windows or any other operating system first. It's great because
it lets virtual machines (VMs)  run incredibly well without a lot of interference. Since there's no
main operating system in the way, the computer can give out more power to the VMs. It's also
safer because there's less chance for viruses or malicious software to get in.
Type 2 Hypervisors
On the other hand, a Type 2 hypervisor is similar to a regular program you run on your
computer, like a game or a word processor. It needs the main operating system, like Windows or
macOS, to work. It does a lot of the same things as Type 1, but it uses more of the computer's
resources to get started.

You can virtualize Windows and Linux inside of each other, inside their own OS, or inside a macOS.
However, you can't virtualize the Apple macOS inside a virtual environment. Apple does not permit
this; they want users to run their OS on their platform.
So what do real hypervisors look like? Here are a few you're likely to run into:
• Hyper - V :  This one is actually built right into certain versions of Windows (Pr o  and Enterprise
editions). It comes with a tool called Hyper-V Manager that lets you create, start, and
stop virtual machines without installing anything extra. Even though it lives inside Windows,
Hyper-V itself acts like a Type 1 hypervisor under the hood.
• VMware ESXi: This is a Type 1 hypervisor you'd find in big server rooms and data centers.
Companies use it to run dozens or even hundreds of virtual servers on a single powerful
machine.
• VirtualBox: A free Type 2 hypervisor that works on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It's a
popular choice for students and hobbyists who want to experiment with different operating
systems without any risk to their main computer.
• VMware Workstation: Another Type 2 hypervisor, but geared more toward IT professionals
who need to test software or set up practice labs on their desktops.
Guest Operating Systems
The guest operating system (OS)  is the term for the operating system that runs inside the virtual
environment. This might surprise you, but sometimes people need to use an older version of
Windows for certain things. And when it comes to Linux, there are hundreds of versions, or
"distros," that can be set up in these virtual machines.
What's most common, though, is putting several Linux or Windows servers inside one physical
computer. This is handy because servers have a ton of power. They often have more than one
CPU with multiple cores (which is like having more than one brain), a lot more memory than a
typical computer, and more storage space as well. With virtualization, you can divide up this
power among multiple guest operating systems. If you wanted, you could even have Windows
running inside another Windows, kind of like Russian nesting dolls, where one fits inside the
other.

Guest OS Uses
Let's try to understand why this is so great. Your computer can pretend to be many computers
at once. Now, each pretend computer can do a different job. For example, one might keep all
the office files together for you and your coworkers, another might keep track of all the printers,
and a third might handle all the emails. These pretend computers can each use a different OS
if a certain system is better for a certain thing, Windows Server on one and Linux Ubuntu on
another, for example.
It's important to make clear that these computers don't affect each other. That's one huge
advantage. If one gets a virus or stops working, it won't cause problems for the others. Each
VM is isolated in its own space, so what happens in one doesn't affect the others.
Hardware and Virtual Machines (VMs)
The magic behind virtualization is done by the hypervisor. It's like the director of a play, telling
everything where to go and what to do. The hypervisor can actually create new virtual central
processing units (CPUs).  Even though it's using the real CPU, the hypervisor divides it up so
that many virtual guest computers can use the CPU at the same time. This division can happen
with other parts of the computer system, such as with memory, for example.
For memory, the hypervisor divides out a portion of the real memory and assigns it to each
virtual computer. And it does the same with storage, giving each virtual machine a slice of
the real computer's hard drive to keep its files on. Sometimes, it even makes virtual graphics
cards for high-end video graphics. The hypervisor also handles the connection of these virtual
computers to networks and the Internet.
One benefit is how fluid everything can be. If one of the guest machines needs more storage
space, the hypervisor can just assign more storage from the real computer's hard drive over
to the guest machine. It's like having a backpack made of expandable material. You can keep
stuffing books in there, and the backpack will keep stretching out.
Organizations and cloud storage providers try to use virtualization for their servers quite a lot.
Instead of having many separate servers, they make one big server pretend to be many smaller
ones. Doing this takes some of the load off their IT workers and technicians. There's also less
equipment in general in the network room, so they can use the space for other things. Less
equipment means less generated heat. Heat is a natural enemy to computers; having a cooler
temperature in the network room means the computers will run better and last longer.
Container Virtualization
Container virtualization is a lighter way to use a computer to run a lot of apps at the same
time without them getting in each other's way. In this scenario, let's imagine that your computer
is a house, and each app lives in its own room. It's a lot like regular virtualization, because
even though they share the same house, there are walls between them. The difference is that
containers are more flexible and don't need a whole computer system for each app or program,
just enough to make the app work. So they don't take up much space, they work very fast, and
you can easily move them from one computer to another. It's a leaner, more portable way to
take advantage of virtualization.
Virtual Servers
You might not realize it, but a lot of websites you visit are actually running on virtual servers.
To you, it looks and feels the same as any other website. But using virtual servers has some
benefits for the professionals who run the websites.
First, it saves them money. Instead of having to buy a bunch of physical machines, they can just
have one machine act like many, and they don't end up spending as much on upkeep. It's also

just easier overall when things aren't scattered everywhere, and it's all in one place. And the
network administrators who manage all these complex operations love virtual servers because
they make their jobs easier, too.
For those professional developers, virtual servers work great because they can test new apps
and programs in a virtual, safe environment, so they don't mess up the whole system if
something goes wrong. It's like having a sandbox to mess around in and then clean up and
start over again. In fact, it actually is called a "sandbox" in the technological world.
Another benefit is that if a virus gets in, it won't spread to other parts of the computer
system. It's confined to its own little virtual bubble. Also, fewer physical computers means less
electricity being generated. That's not only good for saving money but also better for the planet!
So even though you might not see it, virtual servers are a big part of your everyday life on the
internet.
