Lesson 16A
Understanding Technology Risks
Objectives Covered
6.1 Explain fundamental security concepts and frameworks.
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
Every time you connect to the internet or install a new program, you are exposing your
computer to potential threats. Malicious software, or malware, comes in many forms including
viruses, worms, spyware, and ransomware. Each type behaves differently, but all of them can
compromise your data, your privacy, or your ability to use your device.
You will learn about common types of malware and how they spread, and explore the security
tools that help protect your devices. You will discover how firewalls filter network traffic, how
anti-malware software detects and removes threats, and what steps you can take to reduce
your risk of infection.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is malware, and what are the main types of malicious software?
• How do viruses, worms, and ransomware differ in how they spread and what they do?
• What is spyware, and how does it typically get installed on a computer?
• What is a firewall, and how does it help protect a computer or network?
• How does anti-malware software detect and remove threats?
• What steps can you take to protect yourself from ransomware and other malware attacks?
Malware and Spyware
Since the very beginning of the computer age, threat actors have been making harmful code to
attack or to invade computers. Originally, when most of the computers in the world belonged
to governments or to corporations, malicious software or malware evolved as another part of
espionage and spying. Here are some of the common types of malware, or malicious content.
Virus
A virus is the worst kind of malware, intentionally designed to disrupt computer systems or
networks. Viruses need users to get started, but once they are inside a system, they can spread
between computers and corrupt both data and software. It's important to know that viruses
can't actually break the computer's physical components, but they can make programs, and the
computer's operating system stop functioning properly.
Viruses come in many varieties, and they can have different goals, including simple vandalism,
financial gain, or disabling parts of an enemy nation's infrastructure. Some viruses can delete

data, replacing the target files with code or information of their own. Some are designed to
target specific types of programs, and others are designed to move through entire networks as
quickly as possible.
The most famous of all virus infections, designed to damage Iran's nuclear program, is Stuxnet.
Discovered in 2010, this virus used several different types of code to disable machinery and to
cover its tracks. The Stuxnet attack specifically targeted computers that were air-gapped, or
separated from any network. This meant that the attackers had to introduce the virus without
relying on someone clicking a link or downloading a file. They instead used USB or flash drives
with the virus pre-installed, and placed the drives near the nuclear facilities. One or more
employees eventually plugged the flash drives into the air-gapped computers, and Stuxnet was
off and running. In this way, the attack used both a virus and social engineering to accomplish
its goal
Worms
Worms are another type of malware that spreads over a network by themselves, without
needing human intervention. A worm can make copies of itself to move from one computer
to another, taking advantage of weak spots in the network. Within the past 25 years, there
have been many serious worm infections, affecting millions of computers. Sometimes worms
carry another type of malware, which may lock up data, steal sensitive information, or install
backdoors or infect entire systems.
Spyware
Spyware is a type of software that tries to view and record what you do on your computer.
Users may inadvertently install spyware onto their computers because it often comes bundled
with legitimate programs. Sometimes it can include a keylogger, which is a tool that records
what you type, like your passwords and other credentials. This means that the threat actors who
run the keylogger could steal your information.
Most of the time, people use spyware to make money by showing you annoying pop-up ads
or banners. They do this by getting the malware into lots of computers, bundled with legitimate
programs. Companies that sell things want lots of people to visit their website. More visitors
could mean more sales. So, they pay for ads that help bring people to their site. You might see
these ads as banners on different websites. Websites can charge money based on how many
people see the ad or click on it to visit the company's site.
While it's not always illegal, there are many software programs designed just to show you more
ads and pop-ups. If you click on these, the person who made the program gets paid by the
company that's happy to have more people visiting their site.
Ransomware
Ransomware is a type of malware that locks you out of your own files or entire computer and
demands a payment (ransom) to give you access back. It typically works by encrypting your
files so you cannot open them. The attacker then displays a message demanding payment,
usually in cryptocurrency like Bitcoin, in exchange for the decryption key.
Ransomware can arrive on your computer in several ways. The most common delivery method
is through phishing emails that trick you into clicking a malicious link or opening an infected
attachment. It can also spread through compromised websites, infected USB drives, or by
exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in software.
Once ransomware activates, it works quickly. It may encrypt documents, photos, databases,
and other important files within minutes. Some advanced versions can also spread across a
network, locking down multiple computers in an organization at the same time. Victims typically

see a ransom note on their screen with instructions for how to pay and a deadline, after which
the attacker may threaten to delete the files permanently or increase the ransom amount.
Security experts and law enforcement agencies generally advise against paying the ransom.
There is no guarantee the attacker will actually restore your files, and paying encourages more
attacks. Instead, the best defense against ransomware is prevention:
• Keep regular backups: Store copies of important files on an external drive or cloud service
that is not always connected to your computer. If ransomware strikes, you can restore your
files from the backup.
• Update your software: Install operating system and application updates promptly. Many
ransomware attacks exploit known vulnerabilities that patches have already fixed.
• Be cautious with email: Do not open attachments or click links from unknown senders. Even
messages that appear to come from someone you know could be spoofed.
• Use anti-malware software: Keep your anti-malware protection active and up to date so it
can detect and block ransomware before it executes.

Lesson 16B
Applying Basic Security Concepts
Objectives Covered
6.1 Explain fundamental security concepts and frameworks.
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
6.4 Identify common use cases for encryption.
Security is the practice of controlling access to something important, like information or a place.
With computers occupying a large part of personal and professional life, keeping them safe
from threats such as hacking and identity fraud is vitally important. Layers of security come
from understanding industry standards, using common sense, and enforcing rules about who
can do what with a given computer system.
In this lesson, you will explore the foundational concepts that keep computers and data safe.
You will learn about physical device security, security frameworks like the CIA Triad and NIST,
how authentication and authorization control access, how encryption protects data in transit,
and how accounting and tracking monitor what happens on a system.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• Why is physical security important for computers, and what tools can help prevent theft?
• What are confidentiality, integrity, and availability, and why do they matter in cybersecurity?
• What are the different factors of authentication, and how does multi-factor authentication
improve security?
• How do permissions and the principle of least privilege help protect a computer system?
• What is encryption, and how does HTTPS keep your data safe online?
• How do accounting and location tracking help organizations monitor and secure their
systems?
Device Security
The most basic part of cybersecurity is controlling physical access to computers and network
devices. If a threat actor gets physical access to a computer without permission, they can do a
lot of harm to the entire system. Physically touching the computer means someone can begin to
guess passwords, or steal a hard drive to get access to its data, among other attacks.
Computers are high-value targets for two different reasons:
• Physical value: Some computers are expensive because they're made with expensive parts.
The computer is valuable for what it is.
• Data value: Almost every computer stores data of some kind. The computer is valuable for
what it holds.

People who work in cybersecurity also ensure the physical security of the computers and
devices they look after, as part of their job role.
Equipment Locks
Hardware locks for computers and networking equipment have been around for decades. As
computers became smaller and more mobile, it became easier for threat actors to walk away
with sensitive equipment. These hardware locks can attach to any device. In some cases, the
lock will keep the equipment in one place, and in other situations, a different type of lock will
prevent unauthorized people from using the device, even if they are able to steal it.
Most laptops, except ultra-thin laptops, have a small hole on the side or back. This hole is made
for a special kind of lock, called a Kensington lock. This lock looks similar to a bike lock and
comes with a cable. You first wrap the flexible cable around something big and sturdy, like a
pole, a handrail, or another anchor point. Then insert the cable through the laptop and into the
locking mechanism, locking it with a code or a key.
The first company to make these locks was called Kensington. While many different manufacturers
produce this type of device lock, most people just call the locks "Kensington locks.
Image © 123rf.com.
While it might seem like very basic security measures, many times people steal things just
because they see a chance. If a laptop is left sitting alone on a table, it's easy for someone to
grab it and put it in their backpack. A locking cable around a laptop makes it much harder to
steal. When theft requires bolt cutters, crime goes down.
Many organizations use these locks on other devices as well. Desktop computers, monitors,
and projectors are all compatible with this type of cable-based lock.
USB Locks
You can also put a USB lock on an open USB port on a computer to stop users from using these
ports. The lock is easy to install and will prevent unauthorized data transfers through the USB
port. It can also stop the computer from booting up from a USB drive.

Other Physical Security
In addition to locking devices directly, cybersecurity professionals also help prevent theft in
other ways. This usually involves keeping servers in one room where doors are locked, and not
allowing unauthorized people into areas of critical operations.
"I was working for a client who had multiple spaces in an office tower, which also
occupied several other companies. The client's server room was down the hallway
on the same floor. While walking past the server room one day, I noticed that the
server room door was propped open with a door stop. No one was in the server
room, but the door was wide open. On a floor that not only housed my client, but also
several other companies. I asked them why the server room door was propped open,
and they told me it was because there was no ventilation in the room, so they kept
the door open to keep the servers cool. I asked if they were concerned about some
random person walking into the server room. They told me "Well, no one has done it
so far."
-- Greg C., security technician
All employees have a role in cybersecurity. Companies should train every person to understand
how they can help support security measures and how to confidently enforce the rules. Any
person can ask people they don't know, or people without the right security badge, to prove
they should be where they are. A lot of trouble can be stopped if people using computers know
about common threats and take precautions to avoid them. Many businesses make sure their
workers go through training often, so everyone knows about the newest threats.
Security Strategies
Most companies want to believe their computer networks are safe. They create user accounts,
follow strict rules, and check for security issues. But sometimes, people try to break into these
networks from both inside and outside the company. These attempts might be harmful, or just
someone with computer skills wanting to see if they can get in. Because keeping information
safe is so important, working in this part of technology requires a lot of focus, discipline, and a
clear understanding of security concepts.
A cybersecurity framework guides the selection and configuration of devices and behaviors
that keep a computer system secure. Frameworks are important because they stop an
organization from building its security program in a vacuum, or from building the program on a
foundation that fails to account for important security concepts.
Here are two commonly used strategies that many organizations use to guide their work in
security.
The CIA Triad
The field of information security uses the CIA Triad as its primary principles of security control
and management. For information and systems to be considered secure, they must have all
three of these properties:
• Confidentiality: The information can only be read by people explicitly authorized to access it.
• Integrity: The information is stored and transferred as intended, and any modification is
authorized.
• Availability: The information is readily available and accessible to those authorized to view or
modify it.
The triad can also be referred to as "AIC" to avoid confusion with the Central Intelligence Agency.

Nearly all organizations have information that should be kept confidential. For example, the
president of a public company might receive the company's financial documents from the
accountant, but they will not be publicly released for weeks. Other employees do not need
to see the numbers before the release date. Keeping these numbers a secret from the other
employees is an example of information confidentiality.
When the company accountant transmits the balance sheet to the company president,
the numbers should not change. They should be the same numbers when they leave the
accountant and when they arrive in the president's files. This is an example of information
integrity.
If the president of the company needs to review the financials right away, she can easily and
reliably access those documents. There's no barrier to her being able to open or to read those
files. This is an example of information availability.
Some security models and researchers identify other properties of secure systems. The most
important of these is non-repudiation. Non-repudiation means that a person cannot deny doing
something, such as creating, modifying, or sending a resource. For example, a legal document,
such as a person's will, must usually be witnessed when it is signed. If there is a dispute about
whether the document was correctly completed, the witness can provide evidence that it was.
"A user clicked a link he should not have clicked. He ended up forwarding a phishing
email to everyone in his address book. Clients, vendors and coworkers reported
the phish. The user told his boss he did not click the link and did not forward any
phish emails. I performed an eDiscovery search within Microsoft 365. The employee
actually DID forward the phish email. I found evidence in his Sent Items folder. Ten
minutes later, the same evidence was in his Deleted Items folder. The employee's lies
were not credible. He lost to non-repudiation. The employee no longer works there."
-- Mark A, cybersecurity consultant
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework
When we talk about keeping information safe, cybersecurity means making sure the computers
and programs we use are secure. Information security and cybersecurity tasks can be grouped
into five basic functions, following the framework developed by the National Institute of
Standards and Technology (NIS T):
• Identify: Develop security policies and capabilities. Evaluate risks, threats, and weak spots in
the system and recommend security controls to reduce the risks.
• Protect: Develop, install, operate, and retire IT hardware and software assets. Focus on
security as a requirement of every stage of this operation's lifecycle.
• Detect: Perform ongoing, proactive monitoring to be sure that controls are effective and
capable of protecting against new types of threats.
• Respond: Identify, analyze, contain, and eliminate threats to systems and data security.
• Recover: Restore systems and data if other controls are unable to prevent attacks.
Where the CIA Triad is a collection of ideas about security, the NIST framework is something
that companies can apply more actively to the work their employees do. Some companies
choose to organize their cybersecurity departments around these five functions. They might
have job roles that are only associated with the Protect function, for example. Other job roles
focus specifically on the Recovery aspect of cybersecurity.

Authentication Factors
Authentication is the process of ensuring that each account is only operated by its proper user.
There are many different authentication technologies and methods. These different ways of
authenticating a subject are referred to as factors.
Something You Know
This category includes anything that only the user should know. The typical example is the
login credentials. Login credentials are the combination of a username and a password. The
username is not typically a secret, because it's usually some combination of the user's first and
last names, but the password must only be known to the account holder. Some other examples
include:
• Passphrase: A passphrase is a longer password comprising several words. This has
the advantages of being more secure because of its length, and easier to remember.
"PurpleMonkeyDishwasher" will stay in most people's minds longer than " o x94T Y8~3qio7"
will.
• PIN:  A Personal Identification Number (PIN)  is a type of password you remember. It's also
called a passcode, and it can contain both numbers and letters. Using a passcode is a fast
and safe way to get into your device. Many people like to use passcodes because they're
easy to remember.
• Patterns: Devices with touchscreens can offer the option to use a pattern lock as another
security measure. This allows the user to draw a predefined pattern on a grid of 3 columns
and 3 rows of dots.
Another key idea in proving who you are by using things you know is the concept of Personally
Identifiable Information (PII).  This kind of proof is also helpful when you need to reset your
account. For instance, PII is often used for security questions to check who you are when you
call about your account. The person talking to you on the phone wants to make sure you are
really you. For example, PII could be answers to questions like "What is your favorite movie?"
"What street did you grow up on?" or "What is the name of your first-grade teacher?"
Something You Have
This category means that the account holder, or the person with permission, owns something
unique that no one else has. There are several ways to authenticate a user based on something
they have.
One way to prove who you are is to give each person a special hardware token. The most
well-known one used to be the SecurID token. It creates a number code that matches a code on
a server, which you need to enter to log in. The code changes about every 60 seconds. SecurID
tokens were popular until smartphones became more common. Now, with authenticator apps,
smartphones make it easier to use this kind of "something you have" authentication.
Something You Are
This category relies on something unique and virtually unchangeable about the user.
"Something you are" authentication means using a system that recognizes unique body
features. Biometric authentication uses special traits each person has that can prove who
they are. You can use many kinds of biometric information, such as fingerprints, retina or iris
patterns in a person's eye, facial recognition, or even the way someone's voice sounds, to
identify them.
When the system administrator creates the account, the user is there in person to have their
unique body features, like fingerprints or eye patterns, scanned into the system. These scans
are saved in the security system as a template. When the user wants to log in, the system

checks the biometrics that the user provides and compares them to the saved template to make
sure they match.
This is a fast and easy way to figure out who someone is. If the scans match, the person is
allowed in. These unique features are very difficult for someone else to copy, which makes
them an excellent part of the authentication process. Another good thing is that, unlike special
security devices, it's hard to lose your own biometrics!
Windows 10 and 11 provide support for biometrics to authenticate you through something called
Windows Hello. If your computer can use Windows Hello (if your laptop has the right camera or
a fingerprint reader), you'll find this option in Account Settings. Your computer can remember
your face, iris image, or fingerprint and use that to let you in. It's a nice way to get into your
device without needing a password or PIN. Plus, once you're logged in, you can use your
biometrics to sign in to websites or pay for things online.
The biggest issues with using biometrics are that some users find it intrusive and worry about
their privacy. Also, setting up and keeping the system running can be more expensive than
other authentication methods. Sometimes, biometrics can make mistakes, like not letting the
right person in (false negatives) or letting the wrong person in by mistake (false positives).
Multifactor and Two-factor Authentication
Passwords alone are usually not strong enough to protect very important or high-risk
applications like company networks or bank accounts. Any of the factors on this page can
be a key part of two-factor authentication (2F A).  Two-factor authentication adds an extra step
to logging in, on top of using passwords.
Some situations require even more security, an authentication system that's as strong as
possible. Implementing multi-factor authentication (MF A),  using multiple authentication types,
will increase the strength of the system. With two or more steps, it's much tougher for hackers
to get into accounts and devices.
Single Sign-On
Single Sign-On (SSO)  means that a user only has to authenticate to a system one time to
gain access to all its resources. For example, with one set of login credentials on a Windows
computer, a user will also seamlessly be logged into other Windows services, websites, and
programs. This makes life easier because users don't have to remember lots of different logins,
which can be tiring. It's handy because you don't have to keep track of many accounts, but

there's a downside, too. If a hacker gets into your one account, they could get into everything
else you have access to.
Authorization Factors
Authorization is the process of determining what rights, or permissions, users should have on
each resource, such as a file or a program. Authorization also includes enforcing those rights.
Permissions
Every organization has a huge number of programs, files, and folders in its computer
system. Even smaller companies create many files in the course of regular operations. Larger
organizations have the added layer of different departments with different roles, such as
Marketing and Finance. Each department has specific programs and files they work with to
do their jobs, and they don't need to use or look at files or resources from other departments. A
network administrator will set different permissions for those files, based on who needs to use
them.
Permissions can vary between systems, but the IT industry broadly categorizes permissions
into different types, like the ones listed here:
• Read: A user or group of users can view or read the file, but that is all.
• Write: A user or group of users can read the file, and can also modify or edit the file.
• Execute: A user or group of users can run a program or script from the file.
• Delete: A user or group of users can remove the file.
For example, a company may have a mission statement on how it will conduct its business.
Employees may want to review the document from time to time, but no one should change the
mission statement. This document has "read-only" permissions.
Network administrators can also set permissions at different levels. For example, the company's
brand directory, or entire set of files, could have one set of permissions, such as "read-only,"
to make sure that everyone in the company uses the same set of logos and colors. A company
might also set specific permissions that apply only to a single folder or a small group of files.
Network administrators can also assign permissions to individual users or to groups of users.
For example, the entire Development team may need to read or to view the schedule for project
A, but only the individual project manager should be able to edit or write to that schedule.
In other cases, an entire department has different levels of permission related to a directory,
but members of other departments can't access that set of files at all. Financial and human
resource files, containing sensitive information, fall into this category. Setting group permissions
makes the IT department's job much simpler.
Least Privilege
In IT, there's a rule called least privilege. This rule means that a user only gets the access they
need to do their job, and nothing more. You could think of it like keys to a building. Employees
only get keys to the rooms they need to go into and are kept out of places they don't need.
This helps to reduce the risk of security breaches, simple mistakes that expose a network, or
introducing software that may corrupt system data. The concept of least privilege makes IT
management quite a bit easier.
When you give more people access or permissions on a computer or network, you're taking a
bigger risk that someone might use those permissions in a way they shouldn't. The user could
misuse that permission intentionally, or they could cause a problem by accident. To keep things
safer, authorization policies make sure people only get the special access they really need,
based on the concept of least privilege.

Think of it like an invite-only party. If you're not on the party's guest list, you can't come in. In
the same way, access controls work by saying "no" to everyone unless there's a specific "yes"
that lets them in. This is called implicit denial. If there's no clear rule that says you can have
access, then the answer is automatically no.
Administrators and Standard Users
Some special accounts can do anything they want on the entire computer system. On Windows
and Apple macOS, these accounts are called Administrators, and on Linux, they're called
the Root user. Because these accounts can change anything on the computer, network
administrators must be extremely careful when assigning these special user types.
Just below the Administrator, there's a type of account called a standard user. Standard users
can still do their job tasks, such as opening files and using programs, but they can't add new
software or modify important system settings. The goal for the standard user permission level
is to let the workers do their jobs without needing to ask the IT department for help all the time,
while also keeping the computer safe.
In many organizations, it's common to assign these standard permissions to people using the
computers or workstations. This helps to limit changes from being made and lowers the risk
of malicious events. For a virus to get into a computer or network, it has to run, just like any
other program. That's why not allowing the installation of new programs is a key step in keeping
things secure.
Accounting and Tracking
Accounting is the process of documenting user actions on the computer system. Accounting
uses specialized software to log, or record, events that take place on the network. Events are
things like sign-on attempts, software use, and file modification. When you log into a system
that has this type of security logging software, that software will record how you logged in,
what time you logged in, which programs and files you worked on (and at what times), and
when you sign out. Accounting can keep track of different things like computer systems, people
using the computer, files, and even remote connections.
For example, the resources could be the database programs the user opens in the course of
their day-to-day work. This database generates monthly sales reports, and the user prints out
these reports.
Another example is the history of websites visited while browsing the web. This allows the
accounting system to track what users are doing within the system.
Windows Event Viewer can display many of these accounting functions.

Used with permission from Microsoft.
Location Tracking
Location tracking uses technology to record the geographical location of a person or a device.
Different tracking systems use different methods to do this, including the Global Positioning
System (GPS),  cell towers, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi. People and companies use location tracking for
many things, such as using a token to find where you left your cell phone, or for larger logistical
systems like trucking companies.
Location tracking can also be used as a barrier to stop hackers from getting into computer
systems. Geofencing is a security measure that tracks assets by drawing an invisible line
around the specific physical place that holds them. If those important assets move outside the
line, it sends a warning to the IT department that someone might have moved the company's
equipment. This could mean someone stole something from the company.
Web Browser History
Browsers don't just remember the websites you go to; they also know where you're using the
internet from. Are you at home, or are you somewhere else on vacation? There are actually
some valid reasons to let your browser keep doing this, even if it seems intrusive. For example,
if you're hungry and want to order a pizza, searching online will show you pizza places near
you. You can choose if you want your location to be tracked or not by turning this setting on or
off whenever you like.
When you travel to a different part of the world and try to log into common apps such as Gmail,
your account might get flagged. This is because logging in from a location you've never been
to, or don't typically go to, looks suspicious. This could look like someone else trying to get into
your account. The site owners flag your account, or reach out to you through your cellphone or
other backup method, to help stop anyone who shouldn't be getting into your account.

Lesson 16C
Using Device Security Tools
Objectives Covered
6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.
5.4 Explain basic data backup concepts.
Keeping a computer safe requires more than just being careful online. Security tools like
antivirus software and firewalls work behind the scenes to block threats before they can cause
damage. Understanding how these tools work, and how people can use them correctly, is an
essential part of protecting any device or network.
In this lesson, you will learn how antivirus software detects and removes malware, how firewalls
filter network traffic to block unauthorized access, and how layered security strategies like
defense in depth protect organizations. You will also explore recovery options such as patching,
System Restore, Safe Mode, and Reset This PC that help you fix problems when something
goes wrong.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is the primary function of antivirus software, and how does real-time scanning protect
your computer?
• What is a firewall, and how does it use rules to filter network traffic?
• Why is defense in depth important, and how do separation of duties and network
segmentation contribute to security?
• What can happen when people use security tools incorrectly or rely too heavily on
automation?
• Why is it important to keep software patched and updated?
• What recovery options are available when a Windows computer stops working correctly?
Antivirus Software
Antivirus scanners or antivirus software helps to identify and stop harmful attacks on your
computer or network. It primarily works by using a list of known virus patterns, called definitions
or signatures. Another way it works is through heuristic identification. This means the software
looks for actions or behaviors that are similar to what viruses do and tries to block those
actions.
What is Antivirus Software?
Antivirus software, also called security software, usually comes in two types. One type is
a personal security suite, which protects just one computer. The other type is a network

security suite, which protects many computers and is managed from a central server. Most
antivirus software is made for Windows PCs and networks because most viruses target these
systems. However, there is also antivirus software for Linux and for Apple's macOS. Some of
the big companies that make antivirus software are Avast, Norton, AVG, Trend Micro, Sophos,
Malwarebytes, and Bitdefender.
Some companies offer a basic free version of their antivirus software. This free version usually
has the same main engine as the paid version, but doesn't have all the extra features. Corporate
networks don't use the free versions, but it can be a good option for individuals. The most
important thing is to install antivirus software on your computer and keep it updated.
If one antivirus program is good, then two must be better, right? Actually, that's not true. If you use
two antivirus programs, they will conflict with each other and slow down your machine. It's best to
stick with one good antivirus and malware program.
A good IT professional will use antivirus software to protect systems. Make sure you have these
programs installed and updated. Remember, there's no such thing as 100% protection from
every possible attack, so always be careful when you connect to the Internet.
Constant Vigilance
All antivirus software is set up for real-time scanning. Real-time scanning is a feature in
antivirus software that constantly watches your computer for threats. It checks files, programs,
and processes as you open or use them to make sure they are safe. If the software finds
anything suspicious, it can block or remove the threat right away. This helps protect your
computer from viruses, malware, and other harmful attacks as they happen.
Real-time scanning might make your computer a little slower, but it's an important part of
keeping it safe from threats. Just as the software checks files as you use them, the software
can also check system memory, email attachments, removable drives, and network drives for
viruses. Many scanners can even find websites with harmful scripts or code. When setting up
antivirus software, it's important to set the right exceptions, or rules. Scanning some system
files and folders in real-time can cause performance issues.
In addition to real-time monitoring, you can set up scans to run at times that work best for you.
If your computer is busy all day, schedule scans at night when the system activity is lower.
You can choose to scan daily, weekly, or monthly. You can also decide whether to scan only
important files or the entire system on your hard drive.
How Antivirus Software Works During an Attack
Malware such as worms can spread over networks. This means that once they get into a
network, they will copy themselves to other computers. Therefore, if an attack happens, one of
the first things you should do is disconnect the network. Taking a system off the network is a
simple but effective way to stop the threat from spreading.
If a file has a virus, most of the time, antivirus software will find it and neutralize it. You can
set up what the software should do when it finds malware during a scan. You can use antivirus

software to try to remove the virus (called cleaning) or quarantine the file, in which the software
blocks any attempt to open it. Think of quarantining like putting the bad software in a locked
box.
The reason you would not want to permanently delete the file is that sometimes the antivirus
software makes a mistake and thinks a safe file is a virus. This is called a false positive. The
file might be needed by a legitimate system program. If, days later, you notice that an important
program isn't working, it might be because the file is in quarantine. To fix this, you can take the
file out of quarantine and put it back in the right folder.
Sometimes a virus can infect a computer so badly that the only way to fix it is to format the hard
drive or erase everything on it completely and reinstall Windows. Ideally, you have backed up
your data before starting this process.
Security Tools in Practice
The security devices, software, and practices are a very important part of keeping networks
secure. Making sure that people use them correctly is just as important. The way people use
security tools can affect cybersecurity in many ways, both good and bad.
Human Impact on Cybersecurity
When people use security tools correctly, they can make an organization much safer.
Automated tools can find, analyze, and fix security problems quickly, often much faster than
a person could. This means that humans can spend more time focusing on complex problems.
However, if people use security tools incorrectly, they can create weaknesses. For example, a
poorly configured firewall might let in unauthorized users. In another example, people can rely
too much on automated tools, leading them to miss subtle signs of a security breach that the
tool can't catch.
Having advanced security tools might make people feel too safe, causing them to ignore other
important parts of cybersecurity, like training employees and making good policies. Without
proper training and effective security policies, people might misuse or not fully use the tools.
Using Layered Security Methods
Network security must include the concept of layered security, or defense in depth. This refers
to placing security controls throughout the network, so that there are many different kinds
of ways to stop threats. Cybersecurity technicians enforce defense in depth with security
tools and with policies that set out expectations for the way people behave. This includes
behaviors like separation of duties and segmenting the network, in addition to requiring users to
authenticate or prove who they are, using multiple authentication factors.
Separation of duties is a behavioral way to defend against insider threats, meaning abuse by
people who are part of the organization or company. Any tasks that require multiple steps
should be split between different people to prevent ethical conflicts or abuse of power.
Network segmentation is one way to restrict access to different areas of a company's network.
One example would be a company separating its Finance department files from the rest of the
organization. Putting the financial information in its own zone, or network segment, makes it
harder for threat actors to obtain that information.
Any security tool only as good as the person who uses it. Effective training, good policies, and
strong security tools are all necessary to ensure the highest levels of cybersecurity.

Firewalls
Cybersecurity professionals use firewalls as part of defense in depth to establish a secure
barrier at the network edge, where access attempts are most common. This type of security
provides a good first chance to protect the network, but it can still be vulnerable to modern
malware and insider threats. This is why using antivirus software and keeping up with software
updates is so important.
What are Firewalls?
The basic function of a firewall is traffic filtering. Network communications, or traffic, flow
across different areas of the network, out to the Internet, and back into the network from
external sources. A firewall organizes this traffic according to a set of rules that let in or keep
out different types of traffic. Simple firewalls use three criteria or rules when filtering data:
1. Source: Where did the traffic come from?
2. Destination: Where is the traffic going to?
3. Protocol: What transport protocol is the traffic using?
A firewall is an important part of any corporate network. Most home routers also feature a
built-in firewall, which users can configure at a website portal.
Images © 123rf.com.
Firewalls can be hardware devices or software programs. Hardware firewalls, which are
dedicated appliances or devices, typically protect a whole network. A technician would install
these firewalls at the edge of the network so that it can inspect all traffic that passes through it.
Software firewalls typically protect a single workstation or server. These firewalls are installed
as a program or application on the computer and inspect only the traffic addressed to that
computer, and nothing else.
A web application firewall helps protect web applications by filtering and monitoring traffic
between a web application and the Internet. Web application firewalls can be deployed on the
network, on a host, or by using a cloud-based firewall.

Using Firewalls
Different operating systems come with pre-installed firewalls. Windows computers will come
to you with Windows Defender already installed, while macOS devices will include the macOS
Firewall software. You can replace these applications if you prefer. Many people do, for reasons
like increased security or because they prefer the way a different firewall works. It's best not to
run two firewall applications at the same time, because they can conflict with each other.
You can set up any home firewall software to be used on either private or public networks. A
private network would be a connection you trust, such as your home or office. Public networks
include the local coffee shop, your public library, or an airport.
Recovery Options
Even with antivirus software and a firewall in place, there are situations where a computer might
stop working correctly. A virus could slip through, a critical system file could become corrupted,
or a bad software update could cause problems. When this happens, knowing how to recover
your system is just as important as knowing how to protect it in the first place.
Patching and Updating
One of the best ways to keep a computer secure is to install software updates, also called
patches, as soon as they are available. Software developers regularly release patches to fix
security vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit. If you delay updates, your system remains
exposed to known threats that attackers are actively trying to use.
Most modern operating systems, including Windows, macOS, and mobile platforms like iOS
and Android, offer automatic updates. Automatic updates download and install patches in the
background, often while the device is idle or restarting. Keeping automatic updates turned on is
the easiest way to make sure your system has the latest protections.
In addition to operating system updates, it is important to keep all installed applications up to
date. Web browsers, office programs, and media players all receive patches that fix bugs and
close security holes. Many applications can check for updates on their own, but it is a good
habit to check manually from time to time.
System Restore
Windows includes a feature called System Restore that can roll back the computer's system
files and settings to an earlier point in time. The operating system automatically creates restore
points before major changes, such as installing new software or drivers. If something goes
wrong after a change, you can use System Restore to undo those changes without affecting
your personal files, like documents, photos, or music.
System Restore is useful when a new program or update causes the computer to behave
strangely. For example, if your computer starts freezing or showing errors right after you install
a new driver, restoring to a point before that installation can fix the problem. To access System
Restore, search for "Create a restore point" in the Windows search bar and follow the on-screen
instructions.
System Restore does not remove personal files, but it will uninstall any programs or drivers that
were added after the selected restore point.

Reset This PC
When a computer has a serious problem that System Restore cannot fix, Windows offers a more
powerful option called Reset This PC. This feature reinstalls the Windows operating system
while giving you the choice to keep or remove your personal files.
• Keep my files: This option reinstalls Windows and removes all installed applications and
settings, but preserves your personal files. You will need to reinstall your programs
afterward.
• Remove everything: This option erases all files, applications, and settings, returning the
computer to a factory-like state. This is the best choice when selling or recycling a
computer, or when a malware infection is too severe to clean.
You can find Reset This PC in Windows Settings under System > Recovery. Because this
process is significant, make sure you have backed up any important files before starting.
Recovery Drives and Installation Media
Sometimes a computer is in such bad shape that it will not start up at all. In these cases, you
need a way to repair or reinstall the operating system from an external source. A recovery drive
is a USB flash drive that contains the tools needed to troubleshoot and restore Windows, even
when the computer cannot boot on its own.
Creating a recovery drive ahead of time is a smart precaution. Windows has a built-in tool called
Recovery Drive that walks you through the process. Once created, you can boot the computer
from the USB drive and access recovery tools such as System Restore, Startup Repair, and
Reset This PC.
Another option is to download Windows installation media from Microsoft's website. This lets
you create a bootable USB drive or DVD that can be used to perform a clean installation of
Windows. A clean installation erases everything on the system drive and installs a fresh copy of
the operating system.
Safe Mode
Safe Mode is a special startup option that loads Windows with only the most basic drivers and
services. This makes it useful for troubleshooting problems that prevent the computer from
starting normally. In Safe Mode, you can remove a problematic program, update a driver, or run
an antivirus scan without interference from malicious software.
To access Safe Mode in Windows 10 or 11, go to Settings > System > Recovery and
select Restart now under Advanced startup. From the recovery menu, choose Troubleshoot
> Advanced options > Startup Settings, then restart the computer and select Safe Mode from
the list.
If the computer cannot start Windows at all, it will usually enter the recovery environment
automatically after two or three failed boot attempts. From there, you can access Safe Mode
and other recovery tools.

Lesson 16D
Securing Small Networks
Objectives Covered
6.5 Given a scenario, configure security settings for a small wireless network.
A wireless network is only as secure as its weakest setting. Many home and small office
networks are vulnerable not because of sophisticated attacks, but because default settings
were never changed and basic security features were left turned off. Understanding how to
configure a router's security options is one of the most practical skills you can have as a
technology user.
In this lesson, you will learn how wireless encryption protocols like WEP, WPA, WPA2, and
WPA3 protect network traffic, how to secure a router by changing its default SSID and
passwords, and how additional settings like firmware updates, disabling remote management
and WPS, and MAC address filtering can strengthen your network's defenses.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• Why is it important to use encryption on a wireless network, and what are the risks of
leaving a network open?
• How have wireless security standards evolved from WEP to WPA3, and which should you
use today?
• What steps should you take to secure a router when setting it up for the first time?
• Why should features like remote management and WPS be disabled on most home and small
office routers?
• What is MAC address filtering, and why is it not sufficient as a standalone security measure?
Securing Small Wireless Networks
Securing a small home or office network means protecting both your digital data and your
physical equipment. It's just as important to prevent people from stealing your computers as it is
to encrypt your information.
Wireless Network Security
Another important thing to think about is the security of the network. Each new version or
generation of Wi-Fi supports the same or better security protocols than the version before. This
keeps your Internet better protected with each new standard.

A Wi-Fi network doesn't have to be encrypted, but there are risks if it's not. Without encryption,
unwanted people can easily get into the network, see private information, or disrupt the
network.
With encryption, which is set up automatically with wireless security, computers on the network
are safe from tampering. Only people you invite can access the network, keeping everything
private from outsiders. In public places, you might see an open network that doesn't need a
password, making it easy to connect. However, this type of network only connects devices to
the Internet and doesn't have other computer hardware on it, just the modem and router. While
there is no hardware for threat actors to access, data flowing across this unsecured network
can still be at risk.
Routers have a guest network option that you can turn on or off. If you want to let people use
your internet, you can turn on the "guest" option. But make sure to set a password so random
people can't get on your network and use up your bandwidth.
In order to keep others from viewing or intercepting your network activity, the industry added a
security component to wireless transmissions. The first iteration of this encryption came out in
1997 and was called Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP).  It provided for either 64-bits or 128-bits
of encryption. This first generation of security was easily hacked and is now what the industry
calls "deprecated," or no longer used.
WEP limited users to using exactly 10 hexadecimal characters for the password. The password
could not be any shorter or any longer than 10 characters. This limitation caused many people in
the United States to use their phone number, a 10-digit long number of hexadecimal characters that
they could easily remember. Of course, this ease of use also contributed to WEP's vulnerability.
The new standard, Wi-Fi Protected Access (WP A)  came out in 2003 with improved 256-bit
encryption. The industry has continued to improve security, which brought about WPA2, with
the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)  algorithm. Current protocols have evolved to include
Wi-Fi Protected Access (WP A3),  which includes different divisions for personal and business
use, making it much safer. Most routers today support using WPA2 and WPA3 encryption.
Securing a Router
Aside from having strong security, it's a good idea to change the default Service Set Identifiers
(SSIDs)  and passwords that your router broadcasts. The SSID is what you see when you
connect your mobile device to a Wi-Fi network. Sometimes, users might want to change the
SSID for convenience. To do this, you need to use a smartphone app or a web browser to
log into the wireless router. In the main menu, you'll see a box showing the current SSID. Just
replace the text and apply the changes to start broadcasting the new SSID.
Remember, an SSID is one of the few things in computing that is case-sensitive. While today's
Wi-Fi passwords have strong encryption, changing the Wi-Fi password is easy and follows
similar steps to changing the SSID. Just erase the information in the password box and replace
it with whatever you prefer. After making this change, all connected devices will need to
reconnect.

Screenshot courtesy of TP -Link  Technologies Co., Ltd.
Pre-Shared Key
A pre-shared key is a type of password used in offices to let users access a wireless network.
IT sets up the key when they configure the router or access point. Authorized users get the key
so they can connect their devices. However, there's a risk with this method because the key
might get shared with the wrong people.
Physical and Device Security
Make sure to keep all doors and closets locked to stop thieves from taking your computer
equipment, and use cable locks for laptops when needed. In order to protect sensitive personal
or company data, every computer should have a login password. The password should be
strong enough to keep unauthorized people from getting in, but not so hard that it frustrates the
user. Using biometrics, like fingerprint scanners on laptops, is another great way to make it easy
for users to log in while keeping threat actors out.
Routers come with a built-in firewall, which will work for a basic network. But if you have a
larger, more complex network, or you're worried about cyberattacks, you can upgrade your
equipment. A standalone small office firewall can offer stronger protection. For example, an
accounting office that prepares customers' taxes is at a higher risk because tax returns have a
lot of personal information that hackers might want to steal. That type of office may want to add
more levels of security to protect the sensitive information on their networks. These steps are
crucial to keep a small office network safe from potential attacks.

Router Security Options
Setting up a strong Wi-Fi password and encryption is a great start, but routers have many other
security settings that are just as important. Many of these settings are turned off or set to weak
defaults when the router is brand new. Taking a few minutes to configure these options can
make your home or small office network much harder to break into.
Changing Default Admin Credentials
Every router has an administration page where you can change its settings. To access this
page, you open a web browser and type in the router's IP address, which is usually printed
on a sticker on the bottom of the router. The problem is that most routers come with a default
username and password, such as "admin" and "password." These defaults are well known and
easy for attackers to guess.
One of the first things you should do after setting up a new router is change the admin
username and password. Choose a strong password that is different from your Wi-Fi password.
If someone gains access to your router's admin page, they can change any setting, redirect
your traffic, or even lock you out of your own network.
Updating Router Firmware
Routers run their own software, called firmware, that controls how the device operates. Just
like computers and phones, routers need software updates to fix security vulnerabilities and
improve performance. Router manufacturers release firmware updates periodically, but unlike
most computers, routers usually do not update themselves automatically.
To check for firmware updates, log into the router's admin page and look for a section labeled
"Firmware Update," "Software Update," or "Administration." Some newer routers do support
automatic firmware updates, and turning this feature on is a good idea if it is available. Running
outdated firmware is one of the most common security weaknesses in home and small office
networks.
Disabling Remote Management and WPS
Remote management is a feature that lets someone access the router's admin page from
outside the local network, over the Internet. While this might sound convenient, it also means
that anyone on the Internet could try to log into your router. For most home and small office
networks, remote management should be turned off.
Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS)  is another feature found on many routers. WPS was designed to
make it easier to connect devices to a wireless network by pressing a button on the router
or entering a short PIN instead of typing the full Wi-Fi password. However, the WPS PIN is
vulnerable to brute-force attacks, where an attacker tries every possible combination until the
correct one is found. Because of this weakness, security experts recommend disabling WPS
and using a strong Wi-Fi password instead.
MAC Address Filtering
Every network device, such as a laptop, phone, or tablet, has a unique identifier called a MAC
address. Routers can use MAC address filtering to create a list of approved devices that are
allowed to connect to the network. Any device not on the list will be blocked, even if it has the
correct Wi-Fi password.
MAC address filtering adds an extra layer of security, but it is not foolproof. Advanced attackers
can spoof, or fake, a MAC address to match one on the approved list. For this reason, MAC
address filtering works best as one part of a larger security strategy rather than the only line of

defense. It is most practical for small networks where the number of devices does not change
often.

Lesson 17A
Understanding Database Basics
Objectives Covered
5.1 Explain the value of data and information.
5.2 Explain database concepts and the purpose of a database.
5.3 Compare and contrast various database structures.
Almost everything you do online depends on a database. Social media, banking, streaming
services, and school systems all rely on databases to store, organize, and retrieve information
quickly. Understanding how databases work gives you insight into the technology behind the
apps and services you use every day.
In this lesson, you will learn what a database is, why organizations prefer databases over
spreadsheets, and how data is structured within a database. You will also explore the
differences between relational and non-relational databases.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is a database, and why are databases important for businesses and organizations?
• What are the key characteristics that most databases share?
• Why do organizations prefer databases over spreadsheets for managing large amounts of
data?
• What is the difference between structured, non-structured, and semi-structured data?
• How does a relational database differ from a non-relational (NoSQL)  database?
What is a Database?
Databases are everywhere, and most people use them every day.
On the way home from school or work, you stop by the grocery store. You scan your items at
the self-checkout, swipe your loyalty card, and pay with your debit card. Once you get home,
you go to your favorite pizza chain's website, place an order from their online menu, and pay
with your credit card. While you wait for the pizza to arrive, you check your favorite social
media platform and browse for a good movie on your video streaming service. In about an hour,
you have used seven databases without even thinking about it.
The Importance of Databases
A database is a highly organized, multi-table digital storage system designed to hold
information on a computer. You can store any information in the different tables within a
database, including names, dates, files, pictures, transactions, comments, numbers, and more.

Data is vitally important for any group or business. By using databases to gather, store, and
retrieve data, people and companies can use them to make smart choices and plan well for the
future.
This is why databases are so important. Data is an important part of how businesses and
organizations make their decisions, and databases are how those businesses organize that
information. Without a way to organize the information and find the exact right pieces of
information, the data just sits there. Databases provide a logical structure so people can actually
use their data.
Database Characteristics
There are many kinds of databases, and this module will introduce you to each of them.
Each type of database uses different methods to organize data, and each has a different job.
However, most databases share these common features:
• Centralized access: Multiple users can get into, or access, the database at the same time.
This allows people to use the data without waiting or taking turns.
• Security: Databases include security measures to ensure only authorized users can
access the data. Different users have different permission levels. For example, a top-level
administrator can view and edit all the data, while lower-level users might only see records
but not change or delete them.
• Recovery: The information in a database is valuable, and losing it could cause significant
damage to an organization. Databases are easy to back up, so database administrators
(DBAs)  can restore the data if something goes wrong.
• Scalability: Databases can store thousands, millions, or even billions of data points. Imagine
trying to keep track of a billion rows on a spreadsheet. It would not be easy. Fortunately, a
good database makes analyzing a million records just as easy as analyzing a few dozen.
Managing Databases
A database management system is a specific type of software that helps create and manage
each database. It acts as an interface between the raw data in the database and the people who
want to use or analyze it.
With a database management system, people can create, read, update, and delete data in real
time. This means that the database stores any data changes immediately, and other users in the
database can see those modifications right away. Database management systems allow every
user to see the same data all at once.
The database management system decides the format and structure of the database and gives
users the tools they need to work with the data. Microsoft Access, which comes with Microsoft
Office 365, is the most popular consumer database management system. Larger organizations
usually need a system with more features and security. Some of the most common ones are
MySQL, Oracle Database, and Microsoft SQL Server.
Database vs. Spreadsheet
When you think about using databases, especially if you're new to their structure, you might
think of them as overly complex. Why use database software if you're already familiar with
spreadsheets such as Google Sheets or Excel, or simple comma-separated value (CSV)  files?
The reason is that organizations of all kinds are generating more and more data every day.
Managing those data points and their relationships to each other is much simpler if you work
within a database, not a spreadsheet.
Spreadsheets, also called flat file systems certainly have a role in managing information. They
have a simple structure with rows and columns that are easy to understand and organize as you

like. A spreadsheet works great for small to medium-sized sets of data, usually numbers, but it
can also include words. They can be perfect for a single user or for a small group.
Benefits of Databases over Spreadsheets
While flat file systems help transfer information between systems or track sales orders, they
don't always have enough functionality for what a company needs. Most of the time, databases
are the solution. Here are some advantages of using a database over a flat file system:
• Processing speed: Databases store billions of data points and let you quickly search for and
retrieve a single record.
• Backup and recovery: Databases back up information within seconds of adding it, making it
easy to recover lost data through backup and replication.
• Forced data types: Databases control and validate the information that users enter or
provide. This control is called forced data entry. As an example, when you order a product
online, the phone number field only accepts numbers, not letters. This is a situation where
forced data entry helps ensure the data is as clean and accurate as possible.
• Concurrent use: Databases allow many users to access the data at the same time without
waiting. A database can support thousands or even millions of users at once. This is hard
to do with a flat file system, which often locks a file when one person opens it, preventing
others from using it. Online collaboration tools can help, but they usually limit the number of
spreadsheet users, often to around 100.
• Security: Databases ensure only authorized users can access the data.
• Scalability: Databases can handle large volumes of data, and users can extend their capacity
when needed by using external databases or data connections.
In short, databases offer faster processing, better backup and recovery, controlled data types,
support for many users at once, and improved security compared to flat file systems.
Database Structure
In a database, an entity is a real-world thing that an organization uses. For example, a business
considers each customer an entity. Similarly, a product that a business sells is another entity. An
attribute provides a detail or characteristic of an entity. For instance, the customer's name and
phone number are attributes of the customer. The name and price of a product are attributes of
that product. A relationship connects two entities. When a business sells a product to a specific
customer, that sale represents a relationship between two entities.
A database stores a collection of organized information on a computer. Organizations choose
different kinds of databases based on the type of information they need to store.
Structured Data
Structured data divides information into clear, separate categories. For example, consider books
in a library catalog. Each book is different, but they all share the same categories: title, author,
publication date, and call number. This kind of information is easy to store in a structured table,
where every book has a value for each category. This setup is ideal for a relational database. All
data in a structured database follows a strict plan or outline and connects between tables.
Non-structured Data
Non-structured data is information that doesn't have a clear order or pattern. Think about
having a bunch of different things about the US Civil War, like journals, newspapers,
photographs, telegrams, and pamphlets. To keep all these different items organized, people
often use something called eXtensible Markup Language (XML).  XML is similar to HyperText
Markup Language (HTML),  which is used to create websites, but instead of showing how things

should look, XML uses special tags and codes to give structure to the documents or items. This
makes it easier to manage and find different types of data in a database.
Semi-structured Data
Semi-structured data falls between organized and unorganized. This type of data doesn't
fit neatly into rows and columns like a table, but it still shares some common features. For
example, when you classify different types of animals, every species has a scientific name, an
average size, and a known life expectancy. However, you don't need to store information about
a dog's wingspan, and you don't need to include a space for a frog's beak size.
A key/value pair database works best with semi-structured data. A key, also called a field, is a
category of information. Some keys are the same for all items, but other keys can be different.
This type of database doesn't have a search option, so you need to know the key to find the
information you need.
Relational and Non-Relational Databases
One common type of database is the relational database, which keeps data in several
connected tables. Remember that spreadsheet programs use vertical columns and horizontal
rows. But in databases, they are called fields and records. Rows are called records because all
the information in a row goes together.
Records are unique. They collect information about only one entity. The entity in that record
can be a type of vehicle, a specific piece of art, a single park in a national parks system, or a
person. The record is always unique, even if the entity shares some data in common with other
entities.
Imagine you're an administrator at a big company and you need to find an employee named

Managing Relational Databases
A database is made up of many tables full of information, and some of that information can
be located on more than one table. To show that there is a connection between tables, the
software uses a primary key. Each table in a relational database has one field, and only one
field, called the primary key field. This field's job is to give each record a unique identifier, such
as the Employee ID in our example above.
A relational database management system (RDBMS)  is software that lets users create, change,
find, and manage the data stored in a database. These systems use Structured Query Language
(SQL)  is the standard language for working with data. You will explore primary keys, SQL, and
relational database management in more detail in a later lesson.
Non-relational Databases
Not all data fits into strict fields and records. A non-relational database, also called NoSQL,
which stands for "not only SQL", usually stores this kind of data. Unlike relational databases,
these databases don't use traditional rows and columns. Instead, a non-relational database
handles data in different formats, making it easier to organize semi-structured and unstructured
data. They also use different query languages that are best for the specific types of data they
store.

Working With a Database
When new learners start working with databases, it's important for them to understand some
basic ideas and operations. Databases are used to store, find, and access lots of information, as

Import or Input Records
When you create a database, you need to first put data into the system. You can do this either
by importing it from other sources, such as spreadsheets, forms, or other databases, or by
typing it in manually.
Manually transferring your data from one source to another can be time-consuming. It can also
expose your important data to the possibility of human error. For this reason, manual data entry
is almost never your best available option.

Importing records can bring in large amounts of information very quickly and accurately, either
to start a new database or to add to an existing one. People inside or outside the company can
import data into the database.
One example of outside users entering data is when you shop online and enter your personal
information as part of the transaction. You put your information into a series of fields for your
name, email address, and shipping address at checkout. Those data points get added to the
company's database.
As you enter personal information, you create a record and add it to the database. Each piece

field. Fields are like columns on a spreadsheet. A field describes one detail about each record in
the database.
Queries
As you saw in the video, queries let you request specific data from a database. Beyond
retrieving information, you can also use queries to manipulate data. People who work with
databases will typically use the Structured Query Language (SQL).  This language is important
for managing databases, from simple commands to complicated requests involving many
tables.
Queries can add or remove information from a database. For example, if a store customer
buys two new pairs of shoes, database queries update the customer's record to show the new

those specific shoes. After the purchase, the customer remembers that their phone number
changed recently and asks for it to be updated. A query then changes the phone number in the

managing those accounts. The query checks both the customer account and account manager

Reports
You can take the data you asked for in a query and change it into something easy to read and

the day, customers buy shoes, adding customer information and sales information to your
databases and changing your shoe inventory database.
With our shoe store example, you can query your database and get reports of sales that you
can sort in any way you want. You can find out how many sales the store had last month, or how
many sales of children's shoes last month, or how many sales of children's size 3 shoes last
month, or what the difference in total sales was last month compared to the same month last
year.
You can see there are many ways to look at the data. If a full year of reports shows increased
sales in December, you can see a pattern in buying habits and plan for next December.
Database Location and Access
Whether you're running a business, working on your education, or planning your next vacation,
you need reliable information to make good decisions. Databases store a huge amount of data,
in some cases more than you could ever use.
Servers play an important role because they store the database program and data. IT
professionals make sure the data is available to everyone who needs it. The end user doesn't
care where the data comes from; they just want it to be available when they need it. To save
money, an organization might store the information on its own servers. For more flexibility and
reliability, but at a higher cost, they might store the data in the cloud.
Offline vs Online Databases
An offline database can be used without an Internet connection. These are used when
programs don't need Internet access. A big benefit of offline databases is that they reduce
the risk of cyber attacks.
An online database is one that users can access over the Internet. This allows employees or
customers of an organization to reach it from anywhere, not just a physical location. The main
differences between online and offline databases are where the information is stored and how
it's accessed.

Local Databases
Local access means putting the server on the company-owned network so employees at the
office and those outside the local network can use it. It might also be an intranet, set up just for
employees at one location. One benefit of local storage is that you can usually access the data
a bit faster. The IT department controls the hardware and database setup completely. They also
set up internal data security and firewalls to keep threat actors away from the database.
Cloud Databases
Cloud storage means putting the database and data online, hosted and managed by the cloud
provider. You access the data over the Internet, either through a specific program or with a
browser. The cloud provider takes over much of the management work from the local IT team.
Another benefit is that you can expect the data to be available 99.9% of the time, and you can
quickly scale up to meet greater needs.

Relational databases are the most widely used type of database, and understanding how
they work is essential for anyone who manages or interacts with data. A relational database
organizes information into related tables, using a carefully designed schema to keep data
structured, consistent, and easy to retrieve.
In this lesson, you will learn how to plan a database using schemas and data models, explore
how tables use records, fields, and constraints to organize data, and see how primary and
foreign keys link tables together. You will also tour Microsoft Access to see database objects
like queries, forms, and reports in action, learn the basics of SQL for retrieving data, and explore
how big data and NoSQL databases handle information that traditional tools cannot. Finally, you
will examine specific types of NoSQL databases, including key-value and document databases.
Learning Outcomes

• What is a database schema, and what are the three types of data models?
• How do tables use records, fields, and constraints to organize data?

tables?
