Schema in a Relational Database
A database schema is the architecture of how a database is structured and organized. It defines
how data is stored, how the relationships among data are managed, and how data can be
accessed and manipulated.
Creating databases can be a complex process and often involves teams of people. Data
modeling, or designing a schema, is a way to help programmers and others understand the
complex flow of data within an organization. These models help organize tables of data and
ensure consistency in things like naming conventions, default values, and security settings
within the database. It's like a blueprint that an architect creates to show how everything should
fit together. These models can also help you easily spot missing or duplicate data.

There are different kinds of data models, each serving a different purpose and having different
levels of complexity. These include conceptual data models, logical data models, and physical
data models.
Conceptual Data Models
Start by creating a conceptual data model. This is the simplest type of data model because it
only focuses on high-level ideas. It answers the question of what a system contains. It provides
an organized view of the data you need to support your business processes. It looks at the data
being used but doesn't worry about how it's processed or its physical details.
This kind of model organizes and defines business ideas and rules. It shows what all the entities
are, their attributes, and their relationships. You create it without considering hardware details
like storage capacity. This model doesn't use primary or foreign keys. It can show that two
entities are related, but it doesn't specify the attributes that connect them. These models are
usually simpler and easier to read than other types.
Logical Data Models
A logical data model is more detailed than a conceptual model because it explains the data
more thoroughly. It answers the question of how to structure a system, but it doesn't show
how to implement the database with a specific database management system. It also doesn't
consider the system's hardware.
This model aims to create a technical map of rules and data structures. It provides the
foundation for building a physical data model. These models are more technical and can seem
very complex to the average user. They can include primary keys, foreign keys, entity names,
entity relationships, and attributes.
Physical Data Models
The physical data model is the most detailed type of data model. It shows you exactly
how to set up a database using a specific database management system. It also includes
technical details and performance needs for the hardware that will run the database. This

model describes all the data needed for a particular project and provides enough information to
actually build the database.
Tables in a Relational Database
As you saw in the videos, database tables use records (rows) and fields (columns) instead
of the row-and-column terminology used in spreadsheets. Tables form the structure of the
database, and some tables get their information from other tables.
Organizing Tables
The tables within a database work together by identifying specific data from key fields, and
sharing that data between the tables. That specific data could be a field of text, numbers, or
anything else that a table can hold. Most of the time, that field has the same name across both
tables. In every situation, the shared field will be called either a primary key or a foreign key.

Primary and foreign keys are covered in more detail on the following page.
As you'll see in the Microsoft Access tour video, forms provide a convenient way for users to
enter data into their tables, reducing the chances of data entry errors and preventing users from
changing important settings.
A database's schema, its structure, is designed to stop fields from being left blank. This is
called a NOT NULL constraint. It means that a value must be entered into the field whenever a
new record is created. Essentially, constraints are rules about what can or cannot be entered.
Databases allow for constraints, or rules, to be applied to fields in tables. For example, you can
add a rule to make sure an email address field is never empty. Another rule might require the
format of a first name to always have a capital letter in it. You decide the type and format of the
information to be entered. This helps avoid data inconsistency.
Primary and Foreign Keys
Primary keys give each record a unique identifier so you can tell records apart.

Relating Primary and Foreign Keys
The relationship with a foreign key can take on a few different forms, including a one-to-one
and a one-to-many relationship.
In a one-to-one relationship, one record in a table will be associated with only one record in
another table. In a one-to-one relationship, the primary key in the first table is often the primary
key in the other table as well.
Suppose when a student enrolls in school they are entered into the "tblStudents" table. The
student record contains basic student information, like StudentID, date of birth, and other
identifying information. Later, if a student is assigned to the gifted services team, a record
will also be entered into the gifted entry table. The Student ID is the primary key for both the
"tblStudents" table and the "tblGiftedEntry" table.
In a one-to-many relationship, a primary key is joined to a foreign key, meaning there is one
record (in the table in which the key is primary) associated with multiple records in other tables
(in which the key is foreign).
Suppose each time the student enters a new school year, you use their StudentID from
the student information table to associate them with their new enrollment record in the
"tblEnrollment" table. StudentID is a primary key in "tblStudents" but a foreign key in
"tblEnrollment." That means you have one record for each student in "tblStudents," and you
have as many enrollment records for that student as years they are enrolled.

If this student went to school for five years, you would have five records to represent each year
they were enrolled. There can only be one record in "tblStudents" for a student, but an infinite
number can exist for that same student in "tblEnrollment." This is a one-to-many relationship.

Key-value databases handle lots of information that needs to be accessed quickly and often.

Document Databases
A good way to keep track of different resources is by using a document database, which is a
type of non-relational database. Document databases manage and track data that doesn't fit
into neat and orderly tables. This messy data can include nested files, arrays, and more. The file
system on your computer is an example of a document database.
A document database differs from a traditional relational database because it can store multiple
pieces of information in one field. In a relational database, this isn't possible. A document
database stores data in flexible documents, like company inventory or blog posts. It is a type
of NoSQL database that stores data as JSON or XML, which are two popular data formats. This
approach is very different from the columns and rows used in a relational database.
Documents can have layers with different lists and complex data types, making it easier to show
data in a natural way. Other important features include different ways to search the data and
using data models that don't need strict organization. There's also flexibility, so data in the
same collection can have different fields.

Coding Overview
The videos above introduced what coding is and how computers follow step-by-step
instructions. Coding has a long history. English mathematician Ada Lovelace created the first
computer program in 1843 while working with Charles Babbage on his Analytical Engine
designs. Lovelace's notes on the Engine are considered the first description of a computer
program and software. While Babbage's designs were never built into an actual machine, they
advanced the field of computing and changed ideas about what machines can do.

Coding Basics
At their most basic level, computers react to physical signals like positive and negative
electric charges, which humans see as ones and zeros. Computer processors recognize certain
patterns of ones and zeros as commands, which we call machine language or machine code.
Humans find this language very hard to understand because we are accustomed to letters and
the decimal system for numbers, not binary. Luckily, modern developers don't work directly
with machine language. They use programming languages instead, which make it much easier
for humans to read and write instructions for computers.
What is a Programming Language?
A programming language is a system of notation that allows programmers to write code that a
computing device can run.
Syntax in computer programming sets the rules for how to write the language. These rules
include statements, symbols, capitalization, punctuation, and comments. Some computer
languages, like Java and Python, are case-sensitive, so they treat uppercase and lowercase
letters differently. For example, in Java, the variable "MyShoes" is different from "myshoes."
Syntax and other characteristics help programmers collaborate because they can all "speak"
the same language and understand each other's code.
When learning a programming language, you commonly start by writing a program that prints
the words "Hello World" on the screen. In this case, "printing" means showing those words on
the screen when the program runs, and doesn't have anything to do with putting ink on paper.

These examples show that each programming language has a different structure. When
choosing a language, consider things like the platform you are targeting and which operating
system (OS)  that the platform runs on, the performance you need, and personal or
organizational preferences. Programming languages fall into two categories: interpreted or
compiled, also covered in this lesson.
You might have seen Hypertext Markup Language (HTML)  and other markup languages, like
eXtensible Markup Language (XML),  grouped with programming languages. However, they are
usually not considered programming languages for these reasons:
• HTML doesn't make decisions or perform actions like a robot following commands. It simply
tells the browser how things should look.
• XML uses nested tags (similar to boxes sitting within boxes) to show how different pieces of
information should fit together.
Compiled Languages
Compiled programs run fast and have full access to device hardware, but they are platform-
specific and require porting to work on different systems.
Runtime Engines
Some languages, like C# (pronounced C-Shar p )  and Java, mix the ideas of compiling and
interpreting to get the best of both worlds. These are called runtime code or runtime engines.
Think of it like building a model from a kit. Most of the hard work, like molding plastic and
cutting metal, is done in the factory. When you get the kit home, you just need to put the pieces
together and paint the model however you like.
Programs written in these languages follow a two-step process. First, the compiler converts
them into a low-level language called bytecode. Then, a runtime engine translates the bytecode
into the computer's machine language when the program runs. This is faster than a fully

interpreted language but slower than a compiled executable. The key advantage is that
bytecode can run on any computer that has the runtime engine installed.
Scripting Functions
People also call interpreted languages scripting languages. In addition to Python, JavaScript,
Ruby, and Perl, many operating systems have their own scripting languages. For example,
Windows includes PowerShell and Command Prompt, while Linux uses Bash. The Windows
command line can run batch files, which are collections of commands that run one after
another.
Windows PowerShell includes both a command-line shell and a scripting language called
Windows PowerShell Integrated Scripting Environment (ISE).  People often use PowerShell to
perform administrative and management tasks. Sometimes, you can only complete these tasks
using a PowerShell script.
To remember the difference between an interpreted and compiled language, think of an
interpreter for spoken languages. Imagine someone speaking in a language you don't
understand, and an interpreter next to them repeats what they say in your language. This
real-time interpretation is similar to how an interpreted language works.
Interpreted Languages
Unlike compiled languages, interpreted programs don't turn source code into binary ahead of
time. Instead, an interpreter runs the instructions in the source code each time the application
launches.
Interpreted programs have the advantage of being platform-independent. This is often called
portability; you can move a program from one system to another without changing the source
code. Compiled programs, by contrast, must be rewritten and recompiled for each new
platform.
The trade-off is speed and resource access. Interpreted languages are slower than compiled
ones because the code is translated into machine language as it runs. They also have limited
access to the system's hardware. Most applications you use through your web browser,
including the labs in this course, are written in interpreted languages.
One benefit of interpreted languages is that debugging can be easier. Because the code runs
line by line, errors show up right where the problem is, making them quicker to find and fix.
Assembly Language
Assembly language is one of the first human-readable computer languages. It is a low-level
programming language that interacts directly with the computer's hardware, without using a
compiler or interpreter.
Because assembly language is so close to machine language, code written in it is more efficient
and runs faster than code written in higher-level languages. Assembly language allows direct
access to hardware and is very specific to the processor and other components. You can write
a program in assembly language for a specific system with known hardware.
Another capability, and also a challenge, is that assembly language allows direct memory
access, letting you manipulate memory addresses. While programmers still use assembly
language in some specialized areas, they more commonly use higher-level languages for most
programming tasks.

Query Languages
Another type of language specializes in getting information from databases. Are called query
languages, like Structured Query Language (SQL).  They help you find specific data, show only
what you are looking for, or present information in helpful ways.
Queries answer questions about data sets. For example, they tell you the greatest amount of a
product in stock, how many orders the company had last week, or what the weather was like in
January in your town.
For example, if you want to learn more about your favorite movies, you can use the website
IMDb. This is the Internet Movie Database, and it has millions of records about movies, TV
shows, actors, directors, and producers. To get information about a specific topic, you type a
search term on the home page. When you press enter, the website shows a page of results that
match your search. You see the search page taking you directly to the results, but there's a lot
more happening behind the scenes.
When you type a search term and press enter, the computer takes what you typed and
translates it into a query language, like SQL. Then, it uses the query to search the database
and find all the records that match your search. Once it has them, it organizes them into a
nice-looking report and shows it on the screen. Using queries, you can turn the raw data in
database tables into useful information to help you make informed decisions.

Lesson 18B
Planning a Coding Project
Objectives Covered
4.4 Identify programming organizational techniques and logic concepts.
4.3 Explain the purpose and use of programming concepts.
4.1 Compare and contrast programming language categories.
Writing code is only part of programming. Before a single line is written, good programmers
plan what their program should do and how it should work. This planning phase helps catch
problems early, keeps the project organized, and makes the actual coding much smoother.
In this lesson, you will learn how to define the goals of a program, map out its logic using
flowcharts, and write pseudocode to describe each step in plain language. You will also explore
key programming concepts such as branching, looping, logical operators, and functions. Finally,
you will look at the tools programmers use to write and test their code, including text editors,
browser consoles, and integrated development environments (IDEs).
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• Why is it important to plan a program before you start writing code?
• What is a flowchart, and how do the different shapes represent steps in a program?
• What is pseudocode, and how does it help a programmer organize their logic?
• How do branching and looping control the flow of a program?
• What are functions and procedures, and why do programmers use them?
• What tools can you use to write and test code, and how do they differ?
Define What the Program Should Do
Programmers use logic to tell a computer how and when to do certain tasks. They create the
program, the system hardware sits in the middle, and the user interacts with the software on the
other side. Whether a program is simple or complex, all programs instruct a system to follow a
sequence of steps. The code could be for a computer, an IoT device, or even a car.
Programmers design and write their code by following several steps, including using flowcharts,
branching, looping, algorithms, operators, procedures, and functions. Interestingly, some of the
early work of creating a program doesn't always involve computers. The planning process can
take time and shouldn't be rushed. Just like painting a room in your home involves a lot of prep
work before actually putting paint on the wall, creating a well-thought-out program requires
careful planning.

Say you want to create your own electronic version of the game Roshambo or Rock-Paper-
Scissors. Before you start coding, decide what the program should do. The exact features of a
program can be very different depending on your goals.
In this case, you want players to make a choice, and with your program, neither player's choice
will be revealed until both have picked rock, paper, or scissors. Planning this program involves
very little coding; you need to figure out all the variables, inputs, and outputs. How will the user
interact with the program? What will they see on the screen? What are the different possible
outcomes?
What is the difference between a script and a program? The key difference is in how they are
executed. A script is a set of instructions that are interpreted by another program such as a
scripting engine. In contrast, a program is compiled into machine code and executed directly by
the computer's operating system. While scripts are typically used for automating specific tasks,
programs are often more complex and can operate independently.
Map Out the Program Sequence
Any part of a programming sequence that can change (like input from a user) requires
instructions for all possible changes. A flowchart helps you see how each step and variation
fit together. Flowcharts show the flow (sequence) of logic in a program. One advantage of using
flowcharts is that they make programming logic easier to understand, especially for people who
are new to programming.
Sometimes computer programs start at the first line and run one line after another until they
finish. Other times, the program needs to act differently based on what the user does or other
situations. This is called branching and will be covered later.
Flowcharts use standardized shapes to help you see the decisions, actions, and order of steps
the program takes. Some of the more common flowchart shapes include:
• Oval: The start or end of a program.
• Parallelogram: Input or output.
• Diamond: Decisions answered with a Yes or a No.
• Rectangle: Processes.
• Arrow: The logical flow of the program.
You could use a flowchart for your Rock-Paper-Scissors program.

Digital Literacy Module 18:  Telling Computers What to Do by Coding
438

Pseudocode
As your code gets more complex, it's a good idea to plan out what you want it to do before
you start writing. This makes your ideas clearer, helps keep your code neat, and saves you time
fixing mistakes later.
Before you start writing the code line by line, prepare pseudocode. Pseudocode is a simple way
of describing what the code will do using plain language. Pseudocode aims to explain what the
code will accomplish in a clear and easy-to-understand way. Another programmer should be
able to read and follow it easily. After you finish the flowchart, create high-level pseudocode. It
helps break big programs into smaller pieces. You can also use the same piece of pseudocode
more than once.
Specific algorithms are an important part of a program and pseudocode. They provide step-by-
step instructions to solve a problem. They include all the needed logic, like if-else statements,
branches, and loops. Before you write them in code, you often show algorithms in flowcharts or
pseudocode.
Pseudocode and Programming Constructs
Pseudocode is a way to write down six basic programming ideas or constructs always written
in uppercase: SEQUENCE, WHILE, REPEA T -UNTIL,  FOR, IF- THEN-ELSE,  and CASE. These
constructs, also known as keywords, help show how the steps of an algorithm are controlled.
1. SEQUENCE represents tasks that happen in a specific order, one after the other.
Steps in the SEQUENCE construct have their own keywords as well, including:
• The Input step, which obtains data from another section of code or from a human: READ,
OBTAIN, GET
• Output: PRINT, DISPLAY, SHOW
• Compute: CALCULATE, COMPUTE, DETERMINE
• Initialize: SET, INIT
• Add: INCREMENT
• Subtract: DECREMENT
2. WHILE is a loop, or repeated section of code, with a condition at its beginning.
3. REPEA T -UNTIL  is a loop with a condition at its ending.
4. FOR is a different way to loop a section of code.
5. IF- THEN-ELSE  is a conditional statement that changes the flow of the directions or code.
6. CASE is a generalized form of the IF- THEN-ELSE  construct.
Using Operators
Code has operators, just like math problems have symbols that tell you what to do with the
numbers. Each coding language has its own operators. For pseudocode, you should know some
basic operators.
Relational operators:
• = and == mean "is equal to." This means it returns TRUE if both conditions are the same.
• !=  means "is not equal to." For example, a true statement would be "100 !=  5"
• > means "greater than." For example, a true statement would be "100 > 5"
• < means "less than." A true statement would be "5 < 100"
• >= means "greater than or equal to." A true statement would be either "100 >= 100" or "100
>= 95"
• <= means "less than or equal to." A true statement would be either "5 <= 5" or "5 <= 50"

Explaining Your Code
When you write your code, it's very helpful to add comments that explain what each part of
the code does. This way, you or a coworker can easily understand the code when you need to
update or fix the program.
When adding comments, remember that if you want to add notes inside your code, you
need to use a symbol that represents "comment." This symbol can vary depending on which
programming language you end up using, but common symbols are the hash (#), an apostrophe
('), or double forward slashes (//). When it runs, the programming language ignores any lines
within your code that begin with the comment symbol.
Working with Pseudocode
Imagine you’ve agreed to create a shopping cart for a friend starting an online business. Before
you begin coding it, you can use pseudocode to decide how it should work. Pseudocode is a
line-by-line description of what your program needs to do. Pseudocode is not a programming
language; it is a way to represent code using English statements that are easy for a wide range
of people to understand. It provides a good description of the steps and algorithms you need
to implement in your program. Programmers translate pseudocode of the steps and algorithms
they have designed into the programming language they are using to create their code.
Take a look at the pseudocode for the shopping cart we are writing for our friend.
When user clicks "Add to Cart":
If user is logged in:
Add item to cart
Suggest similar items
else:
Redirect user to login page

Our shopping cart pseudocode describes the steps the program needs to perform. It needs to
watch for the user to click "Add to cart." When they do, it checks to see whether the user is
logged in. If they aren’t, they get redirected to the login page.
Once the programmer has reviewed the steps defined in the pseudocode and determined that
they are correct, the programmer translates the pseudocode to the programming language they
are using and includes it in their program code.
Programming Tools
An important decision to make before writing code in JavaScript is what tool you will use to
write your code. You could choose a simple text editor, the coding console in Google Chrome,
or an Integrated Development Environment (IDE).  Depending on the coding tasks you are doing
will determine which coding environment you decide to use as you write a program.
Text Editors
A simple text editor like Notepad++ can be an easy environment to write simple programs
in, but it lacks the helpful features and functions that other coding environments provide. For
example, a simple text editor does not highlight the syntax in your code or identify syntax
mistakes you might have made in your code, like missing a semicolon at the end of a line of
code.
Console Editors
The coding console in Google Chrome is always available, easy to use, and there is nothing
additional that you need to install if you have access to Google Chrome. The console is a good
place to write and test simple programs because it will highlight different keywords, and the
code can be directly run, which makes it easy to test that it's working. To access the coding

console in Google Chrome, launch a Google browser, select the three vertical dots menu, select
the More Tools menu option, and then select the Developer Tools menu option. In the Developer
Tools panel, select the Console. In the console, you can write and run JavaScript code. To add
additional lines of code to your program, press the Shift + Enter keys. When you have your
program written, press Enter to run it.
Integrated Development Environments (IDEs)
IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment, and an IDE is a set of programming tools
that work together to make it easier for a programmer to write code. An IDE helps you to
more easily identify and correct coding errors and bugs by highlighting keywords, automatically
adding closing parentheses and brackets, and allowing you to run the program to test it,
including stopping the program at areas you want to test more deeply using markers called
breakpoints. An IDE also allows many programmers to collaborate on the same programming
project. For professional programmers, an IDE is an essential tool.IDEs provide many helpful
features to make programming easier, such as:
• A code editor
• Auto-completion of coding syntax
• Syntax highlighting and bug identification
• Code execution displayed in a separate window
• Organizing your code into project folders

Lesson 18C
Using Variables, Data Types, and Operators
Objectives Covered
4.2 Identify fundamental data types and their characteristics.
4.4 Identify programming organizational techniques and logic concepts.
Programs need ways to store, organize, and manipulate information. Variables act as named
containers that hold data while a program runs, and data types define what kind of information
a variable can store, such as numbers, text, or true/false values. Understanding how to declare
variables, choose the right data type, and apply operators to transform data is essential to
writing functional code.
In this lesson, you will explore the fundamental data types used in programming and learn how
arithmetic, relational, and logical operators work to compare and transform data.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What is a variable, and how do constants differ from variables?
• What are the fundamental data types, and how do integers, floats, characters, strings, and
Booleans differ?
• How do arithmetic, relational, and logical operators transform data in a program?
• What is the order of operations, and why does it matter when writing expressions?
• How are Boolean operators like AND, OR, XOR, and NOT used to evaluate conditions?
What is a Variable in Program Code?
Computer programs often need to remember data to use later. For example, at a shoe store,
the number of shoes always changes. When customers buy shoes, the number goes down, and
when new shipments arrive, the number goes up. If we call a variable "Shoes," we can assign it
a number, and this number can change based on what happens.
A variable acts like a container that holds numbers, words, phrases, and other values. As
the name suggests, variables can change the values they hold. We call both variables and
constants identifiers, which are unique names given to something in the program. This is
important for how programs run.
In our simple shoe store example, we store the number of shoes in a variable called "Shoes."
The pseudocode might show that Shoes = 7. Using the equals sign, the program sets the value
of "Shoes" to be the number of shoes at the start of the day, which is 7 in this case. Later in the
code, the programmer types the name of the variable "Shoes" to get its value.

Variables can also store Boolean values. If a user logs into an account, the program tracks
whether the user is signed in. When the user logs in, this variable stores the value true. When
they log out, it changes to false.
Constants
Sometimes, a programmer wants to keep track of a value that never changes. For example, a
physicist might want to keep track of the value of pi to fifteen decimal places. Because this
value never changes, they use a constant. A constant is like a container that holds values,
but unlike a variable, constants never change. Once they're set, they're set for good. With this
constant, the physicist just types the name of the constant instead of the whole long number.
Data Types
Programmers use data types to tell a computer what type of data a variable is storing. Common
data types are integer, floating point, character, string, and boolean. Programming languages
use data types to tell a computer how much memory is needed to store variables and objects
during code execution. Data types also define the ways that variables and objects can be used
in programs. For example, two variables with the integer data type can be added together.
Variable Types
Variables store data values in programs and determine what kind of data they hold. Remember
when you learned about numbering systems and how computers use binary numbers?
The ones and zeros create a map to ASCII and Unicode, which set the rules for how all
computer characters are assigned. These same rules apply to programming languages. In these
languages, you will find common types of variables, including the following:
• Integers: Whole numbers, either positive or negative, without a decimal or fraction. Examples
include 23, -7 ,  and 451.
• Floating-point or float: Numbers that can have a decimal place or fractional part. Examples
include 8.02, 99.999, and -1. 01.
• Boolean: Variables that only store one of two logical values: True or False. Programmers
often use them in logical operations.
• String: A sequence of characters, like words or sentences. Examples include "Hello World,"
"3.14," and "555-1212. "
• Character or Char: A variable that stores a single character, which could be a digit, letter, or
symbol. Examples include '7', 'X', and '#'.
• Array: A unique collection of values that must be of the same type and are accessed using
an index. For example, in array [23 , 7 ,451],  the value 23 is at index 0, 7 is at index 1, and 451 is
at index 2.
Different programming languages might have extra types of variables or different versions of
these basic types.
Programmers usually declare variables, define them with a specific data type, and give them
a starting value at the beginning of the routine where they are used. Sometimes, you can use
variables without declaring them first, but this can make the code harder to read and more likely to
have mistakes.
Number Types
Understanding the different data types a computer program can use are important. This is
especially true when you start writing your own programs (coding) or working with database

systems. The central processing unit (CPU)  and storage devices in a computer only process
data as ones and zeros. These hardware parts don't know what the data means.
However, in programming, data types are very important because they determine what kind of
operations you can do. For example, you can treat the characters "51" as a number and use it in
addition and subtraction, or you can treat it as a text string (like a house number). If you store
"51" as a string, you must convert it before using it in a math operation.
Different types of number values include:
• Integers or int: Whole numbers like -7 ,  23, or 65536. An integer data type uses 1 to 8 bytes of
computer storage. They don't have a fraction or decimal place.
• Floating-point numbers: Numbers that can have decimal fractions, like 4.1, 26.4, or 5.62. A
floating-point number (or just "float") uses between 4 and 8 bytes of storage. A float can
also store whole numbers (like 4 . 0).  You use a float when you need more precision.
• Fixed-point: Real numbers with a specific number of digits after the decimal point. They are
common in financial calculations where accuracy is important, like $9.95.
• Double: Similar to a float, but a double variable can store larger and more precise float
numbers.
What the program needs determines the number type you choose. Most programming
languages offer different number types to handle various situations.
Characters and Text
Programmers use characters and strings to represent and work with text data. A character
includes anything you see on your computer keyboard, even the symbols in the corners. A
string is more than one character and includes letters, numbers, or symbols. Programmers use
them in the most popular programming languages. Here are the two types with examples:
• Characters: A character (or char) is a single letter, symbol, or number. Examples include: a,
D, 7, $, @, #. Characters use one byte of storage. Note that when you enter a number as a
character, you cannot do any math with it.
• Strings: A string is a collection of characters. Examples include: XYZ, Hello world, Apartment
#101. There is no real limit on the storage a string can use. Usually, you define the string
length when you set up the data type.
When you use single or double quotes to mark the start and end of a string ("Hello World"), the
quotes are not part of the string itself. If you want to include a quote character (or other special
character) inside a string, you have to use an escape character.
An escape character, usually \, placed in front of the quote, tells the program to include the
quote in the output. For example, the string " John said \"Hello World\" then left." contains two
single quotes, escaped using the backslash character (\). The output of that string would look
like:
John said "Hello World" then left.
Booleans and Logic
Boolean operations follow a format similar to binary numbers, a system of one of two states.
Their 1 or 0, however, represents either True or False.
Boolean operations compare two conditions to determine their state and make a decision on the
outcome. The operations can be combined to make decisions on multiple conditions. They are
fundamental building blocks of programming.

Boolean values are a special type of number that show if something is either TRUE or FALSE
(using 1 or 0).  They use just one bit of storage. You will use them for logical operators, which
test multiple conditions at the same time.
Boolean Operators
• AND:  If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is considered TRUE.
• OR:  If either condition is TRUE, the whole statement is also considered TRUE.
• X OR:  If one condition is TRUE and the other condition is FALSE, the whole statement is
considered TRUE. If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is considered FALSE. In
other words, if the conditions are different from each other, this Boolean operator sees the
statement as correct. If the conditions are the same (either TRUE- TRUE  or F ALSE-F ALSE),
then the statement is incorrect.
• NO T :  The whole statement is not TRUE.
Boolean Operators in Pseudocode
• && (Logic al  AND):  If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is TRUE.
• || (Logic al  OR):  If either condition is TRUE, the whole statement is TRUE.
• ^ (Logic al  X OR):  If one condition is TRUE and the other condition is FALSE, the whole
statement is considered TRUE. If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is
considered FALSE.
• ! (Logic al  NO T):  The whole statement is not TRUE.
With Boolean values, true means something is correct, and false means something is incorrect.
Booleans are often used in conditional statements, like if-then statements. These statements
check a condition to decide what part of the code to run next.
Data Operator
Here's a group of students playing a video game. As they play, computer program code
instructs their computers on how to keep track of game data. Let's look at ways programming
language code instructs computers how to work with data and operate on it.
Identifier Names
Identifier names are the names that a programmer gives to the constants and variables they
create in their program code. Constants and variables are given descriptive names to make

programs easier to read and write. When deciding on identifier names, it is a good programming
practice to make the names meaningful and consistent. In the game example, variables could
be created to keep track of the number of hearts, crowns, and score that a player earns. These
variables could be called numberOfHearts, numberOfCrowns, and playerScore.
Assignment of Values
An assignment statement is used to set the initial value of a constant or variable, or reset the
value of a variable. The assignment operator in JavaScript is an equals sign "=". For example,
the value of the variable hearts could be set to 5 using the following command: hearts = 5;
Relational Operators
Here's a student taking an exam on a computer. The student answers each question on the
exam, and the computer checks whether the student entered the correct answer or not. The
computer uses this information to provide a score for the exam and to give feedback to the
student on what questions they got right and what questions they missed. A programmer uses
relational operators to instruct a computer how to make decisions to grade this exam. Relational
operators are used by programmers to create conditional statements in their code to compare
values and to take action depending on the results. Relational operators are also commonly
used in branching and control statements like if statements, while loops, for loops, and switch
statements, to control decisions a computer makes.
The relational operators are:
• == is equal to. This means it returns TRUE if both conditions are the same.
• != is not equal to.
• > greater than.
• < less than.
• >= greater than or equal to.

• <= less than or equal to.
Often relational operators are used to create test conditions that control program flow and
computer decisions. In our exam scoring example, let's say the answer to question 10 is D. If
the student's response is D, the student gets a correct score on this question. If the student's
response is not D, the student gets an incorrect score on this question.
Logical Operators
Every day, we make decisions and take actions based upon how we logically evaluate certain
conditions. To determine if you are going to go to the beach, you could evaluate two conditions:
Is it sunny outside? AND Is my homework done? AND is one of the logical operators and

Imagine users are playing a computerized card game. Each player gets five cards, dealt to them

While Loops
Using the same card game example, a block of code using a "while" loop might say:
while cardsInHand < 5.
This means, "when the player has fewer than 5 cards in their hand, execute the task."
When the program gets to this block, it checks the number of cards in the player's hand. If the
player discards a couple of cards and has less than 5, the program takes a card from the deck
and puts it into the player's hand. Then, it loops back to the top of the code and checks again. If
the number of cards is still less than five, it deals another card.
Once the player has five cards, the condition is no longer met, so the loop stops running.

While Loop
Repetition is a common part of life. Imagine that you are working at an airplane boarding
counter, helping travelers onto their flight. Before they are allowed to board the airplane, you
must scan each ticket at the gate. This ticket scanning activity is repeated for each person who

While Loops
Computers are very good at repeating the same steps over and over. A programming statement
that instructs a computer to repeat certain instructions is called a loop. While loops continue
to run a block of code until a certain condition is met. A while loop executes a Boolean test
to determine if the result is true or false. The while loop starts by testing a condition. If the
condition is true, the while loop executes a block of code and then repeats, starting with the
condition test. If the condition is false, the while loop terminates, which means it stops repeating
and skips the program to the instructions after the loop code. In our ticket scanning example,
the Boolean condition tested by the while loop is, “Are there passengers waiting to board?” If
this condition is true, the loop will run and then repeat. When the answer is false, the loop will
end.
Advantages of a while loop include:
• It is easy to repeat code instructions.
• Conditions are simple to write.
• Loops help solve complex programming problems.
The while statement in JavaScript creates a loop that runs a block of code statements as long

while (Boolean condition) {
// code statements
}

num = num + num;
}

Infinite Loops
If the loop is created so that the condition can never be false, it is called an infinite loop. If this
happens in your code, it is a bug you will want to fix. When a running program enters an infinite
loop, only forcing the program to quit will end it. Here's an example of an infinite loop:
var num = 1
while (num> 0) {
console.log(num);
}
Because the value of num is never changed in the loop instructions, each time the loop repeats,
num will still be greater than zero, and the loop will repeat. To avoid infinite loops like this, be
sure to include code inside the loop instructions that modifies the variable you're testing in the
loop condition.

Troubleshoot Your Code
Debugging code, or making sure there are no mistakes, is a careful process that needs attention
to detail to fix any errors that appear when the program runs.
The first step in fixing errors is finding and repeating the problem. The programmer needs to
make the problem happen again and again to know if their changes have fixed it. Understanding

Arrays
An identifier called a container holds a set of values. Two common containers are arrays and
vectors.
An array is a special type of variable that holds many values at once. Imagine a shoe store.
The computer program looks up a user's transaction history in the store's database. Because it
needs to keep track of many transactions, the program uses an array to store all of them in one
variable, instead of using a different variable for each transaction.
Arrays are so useful because you can go through all the values one by one using a loop. When
a user wants to see their transaction history, the program uses a for loop to show each value in
the array as a list.

Arrays can also be multidimensional, which means you can have an array of arrays (2-
dimensional)  or an array of arrays of arrays (3-dimensional),  and so on. A table is two-
dimensional, like a grid, and a cube is three-dimensional. Even if you add more columns to
a table, it stays two-dimensional.
Vectors are groups of the same type of variable. During the time that the program runs, the
number of variables within that vector, or group, can change depending on the program's
needs.
Index Notation
Normally, when we're counting items in a list, we start with the first, then the second, then the
third. In programming, however, we start counting at zero.
Consider this array of strings: ["Leonardo", "Michelangelo", "Donatello", "Raphael"]
Since we start counting at zero, Leonardo is the 0th element of this array. Michelangelo is the
1st, Donatello is the 2nd, and Raphael is the 3rd.
The first element in an array is the 0th element, not the 1st!
Index notation is a simple method used to identify values or elements in an array. Programmers
use index notation to work with individual values or elements or groups of values or elements in
arrays as they code algorithms and instruct a computer to perform calculations.
In JavaScript, the first array value or element is assigned index [0],  and the second array value
or element is assigned index [1].  This continues until the last array value or element is added to
the array, which is assigned index [array.length – 1].  Square brackets [] are used as the array
index operator. Valid indices in an array are 0 through 1 less than the length of the array. The
length of an array is the number of values or elements in an array. If you try to access an invalid
array element, your program will have bugs and will not work.

You want to see the entire list of cities in your array, not just one city at a time. One way to do

for (var i = 0; i < cities.length; i++)

Object-Oriented Programming
In the early days of computer programming, programmers wrote most programs as a simple list
of instructions for the computer to follow. However, there is a newer way where you can divide
the program into smaller groups of actions or tasks.
Computer programmers often want to write software about real things in the world. For
example, a program for selling concert tickets needs to keep track of customers, event venues,
seats, and shows. Obviously, you can't put real people and places into a computer program. But
programmers can create models of these things to use in their programs. This idea of modeling
real-world objects in computer code is called object-oriented programming (OOP).
Two of the most important ideas in object-oriented programming are classes and objects.
Classes
A class is like a blueprint or template for creating individual objects.

Classes have properties, which are attributes that objects can have. Classes also have methods,
which are actions that the object can do. For example, a method can take input, generate
output, and change data.

These properties and methods are stored as fields, or private variables, that other programs
can't easily change. This is called encapsulation. Encapsulation keeps those variables secure
inside a class, so that any object created from that class will always have the same properties.
In the example from the image above, each object cup has the property "Material." However,
the travel cup's material is paper, while the mug's material is ceramic, and the trophy's material
is metal.
Objects
Objects are the most basic building blocks of object-oriented programming (OOP).  Objects are
the specific models built from a class. The data inside objects can be variables of different
types, including numbers, strings of text, and functions or formulas that can manipulate other
data. Different programming languages define these variables in different ways.
Depending on the programming language, an object can have its own attributes or properties.
For example, in JavaScript, an object is an entity with its own properties, such as a cup. The cup
can have properties like design (with individual data such as disposable, mug, or trophy), weight
(30  grams, 300 grams, or 3 kilograms), or material (paper, ceramic, or metal).
Objects can also have their own methods or behaviors. Methods can, in some cases, make the
object move around an environment made of code. If the object is a car, the behaviors might
include engine start, accelerate, brake, or start the windshield wipers.
Many common programming languages support OOP, including C++,  C#, and Python. This
widespread support makes it easy for developers to program using objects. Objects can
simplify coding by allowing the programmer to focus on the objects that developers want to
work with, rather than the kind of programming logic needed to manipulate them.

AI Agents
AI chatbots can answer questions and generate content based on your prompts. An AI agent
takes this a step further. Instead of simply responding to one prompt at a time, an AI agent can
work toward a goal on its own by planning steps, using tools, and making decisions along the
way, often with little or no human input between steps.

How AI Agents Differ from Chatbots
A standard AI chatbot waits for you to type a prompt, gives a response, and then waits again. It
handles one exchange at a time. An AI agent, by contrast, can break a larger task into smaller
steps, carry them out in sequence, and adjust its approach if something goes wrong. Think of
it this way: a chatbot is like asking someone a single question, while an agent is like hiring an
assistant who can complete a project from start to finish.
AI agents typically have three capabilities that set them apart:
• Planning: The agent breaks a goal into a series of steps and decides what to do first,
second, and so on.
• Tool use: The agent can interact with external tools and services, such as searching the
web, reading files, running code, or sending messages.
• Memory: The agent keeps track of what it has already done and what it has learned so far,
allowing it to build on previous steps rather than starting over each time.
Examples of AI Agents
AI agents are already being used in a variety of fields:
• Coding agents: A developer describes a feature they want to build. The agent reads the
existing code, writes new code, runs tests, fixes errors, and repeats until the feature works.
• Research agents: A student or professional asks the agent to investigate a topic. The agent
searches multiple sources, summarizes findings, identifies gaps, and compiles a report.
• Customer service agents: Instead of following a rigid script, the agent can look up
a customer's account, check order status, process a return, and follow up all in one
interaction.
• Personal scheduling agents: The agent checks calendars, suggests meeting times, sends
invitations, and reschedules conflicts without the user managing every detail.
Human in the Loop
Even though AI agents can work independently, most are designed with a concept called human
in the loop. This means the agent pauses at key decision points and asks a person to review or
approve its work before continuing. For example, a coding agent might write a set of changes
and then ask a developer to confirm them before applying the changes to a live system. This
approach helps catch mistakes and keeps people in control of important decisions.
As AI agents become more capable, questions about trust, oversight, and accountability will
continue to grow. Understanding how agents work and where human judgment is still essential
will be an important skill in the years ahead.
Robotics
Many industries are taking advantage of robotics to boost productivity. In construction, there
are now robots that can lay bricks and complete a building with great accuracy and speed. In
warehouses, teams of robots help pick and pack items from shelves. Other robots in the same
warehouse might sort packages to make sure they end up at their final destination.
Remember, most robots used in these industries don't look like the sci-fi robots seen in movies.
They are usually specialized robots, often just an arm, a motorized cart, or a lift designed to do
a specific task over and over again.

Robotics Use Cases
Mining robots are helping with underground exploration because they can go places and map
areas that people can't reach. They can also work in dangerous environments that people can't
work in. The automotive industry has been using robots for many years to help with tasks on the
assembly line. These robots can put parts together, weld them, and paint the body of the car.
Each robot is designed to do just one of these jobs.
Other robots are used for precision assembly, such as putting together the small parts in your
phone. Some robots patrol parking lots to monitor people and cars for safety. These robots have
cameras so that someone in a control room can see what the robot sees.
In hospitals, robots assist with surgeries now, and their success is leading to increased usage of
robots in operations. Robots can make very precise movements, which helps reduce the size of
cuts needed for procedures.
Robots are also becoming more important in the self-driving car industry and in farming. Some
companies have started using automated taxis in big cities, which can pick up passengers who
call for a ride using an app. It can be a little unnerving at first to see a car driving without a
person behind the wheel.
In farming, robotics and automation are helping farmers do their traditional jobs better. For
example, Global Positioning System (GPS)  technology helps farmers map out their fields more
precisely, reducing resource waste. These GPS systems create maps that help them navigate
the land and plan efficient routes for planting seeds.
Soft Robots
Another exciting part of robotics is the emergence of robots that look like the ones from science
fiction movies. Companies are working on humanoid robots to help people at home. These
robots are designed to look and talk like humans and help with everyday tasks.
However, there are still many challenges to work out before these robots can be fully functional
in society. Interacting with all the diverse surroundings of everyday human life is one example.
Engineers are working on creating soft robots with hands made of flexible materials, allowing
the robots to handle delicate items gently. This also brings up questions about how robots and
humans will end up interacting with each other in daily life.
Automation
The automation in industries has been in use since the Industrial Revolution, which began in the
18th century and became widespread in the 19th century. Many jobs were either replaced or
improved by machines. Automation happened because machines can often do tasks faster and
more accurately than humans. They can also handle dangerous jobs that wouldn't be safe for
people.
Automation doesn't always mean robots; it can mean specialty devices that perform one
specific task. These devices might look like an arm or a lift. Interestingly, some work that was
once automated was given back to workers because people often notice subtle differences in
products and can make quick decisions that a machine may get hung up on.
The restaurant industry is using automation to make sure customers have a consistent
experience. In the kitchen, robots help prepare food to reduce wait times and lower labor costs.
Often, these automated systems are combined with front-end kiosks, where customers can
place orders on a large tablet.

Automation in Practice
You might not realize how much automation is around you. From home automation to customer
service and transportation, it's more and more a part of our lives. Internet of Things (Io T)  is
essentially different parts of our homes becoming automated. This includes smart thermostats,
appliances, home assistants, and even toothbrushes, toys, and tools. Cleaning floors has also
been automated with smart vacuums and mops, making these chores easier and less stressful.
All of these devices usually have a smartphone app for Android and iOS.
One of the most interesting advances in automation is devices that attach to our bodies and
read our brain waves. You might have seen a simple example of this with a game where two
players try to use their minds, not their hands, to push a small ball to the other end of a table.
Advances in brain monitoring are now able to help people with disabilities by allowing them to
use computers to move a cursor, just like using a mouse. Controlling machines with thoughts
is new and exciting, and it shows great promise for eventually connecting our entire nervous
system to computers.
Virtual Reality
Virtual reality (VR)  can visually pull you out of your current surroundings and put you into a
completely different place and time. Want to know what it's like to be an astronaut or swim in
the deepest ocean? You can do that with VR. The two most popular uses for VR are gaming
and training. There are amazing games you can play with a VR headset that make you feel like
you're truly immersed in the gameplay. As you look around, the virtual world can put you right
in the middle of the action. Many industries are using VR to train employees as well. They can
create scenarios for workers to experience their job conditions without any risks or damage to
expensive equipment.
Mixed and Augmented Reality
The term augmented reality (AR),  also involves putting on a headset. However, with AR, you can
still see your surroundings because images are added on top of what you already see around
you.
There's also mixed reality. Apple has the most advanced mixed reality headset, called the
Apple Vision Pro. It combines virtual reality (VR)  and augmented reality (AR)  into one headset,
giving you an amazing, immersive experience. Another popular mixed reality headset is the
Meta Quest from Meta (F acebook).  It's popular because it costs less than the Apple headset.
The Meta Quest comes with handheld controllers for most apps, but it also uses hand tracking.
Conversely, the Vision Pro uses advanced hand tracking and doesn't need any controllers.
VR Games and Other Uses
Virtual reality games come in the form of classics, like Tetris, to futuristic space adventures.
There are also multiplayer games and social VR experiences that you can enjoy with others from
around the world. It can feel like you're actually in the same place with friends as you interact
and chat, even if you're continents apart. One downside to VR is that some people get motion
sickness from using the headset.
Employee training with virtual reality is extending to industries like healthcare, the military,
and aviation. In safe and low-cost environments, people can learn or improve their skills in
medical procedures, combat scenarios, and flying expensive aircraft. In architecture, they can
go beyond blueprints and let clients walk through a building before it's even built.
One attempt at virtual reality that didn't take off was the Metaverse from Meta (F acebook).
Another attempt that hasn't become as popular as predicted is virtual meetings. Companies

spent a lot of money on the idea of bringing people together virtually for fun and work. Even
though it hasn't taken hold yet, it's still a promising idea and may become the norm in the future.
The Internet of Things
The video above introduced the Internet of Things (Io T)  a network of physical objects that
collect and share information over the internet. From smart doorbells that recognize visitors to
fitness watches that track your health, IoT devices are becoming a part of everyday life. Below,
you will explore some of the most common IoT devices and how they are used.
IoT Televisions
Smart TVs let you watch videos and listen to music online, play games, and look things up on
the internet. Devices that stream, also known as sticks, work a lot like smart TVs. The Roku and
Fire TV sticks are some of the most popular ones. The main thing people do with their smart TV
or streaming stick is watch shows and movies from a wide variety of streaming services.

Smart speakers are IoT devices you can talk to. They can answer back with information from

Smart light bulbs are impressive because you can control them with an app on your phone. You

Security cameras are great for watching over your home or business. They can record any

IoT Wearable Devices
Smartwatches and fitness devices that you wear on your wrist or finger are also part of the

move, like walking or running. A surprising thing they track is how you sleep, which might not
seem like an activity, but knowing about your sleep can help you improve your overall health.

Security with IoT Devices

When Using IoT Devices
When you think about the Internet, you usually think about using a computer or phone to
browse the web, shop online, or send email. However, an increasing number of everyday
objects are being built with internet connectivity. This concept of connecting many kinds of
devices to the Internet is called the Internet of Things (Io T).
The rapid increase of network-connected devices and services has provided consumers and
manufacturers the opportunity to enhance personalization and make personal and business
tasks more efficient. The convenience of using IoT devices makes it necessary for you to share
more data and information than ever before.
IoT Security
IoT technology is growing at an incredible rate, which can lead to significant security
challenges. IoT devices can be susceptible to weak authentication methods and default
settings, a lack of encryption, and overall poor security practices. Manufacturers can be quick
to release the latest and greatest device, which may oftentimes cut corners on security, which
leads to vulnerabilities and potential attacks. Threat actors are constantly on the lookout for
these types of vulnerabilities. IoT devices, especially those that are new and unchecked, are
very attractive to hackers and easy to exploit.
One of the most common attacks on the IoT is called a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)
attack. First, a machine must be infected with malicious software malware that gives an attacker
remote access and full control over that device. The infected computer is typically referred to
as a zombie or bot. The user has no idea the machine is infected since there's little trace of the
zombie process. When triggered, the zombie is activated and begins attacking. The machine,
along with thousands or millions more, is called a botnet, attacks its target, such as a website or
internet-based service, and renders it useless from the overload of all the attacks at once.
A famous example happened in 2016 when attackers gained access to the network by
exploiting thousands of poorly secured IoT devices with Mirai malware. The botnet targeted
Brian Kreb's security blog and infiltrated the domain name server provider, taking down
many websites for an extended period of time. This infiltration resulted in one of the largest
distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)  attacks across the Internet.
Privacy and Patching
Smart devices collect data for many reasons, such as to improve efficiency, enhance
experience, and help with decision-making. The IoT network generates billions of data points
through all of the devices connected to it. The problem is that many IoT devices lack the
security and privacy policies required to protect all this data. Keep in mind that security and
privacy cannot be guaranteed and can bring up protection concerns. Companies that make and
distribute consumer IoT devices could use those devices to obtain and sell users' personal data.
IoT devices may not be supported by the manufacturer in the same way as your personal
computer or smartphone. When software products are released, manufacturers can typically
become aware of weaknesses in their products, which prompts them to issue patches or
updates that include security fixes to protect against known issues. This is not always the case
with IoT devices. Some devices may receive little to no updates or patch support, leaving them
vulnerable to cybercriminals.
Voice Assistants
Digital or voice assistants are based on artificial intelligence (AI)  and a field of computing known
as natural language processing (NLP),  where a computer interprets natural human speech into
commands that it can execute. Many of these assistants can learn and adapt over time to your

speech patterns to become more accurate and helpful. Almost every computer or smart device
on the market today comes equipped with a voice assistant.
Not only are these assistants part of smartphones and computers, but they are now common
in smart home devices such as the Amazon Dot with Alexa or the Google Home. These types
of devices can be ready to reply to your commands by listening for a "wake-up word" (such
as "Alexa" or "OK, Google"). There can be some instances where they might mishear you
or activate and start listening when you are unaware, which may inadvertently allow them
to hear and record sensitive and personal information. Voice assistants may frequently send
voice recordings to the manufacturer. Because of this, you need to make sure your device is
safeguarding your privacy, including paying attention to where in the home these devices are
placed.
Quantum Computing
The idea for quantum computing started in the 1980s, and the first real quantum computers
came into being in the late 1990s. Big tech companies are making these systems more
powerful, and they're improving quickly enough to hopefully solve some really difficult problems
soon.
Quantum computers can be better than supercomputers because they don't rely on binary
code. A regular computer tries to solve problems by checking every possible answer one by
one, which takes a lot of time. However, a quantum computer can do many calculations at the
same time, making it much faster and more efficient. Quantum computers are especially good at
handling big tasks in fields like physics, cryptography, medicine, chemistry, and other areas that
need a lot of computing power.
Quantum computers can do all this because they use something called qubits, in the same way
that regular computers use bits, which can be either 1 or 0. Qubits are different because they
can be both 1 and 0 at the same time, or any mix of the two. This idea is tricky to understand,
but it means quantum computers can handle much more data than regular computers.
Using Quantum Computing
Today, people are thinking about using quantum computers for farming, fighting climate
change, and creating better batteries. Some companies are offering money to researchers who
can find new ways to use quantum computers. At the time of writing, these practical uses have
yet to be implemented.
One potential problem on the horizon is that these computers are so powerful that they could
break even the toughest encryption methods in use today. This could make it easier to hack into
sites and steal passwords. You'll need to find new ways to protect your information as these
machines get better.
But don't expect quantum computers to replace your laptop anytime soon. They're hard to
build and tricky to keep running because they need very specific conditions to work. Quantum
computers are also very expensive and complex machines, designed only to solve the toughest
problems. In your lifetime, they may be used alongside regular computers, but they probably
won't replace them.
Storage
Ever since the first computers came out, people have been constantly inventing new ways to
store data. Computers usually have a solid-state drive (SSD)  and sometimes a mechanical hard
drive inside. You can also add more storage with things like flash drives, memory cards, and
cloud storage.

As technology improves, these storage options can hold more data and cost less money. Some
new types of storage are starting to appear, like heat-assisted magnetic recording and 3D flash
memory. The main reasons for these changes in storage technology are the need for more
space, lower costs, faster speeds, and higher data density.
Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording
Heat-assisted magnetic recording is a new type of hard drive that allows for smaller data bits
that are packed closer together while still keeping the data intact. It uses a tiny laser to heat
the surface of the hard drive for a short time to write the data. Heating the surface makes it
easier to use magnetism to write on a smaller area. This gives it a big storage advantage over
regular hard drives. Seagate, a data storage company based in the United States, developed
these drives and released them in 2024. The first models could hold 16TB of data, and even
larger capacity limits are expected in the future.
3D Flash Memory
Traditional 2D flash memory has been around since the 1980s and is still widely used today.
When discussing SSDs, it usually means flash memory because it doesn't have the moving
parts that traditional hard drives do. It's a type of memory that can be erased and rewritten
electrically and doesn't lose data when the power is off. This is known as non-volatile memory
and is found in memory cards, USB drives, and other internal solid-state drives in computers,
smartphones, and tablets.
3D flash memory is the next big thing. It stacks layers of solid-state flash memory on top of
each other. This stacking method allows for much more storage space at a lower cost than 2D
flash memory, making it a great choice for the future.

Every organization relies on information systems to collect, organize, and use data effectively.

When Tech Goes Wrong
What's the worst that could happen if you don't understand your devices? You might spend a
bit more time looking things up or spend some money to get a professional to help you. That's
a typical experience for the average person. Nothing too terrible is going to happen in that
situation.
The stakes get higher when the average person, someone who doesn't fully understand their
devices, has a little more power. Maybe they have access to a network and can affect more
users. Or perhaps they don't know enough to realize what they're doing. In many cases, they
will disrupt work for a little while, then things go back to normal. Other times, not knowing
enough about your technology can cause major problems.

Tech Fails from the News
In early 2024, high-ranking military officials from Germany met for a video conference call on a
widely used web conferencing platform. In that call, they discussed sensitive topics, including
details about weapons and other countries' troop presence in Ukraine. While the call was in
progress, someone from Russia dialed in and listened to the conversation. Nobody else noticed.
Russia later leaked the details of the call to its state-controlled news, and the details were
shared around the world.
In 2014, a Twitter account posed as a United States congressional representative from
Georgia's 15th district. The account posted divisive views regularly, shared posts from the
representative's chief of staff, and gained nearly 5,000 followers. Regular people and news
media alike believed this person was a member of the United States Congress, even though the
state of Georgia did not have a 15th district!

protocol (IP)  addresses to devices all over the organization. Reports started coming
in about devices that would not reach the Internet. (On  a Windows network, this can
be prevented using server restrictions. Unfortunately, this was a Linux network.)"
-- R. T., network administrator
This example talks about the dynamic host configuration protocol (DHCP).  This is a set of rules
used to automatically assign IP addresses to devices when they connect to a network.
"One time I got a ticket from a manager whose computer was running slowly. We
found that it was overrun by malware. Hackers were using it as a server for an illicit
website! Check your links carefully!"
-- Anonymous, support technician
This example mentions malware, which is software that serves a malicious purpose. It's
typically installed without the user's consent or knowledge.
SDLC Models
There are five phases of the System Development Life Cycle (SDL C):  planning, analysis, design,
implementation, and maintenance. Beyond understanding those phases, it's important to know
the different models that organizations use to move through them.
Table 4 1:  SDLC Models
Model Description
Waterfall Model The waterfall model has historically been the most widely used
development model. It divides the SDLC into a series of sequential or
linear phases, from preliminary analysis and design to implementation and
maintenance.

Model Description
Iterative Design Today, most information systems are developed using an iterative
process that involves designing, implementing, and testing smaller pieces
of the overall project; then cycling back and doing more analysis
and design. For example, rather than redesigning the entire system at
once, an organization might start by implementing a single enterprise
application, such as new sales and marketing software. This process
continues until the entire system is in place. The Agile method is one of
the most popular iterative models, especially in the software development
industry.

fields like cloud computing, data science, software engineering, and cybersecurity. You will also
examine detailed job profiles for IT support technicians, network administrators, and system
