Careers in Internet Technologies
Tech job roles begin from so many different paths. Check out how one web developer began his
tech career from an Uber driver’s seat. You can find out more about these careers and more at
CompTIA’s Career Explorer.
Internet Service Technician
If you love solving mysteries, helping people, gadgets, and adventure, being an Internet Service
Technician may be a great career for you. Internet Service Technicians are solving mysteries

every day. They use clues, like codes and signals, to find out why someone’s Internet service
isn’t working. Many people depend on the Internet to work, to provide for their families, or to
help others. By getting their Internet service working again, you are like a hero to them.
If you love computers, gadgets, and technical things, this career lets you dive deep into how
they work. You will learn about networks and cool tools that keep everything running smoothly.
If you would rather be climbing a pole than sitting in an office, an Internet Service Technician
career can offer hands-on work that can be an adventure. You may be working on a rooftop,
exploring underground tunnels, or climbing poles to get networks connected and maintained.
Web Designer
Are you both logical and creative? If so, becoming a Web Designer may be just the career for
you. A Web Designer is like an architect of the digital world. As a Web Designer, you would get
to choose layouts, colors, fonts, and images to create beautiful and functional websites.
Web Designers combine problem-solving and tech skills to use software and coding languages
to make everything fit together so that website users can have a great experience. Every
website you create can make a real impact. Whether it’s promoting a small business, sharing
information about a cause close to your heart, or creating a fun place for gamers, your designs
can reach and connect people globally.
Social Media Marketing Manager
If you are a trendsetter and you love numbers and data, a career as a Social Media Marketing
Manager may be a good fit for you. Imagine getting paid to be on social media, but not just
for fun, for work! You get to discover what’s cool and popular online, and then help businesses
use that information to connect to their customers. From crafting catchy posts to designing
eye-catching graphics and videos, social media marketing lets you unleash your creativity.
Social media is also about numbers and analytics. You’ll use data about what’s working, or
not working, to fine-tune your strategies for even better results. As a Social Media Marketing
Manager, you’ll always be in the loop about the latest trends, memes, and viral content. Plus,
you’ll get to interact with people all over the world. Your work could potentially reach millions of
people.
Browser Extensions Developer
Imagine being the creator behind the scenes of your favorite web browser, adding cool features
that make browsing the Internet even more awesome. As a creator of browser extensions or
add-ons, you get to blend your love for technology with creativity in fun and interesting ways.
Browser extensions allow you to customize how you experience the Internet. You can create
tools that block ads, improve productivity, enhance security, or even add fun features like
custom themes and emojis to your browser. If you enjoy coding or want to learn, creating
browser extensions is a fantastic way to dive into programming languages like JavaScript,
HTML, and CSS. You'll learn how to bring your ideas to life through code.
Picture inventing the next big thing that everyone wants on their browser. Whether it's a game-
changing tool for developers, a time-saving feature for students, or a fun add-on for social
media enthusiasts, your creations can leave a lasting impact.
Careers in Networking
Every company with an office has computers, and every school nowadays has a computer lab.
These computers will be connected to each other and to the internet through networking. If
you're interested in managing these networks, there are many opportunities available for you as
a network professional. You might focus your training on handling large, complex networking

systems. Remember that small networks need someone to set them up, but they usually
don't need someone to take care of them all the time. CompTIA’s Career Explorer has more
information on these job roles, as well as stories from individual network administrators.
Network Administrator
Imagine being part of a team running an organization's communication system, making sure
that every connection is strong and safe! As a Network Administrator, you'll dive into the world
of networks. Routers, switches, and firewalls play a crucial role in keeping businesses and
organizations connected and protected.
Because keeping the network safe is vitally important, you'll set up security tools like firewalls,
intrusion detection systems, and other security measures to protect networks from cyber
threats and unauthorized access. When network issues arise, you'll step in, diagnosing
problems, analyzing network performance, and implementing solutions to keep everything
running smoothly.
Network Engineer
Imagine designing cutting-edge solutions that power the digital age! As a Network Engineer,
you'll combine creativity and technical expertise to build reliable, high-performance networks
that connect LANs and/or WANs. You'll design network topologies, the physical or logical
arrangement of nodes, set up devices, and make sure data travels smoothly.
Network engineers work closely with network architects, administrators, cybersecurity experts,
and other IT professionals. So, you must be good at working in a team, communicating
effectively, and adapting to changing situations.
Network Architect
As a Network Architect, you'll mix creativity, tech skills, and big-picture thinking to create
strong, flexible, and safe networks that help people communicate easily. While network
engineers make and look after networks, architects plan how everything should fit together.
You'll make network plans, set rules for how things work, and create guidelines for building and
improving networks.
Network architects are strategic thinkers. You'll analyze business requirements, assess
technical needs, and make sure the network designs work within the organization’s goals and
objectives. Your designs focus on performance and reliability, while minimizing costs and risks.

Careers in Apps and Software
Take a look at one person’s experience in the world of software development. You can find out
more about application and software development at CompTIA’s Career Explorer.
Application Developer
Imagine being the person who designs and builds your favorite apps and games. You get to
bring your ideas to life and create something millions of people might use and enjoy. Learning to
write in coding languages, like JavaScript, Python, or Swift, is a lot like learning a new language
that tells the computer what to do. You'll collaborate with other developers, designers, and
testers to make your app the best it can be. It's a lot of teamwork and creativity all rolled into
one.

Think about it if you love technology, solving problems, and being creative; becoming an
application developer might just be the perfect career for you. Imagine people all over the world
using something you created. How cool is that?
Full Stack Developer
While an Application Developer usually specializes in either the front end or the back end of
application software, a Full Stack Developer creates both the front end, what users see and
interact with, and the back end, the behind-the-scenes stuff that makes everything work, of a
website or app.
As a Full Stack Developer, you get to design and build the parts of a website that users interact
with, making sure it’s easy and fun to use. It’s like creating a digital experience for people. You
also make sure that everything works correctly, from the user clicking a button to the data being
stored and processed in the database. It’s like being able to design the outside of the car and
also build the engine and mechanics.
Software QA Analyst or Test Engineer
Do you know how frustrating it can be when a game crashes or an app doesn’t work the way
it should? There are special tech heroes who make sure those problems don’t happen. They’re
called Software Quality Assurance (Q A)  Analysts or Software Test Engineers.
Imagine playing a game and discovering bugs or issues before anyone else does. Your job is to
find these problems and help the developers fix them, so everyone has a smooth experience.
You’ll create plans and strategies to test every part of the software, making sure nothing is left
unchecked.
If you have an eye for detail, enjoy solving puzzles, and like to make sure things work properly,
becoming a Software QA Analyst might be a perfect career for you.
Careers in Operating Systems
Systems administrators and technicians are the backbone of many organizations' IT
departments. CompTIA's Career Explorer lets you explore these job roles, see personal stories
from real people, and find a career path tailored to your strengths.
Systems Administrator
Have you ever wondered who keeps all the computers in a school or company running
smoothly? That's the job of a Systems Administrator. They install, configure, and maintain
operating systems across an organization's servers and workstations. When something goes
wrong, like a server crash or a software update that breaks things, they're the ones who jump in
to fix it and get everyone back to work.
As a Systems Administrator, you'll manage user accounts, set permissions, and ensure
systems stay secure and up to date. You might work with Windows Server, Linux, or macOS
environments, sometimes all three at once! If you enjoy solving problems, keeping things
organized, and being the person everyone counts on when technology acts up, this could be a
great fit for you.
DevOps Engineer
DevOps Engineers live at the intersection of software development and IT operations. They
build and maintain the systems that allow developers to release new software quickly and
reliably. Think of them as the people who design the assembly line for software, automating
testing, deployment, and monitoring so that updates can go live without breaking anything.

In this role, you'll work with tools that manage operating system environments in the cloud
and on-premises, write scripts to automate repetitive tasks, and set up systems that can heal
themselves when problems occur. If you like the idea of making complex processes run like
clockwork and enjoy working with both code and infrastructure, DevOps engineering is an
exciting and in-demand career path.
OS Developer
Have you ever thought about what it takes to actually build an operating system? OS Developers
write and maintain the core software that makes hardware and applications work together. They
design the kernel, develop device drivers, and create the system services that every other
program on the computer depends on. It's deep, challenging work that forms the foundation of
all modern computing.
As an OS Developer, you'll work with low-level programming languages like C and C++
and need a strong understanding of how hardware communicates with software. You might
contribute to open-source projects like Linux or work at a major tech company improving
Windows, macOS, or mobile operating systems. If you love digging into how things work at the
deepest level and want to build technology that millions of people rely on every day, this career
could be your calling.
Careers in Computer Hardware
CompTIA’s Career Explorer is ready to help you dive into these job roles with information about
hiring practices, job outlooks, and potential salaries.
Computer Hardware Design Engineer
You know how your computer, phone, and all those awesome gadgets work on the inside? Well,
that's where Computer Hardware Engineers come in! They're the ones who design and build the
brains and muscles of our tech world. Imagine designing the next generation of smartphones,
gaming consoles, or super-fast computers. As a Computer Hardware Engineer, you get to turn
your ideas into real, tangible technology!
You'll get to figure out how to make devices faster, smaller, and more efficient. To do this, you'll
work with teams of engineers, designers, and developers to bring your hardware designs to
life. If you love tinkering, experimenting, and creating new things, this career lets you push the
boundaries of what's possible in the tech world.
Electrical Engineer
Have you ever been curious about how your beloved computers and gadgets come to life?
Well, that's the realm of Electrical Engineers in computer manufacturing! They're the experts
who skillfully integrate electronic components to craft incredible devices. Being an Electrical
Engineer could be an exciting career.
As an Electrical Engineer, you'll be at the forefront of innovation, designing the circuits, chips,
and hardware that power the next generation of computers and gadgets. It's like being a tech
pioneer! Have an idea for a new feature or a faster processor? As an Electrical Engineer,
you'll turn those ideas into reality by designing and testing the electronic systems that make
technology work.
Industrial Engineer
Industrial Engineers in computer manufacturing shine are like the master planners who make
sure everything runs smoothly in creating our favorite devices and computers. Imagine you
have a giant puzzle of how to make computers faster, cheaper, and eco-friendly. Industrial

Engineers solve this puzzle by designing efficient processes and systems to streamline
production.
Ever heard of smart homes? Industrial Engineers design smart factories where machines
talk to each other, making production faster and more precise. Industrial Engineers focus on
sustainable manufacturing practices, reducing waste and energy use. They ensure that every
gadget coming off the assembly line is top-notch. It's about making sure your favorite devices
work flawlessly every time.

Careers in Data and Privacy
How does a data mining analyst get their start? For more information about these careers and
others, take a look at CompTIA's Career Explorer. Discover what types of companies are hiring
in these roles, what they look for, and what they might pay.

Data Privacy Attorney
Imagine being a digital guardian of people's most sensitive information, ensuring their privacy
and rights are protected in the fast-paced digital age! As a data privacy attorney, you step into
a vital role where law meets technology, advocating for data protection and helping shape the
future of privacy rights.
You'll advocate for strong data protection laws, ensure companies comply with privacy
regulations, and represent individuals whose privacy has been violated. You'll dive into complex
legal frameworks like GDPR, CCPA, and others, applying legal principles to evolving digital
landscapes.
Data Privacy Specialist
A good data privacy specialist possesses a blend of technical, analytical, communication, and
ethical skills. As a Data Privacy Specialist, your focus is on understanding and implementing
privacy regulations, ensuring organizations handle data responsibly. You'll analyze data
practices within organizations, assessing potential privacy risks and vulnerabilities. Your
insights help mitigate risks and strengthen data protection measures, ensuring that individuals'
privacy rights are upheld.
While Data Privacy Attorneys focus on legal interpretations, you bridge the gap between
law and technology. You'll work closely with IT teams, understanding data flows, encryption
methods, and security protocols to ensure data is handled securely. You must also have
a strong ethical compass, understanding the importance of respecting individuals' rights,
ensuring data accuracy, and promoting transparency in data practices.
Data Analyst
A Data Analyst is like a sleuth who solves puzzles using numbers! They look at lots of
information about things like what people buy, what they like, or how they use apps and games.
Then, they use special tools to organize and study this data to find cool patterns and insights.
These insights help companies make smart decisions, like what new features to add to a game
or how to make a website easier to use. It's all about using numbers to understand what people
love and how to make things even better.
If math is your thing, you'll love working with numbers, charts, and graphs to tell stories about
what the data is saying. You get to use tools like Excel, Tableau, or Power BI to analyze data and
create visualizations that make complex information easy to understand. It's like being an artist
with data!
Careers in Databases
Database Administrator (DBA)
Have you ever wondered where all the information from your favorite apps, games, and
websites gets stored? That’s where database managers come in. They are the experts who
organize, store, and protect data. Database Administrators (DBAs)  set up databases to store
data securely and efficiently. It’s like being the librarian of the digital world. They make sure
databases run smoothly and quickly, so your apps and websites don’t lag. DBAs protect data
from hackers and ensure only authorized people can access it.
Data Engineer
Imagine you have a giant treasure chest filled with all sorts of amazing stuff, but it's a bit messy
and hard to find what you need. A Database Engineer is like the expert who organizes this
treasure chest so that everything is easy to find and use.

Database Engineers create and manage digital treasure chests called databases. They make
sure all the information (like usernames, game scores, or shopping data) is stored neatly
and can be found quickly when needed. They use special tools and coding tricks to design
databases that work super-fast and can handle lots of data without getting confused.
Data Scientist
A Data Scientist is like a super smart problem-solver who uses computers and math to learn
about the world and make predictions. They look at lots of information (data) and find patterns
or trends to help companies and scientists make better decisions.
Data Scientists often work on complex problems that require advanced statistical and machine
learning techniques, while Data Analysts focus more on analyzing data to answer specific
questions or solve defined problems using tools like Excel or SQL. For example, Data Scientists
might figure out what products people will like in the future or how to improve things like
healthcare or the environment, whereas Data Analysts might analyze sales trends or customer
behavior to help a company make marketing decisions.

Careers in Coding
CompTIA’s Career Explorer is ready to help you dive in to these job roles and more with
information about hiring practices, job outlooks, and potential salaries. You can also take a
quiz to see what job roles might best suit your talents.
Web Developer
A Web Developer is someone who creates websites and makes sure they work well. They
design how the website looks, and they also make sure all the buttons, links, and features work
properly. Web Developers use different coding for the front-end development and back-end
development.
Front-end development is all about how the website looks and feels to users. Front-end
developers write code using languages like HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to create the layout,
design, and interactive elements of a website. They make sure everything looks great on
different devices, like computers, tablets, and phones.
Back-end development is about what happens behind the scenes. Back-end developers
write code that powers the website’s functionality, like storing user information, processing
transactions, and retrieving data. They use languages like Python, Ruby, or PHP, and work with
databases to ensure the website runs smoothly.
If you love technology, enjoy being creative, and want to build the future of the Internet, a
career as a Web Developer could be perfect for you.
Cloud Architect
Think about all the cool apps and games you use on your phone or computer. A lot of them
rely on "the cloud" to work smoothly and store all your data. A Cloud Architect is a tech expert
who designs and manages these cloud systems to make sure everything runs efficiently and
securely. The cloud is like a giant, powerful computer that you can access over the Internet.

As a Cloud Architect, when you set up new servers or databases in the cloud, you use code
to do it. This makes the process faster, more efficient, and less prone to mistakes. Cloud
Architects write code to automate tasks, which means you create scripts to make computers
do things on their own. By coding, you can make sure that cloud systems run smoothly and
efficiently. You might write code to balance the load between servers, so everything works
quickly and reliably even when lots of people are using the service at the same time.
In short, coding is a powerful tool that helps Cloud Architects design, build, and maintain cloud
systems efficiently and securely. It’s a key part of making sure everything works well and stays
protected. If you like the idea of using coding to control and improve big tech systems, being a
Cloud Architect could be a really exciting job for you!
Video Game Designer
Think about your favorite video games and how much fun you have playing them. Video Game
Designers are the people who create those games. As a Video Game Designer, you get to bring
your ideas to life. You can create characters, worlds, and stories that other people will enjoy and
experience.
This job is perfect if you like both creativity and technology. You’ll use your artistic skills to
design graphics and your coding skills to make the game work. Developing games involves
solving lots of interesting challenges, like how to make characters move realistically or how to
make levels more fun. Game development is often a team effort. You’ll get to work with artists,
writers, musicians, and other programmers.
There’s nothing quite like seeing people enjoy something you created. When you develop
games, you get to share your work with players all around the world.

Careers in Cybersecurity
From cybersecurity engineer to penetration tester, CompTIA’s Career Explorer has details on
everything from job outlooks to current hiring numbers.
Cybersecurity Analyst
Are you analytical, detail-oriented, and enjoy problem-solving? A cybersecurity analyst uses
these skills to defend networks, systems, and data from cyber threats like hackers, viruses, and
cyberattacks. Imagine you're the digital Sherlock Holmes, solving mysteries and outsmarting
cyber villains in the virtual world! As a cybersecurity analyst, your job is like being a detective
for the internet, but with cool tech tools and skills.
Your main task is to monitor the digital networks for any suspicious activity. You'll dive into logs,
which are like digital footprints left behind by users and systems.
You'll also conduct vulnerability assessments to find weaknesses in systems before bad guys
do. If a security incident does happen, you're the hero who jumps into action! You'll respond
swiftly to stop cyber threats in their tracks, protecting data and systems from harm.
Cybersecurity Engineer
As a cybersecurity engineer, you embark on an adventure where technology meets strategy
to defend against hackers and cyberattacks. Cybersecurity engineers design and create digital

fortresses for data and systems. You'll use your tech prowess to implement robust security
measures that keep hackers at bay.
Your main focus is on designing and building secure networks, systems, and applications right
from the beginning. You'll dive deep into networking, encryption, and security protocols. Every
day presents new challenges and puzzles to solve. You'll tackle tasks like configuring firewalls,
conducting security assessments, and developing security policies.
Cybersecurity experts are in high demand globally. Companies, governments, organizations of
all sizes, and even celebrities need skilled analysts and engineers to protect their digital assets.
Penetration Tester
Penetration testing is like a hacking adventure, but with a noble purpose. As a penetration tester
in cybersecurity, you get to wear the hat of an ethical hacker, testing systems and applications
for weaknesses before the bad guys do. You'll use your tech skills to simulate cyberattacks,
finding and fixing vulnerabilities to strengthen digital defenses.
Your main task is to think like a hacker, identifying loopholes and entry points that could
be exploited. If you love coding, networking, and technology puzzles, penetration testing is
a playground for your skills. You'll delve into security protocols, encryption methods, and
cybersecurity tools.
As an ethical hacker, you uphold ethical standards and use your skills for positive purposes.
You'll work within legal and ethical boundaries to help organizations fortify their defenses
against malicious hackers. Your work directly contributes to making the digital world safer.
Whether it's protecting sensitive data, securing financial transactions, or safeguarding critical
infrastructure, your efforts will have a tangible impact on cybersecurity.

Careers in Creative Technology
Technology is not just about code and data. Creative professionals use digital tools every day
to design visuals, capture images and video, and bring characters to life through animation. You
can find out more about these careers and others at CompTIA's Career Explorer.
Graphic Designer
Do you enjoy drawing, picking colors, and making things look great? Graphic Designers use
their artistic skills along with professional software to create logos, advertisements, websites,
and social media content. They turn ideas into visual designs that communicate messages and
capture people's attention.
As a Graphic Designer, you'll work with tools like Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop, and other design
software to create everything from brand logos to marketing materials. You'll collaborate with

clients and teams to understand what message a design needs to communicate, then bring that
vision to life. If you have an eye for color, layout, and detail, graphic design is a career where
your creativity meets technology.
Photographer and Videographer
Photographers and videographers use cameras, lighting, and editing software to tell stories
through images and video. Whether it's capturing a live event, shooting a commercial, or
creating content for social media, these professionals combine technical skills with artistic
vision to produce compelling visual media.
In this career, you'll learn to work with professional camera systems, lighting equipment, and
editing tools to produce polished results. You might shoot weddings, create promotional videos
for businesses, or document events. Technology plays a big role, from drones for aerial shots
to advanced software for editing and color correction. If you love capturing moments and telling
visual stories, this could be the career for you.
Animator
Animators are the artists behind the moving characters and worlds you see in movies, video
games, and apps. Using specialized computer software, they create 2D and 3D animations that
bring stories and ideas to life. From cartoon characters to realistic visual effects, animation is

As an Animator, you'll use tools for modeling, rigging, and rendering to make characters move

artists to make sure the animation fits the project's vision. If you love drawing, storytelling, and
seeing your creations move on screen, a career in animation lets you turn your imagination into
something everyone can experience.

The IT field is full of exciting career opportunities, from computer support and network
administration to cybersecurity and software development. Whether you prefer working as a
generalist who handles a little bit of everything or as a specialist who focuses on one area, there
is a place for you in tech. The key is knowing how to get started and how to prepare yourself for
the career you want.
In this lesson, you will explore the wide range of careers available in IT, learn how to set
achievable career goals using the SMART framework, and discover the education and training
options that can help you get there. You will also learn how to build a professional network,
write an effective resume, and prepare for job interviews so you can put your best foot forward
when it is time to apply.
Learning Outcomes
As you study this lesson, answer the following questions:
• What types of careers are available in the IT field, and how do generalist and specialist roles
differ?
• How can you use the SMART framework to set achievable career goals?
• What education and training options can help you prepare for a career in IT?
• How can professional networking help you find job opportunities?
• What are the key sections and formatting tips for writing an effective resume?
• How should you prepare for different types of job interviews?
Careers in Tech
CompTIA Tech+ helps you learn more about the technology you use every day and also shows
you the different kinds of jobs you can have in tech.

The world of IT is full of many different job roles that help keep our digital world running
smoothly. From fixing computers and setting up networks to designing websites and protecting
against threats, there is a job for everyone.
Some people work as computer support specialists, helping others solve their tech problems.
Others might be software developers, creating the apps and programs we use every day. There
are also network administrators who make sure our Internet connections are fast and reliable,
and cybersecurity experts who keep our information safe. No matter what your interests are or
turn out to be, there's likely an IT job that fits you perfectly!
Check out explore.comptia.org for a deep dive into the wide variety of IT jobs, including salaries
and requirements.
Your Place in the Future of Tech
As a new learner stepping into the exciting world of IT, you are starting a journey of personal
growth and discovery. You are also putting yourself at the front of an industry that shapes
the future. The IT field is full of endless possibilities, where new ideas meet opportunities and
challenges turn into successes.
Your curiosity, hard work, and passion are the building blocks of tomorrow's big breakthroughs.
Enjoy the learning process because it is the key to unlocking a future where you are not just
taking part but leading the way, making a big impact in a world that relies more and more
on technology. The future of IT is bright, and with your unique talents and constant quest for
knowledge, you are set to make it even brighter.
Finding a Job in the IT Field
Most IT jobs fall into two main categories: jobs where you do a bit of everything, and jobs
where you focus on just one thing. Small- to medium-sized companies usually can't afford to
hire people to focus on just one part of IT, such as only taking care of the computer network
or managing the servers. Instead, in these smaller companies, the few IT staff members have
to handle many different tasks. They often take care of the network, the servers, and every IT
problem that comes up.
In larger organizations, there are usually more systems, so they have technicians focus on just
one part of IT. For example, one IT worker might be in charge of the network, making sure
the routers, switches, and access points are all working well. Another might take care of the
servers, keeping them running, upgrading them, and ensuring that they're secure. As you start
to grow in your career, think about what you've experienced and what you prefer. Do you want
to be an expert in one specific area, or do you like juggling a bunch of tasks at once? There's no
right or wrong answer; it's about what suits you best and what you enjoy. Be sure to check out
CompTIA’s Career Explorer, where you can find more about jobs in robotics, virtual reality, and
so much more.
Make sure to gravitate towards areas of IT you're interested in, and make sure that you have some
aptitude in those areas. Don't jump into and struggle in a particular area because someone told you
it was a good field to get into, or because it seemed cool or exciting to you after watching a video
online.
Career Goal Setting and Preparation
Career Goal Setting and Preparation
Identifying a career path can be daunting when there are so many careers to choose from.
Many jobs may seem interesting, but how does that translate into a career? Narrowing down
your career choices to one or two can include the following options:

• Take advantage of career centers at your local high schools, colleges, and even community
centers. You can ask to speak with a career advisor about your interests and goals to help
you decide what you might want to pursue.
• Career assessment tests can help you concentrate on particular career possibilities by
asking a variety of questions that assess your skills, values, personality, and interests. Your
answers to these questions will result in a report of potential careers that you might be
interested in. Both paid and free assessments can be found online and at career centers.
• Job shadowing provides an opportunity to spend a day observing a professional at work.
During this time, you can see exactly what they do on a day-to-day basis and get a better
feel for the job.
• Interviewing career professionals is a great way to learn from an expert about career paths
and ask for advice on how to enter their field. You can work with your local career center or
career advisors to help you set up opportunities to job shadow, intern, or interview a working
professional.
Once you've decided on a career path, it's a good idea to set achievable goals regarding your
next steps.
• Pinpoint potential employers and specific job descriptions that you could see yourself
applying for, and review their job requirements.
• Evaluate your strengths, education, and experience, and compare those to the posted
job qualifications. What do you still lack? Do you need more education? Do you need a
certification or a degree? What about experience?
• Once you have established the things you still need, it's important to write down your goals
and plans for achieving them.
• Get feedback on your plan from an advisor, mentor, or friend. Remember, there's more than
one way to get where you want to go professionally, so don't get discouraged if you need to
adjust your plan.
SMART Goals
You can also use the SMART acronym to help organize and plan your goals. SMART stands
for specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-based. This acronym can help you set
clearly defined goals that are easier to track.
Step Description
S: Specific Goals should be clear and specific so that it is
easier to determine the next steps.
M: Measurable Setting up milestones or checkpoints along the way
will help you determine if you are making progress
towards your goal.
A: Achievable Is this goal something that you can accomplish
now, or do you need to gain additional education,
experience, or skills that would be essential in
earning that position?
R: Relevant Consider whether or not your goals align with your
values and objectives. Do your goals contribute to
the overall big picture?

Step Description
T: Time-based Creating a realistic time frame for achieving your
goal can help keep you motivated and focused.
Setting a deadline can help you to better prioritize
the steps needed to achieve your goal. If your goal
is to earn an industry certification to qualify for an
IT tech position, you may want to give yourself three
months to do so. If you do not meet that deadline,
then you might have to evaluate the reasons why
that deadline wasn't met and set a more realistic
end date.
Gaining Education and Experience
Gaining Education and Experience
Do you know what education or training it takes to land your dream job? Look at some common
college program options to help you achieve the education and skills necessary for your career
goals, and explain how you can gain valuable work experience.
Career or Technical Schools
Career or technical schools have programs that are dedicated to helping you prepare for
specific careers. Some common programs include automotive technology, culinary arts,
cosmetology, and information technology (IT).
The greatest benefit to attending a career school is that you only take the classes you need
for that career. The programs at these schools usually take one to two years to complete, and
graduates leave with either a certificate or an associate's degree. Upon graduation, students
will be able to quickly start a job at an entry-level position within their chosen field.
Community and Junior Colleges
Another option for schooling is at the community or junior college level. At these institutions,
students receive an education for an associate degree, which typically includes courses in
general studies, with a few career-specific majors and classes. Associate degrees typically take
two years to complete.
Another option given at community colleges is career or vocational programs, similar to what
you'd get at a vocational school. An advantage to this is that the schools themselves are state-
funded, so tuition will likely be considerably cheaper. Also, class sizes are smaller, which usually
translates into better teacher-student interaction. A final benefit is that community colleges offer
open enrollment, so that anyone who applies to the school is accepted.
Since credits from a community college associate degree can be transferred to a four-year
university, many graduates go on to receive their bachelor's degree. An associate degree in
applied science is typically designed to get you a career, while an associate in science is
typically designed to transfer to a four-year college or university.
Four-Year Colleges and Universities
Universities are larger colleges that offer a greater variety of majors and minors. Graduates
leave with a four or five-year bachelor's degree. At a college or university, you can pursue a
liberal arts degree or a career- specific program, like nursing, accounting, or computer science.

Universities are more competitive institutions. The application process includes a review
of educational performance, including high school or community college GPA and college
entrance exams, like the SAT or ACT. A disadvantage is that classes at these institutions can
have higher student enrollment. This may make it more difficult to build relationships with
professors.
However, in competitive job markets, some students see the value in receiving a bachelor's
or master's degree. These degrees can give candidates an edge in certain higher-paying IT
careers, such as systems analysis, software engineering, and data science.
Many high school students can also take advantage of AP courses, dual-credit, or dual-
enrollment opportunities. They can earn 16 or more college credits while still in high school.
Gaining Work Experience
• Internships are short-term employment opportunities at an organization or company that are
available to people at the beginning of their career in order to gain experience. Depending
on the type of internship, some may offer a small salary, whereas others may be unpaid
positions. An internship is a good way to earn on-the-job experience and help you decide if
that's what you want to do in the future.
• Volunteering is a great way to add valuable experience to your resume if you have little to
no experience in a job environment. Working with charities and non-profit organizations can
be a good way to learn how to work with others in a business atmosphere, and help you
build a strong work ethic and good communication skills. While you may not be necessarily
working in the job position of your choosing, you could be developing a teamwork mentality
and leadership abilities that are highly valued by employers.
• Work-based learning can be offered by your educational institution and can be an efficient
way to participate in on-the-job training to gain career experience, enhance your resume,
and utilize any skills and knowledge learned from the classroom. High school students may
be exposed to work-based programs such as high school internships, pre-apprenticeships,
and cooperative education. These options can be either paid opportunities and/or for high
school credit. Colleges and universities may also offer work-based options that align with
different programs of study, such as engineering or building science. Keep in mind that there
are typically eligibility requirements and an enrollment process that may have to take place
before you can participate in a work-based program.
Networking
Networking
Looking for job opportunities that are in your career field can be a daunting task. Applying for
jobs through websites and social media platforms can seem impersonal. Job hunting should
not be something you have to do alone. Finding a job is much easier when you leverage your
network of personal and business connections. Networking might sound intimidating, but in its
simplest form, networking is essentially making real and authentic connections with people.
While it isn't impossible to land a job based purely on your own reputation, you'll typically have
better chances of getting a job when reaching out to your network, rather than relying solely on
your resume. These connections can prove to be valuable for you and for employers who prefer
to hire new employees through people they know and trust.
Networking can not only help you find new job prospects, but it can also make opportunities
available that you may not find on a company website or online job search. Some positions
may be shared internally and are not listed on company websites or networking sites, but
can come up in conversation during networking events. Although you can network practically
anywhere and anytime, a great deal of networking happens at events specifically designed for
networking. These can be hosted by colleges, professional groups, or companies. Anyone who
wants to bring like-minded people together can plan a networking event.

The following are networking opportunities that can help you connect with professional
contacts:
• Join a club or professional organization that relates to your interests.
• Attend a campus or company social event.
• Volunteer for local events and causes that are significant to you.
• Attend a professional conference or workshop in your related field.
• Join a social media group focused on connecting business professionals.
Networking never ends, and you should always work on expanding your network by building
more connections with people. As soon as you've started networking, you can start using your
contacts to help guide you towards certain types of jobs or internships. A good tool to apply
in making use of your network is requesting informational interviews, where you meet with a
professional in a career you're hoping to get into. This is not necessarily the place to ask for a
job, but a way to learn more about a particular career or industry. You can also ask for advice
about your education and intended career path.
Resume Writing
A resume is a brief written summary of your education, work experience, skills, and
qualifications. When you apply for jobs or internships, companies request a resume as the
initial step in assessing your ability to handle the duties of the job. Remember, the purpose of a
resume is not to help get you the job. It is to help you get the job interview.
Keep the following tips in mind when planning a resume:
• Creating a good resume takes time. Make sure you plan.
• Choose a resume template and format that helps highlight your professional history and
skills, and helps you stand out above the other job applicants.
• Most job posting websites will offer free resume-building features that can help you get
started.
• Make sure you include keywords and relevant skills from your target job posting to give
your resume the best opportunity of being generated from automated searches used by
employers.
Resume Formatting
Consider the following formatting options when creating a resume:
• Creating a good resume takes time. Make sure you plan.
• Use 1-inch margins on all sides. In cases where you need more space, you can adjust the
margins to .5 inches on all sides.
• Use a line of blank space between sections to allow for easier readability.
• Consider the use of italics, bold, and underlining to emphasize key points.
• Keep the resume down to one page in length and summarize the experience most relevant
to the job you're applying for. In cases where you have a lot of work experience, you can
include up to two pages, but never more than this.

Section Description
1. Header This is where you put your name and any relevant
job title or description that matches your experience
and goals.
2. Objective This is where you put the type of work you are
looking for and the types of experiences you hope
to have in the position.
3. Education and Relevant Coursework This is where you list your educational experiences.
Don't list every course you've taken, but if there is a
course that has relevant material to the position, list
that course and the skills learned.
4. Experience This is where you list experience and work history,
along with short descriptions of what you did in
those roles.
5. Skills and Training This is where you list any specific skills you've had
or training and certifications you've received. The
skills you list must overlap with the desired skills on
the job posting. Never list skills you don't actually
have.

Section Description
6. Optional Sections This is where you put anything else that is relevant,
but that doesn't easily fit into any of the categories
listed above, like extra-curricular activities, awards
and accomplishments, or other things related to the
job you're applying for.
Interviewing Skills
Interviewing Skills
Congratulations! You got an interview. Now what? Well, the best way to land that job is to ace
your interview. First, you have to prepare. You can't just plan on winning over your audience
with your good looks and charming personality. In order to be ready for what might come in
the interview, you have to know your target audience. Be sure to study as much about the
company as possible before you go. You could do this by visiting the company's website to
learn more about its mission and what they offer to customers. If at all possible, be sure to
sample their products or services or talk to someone who has. It's also a good idea to learn
about the company's culture by talking to any contacts you may have at the company or visiting
the company's LinkedIn page.
Types of Interviews
You need to be aware of the interview process and the different types of interviews that may be
conducted. Most of the time, job candidates will go through a couple of interviews during the
interview process. This could be done all on the same day or across a couple of days as you're
considered for the next stage in the process. The types of interviews you might have include
traditional, phone, or video conference, panel, and group interviews.
• A traditional interview is the typical one-on-one, in-person meeting with a hiring manager
or potential supervisor where you'll be asked about your skills, education, and work
experience.
• A phone or video conference interview is similar to a traditional interview except that it's
done over the phone or through a video conference call. Recently, it's become common for
these types of interviews to be done as video recordings of your answers instead of an
actual conversation with a person.
• A panel interview is also similar to a traditional interview, but you're interviewed by a panel
of hiring managers. This is often done to save time in the process, but also to give the hiring
manager another opinion of the candidates.
• A group interview is a meeting with a hiring manager or a panel of interviewers and a group
of potential employees. It's especially important to come prepared for a group interview
because you don't want to sound uncertain or underqualified in your answers and appear
less capable of doing the job compared to other candidates.
Interview Attire
Interview attire is important in making that first impression. A general rule that's safe to go by
when deciding what to wear to an interview is to dress a step above what the position would
require you to dress. For example, if you were applying to be a lifeguard, you probably wouldn't
need to dress up in a suit and tie. You would just wear some nice casual clothing. If you're
unsure about what to wear, just ask. Don't be afraid to reach out to a contact you may have at
the company or the recruiter working with you in the interview process.
Typically, you can either go business professional, business casual, or smart casual.

• Business professional is the typical nicely pressed business suit with a light-colored button-
up shirt, a tie, and well-polished shoes.
• Business casual is the next step down. Wear a nice dress shirt, slacks or a skirt, and
polished shoes. A tie is optional in this case.
• Smart casual is the next step down. You can feel free to wear chinos or khakis, a nice
finger-length skirt, with a collared or polo shirt. Here you can experiment a little more with
more colors and patterns in your attire.
Whatever you decide to wear, just remember that it's better to be a little overdressed than
under. Just make sure you are well-groomed and appropriate for the occasion.
Potential Interview Questions
Once you know more about the company and the type of interview you'll likely be having, it's
time to start practicing for the interview. It's important to know how to respond to some of the
most difficult questions that might come up. Each interview can be different, but there are some
general questions that interviewers commonly ask to help them get to know you as a person.
Question Question Tips
"Tell me a little bit about yourself." This question is one of the most asked questions in
job interviews. This question is not the time to talk
about where you're from, what you like to do in your
free time, or any other trivial thing about yourself.
Use this opportunity to talk about how your skills
and personality are a great fit for the position you're
applying for.
"Why do you want this job?" This question is where your preparation comes into
play. As we mentioned before, you should learn as
much as you can about the company, its products
and services, and the company culture before your
interview. In responding to this question, you can
confidently explain why your experience, interests,
and education align well with the company's goals,
mission, and culture.
"What makes you a good fit?" Questions like this allow you to talk up your
experiences and abilities, as well as mention your
goals and hopes. Focus on how you and your skills
can add value to the company and its customers.
"What is your greatest strength?" This question is your chance to tell the interviewers
why you're qualified for the job. Your greatest
strength should be directly tied to your ability to
execute your job well and efficiently. Make sure to
state not only your strength but also give examples
of how your strength has helped you in previous
experiences.

Question Question Tips
"What is your greatest weakness?" This question is hard because we naturally
don't want to show too much vulnerability.
But many employers like to see humility in
potential employees. Unfortunately, they likely won't
buy into the "I'm a perfectionist" or "I'm a
workaholic" weaknesses. Be honest and pick a
genuine weakness that you've recently worked on
overcoming. By giving examples of your ability to
cope with a personal weakness, you can put a more
positive spin on it.

Throughout this module, you explored the technology industry, learned about dozens of career
paths, and built the job-readiness skills you need to get started. Now it is time to put it all
together. You will complete three hands-on activities that challenge you to research, compare,
plan, and apply what you have learned.
You will begin by comparing two technology careers side by side to understand how they differ
in responsibilities, education, and skills. Next, you will build a complete career action plan that
includes a SMART goal, an education roadmap, networking strategies, and a draft resume.
Finally, you will find a real job posting and prepare a mock application package with a tailored
resume, cover letter, and interview responses. By the end, you will have a set of practical
documents you can refine and use as you begin your career journey.
Learning Outcomes
As you complete this lesson, you will:
• Research and compare two technology careers from different areas of the industry.
• Create a structured career action plan with a SMART goal and an education roadmap.
• Draft a resume tailored to a specific technology career.
• Prepare a mock job application package, including a cover letter and interview responses.
• Reflect on how information systems and ICT industry knowledge connect to the career you
want to pursue.
Activity: Career Comparison Report
You explored a wide range of technology careers in areas such as networking, software
development, engineering, data, cybersecurity, and the creative arts. In this activity, you will

compare two careers from different areas of the technology industry. Your goal is to research
both careers and determine which one is the best fit for your interests, skills, and goals.
1. Choose two technology careers from different areas of the module.
Select one career from each of two different lesson areas. For example, you might compare
a network administrator with a cybersecurity analyst, or a web developer with an animator.
The two careers should come from different categories so you can make a meaningful
comparison.
2. Research each career using the module content and online sources.
For each career, gather the following information:
• Which ICT sector does the career belong to?
• What are the typical day-to-day job duties?
• What education, certifications, and experience are required?
• What is the expected salary range?
• What soft skills are most important for this role?
3. Create a side-by-side comparison of the two careers.
Organize your comparison in a table or two-column format. Include rows for job duties,
education, certifications, salary range, and soft skills. Highlight the key similarities and
differences between the two careers.
4. Write a one-paragraph reflection explaining which career is a better fit for you and why.
Consider your personal interests, strengths, and long-term goals. Explain what draws you to
your preferred career and how it aligns with who you are.
5. Write a SMART goal for pursuing your preferred career.
Your goal should be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. For
example: "Within the next 12 months, I will complete an introductory cybersecurity course
and earn the CompTIA Security+ certification to prepare for an entry-level security analyst
role."
Activity: Career Action Plan
Now that you have explored the technology industry and compared different career paths, it is
time to build a plan for the career you want to pursue. In this activity, you will create a career
action plan that connects what you have learned about information systems, ICT sectors, career
requirements, and job-readiness skills into a single, structured document.
1. Choose a technology career to focus on.
This can be the career you selected in the Career Comparison activity or a different one.
Pick the career that genuinely interests you the most.
2. Identify the ICT sector and describe how information systems support the role.
Write a short paragraph that names the ICT sector your career belongs to and explains how
information systems (people, technology, and procedures) are used in that role on a daily
basis.
3. Write a SMART career goal.
Define a goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Your goal
should describe a concrete milestone you want to reach within a specific timeframe, such as
earning a certification, completing a degree, or landing your first role in the field.
4. Create an education and certification roadmap.
List the education, training, and certifications you will need to qualify for this career.
Organize them in the order you plan to complete them, and include estimated timeframes.
Consider options such as:
• College degrees or technical programs
• Industry certifications (such as CompTIA, Cisco, or A WS)

• Online courses, boot camps, or self-study resources
• Internships or volunteer opportunities for hands-on experience
5. List three networking strategies you will use to build professional connections.
Describe three specific actions you can take to grow your professional network. Examples
include joining an online community, attending a local tech meetup, connecting with
professionals on LinkedIn, or reaching out to a mentor in the field.
6. Draft a resume tailored to your chosen career.
Create a one-page resume that highlights the skills, education, and experience most relevant
to your chosen career. Include the following sections:
• Contact information
• Professional summary or objective statement
• Skills
• Education and certifications
• Work experience or relevant projects
If you do not yet have work experience in the field, include relevant coursework, school
projects, volunteer work, or personal projects.
Activity: Mock Job Application
You have explored technology careers, built a career action plan, and drafted a resume. Now it
is time to put your job-readiness skills to work. In this activity, you will find a real or realistic job
posting for a technology role and prepare a complete application package, just as you would if
you were applying for the position today.
1. Find a job posting for a technology career that interests you.
Search a job board such as Indeed, LinkedIn, or Glassdoor for an entry-level or early-career
position in a technology field you studied in this module. Choose a posting that includes a
job description and a list of qualifications. Save or copy the posting so you can reference it
in the following steps.
2. Tailor your resume to the job posting.
Using the resume you drafted in the Career Action Plan activity, or a new one, customize it to
match the job posting. Adjust your professional summary, skills, and experience descriptions
so they align with the qualifications the employer is looking for. Keep the resume to one
page.
3. Write a brief cover letter.
Your cover letter should be three to four paragraphs and include:
• An opening paragraph that states the position you are applying for and why you are
interested in it.
• A body paragraph that highlights your most relevant skills, education, or experience and
explains how they make you a good fit for the role.
• A closing paragraph that thanks the employer and expresses your interest in an interview.
4. Write answers to three common interview questions.
Prepare written responses to the following questions as if you were in a job interview:
• Tell me about yourself and why you are interested in this role.
• What skills or experiences make you a strong candidate for this position?
• Where do you see yourself in your technology career five years from now?
5. Write a short reflection connecting the role to what you learned in this module.
In one to two paragraphs, explain which ICT sector the job belongs to and how information
systems are used in the role. Describe how the skills and knowledge you gained in this
module helped you complete the application package.
